bodyText:
My brother in law planned the October cabin weekend around my feet and typed short loops next to my name on the hike sheet. Twelve days after I opened a shoe box I walked the whole 4.1 mile ridge.

My name is Renee. I am 62.

Six hours and forty minutes on that ridge. Zero pain. Nine thousand eight hundred steps. And I was the one who came down last.

Dale's family has rented that cabin in the Blue Ridge for twenty two years, and I have been going for eleven. Fourteen of us this year, three generations around one long table.

Wendell is Dale's older brother. He runs the whole weekend and he runs it well.

He prints a hike sheet every year. Trails, mileage, start times, who is going where.

This year he handed them out at the August cookout, in his own backyard, off a folding table next to the potato salad.

I found my name near the bottom of the page.

Short Loop Renee.

It was not a joke told to my face. It was a line item, typed in under Sunday.

Wendell saw me reading it. "I built you an easy one this year. The creek path. Flat the whole way."

"I can walk the ridge."

"You could. But why put yourself through it."

He meant it kindly. That is the part that sat in me all through September.

Kayla read hers and laughed. She is my niece and she loves me.

"Short Loop Renee," she said. "That is kind of cute, Aunt Renee."

Nobody said it again after that day. They did not have to. It was printed.

Here is what they were all being so careful about.

I have wide feet, and I have had them since I was nineteen.

Size eleven, wide across the ball, and nothing in a store has ever closed on me right.

I am a heavy woman too. I have been one since my forties.

Every pound of me lands on those two feet.

The stairs in my own house make me stop and breathe at the landing.

By three in the afternoon my feet swell. Then whatever I am wearing turns into a clamp.

The burn starts across the ball, then the outside edge. Then I am looking for a chair.

For eight years I was the one who turned back.

At the pumpkin farm, at the outlet mall, at the county park with the grandkids.

I turned back so often that people stopped asking me to come.

The short loop used to have somebody else on it.

Ada was Dale's mother. She started the cabin weekend before I ever met this family.

She had wide feet too, worse than mine.

Every October she and I took the creek path while the rest of them took the ridge.

She always stopped at the second bridge and looked up at the ridge line.

"That is a pretty walk up there," she said once. "I hear."

She died three years ago in March. That October I walked the creek path by myself.

I sat on the second bridge a long time.

I was not sad about a trail. I was sad about the hearing about it.

The last Saturday in September I helped Maxine load mums into her truck.

Maxine has worked the garden center on Route 9 for nineteen years. Concrete floors, gravel lot, ten hour days through the fall rush.

She is sixty four and she outlasts every teenager they hire.

I told her about the sheet, about the short loop, about Ada.

She let me finish the whole thing, and then she pointed down at my shoes.

"How long have you had those?"

"Two years. Maybe three."

"And your feet hurt at three o'clock every single day."

"Every day."

"Renee. It is the shoe. It is not your feet."

"My feet are the problem, Maxine. They have always been the problem."

She stuck her boot out on the gravel. "Then look at what I stand in all day."

"Nimbao. The Cloud Walk," she said. "Nineteen years on that concrete and these are the first ones that quit hurting me."

She sat down on the tailgate and pulled one off.

"Put your thumb in there."

It was a knit upper. Soft, stretchy, no seam biting anywhere.

I pushed from the inside and the fabric moved out with me, then came right back.

"It just gives," she said. "I do not know how else to say it."

She took it back and stretched it flat between her hands.

"It goes where your foot goes. That is the whole thing."

"My width, Maxine. Nothing has ever gone around my width."

"It went around mine. And I am wider than you are."

She turned the shoe over and showed me the front.

"Look at that toe box. My toes actually spread out in there."

She stood up and put the shoe back on without bending over. Just slid her foot in.

"I have not sat down to put my shoes on since June."

Then she was already on her phone.

"Write that name down before you forget it," she said.

"They are doing buy one get one free right now. I picked up my second pair the same week."

"Which color?"

"Grey Stone. In our size that one goes first, so do not sit on it for a month."

That night I sat on the porch with my glasses on and ordered them.

Monday I opened the box on the kitchen table.

I put the first one on standing at the counter, no bending over and no hands.

My foot went in and the knit opened around the wide part and just held me.

Nothing pressed anywhere. Nothing sat down on the bone.

My toes went out flat, the way they only do in the bath.

I went down the hall to the back door and came back. Then I turned around and did it again.

Dale looked up from the paper. "What are you doing?"

"Walking."

"In the house?"

"In the house."

Wednesday I ran the errands.

Bank, pharmacy, the market on Third, the feed store for Dale.

Two hours and ten minutes. Thirty nine hundred steps.

At the last stop I stood in the checkout line and noticed I was not shifting.

That is my tell. I always shift, left foot to right foot to left foot again.

I stood there still, like a woman who is not counting.

Maxine called me Friday night.

"Well?"

"I ran all four stops. Two hours on my feet."

"And?"

"And I forgot about them. I never once thought about my feet."

"That is the whole thing, Renee. You stop keeping track of them."

"I have kept track of my feet every afternoon for eight years."

"Not anymore you do not."

Saturday I cleared the garden beds.

Six hours in and out of the house. Kneeling, standing, hauling buckets.

Then the neighborhood loop after supper, because I wanted to see what would happen.

Sixty two hundred steps that day. My highest in four years.

That night I took them off and looked at my feet.

No red stripe across the top, no angry line down the outside edge.

Nothing to soak and nothing to prop up on a pillow.

We drove up the second week of October.

The mountains had turned gold and rust the whole way, with wet leaves packed down on the road.

Wendell had the hike sheet taped inside the cabin door.

Saturday: Ridge Loop, 4.1 miles. Sunday: Creek Path, 1.6 miles, short loop Renee.

I read it standing there in my coat, and then I went and unpacked.

Friday afternoon we walked down to the water. Half a mile of gravel and roots.

I got there first, and not on purpose.

Kayla caught up at the dock. "Are you speed walking?"

"I am just walking."

Saturday morning at seven forty, and forty one degrees on the porch thermometer.

Twelve of us at the trailhead in the cold. Boots, packs, poles.

Sharon next to me, taping her knee. She is Dale's cousin and she has walked that ridge every October of her life.

Wendell had the sheet folded in his hand. "Renee, the creek path is tomorrow. Nobody would think anything of it if you waited here today."

Dale looked at me.

"I am walking the ridge," I said.

Wendell hesitated. He is not a cruel man. He was doing the math on my feet.

"It is four point one," he said. "With the climb it walks a lot longer."

"I know what it is. I have been hearing about it for eleven years."

Nobody said anything. Then Kayla said, "Let her go, Uncle Wendell."

We went.

The first mile is switchbacks. Loose rock, roots, leaves over all of it.

Wet leaves are the real problem. You cannot see what is underneath them.

I put my feet down flat and slow, and nothing rolled out from under me.

Mile two was the climb. Nine hundred feet of it.

By then it was past the hour my feet always swell. I felt them go wide inside the knit and the knit just went wide with them.

Nothing clamped down. Nothing had an edge to press on.

My lungs complained and my legs complained the whole way up.

My feet had nothing to say at all. That was the strange part.

Through the sole I could feel every root and every stone of it. I always knew where I was standing.

At the top there is a shelter. Three walls, a roof, a register in a metal box.

The caretaker was up there splitting wood. A man about seventy, named Roy.

He watched me come over the last pitch and set my pack down.

"You are not favoring anything," he said.

"No."

"Most people come over that pitch favoring something."

He nodded down at my feet. "Those are not boots."

"They are not."

"What are they?"

"Nimbao. The Cloud Walk."

He put the maul down and opened the register box.

He wrote the date and the party count, the way he does every day.

Then he wrote it in the margin, saying it out loud while he wrote.

"Nim. Bao. Cloud Walk."

"My wife Marie has one foot wider than the other," he said. "Forty years of that."

"She will get into these standing up," I said. "She will not have to bend down over them."

He looked at that a second, and then he closed the box.

Kayla took the group photo at the overlook, twelve of us strung across the rock with the whole valley in color behind us.

Coming down I ended up last. Not because I was slow.

Because Sharon's knee locked up at the top of the switchbacks, and somebody had to stay back with her.

Eleven years, and I had never once been the one who stays back for somebody else.

I walked her the whole way down. Four point one miles. Nine thousand eight hundred steps.

Two miles of downhill, and my heel never once slid forward in them.

We came out at the road at two twenty in the afternoon.

Kayla turned around and took one more picture there.

Sharon and me, coming out last, the two of us.

That is the one that went in the family album.

Twelve days from the morning I first put those shoes on to that photograph.

I was hungry. I was not hurt.

That night Sharon found me at the wood stove with my feet on the hearth.

"You could have gone on ahead of me," she said. "You had it in you."

"I did not want to."

"You walked that whole ridge and then you walked me down off it."

"I know what I did."

She looked at my shoes drying by the stove. "Are they going to be bad tomorrow?"

"I do not think they are going to be anything tomorrow."

Dale heard that from the kitchen and did not say a word. He just kept drying the same plate.

Sunday morning I was up first.

I put them on standing at the door and went down to the creek alone.

Six thirty in the morning, with frost on the boards of the dock.

My feet were the same feet I went to bed with. No swelling, no ache, no first step to brace for.

I stood on the second bridge a while, where Ada always stopped.

Then I walked the creek path. Because I wanted to, not because it was assigned to me.

When I came back Wendell was making coffee.

The hike sheet was still taped inside the door.

I took the pen out of the kitchen drawer and crossed out my line.

Short Loop Renee. One clean stroke through it.

He watched me do it, and he did not say anything for a minute.

"You closed that loop yesterday," he finally said.

"I did."

"I should have asked you before I printed it."

"Yes."

He went back to the coffee. That was the whole apology and it was enough.

Next October I am making the sheet. He offered it in the driveway and I said yes before he finished.

I already know what Saturday is. The ridge, plus the spur out to the falls.

Sunday can stay the creek path. Somebody will want it.

I will walk it with them because I want to. Then I will go back up.

Nobody handed me that ridge. They just ran out of reasons to keep me off it.

Roy came down to the trailhead kiosk while we were loading the cars.

He had the register page folded in his shirt pocket.

"I ordered them for Marie last night," he said. "The Grey Stone was already gone in her width."

"Then she waits on the Grey Stone."

"She has waited forty years. She can wait on a color."

I sat in the truck with the pen still in my coat pocket, already planning next October.

If your name has ever been typed next to the easy option before anyone asked you.

If your feet have ever swollen by three in the afternoon until the shoe turned into a clamp.

If you have ever turned back at the trailhead and told everybody you did not mind.

You need these shoes. Not because they are pretty. Though they are.

But because you have been walking the short loop for years on feet that were never the problem.

One pair. Twelve days. Four point one miles. Zero pain.

Maxine asked me to text her the link, so here it is for you too: https://nimbao.com/cloudwalk

Your move.

bodyText:
Twenty-two years on a three-mile loop. Then a year on the same bench every morning, laces undone. My husband set the alarm later. Two miles, he said. Last Sunday I walked past it. Fifty-four minutes.

My name is Jeannie. I am sixty-four.

I retired last spring after thirty-eight years in the office of a construction company. I kept the schedules and the payroll for the crews. My husband Hal framed houses for the same outfit.

Since 2003 I have walked the loop around the reservoir every morning at 6:15.

Hat in the summer. Headlamp in the winter.

I walked it the morning after I buried my father.

When I am moving well, the loop takes fifty-two minutes.

The bench comes at the two-thirds mark. A wooden bench under an oak tree, with a small brass plate on the back. Donated in memory of someone I never knew.

For nineteen years I walked past it.

Two years ago I started sitting on it.

It was April. My heel had been stabbing me at the first step out of bed for months. Like stepping on a nail. By the oak tree the whole sole was on fire. My toes had gone numb inside my walking sneakers.

By the end of that summer the bench was part of the walk. Six minutes, laces open, toes spread on the wood. Then tie them up and finish the last mile.

That September I went to a podiatrist. I told him straight.

"For five months I have not finished my walk without sitting down. I take my shoes half off. That is new. Tell me what it is."

He took the X-rays. He pressed on the heel.

"Does that hurt?"

"Yes."

"And that?"

I said a word I do not use in church.

"Plantar fasciitis," he said. "And the bunions are pushing your second toe over. No heel spur. Nothing to operate on. These are feet of your age carrying your weight."

He slid a pair of rigid insoles into my sneakers. They cost more than the sneakers.

"Rigid. They will hold the arch."

"Where do my toes go?"

"They will adjust. Keep walking. Come back if anything changes."

He was honest.

The next morning I sat on the bench, same as before. The insoles just gave my toes less room.

Every morning. For a year.

I was not scared. I was faintly embarrassed. A woman who did the loop in forty-eight minutes at fifty, sitting on a memorial bench with her laces undone.

You cannot take that to the doctor. He already took the pictures.

You cannot take it to your husband. He loves you and he will worry.

So I did not tell Hal.

Dot is sixty-eight, a widow, built like me. We have had coffee after the loop for eleven years. In June she came into the coffee shop in black knit shoes I had never seen on her. She walked like her feet did not hurt. I did not ask.

But Hal can count. He saw I came in twenty minutes later than I used to.

One morning in August the alarm went off at 6:40 instead of 6:15. I looked at him.

"Thought you could use the sleep," he said.

A week later, at dinner: "Two miles is plenty. At our age that's reasonable. I could drop you at the far lot."

"I like the road part."

"I'm just saying."

He thought it was my heart. He was shortening my loop for me. I let him. I could not tell him why I sat.

A Saturday in September, a year ago. I finished the loop, bench included, and came in for coffee.

Dot was already at our table. She did not say hello.

"You sit on Ellen's bench every morning," she said. "I've watched you do it for a year. You come in twenty minutes after me with your shoes half untied."

I sat down. "It's just my age."

She pushed her phone across the table. A page was open on it.

"These are the Cloud Walk. The ones you looked at in June and didn't ask about. I got them for my bunions."

"Dot, it's my age."

"It's not your heart, Jeannie. It's not your age. It's your feet. Look at how you walk. You land on the outside edge like you're scared of your own heel."

"I have spent money on insoles that did nothing."

"These aren't insoles. The top is a stretch knit. The toe box is round and wide. Nothing presses. You step in standing up, no laces to fight."

"Dot."

"They are buy one get one free right now. I took the Full Black because it goes with everything. The Full Black is the one that goes first. Don't wait on that one."

I did not order anything that day.

But I thought about it on the bench that week.

Then I did what I did with every vendor for thirty-eight years. I read the complaints first. Two evenings with my glasses on.

The bad reviews were about color, not feet. The women with bunions said the top stretched at the bump. It did not fight it. The women with my heel said the shoe did not fix the heel. It gave the toes room and the heel took its own time.

That was honest enough for me. I ordered the Full Black on the Thursday. Two pairs, the way Dot said.

The box came. The second pair went in the hall closet that day, next to the hat and the headlamp.

Now the honest part.

The first morning I stepped into them standing in the hallway. Hal was on the stairs with his boots.

"Where are your laces?"

"There aren't any."

My toes spread out. Nothing pressed on the bunion. I walked the hallway twice to make sure.

"Those the ones Dot wears?"

"Yes."

"Huh." He went back to his boots.

Then I did the loop.

I sat on the bench. Same as every morning for fifteen months.

But I did not unlace anything. There was nothing to unlace. My toes had not gone numb.

I sat because of the heel. The heel was still the heel.

Nothing changed in the heel the first week. Nothing the second week.

I almost put them in the closet with the other pair. On a Tuesday I counted. Two weeks of walking. Same bench.

But I ran a construction office. You do not walk off a job three weeks in because the concrete has not cured.

So I kept going.

I cannot tell you which morning it was.

Somewhere in the fifth or sixth week I came up on the oak tree. I thought about sitting. I did not need to.

I stood next to the bench for a second, checking myself. My toes were moving. Nothing was burning.

I kept walking.

Fifty-six minutes. The first complete loop without sitting in fifteen months.

I want to be careful here. The next morning I sat. I was tired.

"You sat," said Dot, at the table.

"I sat. I'll pass it tomorrow."

I did. Then I sat again two days later.

It was not a switch. The bench went from every morning to some mornings.

By the end of the second month, once a week. By the end of the third, once a month.

In November Kristen, our daughter, met me at the historical society. Two flights of stairs, no elevator. Then across to the last outdoor market of the year, at the corner of the reservoir.

One hour and forty minutes on my feet. Concrete, then gravel. A full bag of squash and apples on my arm.

She watched me stand in the cider line for twenty minutes.

"Mom. You haven't moved off that foot once."

"I know."

"What happened to your feet?"

"Dot happened."

"Mom, you have limped through every market since I was thirty."

"I know that too."

I did not sit once. I walked home the long way. No cutting through by the road.

That night the bag of frozen peas stayed in the freezer. I keep it for my arch.

Kristen opened the link that night for her mother-in-law, who has the same bunions I do.

I went back to the podiatrist in May.

He took the same X-rays. Same bunions. Same second toe. Nothing new.

"I walked past the bench, Doctor. Fifteen months I sat on it."

"In what?"

I showed him.

"Those are not the insoles I gave you."

"The insoles are in a drawer."

He pressed on the heel. "And that?"

"That's fine."

He listened to the rest. "Jeannie, I told you last September there was nothing to operate on. There still isn't. But whatever you're doing is sensible. Keep doing it."

I walked the loop that afternoon. I did not sit.

I cannot tell you the shoes did all of it. A dozen things were moving that year. A heel that has burned for two years calms down on its own schedule.

What I can tell you is what I did and what happened.

Then came the wedding, last Saturday. Kristen's husband's niece. Outdoor ceremony, reception in a barn with a plank floor.

Six hours. We stood for the ceremony. Stood for the pictures. Stood in the bar line behind forty people.

At my own daughter's wedding four years ago, my shoes came off under the table. Before the salad.

Hal leaned over around nine. "You want to sit?"

"No. Dance."

"Since when do you dance?"

"Since when do you?"

We danced twice. Hal has not danced since our own wedding.

The drive home was an hour and fifteen minutes. I kept the shoes on the whole way.

Sunday morning, 6:15. First step out of bed. No nail.

Hat. No headlamp yet. Past the bench without thinking about it. Fifty-four minutes.

I wrote the time in the notebook where I used to write the crews' hours.

The alarm had gone off at 6:15. I had not reset it.

"You moved it back," I said.

"You're walking like you used to," Hal said.

Then on Thursday: "What size would they run in a man's?"

"What for?"

"I'm tired of the stairs."

I ordered him his own pair that night. The closet pair stays where it is. A woman who sat a year on a bench does not run out of the thing that got her off it.

The brass plate on the bench says Ellen. She died in 1998. I looked her up at the historical society during the year I sat there. A librarian. Married forty-one years. Seventy-two when she died.

I sat on her bench for a year not knowing her name. I have walked past it for months knowing it.

This morning was cool. Fall coming in.

I did the loop and went to the coffee shop. Dot was at our table. I sat by the window.

A woman about my age I did not know came up the path. Doing the loop for the first time by the look of her. She got to the oak tree and sat. She bent down and untied her shoe.

Ten minutes later she limped into the shop and took the table next to ours.

She looked at my feet for a while. "Excuse me. What are those?"

"Cloud Walk," I said. "The Full Black."

"Do they run true to size?"

"Order the one you wear."

She wrote it on the paper napkin under her cup and folded it into her pocket.

I did not tell her anything else. I do not know if that bench is hers yet. Maybe this was her first morning on someone else's.

I drank my coffee and I hoped for her the way Dot hoped for me. Quietly, across a table.

Kristen's mother-in-law is still waiting on the Full Black in a nine. She is wearing the Grey till then. Kristen says she has stopped talking about her feet.

If you have your own bench under your own oak tree, where your feet started asking for something new, and the pictures came back clean:

If your husband has started setting the alarm later and offering the far lot, and you have let him, because you cannot tell him why you sit:

If you are standing in a cider line shifting your weight, or sitting under a wedding table with your shoes off before the salad:

You need these shoes. Not because they are pretty. Though they are. But because a woman who walks her loop without sitting down is a woman nobody has to shorten the loop for.

One pair. Six weeks. Past the bench.

Dot pushed her phone across the table, so here it is for you too: https://nimbao.com/cloudwalk

Your move.

bodyText:
I've done every level of my physical therapy program. I've been stuck at the top for four months. My PT said there's nothing left to try but a shot. Then I found out a woman in the same waiting room was improving every week on a THIRD of my exercises. Now I know why.

There's a moment I want to tell you about, because if you're anywhere near the top of your PT program for plantar fasciitis, you're headed toward it.

It's the moment your physical therapist runs out of program.

I'm 56. Fourteen months of PT for my left heel. And four months ago, at my re-evaluation, my physical therapist looked at my chart, looked at me, and said the sentence I'd been dreading since around month six.

"Lisa, you're at the top of the program. You've plateaued. There's nothing left for me to add."

And then, because she's kind, she offered me the consolation prize.

"I can send a note to your podiatrist about a cortisone shot. And if that doesn't hold, he might want to talk about a surgical consult."

A shot. Then maybe surgery. Fourteen months in. Or accept where I was.

Let me back up, because I know that program. I climbed every level of it.

I started fourteen months ago. Level one was towel stretches and rolling a frozen water bottle. Six good weeks. My first step went from a 9 to a 7. Then it slowed, and we moved up.

Level two: calf raises on the floor, three sets of fifteen. That bought me a few more good weeks. Then it slowed. We moved up.

And that became the shape of my whole year. Every level up bought me a few weeks of progress and a lot of soreness. Then the progress would slow, then stop, and we'd move up again. Each level bought a little less than the one before.

Calf raises on a step. Then single-leg. Then single-leg with a backpack full of books. Then three sessions of shockwave therapy at $300 each.

My first step went from a 9 to a 5. I'm not ungrateful for that. But a 5 is still a stab every morning. And I'm a pharmacy tech. I stand nine hours a day. My job is counting on getting the rest of the way there.

And at the top of the program, the pattern I'd been outrunning for a year finally caught me.

Four months. The hardest level. Nothing.

And here's what the top level actually felt like, since nobody talks about it.

The pain wasn't even steady. That's the part that made me feel crazy. On the hardest, most advanced program, a quiet week was okay. But a hard week, a double shift, my mother's move into assisted living, and the nail came straight back. Me, at the top of my PT program, standing at the pharmacy counter at 4 PM shifting from foot to foot, unable to stand still.

Like stress and long days had a manual override on the strongest program there is.

My podiatrist took X-rays. No heel spur. No fracture. My PT measured everything. My ankle flexibility was "great." My calf strength was "excellent for your age."

Everything came back fine.

So I posted in my plantar fasciitis group. Top of the PT program, four months stuck, PT says nothing left. And I got forty answers.

"Get the shot. Mine lasted six months." And for some women it does. But other women in that group got the shot, felt great for six weeks, and were back worse than before. Nobody talks about them.

"Try PRP injections." $1,200, not covered.

"Some feet just don't fully heal. A 5 is a win."

"Lose weight, it takes pressure off." I'd already lost 18 pounds since this started, eating salads at my desk.

And then the one I still think about.

"Honestly, if the hardest PT isn't working, it's not the PT anymore. It's just your feet."

I read that one in the break room and just sat there. Because that's the thing about the top of the program. On every other level, there was somewhere to put the blame. The exercises were too easy. Now there was nowhere left. If the hardest program doesn't work on you, you're not under-treated anymore. You're broken.

That's what "nothing left to try" means when you take it home. It doesn't mean the PT ran out. It means you did.

And here's the part nobody could explain.

My next-morning soreness got worse every time we added weight. By the top level, the morning after a PT session was the worst first step of my week. Every time. My heel was screaming that something was wrong, while every test said I was fine.

bodyText:
I'm going to say something that no woman who's been through the menopause and had plantar fasciitis for years wants to hear. And I don't give a sh*t if it upsets you.

The Voltarol won't fix this. The Scholl insoles won't. The cortisone jab in the heel won't. That night splint you can't sleep in won't. That compression sleeve all over your feed, buy 1 get 1 free? That won't either. And the next "just keep stretching your calves" won't.

And that physio referral you're waiting on? The one that's 14 weeks away, for 3 stretches off a printout? It's just going to sit there and watch your heel get worse. And podiatry, where I live, is for diabetics now. So if you're not diabetic, there is no list. There's just you and a frozen bottle of water.

Not 1 thing on that list is touching what's really causing the pain. I know. I watched the same thing take my mum.

12 years it had her. Gels. Insoles. Jabs. Then the "special shoes" that were meant to fix it all. They never did. First she stopped the walks. Then the shops, because it's an hour on your feet. Then she stopped answering the front door, because she couldn't get there before they'd gone. By the end she was on a mobility scooter at 71 for a foot. The last thing she ever said to me about it was, "Don't let it get you like it got me, love."

Then, 1 year ago, I sat on the edge of the bed at 6:12 in the morning with my right foot held in the air, because I already knew what it was going to feel like when it touched the carpet.

It's happening to me. And if you're reading this with your slippers already lined up beside the bed so your heel never touches the floor, it's happening to you too.

So read every word. It's long. But the answer is in here. And it is NOT another treatment.

I'm Beatrice Morgan. I'm 56, from Columbus. I've been a hairdresser for 32 years. On my feet all day, on a hard salon floor, 9 hours, no sitting down between clients.

For me it started small. A stiff heel getting up off the couch after Wheel of Fortune, like I'd been sat on my foot. A few steps and it went.

3 months later it wasn't small. It was a nail straight up through my heel the second my foot touched the floor in the morning. I'd sit back down on the bed and hold my foot and swear.

And here's the bit I could never work out. It was murder for the first 10 steps, then it eased. By the time I'd made a cuppa I could walk almost normal. Sit down for half an hour, and it started all over again. Some weeks it screamed. Some weeks it went almost quiet. I thought the heel was just worn through for good. It wasn't. (Hold that thought. It matters later.)

I did what you're meant to do. I rang the medical center. Waited 2 weeks. Got 8 minutes with a family doctor who'd never met me. She pressed her thumb into my heel, I nearly went through the ceiling, and she said "Plantar fasciitis. Very common. Stretch your calves, roll it on a frozen bottle, take some ibuprofen. It settles on its own in a year." Out the door.

The drugstore sold me Voltarol. For 2 weeks it was almost a miracle. Then it stopped. And when the pain came back, it came back meaner. Deeper. The kind no gel could reach, because it wasn't coming from the skin on my heel. It was coming from somewhere else entirely, though I didn't know that yet.

By then I'd joined 1 of those Facebook plantar fasciitis groups. Thousands of us. All awake at 5:00 AM dreading the first step. All with a tip. Scholl in Balance insoles at $20, then the "proper" ones at $38. Gel heel cups off Amazon. A spiky ball. A wooden roller. Deep Heat. Biofreeze. A night splint like sleeping in a winter boot, and I lasted 4 nights. Those orange massage insoles. That compression sleeve with the straps. Copper socks. A pair of FitFlops. A pair of Hokas. A cortisone jab in the heel that was lovely for 5 weeks then wore off. Naproxen. Co-codamol that turned me into a zombie and bunged me up for 1 week.

I spent over $1,100 on crap in 3 years. And I still couldn't get from the bed to the toilet without a hand on the wall.

Then it hit me like cold water. I was doing exactly what my mum did. The same gels. The same insoles. The same "give it time." Walking her road, step by step. Towards the same front door she stopped answering.

They'd always told me bad feet "run in families." Nobody told me the truth. We were both treating the wrong bloody thing.

By summer I was a ghost. Every morning I sat on the edge of the bed for 10 minutes writing the alphabet with my foot before I dared put it down. I went down the stairs sideways, one at a time, both hands on the rail, like my nana. I couldn't stand at the basin for a full color without leaning on the chair. I stopped taking my grandson to the park because I couldn't get across the grass if he ran off. I stopped the Saturday market with my sister, because it's an hour on cobbles. And every night I lay there with my heels throbbing under the covers, dreading a step I hadn't taken yet. Crying, some nights. Swearing into my sleeve so I didn't wake Steve.

The woman who used to do 12,000 steps a day round a salon and then walk the dog after was googling "mobility scooter" at 2:00 in the morning. Googling my mum's scooter. I thought I was just getting old. I thought it was the change, on top of everything else the change had done to me. I wasn't just getting old. That was wrong too.

Back to the family doctor. They sent me to physio. The wait was 14 weeks. I asked about podiatry and got told it's mostly diabetics now. I'm not diabetic. So that was that.

I paid for 1 private podiatrist I couldn't afford. $45 for 10 minutes, a look at my feet, and 3 calf stretches off a printout. "Keep at them. Give it more time." More time. While I did 9 hour days on that floor and crawled to the toilet every morning.

So I did the calf stretches. Morning and night, foot against the skirting board. And here's the thing nobody warned me about: some days they made it worse. Tighter. I know why now. You can stretch a clenched muscle for a minute and it'll give a bit, and then it snaps straight back, because you haven't given it what it needs to STAY let go. Every stretch was me yanking a rope that was already too tight.

Then I finally got the X ray everyone waits for. You know what it showed? "A small heel spur. Common at your age. We don't do anything about it." Nothing that explained why some mornings I could barely stand and some I could. And that's when the penny dropped. 1 in 6 people over 50 has a spur on an X ray and no pain at all. A spur on a picture doesn't tell you where the pain's coming from. They looked at the heel, because that's where I pointed. Nobody looked 18 inches higher, at the muscle pulling on it. And remember how it was murder for 10 steps and then eased? A torn band can't do that. A band doesn't heal by 8 o'clock and tear again by midnight. Whatever was tightening and loosening hour to hour, it was never the heel.

The letter even admitted it: "Recovery times for plantar fasciitis vary widely." I was a number on a list. And the list was not moving.

So I stopped hunting for another treatment. And I started hunting for the cause.

Once I saw it, I couldn't unsee it. Look at the road they marched me down. My mum before me.

A stiff heel. Ibuprofen. A gel. It fades. Insoles. A splint. A jab. Special shoes. A scooter.

Every step just managed the pain. Not 1 step ever asked WHY it was there. We were all sanding rust off a pipe and wondering why the bastard kept coming back.

I'd already ruled out the easy stuff. Cushioned trainers. A stool at the basin. A stone gone, they were right about that much, but it barely touched it. Because none of it reached where the pain really started. Not the skin. Not even the heel. The calf muscle above it, clenched like a fist, dragging the heel bone up all day and all night.

I spent 2 weeks reading. Not the sponsored stuff. The real threads. Reddit at 4:00 AM. Forums full of people who'd suffered 10 years. Podiatrists on YouTube who'd gone "off grid" from the usual advice.

Then I found 1 comment. Buried under a post. From a woman in Denver. "Heel pain 3 years. Tried it all. What finally freed it wasn't a splint or a jab or another insole. It was getting magnesium deep into my calves, not my heel. 5 weeks, and the first step of the morning just stopped."

Magnesium. Into the calves. Not the heel. Not down your throat, into the muscle. I read it 10 times.

So I ordered the first magnesium thing I could find. A $7.49 spray off Amazon. Thousands of 5-star reviews. Week 1: nothing. Week 2: nothing. Week 3: still coming down the stairs sideways on the rail. I nearly wrote it all off as more snake oil.

What saved me was a chat over the back fence.

My neighbor Brenda is 68. She was a hospital podiatrist for 31 years. Most of them in a foot clinic. She saw me stood at the washing line with one heel lifted off the ground like a horse resting a leg, and came over. I showed her the spray. She laughed, kindly. "Oh, love. This is next to useless. No wonder it's done nothing. Do you want to know why?"

And stood there in her slippers, she told me the thing no 8-minute appointment ever had.

"The heel is where the pain shows up. The calf is where the pain starts. Your calf and that band under your foot are hooked onto the same bone, the heel bone. The calf pulls it from behind, the band pulls it from underneath. It's 1 rope, and your heel's the knot in the middle. Now, every muscle needs 2 things to work. Calcium to tighten. Magnesium to let go. After 45 your body holds a lot less magnesium. And here's what nobody tells women: it's the estrogen that helps you hang on to it. When that drops at the change, you take in less and your kidneys let more go. Think of it like a phone. A phone needs charge to make a call. No charge, no call. No magnesium, no message to let go. So the calf never fully lets go. It stays a fraction short, all day, every day, dragging your heel bone up from behind, and that band underneath gets stretched like a guitar string. Every step, a tiny tear. That fire in your heel? Your heel's the victim. The calf's the one doing it. And the mornings? You lie there 8 hours with the calf clenched. Your body knits the tears back together overnight. Then you stand up, the calf's still pulling, and the very first step rips the night's work straight open. 10 steps of walking warms the calf and it loosens a bit, so it eases. Sit down, it shortens again. That's your proof it's a muscle. The spur never moved. Your pain did.

"The 'plantar fasciitis' everyone keeps managing is just what you feel when the rope's pulled too tight. Feed the calf the magnesium it's missing and it finally lets go. The heel bone stops being dragged up, the band gets some slack, and the tearing stops. But the magnesium has to get down INTO the calf. Through the skin, right over the muscle. Not sit on top. And not go down your gut, where almost none of it ever arrives."

First time in 3 years, something made sense.

Then she told me why everything I'd bought had failed. And it wasn't bad luck. "The gels? Voltarol, Deep Heat, Biofreeze, they're built for the top layer of skin, and that's where they stay. 20 minutes, then gone. They never reach a calf muscle 18 inches above where you're rubbing them. It's like watering the leaves of a plant when the roots are dry. The insoles and heel cups cushion the landing, but the calf's still pulling the bone up. The night splint holds your foot at 90 degrees and drags the calf from the OUTSIDE for 8 hours, but never gives it the mineral to let go on its own. Take it off, it clamps straight back. That's why you wake up stiff, not better. The jab settles the band where the needle went in, the calf carries on pulling, so it's back in 5 weeks. The tablets? You swallow magnesium and your gut burns most of it off. Barely any gets through, and it's the wrong place anyway. That cheap spray, that sleeve, those orange insoles? Not 1 of them gets real magnesium down into the muscle that's doing this. You were rubbing on hope. 18 inches too low."

Not all magnesium is the same, she said. It's the type. The strength. And whether it can actually get through.

"This," she said, "is what I'd have put my patients on. If we'd ever been allowed to sell anything."

It's called Calvera. A cream, not a pill. It uses magnesium chloride, the 1 type that soaks through the skin and gets down into the calf muscle. It gives that muscle what it needs to let the heel go. The MSM breaks the magnesium into tiny bits, so it slips through the skin and reaches the muscle instead of sitting on top. The vitamin B6 switches the nerve's signal back on, so the calf keeps letting go instead of clamping again. There's arnica for the damage the pulling has already done under your heel. And menthol, so the heel goes quiet in minutes while the slow part gets on with the real work. You rub it on your CALVES first, both of them, then the heel. It feeds the muscle. It doesn't go down your throat. That was the whole difference. The 1 thing I'd been missing for 3 years.

You rub it in 2 times a day. A good minute on each calf, from the back of the heel up to behind the knee, then the heel and arch. Last thing at night. And in the morning, sat on the edge of the bed, before your foot touches the floor. Give it 8 weeks. The first night you feel the cold and the heel goes quiet. But the real job, feeding the calf until it lets go and stays let go, takes weeks. It's a cream, not a drug. Nothing to swallow. Nothing to fog your head. Nothing to clash with your HRT or your blood pressure tablets. And it comes with a 60-day money-back promise. Finish the jar, and if you still can't put your foot down without bracing for it, send it back empty. So the only thing I could lose was a few more weeks of the same.

And here's what made me cry with anger. All they're really allowed to give you for this is a gel, a printout of stretches, and "it settles in a year." Podiatry if you're diabetic. Nothing that goes near the muscle pulling your heel apart. So they manage you while you wait for it to settle. It's been 3 years. It didn't settle. Nobody gets paid to tell a hairdresser in Columbus to rub magnesium into her calves.

The system's hands are tied. Yours are not.

So I started. Every night. Calves first. No excuses.

Morning 6: I put my foot down and it was sore, but it wasn't a nail. I stood there next to the bed and waited for it, and it didn't come.

Week 3: I came down the stairs foot over foot, like a normal person, not sideways on the rail.

Week 5: I did a full Saturday on the salon floor, 9 hours, 6 colors, and never once leaned on the chair.

By week 8 I walked the dog to the end of the street, then past it, all the way round the park and back, and the heel never lit up once. And when my grandson ran off across the grass at the park, I ran after him. Ran. And caught him. And swung him round.

The 6:12 dread. The stairs. The salon floor. The park. 1 by 1, they came back.

Brenda checked me over a few weeks in. The way she'd checked 1,000 feet. She had her thumbs in the back of my calf. "It's let go," she said. "There's give in it. Last time it was tight as a rope, dragging that heel up. In 31 years I hardly ever saw both heels this far gone settle this well without a jab. And you did it with a cream and a bit of patience."

That was 7 months ago. Not 1 dreaded morning since. My heels are quiet. I gave a tub to my sister, whose feet had started going down the same road, the same year as her change. Hers are easing too. This isn't a good week that wears off. It held. It's still holding.

I think about my mum every single day. The walks. The shops. The front door she stopped answering. That scooter. And the last thing she said to me.

If you're sat on the edge of the bed with your foot in the air, dreading the carpet, with a printout of stretches and a heel that's supposed to "settle in a year," do not walk her road. Do not wait for it to settle. Do not hand your good years over the way she did.

bodyText:
I've done every level of my physical therapy program. I've been stuck at the top for four months. My PT said there's nothing left to try but a shot. Then I found out a woman in the same waiting room was improving every week on a THIRD of my exercises. Now I know why.

There's a moment I want to tell you about, because if you're anywhere near the top of your PT program for plantar fasciitis, you're headed toward it.

It's the moment your physical therapist runs out of program.

I'm 56. Fourteen months of PT for my left heel. And four months ago, at my re-evaluation, my physical therapist looked at my chart, looked at me, and said the sentence I'd been dreading since around month six.

"Lisa, you're at the top of the program. You've plateaued. There's nothing left for me to add."

And then, because she's kind, she offered me the consolation prize.

"I can send a note to your podiatrist about a cortisone shot. And if that doesn't hold, he might want to talk about a surgical consult."

A shot. Then maybe surgery. Fourteen months in. Or accept where I was.

Let me back up, because I know that program. I climbed every level of it.

I started fourteen months ago. Level one was towel stretches and rolling a frozen water bottle. Six good weeks. My first step went from a 9 to a 7. Then it slowed, and we moved up.

Level two: calf raises on the floor, three sets of fifteen. That bought me a few more good weeks. Then it slowed. We moved up.

And that became the shape of my whole year. Every level up bought me a few weeks of progress and a lot of soreness. Then the progress would slow, then stop, and we'd move up again. Each level bought a little less than the one before.

Calf raises on a step. Then single-leg. Then single-leg with a backpack full of books. Then three sessions of shockwave therapy at $300 each.

My first step went from a 9 to a 5. I'm not ungrateful for that. But a 5 is still a stab every morning. And I'm a pharmacy tech. I stand nine hours a day. My job is counting on getting the rest of the way there.

And at the top of the program, the pattern I'd been outrunning for a year finally caught me.

Four months. The hardest level. Nothing.

And here's what the top level actually felt like, since nobody talks about it.

The pain wasn't even steady. That's the part that made me feel crazy. On the hardest, most advanced program, a quiet week was okay. But a hard week, a double shift, my mother's move into assisted living, and the nail came straight back. Me, at the top of my PT program, standing at the pharmacy counter at 4 PM shifting from foot to foot, unable to stand still.

Like stress and long days had a manual override on the strongest program there is.

My podiatrist took X-rays. No heel spur. No fracture. My PT measured everything. My ankle flexibility was "great." My calf strength was "excellent for your age."

Everything came back fine.

So I posted in my plantar fasciitis group. Top of the PT program, four months stuck, PT says nothing left. And I got forty answers.

"Get the shot. Mine lasted six months." And for some women it does. But other women in that group got the shot, felt great for six weeks, and were back worse than before. Nobody talks about them.

"Try PRP injections." $1,200, not covered.

"Some feet just don't fully heal. A 5 is a win."

"Lose weight, it takes pressure off." I'd already lost 18 pounds since this started, eating salads at my desk.

And then the one I still think about.

"Honestly, if the hardest PT isn't working, it's not the PT anymore. It's just your feet."

I read that one in the break room and just sat there. Because that's the thing about the top of the program. On every other level, there was somewhere to put the blame. The exercises were too easy. Now there was nowhere left. If the hardest program doesn't work on you, you're not under-treated anymore. You're broken.

That's what "nothing left to try" means when you take it home. It doesn't mean the PT ran out. It means you did.

And here's the part nobody could explain.

My next-morning soreness got worse every time we added weight. By the top level, the morning after a PT session was the worst first step of my week. Every time. My heel was screaming that something was wrong, while every test said I was fine.

On the strongest program. Hurting the most after it. Nobody found that strange but me.

Meanwhile my group was a highlight reel. "Back to running!" "Pain-free in 8 weeks!" And the ones who'd plateaued, quietly getting the shot, disappearing from the group for a few months, and coming back with a boot and the same story.

One night at 1 AM I googled "plateaued in PT plantar fasciitis."

Reddit threads. "Chronic plantar fasciitis" articles. "Some people never fully recover" pieces. And the surgery forums, full of people on their second and third procedures. I read it all with my heart pounding and thought, that's my future.

I drafted the email to my podiatrist asking for the shot. It sat in my drafts. Unsent. Because something about it felt like admitting the problem was never going to be fixed, just numbed.

Then I asked a stranger the question that changed everything.

There was a woman in my PT's waiting room, I'll call her Gina, who came in on Tuesdays like me. We'd started chatting. Same heel problem. Started PT around the same time. I'd watched her through the glass. She was doing a third of my program. Floor calf raises, a few stretches, a walk on the treadmill. And every week she was telling the front desk she was better than the week before.

I'd been quietly furious at her for two months, if I'm being honest.

One Tuesday I just asked.

"Can I ask you something? How are you still getting better on that program? I'm doing three times as much and I've been stuck since spring."

She smiled a little.

"You're going to be mad."

"Why would I be mad?"

"Because it's something my PT made me start before my very first session. It's about $35 a month. And I figured every PT did that, until I talked to you."

Before Gina's first appointment, her physical therapist, at a different clinic before she moved here, told her something she'd written in her phone. She showed me.

"Every patient I put on loading starts collagen with vitamin C first, an hour before every session. Because the exercises are about to create a demand for new tissue that their body can't meet. And the harder we push the load, the bigger the bill."

I read it twice. Then I said:

"Collagen? I TAKE collagen."

Every night. Since month three. The big tub from Target, a scoop in my tea before bed. It was on my kitchen counter right now.

"What kind?" she asked.

The kind with a woman's face on the label. I had no idea.

"That's the problem. Wrong kind, and wrong time. Let me explain it the way she explained it to me. Because it explains your whole program."

So here it is, the way Gina gave it to me in a PT waiting room, from a woman doing a third of my exercises.

Your plantar fascia is a band of tissue made almost entirely of one material: type I collagen. When you have chronic heel pain, that tissue isn't mostly inflamed. It's worn. Frayed, tangled collagen that's been patched over with weak material.

PT is how you rebuild it. Every time you load the tissue with calf raises, steps, walking, you're telling it: break down the weak stuff and rebuild stronger.

But rebuilding takes material. New collagen has to be built out of something. And your body needs vitamin C to build it at all. Without vitamin C, it can't link the fibers into strong tissue.

The exercises are the order. The collagen and vitamin C are the delivery.

Now here's the trap, and fourteen months of appointments never once covered it.

Most women over 50 are already making a lot less collagen than they used to. Your body's own production drops every year after your mid-twenties, and menopause drops it hard.

Then you start PT, and the exercises do exactly what they're supposed to. They ask your heel to rebuild.

And at the same time, half of us get told to lose weight. So we eat less. Less protein. Fewer of the foods that give your body building blocks.

More orders. Fewer deliveries.

"Now look at your program," Gina said. "Every time your PT raised the load, she asked your heel to rebuild more than the level before. Same short supply. Bigger bill. The level that's supposed to be the strongest is the level where you're asking your body for the most it's ever had to build, with the least it's ever had to build with."

"That's why each level bought you less than the one before. The program got harder and your supply got thinner at the same time. And that's why I'm still improving on my easy program. My exercises are lighter. But my body has what it needs to answer them."

"The program was never measuring the exercises. It was measuring the supply."
