bodyText:
My husband and I got home two weeks ago from a seven day Western Caribbean cruise out of Galveston. Four port days, three sea days, and one pair of shoes I wore from embarkation to debarkation without switching once. I have done six cruises in the last ten years. My feet ruined every single one of them. Then on this trip, three women stopped me in the street in Cozumel to ask what I was wearing.

My name is Ruth. I am 68. I live outside Houston with my husband Gary. I kept a little diary on this cruise, day by day. I am going to give it to you straight.

First, the history. Because the history is the whole point.

Cruise number one, I brought cute sandals. Thin straps, tiny heel, adorable in the mirror. They lasted until lunch on day two. My feet swelled in the heat and the straps cut red lines into them. The sandals spent the rest of the week in the cabin.

I bought flip flops in the gift shop. Gary still brings it up. "Best souvenir of the whole trip," he says. He thinks he is funny.

Cruise number three, I went the other way. Big chunky white walking shoes, the wide ones. The kind they sell on the rack next to the compression socks. They did not hurt, they just made me look like a tourist who had given up on life.

My granddaughter saw the photos. She said, "Grandma, whose shoes are those?" They were mine. That was the problem.

That is the choice they give a woman my age. Shoes that hurt or shoes that surrender.

Here is my real problem, and maybe yours. My feet swell in the heat. Every afternoon, like clockwork. By dinner they are a full size bigger than at breakfast. Anything with a strap cuts. Anything stiff pinches. By evening my feet ache down in the bones.

On a Caribbean cruise, heat is the whole show. So every night of every cruise ended the same way. Me on the bed, feet up on a pillow. Gary at the show alone.

After the last cruise I complained to my best friend Elaine. I said, "My feet just cannot do cruises anymore. Maybe I am done."

She did not let that sit for one second. "Ruth, there is nothing wrong with your feet," she said. "There is something wrong with every shoe you have ever bought."

I thought about that for a whole year.

So this spring, when we booked Galveston, I went looking. Really looking, not just grabbing the white rack shoes again. I found a pair called the Cloud Walk, from a company called Nimbao. A stretchy knit shoe with no laces at all, and room for the toes to sit flat. The whole upper flexes like a good sock. I read every review written by a woman with swollen feet. There were pages of us.

I ordered them in Turquoise, because I am 68, not dead.

The box arrived on a Tuesday. I slipped them on standing up at the kitchen counter. No bending, no chair, no shoehorn. Two seconds. My toes spread out flat inside that toe box. Nothing pressed anywhere. Nothing waited to rub.

I walked the hallway twice and said, "Well."

Gary looked up from his paper. "Well what?"

"Nothing hurts."

"Give it a week," he said.

He is a give it a week man. He wears the same old cushioned sneakers he has worn for years. Worn down flat on the inside edges. He calls them broken in. I call them broken.

When I packed, I almost threw in the sandals as backup. Six cruises of habit. I left them on the closet floor. One pair of shoes for seven days. Gary watched me zip the suitcase and shook his head slowly.

"Bold," he said.

Now the cruise. Day by day, exactly how it happened.

Day 1. Embarkation.

Anyone who has sailed out of Galveston knows that terminal. The line wraps around itself twice and the floor is bare concrete. We stood for over an hour before we ever saw the gangway.

The woman ahead of us took her sandals off right there in line. She stood on that concrete holding them, wincing. I wanted to hug her. I have been her six times.

My feet did not say one single word. We got to the cabin and Gary dropped into the chair. He pulled off his sneakers with a groan.

"An hour on concrete," he said. "My feet are barking already."

Mine were not. I wrote it in the diary. Day one, zero complaints. I did not trust it yet.

Day 2. Sea day.

Pool deck all morning. Before breakfast I walked four laps around the promenade deck. That is more than a mile. Then it was lounge chairs, the buffet line, the art auction we always wander into and never buy from.

In the afternoon the real test came. The heat came up and my feet started their swelling. I know the feeling by heart. That tight, hot, growing feeling. I sat there and actually watched for the moment the shoes would start to bite.

They never bit, the knit just stretched. It gave exactly where my feet grew. No line, no cut, no pressure point. By dinner I still had shoes on my feet. On a ship. In the heat. That has never once happened to me.

A woman at the towel station looked down at my feet. "Those look comfortable. Are they?"

"You have no idea," I said.

Day 3. Cozumel.

First port day, ninety degrees by ten in the morning. We walked five hours. The market, the little shops, the whole long waterfront. Gary wanted to quit at hour two.

"My feet are done," he said. "Are yours not done?"

They were not done. They were swollen, sure. It was ninety degrees and I am 68. But the shoes swelled right along with them, and nothing cut in, and nothing rubbed raw. Somewhere around hour two I forgot about my feet completely. I have not forgotten about my feet in fifteen years.

Then came the part I still cannot get over. Three separate women asked me about my shoes. In one port. In one day.

The first was at the market, by the vanilla stand. She pointed at my feet. "Excuse me. What are those?"

The second one crossed the actual street to reach me. She said her feet were killing her and mine looked happy. Her word. Happy.

The third was from our own ship. She said, "I have been watching you all morning. You are the only woman our age out here not limping."

Then she pulled out her phone right on the sidewalk. "Spell it for me," she said. So I spelled it. Cloud Walk, by Nimbao. She typed it in and saved it in her notes.

Gary witnessed all three and did not say much. But at dinner he looked at my Turquoise shoes for a long moment and said, "Huh."

Day 4. Sea day. Casino night.

That night I stood at the craps table with Gary for three hours. Standing, not perched on a stool, on thin casino carpet over a steel deck. On every other cruise of my life, I am back in the cabin by ten. Feet up on the pillow. Listening to the fun through the wall.

At midnight Gary looked over at me, confused. "You are still here."

"I am still here."

"Your feet?"

"What feet?" I said. He laughed so hard the dealer looked up.

Back in the cabin I called Elaine on the ship wifi. I know it was late. Some things cannot wait for morning.

"Elaine. I stood at a craps table for three hours. It is day four and nothing hurts. Nothing. You were right the whole time. It was never my feet. It was forty years of wrong shoes."

She had already looked them up after my text from Cozumel. Of course she had. That is Elaine.

"Ruth, listen to me," she said. "They are running buy one get one free right now. So you are ordering for me tonight. I want the Apricot, and the free pair is mine too. A spare, before the rest of you buy them all."

So I sat on the bed in my Turquoise pair and ordered Elaine both her Apricot pairs, from the middle of the Gulf of Mexico, at half past midnight. Gary watched me do it and did not say one word about money. That is how you know he was convinced.

Day 5. Grand Cayman.

Tender port. There is no dock at all, so they load you into a small boat, and the small boat bounces, and you step across a moving gap in front of forty watching strangers.

I am 68 and I do not bounce well anymore. Balance is a real thing at my age. I need both hands on that railing. Which means I need to trust my feet completely, with no hands to spare for doubt.

I stepped across that gap like it was my own kitchen floor. The soles gripped and my feet sat flat and sure inside them. Both hands free for the railing, both times, on and off.

Gary came behind me in his worn out sneakers. He wobbled on the step. A crew member caught his elbow.

"Sir, take your time," the young man said.

We still walked the waterfront after that. Two slow hours of shops and shade. My feet never once asked to sit down.

Gary was quiet on the ride back. Then he said, "Maybe there is something to your little knit shoes."

Six cruises, that is what it took.

Day 6. Roatan.

Beach in the morning, then lunch at a white tablecloth restaurant an hour later. Same shoes, and that is the part nobody believes.

The shoes that walked me down the boardwalk to the beach walked me straight into a nice restaurant. And in Turquoise, they looked like I had planned the whole outfit around them. Cute and comfortable used to be a choice. Pick one, lose the other.

Gary looked under the tablecloth at my feet. "You wore those to the beach an hour ago."

"Same shoes," I said. "Keep up."

Six cruises I packed sandals for pretty and big white shoes for walking. I wore neither one happily. This cruise I packed one pair. One.

Day 7. Debarkation.

Customs line, luggage hall, parking garage, all concrete, all standing, all the parts of a cruise nobody photographs. My feet handled it like it was nothing, because by then it was nothing.

In the car I added up the diary. Seven days. Four ports. Five hours in Cozumel heat. Three hours standing at a craps table. More than four miles walked across Grand Cayman and Roatan together. Every dinner in real shoes instead of surrender shoes.

Zero blisters. Zero red strap lines. Zero nights with my feet up on a pillow while Gary had my vacation for me.

One more thing happened in that customs line. The woman from our ship found me, the one who typed the name into her phone. "I ordered mine last night from the cabin," she said. "They were out of your Turquoise. I am waiting on the restock."

Elaine has worn her Apricot pair every single day since it came. Her words, not mine. Then she called me with her official verdict.

"Ruth, I have walked more since that box came than in the last two years," she said. "And you know the worst part? In my old sneakers I felt like a tourist in my own town. In these I feel like a person."

Gary ordered his own pair on Sunday. Full Black, because he is Gary. He would tell you his feet made him do it.

If you have a cruise coming up and you are already dreading the shoe question, stop dreading it. You do not need a suitcase of compromises. You need one pair that stretches when the heat comes.

If your feet swell every afternoon and every strap you own cuts into them by dinner, hear me. That is not your feet failing you. That is stiff shoes refusing to move. Knit moves.

If you have ever sat alone in a beautiful port, feet throbbing on a bench, watching your family walk on without you, I was you. For six cruises I was you. I am not anymore.

You need these shoes. Not because they are pretty. Though they are, my Turquoise got compliments in Cozumel and on the ship. But because you only get so many cruises, and your feet should not be allowed to steal another one.

One pair. Seven days. Four ports. Zero pain.

Elaine made me promise to pass the link along to the next woman with feet like ours, so here it is for you too: https://nimbao.com/cloudwalk

Your move.

bodyText:
I was seven when Princess Marcy implanted lizard eggs in my throat. Because she feared my beauty would one day make the Alpha King choose me as his Luna.
At eight, the eggs hatched. Lizards crawled from my throat and spread across my body. Marcy was certain the excruciating pain would kill me.
But that night, my powerful wolf healed me. When Alpha Edward, Marcy’s father, discovered the truth, he tore my wolf apart.
“She’s a cursed witch. Tame her. She’s your pet from now on.”
That was the day Marcy stopped treating me like a person.
“Dogs don’t walk. They crawl, bitch.”
And for the next fifteen years, I lived like an animal.
I slept in a doghouse.
When Marcy and her friends ate, I sat on the floor beside their table—not like a beloved pet waiting for treats, but like a stray waiting for its next kick.
My knees bled from crawling. My back permanently bent from living on all fours.
When Marcy was angry, she yanked my leash.
When she was bored, she kicked me.
And when she wanted entertainment, she left me in a pitbull pen.
“Bad dog. Go play with your kind.”
I grew up never knowing what it felt like to be human.
Never knowing what it felt like to be loved.
Every night, I prayed to the Moon Goddess.
“Please… change my fate. Let me live like a human.”
I had no idea my prayer was about to be answered.
Because that very night, whispers spread through the palace.
The packhouse doors opened.
And Alpha Damon—the most powerful Alpha in the realm—walked into the Red Moon Pack for the first time.
He was about to see the “pet” everyone else had learned to ignore.
Alpha Damon entered the Red Moon packhouse for the first time. 
Leader of the Dark Howlers, fiercest pack in the realm. He was the most powerful Alpha in all of North America. Women threw themselves at him. Rulers feared him. He could seduce a she-wolf with a glance, or tear out a man’s throat just as easily.
Damon was untouchable. 
He scorned the idea of love. Rejected every political match. Not a single potential bride, despite the many presented, could win his affection. None were worthy of being his Luna, the proud she-wolf to rule by his side.
Love was a distraction, an attempt to tame him. And Damon would never be tamed. 
Still, there were those who tried.
Alpha Edward was desperate to secure his political power. He invited Damon to meet his daughter, Princess Marcy, beautiful, cunning, cruel. She intended to make him hers.
Talia feared their union. Would Marcy succeed where so many others had failed? Would Marcy’s cruelty only intensify as Luna to such a powerful Alpha?
The moment Alpha Damon stepped onto Red Moon Pack grounds with his mated Betas, Caden and Maya, something felt off. His wolf stirred uneasily beneath the surface. Damon didn’t need confirmation, he already knew: no one in the Red Moon Pack could be trusted.
They all sat down in the dining hall, its gaudy opulence a reflection of Red Moon’s inflated ego.
Marcy arrived fashionably late, every detail of her appearance sharpened like a blade. Shimmering blond hair, a sculpted figure. She was the type of girl who got what she wanted.
Her friend, Nora, wasn’t as restrained. She eyed Damon with hunger, her gaze sliding over him like a caress. The rumors had reached her ears: about his appetite, his stamina, his size. She didn’t care that Marcy was supposed to win the Alpha’s hand. Nora wanted a taste for herself.
Marcy’s mother, Luna Layla, noticed the heat in Nora’s stare… and the flicker of fury in her daughter’s eyes.
“Marcy,” Layla said, too sweetly, “Why don’t you show Alpha Damon to his room so you two can… talk?”
While the Red Moon Pack celebrated Damon’s arrival, elsewhere in the kitchens, Talia worked until the sweat stung her eyes. All she could dream of was the scraps she might scavenge when the feast was over.
The other Omegas had different plans for her.
Anna, their cruel ringleader, stepped into Talia’s path, towering over her, “Listen up, slave.” The other Omegas giggled behind her like hyenas. 
Anna’s lips twisted into a cruel smirk. “You’re going to deliver towels to Alpha Damon’s room.”
Talia froze. “Right now? But... what if he’s inside?”
Anna raised her hand, ready to strike. “Are you questioning me?”
Talia flinched, her heart pounding. Without her wolf, she was defenseless against the bullies. 
Without another word, she took the towels and hurried off, every step dragging her closer to the Alpha’s quarters and whatever fate awaited her behind that door.
When Talia entered the room, she froze. Damon was in his room. But he wasn’t alone. 
There was Marcy. On her knees. Between Damon’s legs. 
Marcy whipped around, her eyes blazing with fury as they locked onto Talia’s. The insolence! 
A jolt of fear shot up Talia’s spine. Retribution would be certain.
Damon’s eyes snapped to Talia.
“Stop!” he barked.
But Talia was gone, bolting from the room, too terrified to look back.
What Talia didn’t know, what she couldn’t have known, is that in that moment, Damon’s world had shifted.
Her scent. It hit his veins like a spark of kindling, igniting something primal within him.
Could it be? His inner wolf howled the truth within him, again and again. She, a lowly omega, a serving girl without a friend, was his fated mate?
Ignoring the mocking laughter of Anna and the others, Talia ran until she reached the attic, shoving the cabinet against the door before collapsing in the corner, struggling to quiet her frantic breathing.
'Is this it? Is this the day I die?'
Back in Damon’s room, Marcy landed clumsily on her backside as Damon shoved her away, his expression thunderous and unreadable.
"Who was that girl?" he demanded, hastily buttoning his pants.
Marcy knew exactly who she was. Talia. Her wolfless collared pet. How dare she step into an Alpha’s chambers uninvited? And worse, if word got out that Marcy had been pleasuring Damon before he’d even proposed... she’d be humiliated. A laughingstock. Her reputation would be in shreds.
Marcy’s jaw clenched with fury. She should’ve done more than just beat the girl this morning.
But Damon didn’t notice Marcy’s simmering rage. He was too distracted, his mind replaying the moment when she walked in. How that intoxicating scent, freesia and citrus, had struck him. How his wolf had howled, wild and urgent. All he could think about was pulling her into his arms.
'Mate.' His wolf howled in confirmation. 
He had never expected to hear that word. Never wanted to. And yet, the moment Talia entered the room, something inside him had shifted, changed.
His wolf growled inside him. 'Find her!'
Damon clenched his jaw. "Find her,” He ordered. “Now."
Marcy hesitated, she was confused. Why would an Alpha give a shit about a slave? Damon’s Alpha energy radiated off of him, making her lower her head. "Yes, Alpha Damon."
But Marcy already knew. She’d be doing much more than just finding her… 
Meanwhile, Damon paced, running his tongue over his teeth, irritated beyond reason. His body still ached with unfinished release, but the thought of Marcy’s coconut scent made him recoil. It wasn’t her scent he wanted, it wasn’t her body against his that he needed.
It was her. Talia.
The girl with the smart doe eyes and copper-colored hair.
Damon prowled through the packhouse, inhaling deeply. Nothing. No trace of her scent.
His wolf snarled. 'Find her!'
'If she was really my mate, why did she run? Why didn’t she feel it too?'
'You had another woman on her knees in front of you,' his wolf sneered. 'What did you expect? That she’d throw herself into your arms?'
Damon scowled. His instincts screamed at him to chase, but logic held him back. He needed to stay in control. If he lost control and Marcy found out the truth, there was no telling what they would do to her! 
For now, he would wait.
Later that night, Marcy returned to Damon’s chambers. She couldn't wait to tell him how she put the girl in her place, that wretched, wolf-less slave. But when she saw Damon standing there, Marcy forgot all about the girl.
And she would make him forget all about her too.
But Damon barely acknowledged her, his mind consumed by the memory of that freesia scent.
Marcy advanced, “Hello, Damon.”
Damon swiftly turned toward the door to see Marcy peeking in. He wondered if she even knocked, but even if she did, he probably wouldn't have noticed.
He never felt this distracted!
What if that was an enemy? That copper-haired girl already caused him to be weak, and he didn't even acknowledge their mate bond.
"Why are you here?" Damon asked.
"You look tense..." Marcy said while reluctantly putting her palms on Damon's firm chest. 
"I can help you relax."
Damon's lips lifted into a half-smirk. "And how would you do that?"
"I know that nothing is confirmed, but technically, we are engaged,"
Damon observed her fingers as they moved slightly. 
She felt him out over the thin fabric of his shirt.
He noticed a big ring on her right middle finger, an oval-shaped ruby with small diamonds surrounding it. 
Damon looked at her almond-shaped blue eyes, straight nose, and full lips, and he confirmed that she objectively appeared attractive.
Damon felt his wolf's anger and dejection, but he decided to ignore it.
Unaware of the conversation Damon had with his wolf, Marcy inched closer to Damon and she smiled seductively.
"I can..."
Before Marcy could finish her sentence, Damon's hand landed at the back of her head, and he pulled her closer for a kiss, pulling her toward the bed.
“Wait,” Marcy breathed.
"Wait?” Damon replied, “What happened to were technically engaged? Get out."
Marcy didn't understand.
"What?"
"I said... GET OUT!"
The clock struck two. Damon lay restless, tension coiled in his muscles, his thoughts tangled in a torment he refused to name. The oppressive stillness of the Red Moon packhouse suffocated him. He needed air. Control. Escape.
He moved silently, intent on a midnight run—until it hit him. Freesia.
That intoxicating scent. Sweet citrus and wild temptation. His pulse pounded, his body moving before his mind caught up, drawn to the scent like a predator to prey. His hunt led him to the kitchen, shadow pooling in the corner, the hum of the refrigerator filling the quiet.
And there she was.
A small figure bathed in the cold glow of the open fridge, unaware of the danger lurking just behind her.
Damon closed the distance. Too close. Close enough that his heat ghosted over her nape, close enough that he could imagine how she’d feel beneath him. Soft. His.
"Mhm." His voice came unbidden, dark, possessive.
Talia gasped, jerking back—right into him.
She spun, eyes wide, body trembling. Fear. A scent he despised on her.
"Aw," she whimpered, rubbing the back of her head, shrinking under his gaze. Wrong move, little one. You’re not leaving.
She scurried sideways, but Damon was faster, his arm blocking her escape.
"What are you sorry for?" he murmured, his voice low, dangerous.
She stammered, refusing to meet his eye, her lip caught between her teeth—a sight that shouldn’t send heat curling in his gut, but damn it, it did.
He cupped her chin, tilting her face toward the light. Sparks. A wildfire licked up his arm, searing through his vein. His wolf howled, triumphant. Mate.
But that momentary euphoria crashed when he saw her bruise.
His grip tightened. Rage.
"What happened?" His voice was no longer smooth. It was a blade, sharp with violence.
She flinched. "I—I fell."
"Lies." His thumb ghosted over the mark on her cheek. It was shaped like—a ring.
Marcy.
His wolf roared inside him, demanding blood. Demanding vengeance.
"Who did this?" he growled.
Talia shuddered. "No one."
A lie. A plea. A desperate attempt to protect the monster who hurt her.
Damon inhaled deeply, trying to rein in the storm inside him, but her scent—the sweetness, the fragility—it wrecked him.
"I will not hurt you," he swore, his tone softer now, but she didn't believe him. He could see it in the way her body coiled, ready to run.
Then, she did.
Gone. Vanished.
She had run from him AGAIN, Damon couldn’t believe it.
Damon stood frozen for a second. Then—"Damn it!"
His wolf snarled. Find her.
Damon’s body moved on instinct, chasing the fading scent of freesia into the night.
Damon halted in the middle of the garden, nostrils flaring as he inhaled deeply, searching for her scent. 
The freesia and citrus still lingered in the air, but it was interwoven with the overpowering fragrance of hydrangeas and roses, scattered wildly by the wind.
"Shit!" he cursed, his fists clenching. "I lost her. Why did she run?"
'Maybe because you scared the soul out of her.' His wolf growled.
Damon frowned. 'I scared her?'
'You grabbed her, cornered her, demanded answers... You think she’s not used to being mistreated? 
And let’s not forget, the first time she saw you, another she-wolf was on her knees for you, and you barked at her to stop. Hardly a warm introduction, if I may say.'
Damon cursed under his breath. He hadn’t considered it from that angle.
The girl haunted him. Her wide, fearful eyes. The bruises marring her delicate face. The way she shrank when he spoke. It made something primal inside him snap.
'If she’s my mate, why didn’t she feel it? She should have wanted to be near me, not running for her life.'
'Maybe she doesn’t know you’re her mate.'
'Is she too young?'
'No, she’s small and malnourished, but she’s definitely over eighteen.' His wolf hesitated. 'The problem is... I can’t sense her wolf.'
Damon’s body stiffened. 'She’s a human?'
That thought made him recoil. A human? The Moon Goddess paired a fragile human with an Alpha like him? That was insanity.
'No,' his wolf corrected. 'She’s a she-wolf. But for some reason, her inner wolf hasn’t awakened. It could be abuse. Starvation. Or something darker. Maybe… her wolf has been silenced.”
Silenced? Who would do such a thing? What reason could they possibly have to justify such cruelty? Ripping a wolf from her other half, severing the sacred bond between soul and beast.  Damon couldn’t imagine a fate more brutal. More inhumane.
Damon raked a hand through his hair, his frustration mounting. He’d frightened her. He let her leave without food. And now, she was out there—alone, vulnerable.
'How do I fix this?'
His wolf growled. 'Fix what? 
You came here to seduce Marcy, ruin Alpha Edward’s plans, and leave. 
What changed? You want to apologize for being an ass and take her out for dinner?'
Damon scowled, staring at the darkened tree line in the distance.
He wasn’t the kind of man to coddle or chase after anyone. He told himself to forget her, to move on. 
But the truth was, he wasn’t sure if he could.
Damon stormed up the stairs, each step heavier than the last. His blood ran hot, his chest tight with frustration he couldn’t shake.
She ran from him.
The copper-haired girl with those wide, frightened eyes and the scent that still clung to his skin. Like she wanted nothing to do with him.
Fine. Let her go.
He threw the bedroom door open without thinking—and froze.
Nora was already there, draped across his bed like she belonged, wearing nothing but a wicked smirk.
“I figured you’d need company,” she purred, stretching, letting her fingers trail across his pillow. Marking her territory. "Rough night?"
Damon exhaled hard, his fists clenching at his sides. The girl’s scent was still in his head, citrus and freesia, clinging like a curse.
But Nora smelled of want. Willing. Available.
A distraction.
That’s all he needed. That’s all this was.
He closed the door with a snap and stepped toward the bed, gaze dark and unreadable.
“Shut up,” he growled.
Then he grabbed her.
Damon sat on the edge of the bed later, running a hand through his damp hair. The shower hadn’t washed away the frustration, nor the bitter aftertaste of what just happened. Nora was already gone.
He glanced down and saw a pair of torn panties near the foot of the bed.
Not Marcy’s.
Nora’s.
His lip curled. Perfect. Just another mess to clean up.
"You’re a damn fool." His wolf's voice slithered into his mind, thick with disgust. "Did that make you forget her? Did she feel like our mate?"
Damon clenched his jaw. No.
Nora had been warm, willing—everything he should’ve wanted. But it had been empty. Pointless. The moment his release faded, the hunger in his chest only grew sharper.
His wolf sneered. "I warned you. She is the only one who can satisfy us."
Damon growled under his breath. He didn’t want this to be true. He didn’t want to need the girl with the copper-colored hair.
And yet… he did.
If he was ever going to find peace again, he needed to find her.
His frail, elusive mate.
The Omega who kept slipping through his fingers.
The next morning, Damon contacted Caden and Maya through their mind link.
'Are you guys up?'
'We are now,' Caden grumbled.
They had an agreement—nights were private between him and Maya, and Damon only disturbed them if something urgent came up.
Maya’s voice grew alert. 'Did something happen?'
'Caden, come to my room.'
There was a pause before Caden responded. 'On my way.'
When Caden arrived, he gave the room a once-over before raising a brow at Damon. "You look like shit. Were you attacked?"
His gaze fell on the shredded panties discarded on the floor. "Oh. Never mind. Guess you had a long night."
Damon wasn’t in the mood for jokes. 
He tossed and turned the entire night, plagued by nightmares. He saw the copper-haired girl trapped in darkness, shadowy hands choking her, bruising her skin. He clawed at an invisible barrier, screaming her name.
Except he didn’t even know her name.
"How did you feel when you met Maya?" Damon asked abruptly.
Caden’s grin faded. "Why? Is Marcy your mate?"
Damon rolled his eyes. "Just answer the damn question."
"Attraction, sparks, happiness. I needed Maya to be happy so I could be happy. I thought I knew what happiness was before, but after meeting her, I realized I’d been clueless."
Damon clenched his jaw. That wasn’t what he felt. He felt restless, furious, out of control.
"Did you ever think about resisting it?"
Caden looked appalled. "Why the hell would I? She’s the best thing that ever happened to me. I waited my whole life for her. Why would I reject her?"
Damon’s stomach twisted. "What if Maya was in danger because of you? Would you pick her safety over your happiness? What if the only way to protect her was to reject her?"
Caden frowned. "What kind of twisted scenario is that? I wouldn’t be happy if she suffered. Rejection would break us both, so I’d rather face danger together."
He eyed Damon sharply. "What’s going on? Did last night fry your brain?"
Damon exhaled harshly. "I don’t know what’s going on."
Caden shrugged. "Alright. We’re still leaving after breakfast, right?"
Damon hesitated. Could he really leave without seeing her again? Just one more time—to make sure she was okay, to confirm that the sparks weren’t in his head?
"Let me think about it.”
Caden studied his Alpha, his oldest friend. There was something Damon wasn’t saying. He could feel it. But he didn’t press. Damon would talk when he was ready, and when he did, Caden would be there. He always was.
He couldn’t have known Damon’s mind was consumed by the copper-haired girl, his true fated mate. Or that beneath his calm exterior, he was seething over the bruise Marcy had left on her skin. That cruel woman. His so-called betrothed. He could tear her apart if it wouldn't start a damn war. Though maybe there were other ways to destroy her…
Caden turned toward the door when Damon’s voice stopped him. “Could you look into Marcy for me? Anything we can use to discredit her: past scandals, secrets, whatever you can find.”
Caden nodded without hesitation. “Anything, Damon.” He slipped out, closing the door softly behind him.
'Are you thinking about her?' his wolf asked.
Damon sighed. 'I need to protect her.'
'Then keep her close. Don’t reject her.'
His wolf had explained that, without her wolf, Talia didn’t feel the bond. She wasn’t drawn to him the way he was to her. To win her, he’d have to do it the human way; court her, earn her trust. 
But without the bond, nothing guaranteed she would stay and that terrified Damon the most!
Damon didn’t know the first thing about romance, but he knew one thing—no one could know she was his mate.
If Alpha Edward learned, he’d use her against him. She’d become leverage, a hostage. Damon couldn’t allow that.
After breakfast, Damon met with Alpha Edward in his office.
"I wonder if you’re aware of how your Omegas are treated," Damon said.
Alpha Edward frowned. "Elaborate."
"Do they get paid? Fed? Protected?"
Edward bristled. “We provide accommodations, three meals a day. They have access to the kitchen. We train them, discipline them if necessary, but no one is mistreated."
Damon leaned forward. "Then why did I see one yesterday, perfectly fine—and hours later, covered in bruises?"
Alpha Edward’s jaw tightened. "Disputes happen."
Damon smirked. "Then maybe you should have a chat with your daughter."
Edward’s eyes sharpened. "Marcy?"
"A Luna should protect her people—not beat them to a pulp. If my mate was ever treated like that—" Damon cut himself off, clenching his fists.
Edward narrowed his eyes. "I’ll speak with her."
Damon smirked. "I’m counting on it."
Later when Marcy entered Edward’s study, he cut straight to the point.
"How is your relationship with Damon?"
Marcy smiled. "We’re getting along well. I think he plans on making me his Luna."
Edward’s voice darkened. "Then explain why he thinks you beat Omegas half to death."
Marcy paled.
"What were you thinking?!" he roared. "You don’t beat an Omega when an Alpha you’re trying to impress is watching!"
Marcy swallowed hard. She had just made a very dangerous mistake.
"Do whatever it takes. Do you understand me?"
Alpha Edward’s voice was razor-sharp, slicing through the thick air between them. His hand slammed against the desk, the loud crack making Marcy jump.
Marcy swallowed hard, nodding fervently. "Yes, Father."
"Don’t just ‘yes, Father’ me!" he snapped, eyes gleaming with fury. "I gave you everything. Position, power, the opportunity to become Luna of the strongest pack! And you’re ruining it because of your carelessness. Do you know what happens if you fail me? If you mess this up?"
Marcy’s breath hitched. "I—I can fix it. I promise."
Edward’s jaw clenched. "You’d better. Find Damon. Make him yours. By any means necessary."
Marcy rushed to her room, slamming the door shut behind her. Her hands trembled as she braced herself against the vanity. That was close.
And it was all her fault. That lowly mutt, Talia, who needed a muzzle. A constant thorn in Marcy’s side. 
Why would Alpha Damon, of all people, care so much about such a useless little omega? It made no sense. 
After a deep breath, Marcy steeled herself. She wouldn’t fail.
She stripped off her dress, selected something more daring—plunging neckline, fabric that clung in all the right places—and touched up her makeup before making her way to find Damon.
She found him outside his room, speaking with his mated betas Caden and Maya.
"Are you guys going out?" she asked, feigning casual interest.
Caden nodded. "James offered to show us around the warrior training grounds."
Marcy barely suppressed her grimace. The training grounds reeked of sweat and desperation, two things she had no interest in.
Damon’s eyes were cold as they landed on her. "Can I help you, Marcy?"
She nearly flinched. His tone was ice. It was worse than anger—he was indifferent.
He found out.
The bruised stray rat had reached his ears. Her father had been right. She needed to fix this—fast.
She smiled sweetly. "I was hoping we could talk. Just the two of us."
Damon glanced at Caden, who gave him a knowing nod before leading an eye rolling Maya away. 
Once they were alone, Marcy stepped forward and, without hesitation, wrapped her arms around Damon’s waist.
He didn’t return the embrace.
Instead, his hands gripped her wrists and peeled her off him as if she were something repugnant.
"What are you doing?"
"I’m sorry," Marcy said quickly.
Damon arched a brow. "For what?"
She hesitated. Did she mean last night? Or the Omega? Or both?
"My behavior yesterday was… unacceptable."
Damon leaned back against the chair, his arms folding over his chest. "You came here to apologize. Do it without touching me."
Marcy took a breath. "I also want to fix things."
His brow lifted. "Fix what, exactly?"
She clenched her hands at her sides. Just do it. Give him what he wants. You can control him once you’re Luna.
"I wasn’t thinking straight last night," she admitted. "I said things I didn’t mean."
Damon smirked. "You didn’t mean what you said? About your limits? What you’d do?"
Marcy’s cheeks burned. "I mean… I said we needed to know we were heading toward marriage first. And we are. So… I’m fine with whatever you want to do."
Damon leaned forward, his smirk darkening. "Whatever I want?"
Marcy swallowed. "Yes."
"Undress."
She blinked. He’s serious.
With slightly trembling fingers, she unbuttoned the front of her dress, letting the fabric pool around her ankles. She stood before him in lace lingerie, heart hammering.
Damon’s gaze swept over her body, unreadable.
"All of it."
She hesitated for only a second before obeying. The bra slid from her shoulders, the panties kicked to the side. She stood bare, feeling powerful and vulnerable all at once.
Damon’s smirk remained. "Turn around."
She did. Slowly.
Gritting her teeth, she obeyed. Damon circled her slowly. 
And then—
Smack!
Marcy jolted as his palm connected with her bare skin, leaving a bright pink imprint on her skin. The sting melted into pleasure, making her whimper.
She arched her hips, offering more. But Damon stepped away.
She turned, confused, just in time to see him buttoning his cuffs.
"What?" she gasped. "What are you doing?"
Damon smirked, voice dripping amusement. "Parting is such sweet sorrow."
And with that, he walked to the bathroom, washed his hands as if cleansing himself of her, and left without looking back.
Marcy stood there, naked, humiliated.
He. Just. Left.
Damon used his mind link to check on Caden and Maya. 
"That was fast," Caden teased as Damon joined them.
"Shut up," Damon replied.
Maya crossed her arms. "Did you get anything we can use against Marcy?"
Damon exhaled. "No."
Caden and Maya exchanged a look.
"She’s been careful," Caden admitted. "No photos. No proof of her messing around. Just whispers."
Damon’s jaw tightened. "Keep digging. Someone has something."
“We did find something else,” Maya said, holding up a sealed envelope.
Damon’s eyes narrowed. “About Marcy?”
“No,” Caden shook his head. “Another girl from the Red Moon Pack. A servant girl. With copper hair.”
Damon’s eyes widened, his entire body stilled. He snatched the envelope from Maya’s hand and tore it open. He couldn't believe his eyes. 
His grip tightened, voice low and urgent. “We need to find her. The copper-haired girl. Now.”
"You don’t even know her name," Maya pointed out.
Damon clenched his fists. But I know her scent.
He turned abruptly. "I’ll be back in ten minutes."
Maya and Caden exchanged another look as he strode off.
"What’s gotten into him?" Maya asked.
Caden sighed. "Hell if I know. But I think we just found his weakness."
As Damon searched the grounds more desperately, he hatched an idea. Damon knew that as a guest he couldn't go anywhere he wanted, so he asked Alpha Edward to assign him an escort.
"Can Marcy accompany you?" Alpha Edward asked. He obviously wanted to increase the time that Damon and Marcy spent together.
He immediately contacted Marcy through the mind link and after a brief pause, he said, "Oh, sorry. She's busy right now. Can you wait a little bit?"
Damon guessed that Marcy sulked after he left her hanging in his room. That made him feel good.
Damon didn't care who accompanied him. He had no clear goal in mind and as long as that person didn't get in his way, it seemed fine. "I'd like to start now if it's OK with you. You can tell Marcy to join me whenever she's ready."
Alpha Edward wondered why Damon seemed in a rush, but he didn't question it. Damon wanted to walk around, and he even acted considerate enough to ask for someone to escort him.
It took Alpha Edward two seconds to find his next candidate. A person who knew what went on and wouldn't embarrass him.
Nora waited for Damon in front of the study with a big smile on her face. "Alpha Edward asked me to escort you and to answer any questions you might have."
Damon hummed in understanding. "Take me to where Omegas stay."
"Sure."
Damon eyed Nora. If she was surprised by this demand, she didn't show it.
Damon observed the two-story high building. The bottom floor had a kitchen, a common area that doubled as a lounge and dining room, and four bedrooms. The upper floor had ten bedrooms.
Based on the information they received about the Red Moon pack, each room housed six to eight people, so Damon estimated about one hundred people in each building.
Nora didn't understand why Damon asked to visit this place, but other than walking through the hallways, he didn't stop.
"Do you want to see inside rooms?"
Damon refused. "That's not necessary. Is this the only building for Omegas?"
"No, there are three more," Nora responded.
"I want to visit them."
Three buildings later, Damon lost hope that he would find the mysterious copper haired girl.
Not a single whiff of freesia appeared, no matter how much he searched.
After four buildings without any hints of the copper haired girl., Damon was frustrated.
"Are you looking for anything in particular?", Nora asked when she saw Damon spacing out in the middle of the hallway.
Damon shrugged and shook his head. He was not sure himself.
Nora stepped closer to him and spoke in a sultry voice, "Whatever you want, I can give you…"
Damon frowned. "Keep your distance, Miss Nora, or people might get the wrong idea." She didn't move and his expression darkened.
"Do you want to start the rumors about us? I wonder, what would Alpha Edward say if he thinks there is something going on between us? I'm sure you are aware of my reputation. One more girl won't make a difference, but for you who tried to ruin Marcy's chances of becoming the Luna of the Dark Howlers pack..." Damon clicked his tongue.
Nora gave him a tight smile and increased the distance between them. She got the message to stay away. For now.
Damon became immersed in his thoughts, completely ignoring Nora who fidgeted by his side. He was recollecting everything he knew about the copper haired girl and trying to come up with something that made sense. Damon assumed that she was an Omega because she brought towels into his bathroom, and because of the poor treatment she received.
If she had any standing, Alpha Edward wouldn't be oblivious that she was mistreated. Of course, there was a possibility that Alpha Edward knew about it, and he was pretending to be oblivious. However, if he was concealing the issue, he would deny it and not tell Damon that he would talk to Marcy.
Damon spent the last decade among Alphas, and he learned a thing or two about reading them. He was confident that Alpha Edward didn't know that Marcy (and maybe someone else) was physically punishing Omegas.
Damon wanted to ask Nora if she knew something about beatings or the girl with copper-colored hair, but he quickly decided not to. He didn't want to appear to be snooping into something that was not his business and if anyone suspected that he was specifically interested in one girl with poor standing, that could backfire big time.
The last thing he wanted was to jeopardize her in any way. He had to connect the dots on his own.
Anyone with such injuries would probably stay in bed, either in the pack hospital or in her room, and an Omega would help her out. Hell, even if she was an Omega, someone should take care of her and not let her search for food in the middle of the night.
The fact that she was looking for food in the middle of the night while injured, meant that she didn't have dinner, and her skinny appearance told Damon that she skipped many other meals as well. His heart ached.
He thought that maybe she committed some crime and was being punished, but if she was imprisoned or tortured, she wouldn't be able to come to the kitchen, so he crossed off that as a possibility.
If she truly was an Omega, she would live in one of these common buildings, and Damon could pick up her scent. Another mystery was, why would she look for food in the packhouse when there was a kitchen in each of these buildings?
The more Damon thought about it, the less sense it made. It all felt like he was trapped in a game of hide-and-seek. He was exasperated and his mind was a mess.
His life was so much simpler before he saw that girl sneaking out of his room while Marcy was pleasuring him.
Damon didn't want to think about the copper haired girl, and he couldn't believe that he spent so much time searching for her. The girl ran away, and she probably didn't care about him.
The smartest thing to do was leave this pack and return to his routine. Eventually, her addictive scent would fade from his mind, and he would be normal again.
Damon wanted to leave the Red Moon pack and go home. He really did. But as time passed, Damon realized that he couldn't leave without seeing the girl with the copper-colored hair again. Just one more time.
He wanted to ensure that she was fine. At least that's what he told himself. Damon hoped that if he could inhale her sweet citrusy scent of freesia a few more times, he might get sated, or maybe he would find out that it didn't affect him anymore. And then there were those sparks that felt divine. Yes, he needed to feel those again also.
Just once and then he would leave. Definitely.
Damon came up with a million reasons to see the girl he couldn't get out of his mind, and he roamed around the packhouse and community buildings, but with no luck.
It was like the girl simply disappeared.
Damon was desperate. Was she a ghost who came to torture him? He was never this anxious.
Caden and Maya realized that Damon was acting strangely, but he didn't explain anything, no matter how many times they asked.
Damon was irritable and he said more than once that they were leaving, only to turn around and tell them they were staying longer.
To say that Maya and Caden were confused, was an understatement.
When Damon announced that they would stay another night, Caden and Maya started suspecting that Marcy or Alpha Edward drugged Damon or cast some mind-muddling spell on him because this was not Damon they knew.
Damon was never indecisive, and he never refused a naked woman and this was enough proof for Caden and Maya that Damon was losing it.
Caden and Maya agreed that if Damon's behavior escalated, they would take him away by force. The plan was that Maya would distract Damon, and Caden would whack Damon in the head, and then they would drag him into the car and drive away.
Oblivious to Caden's and Maya's plans, Damon thought about his situation and realized that there was only one thing for him to do. He left his room around midnight and headed downstairs.
Damon sat in the kitchen of the packhouse with the lights off and waited. That's where he saw the copper-haired girl, so he hoped that she would show up again.
Damon didn't sleep the previous night, and he was not in his best shape, but every one of his muscles was tense, and he didn't feel like sleeping.
His mind was going through numerous scenarios of what he would say when the mysterious girl showed up, and how she would respond.
Would he play it cool and ask casually how she was doing?
Or maybe he should show a stern expression and demand an explanation to why she disappeared last night without a goodbye?
Or maybe he should make a pitiful expression and say how she hurt his feelings? Based on the internet, girls liked it when a man exposed his vulnerable side.
Damon was still not sure if he should embrace this madness or reject her, but he knew that he had to see her.
His wolf would growl in displeasure whenever Damon thought about rejecting her as his mate, and whimper sadly when Damon worried why she was not there yet.
What if she is hurt? Did she leave? Was she hungry? Damon shoved his hand into his hair. Maybe the girl was fine and sleeping and he was an idiot for spending the night in the kitchen.
Seconds ticked into minutes that turned to hours, painfully slow, and Damon was exasperated when he saw dawn cracking through the window. She didn't come.
Damon was about to give up and head to his room when footsteps from the hallway got his attention.
He impatiently jumped to his feet, in the hope that it was the copper haired girl.
Damon's handsome eyebrows came together when he saw a woman with a duster in her hand. A blonde Omega in her late-twenties.
Her eyes widened in surprise, and she stuttered. "Can… can I help you, Alpha Damon?"
Damon rubbed his chin. Could she help him? Maybe. He looked around, making sure they were not overheard.
"Can I ask you something, but you make sure it stays between us?"
The woman nodded fervently in small jerky movements.
"I'm trying to find a girl. I believe she is an Omega. This tall…" He gestured with his hand. "Skinny. Waifish. Copper-colored hair this long…" He pointed below his shoulder.
The woman shook her head, indicating that she didn't know the person Damon was searching for.
Damon remembered one more detail. "She wore old clothes that were oversized for her."
The woman made a thoughtful expression.
"You know her?", Damon asked in an urgent whisper while inching closer to the Omega who was now blushing profusely.
"I… I…" The words were stuck in her throat. He was too handsome and too close, and all this was too sudden. "She… maybe…"
"Yes? Yes!?" He asked impatiently.
She blinked rapidly. "The attic. There is a girl living in the attic."
Damon climbed to the attic faster than the wind and his lips curved into a smile when he inhaled the scent of freesia he was craving for.
The girl was there.
He stared at the closed door in front of him and took a moment to compose himself.
Damon thought about how he went all around the Red Moon pack's properties in search of the girl. Why didn't he think of checking the packhouse thoroughly?
He already knew that the girl was not in the common buildings because she came to the kitchen in the packhouse.
Now that he was standing in the attic, he realized that the obvious places would be to check the basement and the attic, as well as any isolated places where guests didn't venture. It seemed that his mind was muddled and he didn't think straight.
Well, it didn't matter. The time had come. She was right there. Behind that door. Hopefully.
Damon knocked on the door lightly and waited.
Nothing. He knocked again, this time with a bit more force.
Damon thought that he heard some shuffling from inside, but he was not sure because his heart thundered in his ears. He was never this anxious.
He gave it another knock and His patience snapped. Damon turned the handle, stepping inside. 
The attic was dark, the only light filtering through a small window, illuminating a frail figure curled in the corner.
Copper-colored hair spilled over her face, but he could see her wide, honey-brown eyes locked on him.
His breath hitched.
He had found her.
Talia looked up…and froze.
Her eyes went wide, not with relief, but fear.
“No,” she whispered, scrambling back until there was nowhere left to go. “You—you can’t be here.”
Damon stopped immediately, hands lifting in a placating gesture. “I won’t hurt you.”
Her breath came fast, shallow. She shook her head, panic flashing across her face.
Why him?  The thought screamed through her mind. Why does he keep finding me?
Then he saw it—the bruises, fresh ones layered over the old. And when she shifted, her sleeve hitched, revealing a swollen wrist.
Marcy.
A savage growl rumbled deep in his chest. "She hit you again, didn’t she?"
Panic flickered across her face. "Please don’t say anything. If you do, she’ll hurt me more."
His wolf roared in fury. She fears more punishment because of me.
Then he saw it hanging on a hook—the dog collar. Damon squinted his eyes. “Marcy’s Pet” was engraved on the name tag.
Damon clenched his fists, barely restraining the need to storm out and rip Marcy apart. But the girl in front of him—his mate—was trembling. 
The need to protect her was all-consuming—like it was his sole purpose in life.
He forced his anger down. He did the only thing that made sense in that moment.
He sat down beside her and wrapped her in his arms.
She froze. Then squirmed out of his grip.
“No…” She struggled. “Let go. Please…”
He released her immediately, hands lifting away. “All right. I’m sorry.”
She pulled her knees to her chest, eyes darting to the door, then back to him. His presence wasn’t comfort. It was danger.
‘She doesn’t trust you’, his wolf said quietly. ‘You will have to be patient. Court her. Earn her trust.’
Damon swallowed. That went against every instinct screaming inside him, but his wolf was right.
“I’m not here to hurt you,” he said carefully. “I want to protect you. You don’t belong here. You don’t have to stay.”
She shook her head at once. “You don’t understand.”
“Then help me,” he said. “Come with me.”
“Why?” She asked, as if she couldn’t bring herself to believe him.
"Because I’ll give you what you deserve. A home. A room of your own. Clothes that fit. Food whenever you want. A doctor for every scratch. No one will ever lay a hand on you again. And if they do, I’ll deal with them myself."
His wolf let out a low, possessive growl.
Talia stared at him as if he’d lost his mind. And maybe he had.
"Why do you want to help me?" she whispered.
"Because."
Because you’re mine. He thought. 
She didn’t believe him. He could see it in the way her shoulders stayed tense, in the way she never stopped watching the exit.
Damon knew time was of the essence. He feared that at any minute, Edward or one of the other guards would begin to inquire where Damon had gone.
“We have to leave,” Damon said. “Now. You can trust me!”
Talia’s gaze flicked to the door, then to the small window, then back to him. Escape routes. Distances. Survival. She began to hyperventilate.
“You don’t have a choice,” Damon said, the words heavy with desperation. “Please. You must come with me…You’re in danger. We all are.”
Danger?! What does that mean? From who? From what?
Her chest rose and fell rapidly. 
What would she do… what could she do?!
Trust him and risk everything. Stay and suffer what she knew was coming. Run—and face the unknown alone.
The estate groaned softly around them, footsteps echoing somewhere below.
Talia looked at Damon, her expression unreadable.
She bit the inside of her cheek while considering her options.
One was staying at the Red Moon pack. Anna's bullying was escalating, and Marcy was unpredictable. Yesterday Marcy came to the attic and Talia got a beating for something she didn't do.
The second option was to go to the Dark Howlers pack. Alpha Damon said that in his pack people were accepted. Could it be worse than here? Probably not.
Of course, there was also the third option for Talia to leave on her own somewhere, but that option was scary and uncertain, and it will exist even if she goes with Alpha Damon.
“Come with me.” Damon asked, holding out his hand.
"Just like that?"
Damon nodded. "Just like that."
Talia paused and decided to ask the question that was bothering her from the moment he came to the attic. "How do I know that you are not tricking me?"
Damon stood up and Talia felt chills surround her when his body separated from hers.
He extended his hand toward Talia, palm up. "Let me prove it to you."
***Now that Damon has found his fated mate, can he help her escape a life of imprisonment? ***
Will Talia risk everything for a chance to discover freedom?
What will happen when Edward and Marcy discover Damon has found Talia?
Will the bond between Damon and Talia ignite a war between packhouses?

bodyText:
I watched plantar fasciitis turn my husband into a man that depended on others. 

My husband is 47 and he's a carpenter. Runs his own small crew. Decks, framing, additions, whatever the job is.

His whole life is his hands and his body. He framed most of our house himself. He built our back deck one summer, the good one with the wraparound bench. He built our son a treehouse when the boy was seven that half the kids on the street ended up in. He was never a man who sat down. Full day on a job, then home, then out to the garage to start something else. Busy, strong, never still. That was him.

I'm telling you that so you understand what this took.

For almost two years, my husband couldn't walk across our own backyard without it showing on his face.

It came on slow. He mentioned his heel hurt, which he never does, so it stuck with me. He blamed his boots. He's the type who buys the cheap forty dollar work boots and wears them down to the ground, so he got $300 boots that didn't help.

Then I started seeing it in the mornings. We wake up together, and he'd sit on the edge of the bed and put his foot down and stop. Just sit there a second, bracing, before he could take a step. He told me the first step felt like standing on a nail and he had to walk it off before his foot worked right. He's not a complainer. When a man like that tells you it feels like a nail, it's felt like a nail for a long time.

Then it got into his work. He came home one day quiet and it took me a while to get it out of him. One of his young guys had carried the loads up from the truck all day because my husband couldn't, pretending to be fine wasn’t an option for him anymore. That one hit him hard. Carrying the weight of the crew was his job. But he couldn’t carry his own anymore. 

Here's the road we went down, the whole thing, because I want you to hear it.

We started buying shoes, like everyone does. The Oofos everyone online swears by, that he wore around the house. The big cushioned Hokas, because a guy at the store said those were the plantar fasciitis shoes everyone loves. He wore them everywhere and his foot still hurt.

When the shoes didn't do it, we started going to doctors.

Our GP first. Anti-inflammatories and a photocopied sheet of stretches. The calf stretch against the wall. The one where you loop a towel around your foot and pull it toward you. Rolling his arch on a frozen water bottle. He did all of it, every day, for weeks, and it did nothing. 

The GP sent us to a podiatrist. Plantar fasciitis, he said, and made custom orthotics, three hundred dollars out of our pocket, that dropped into his $300 boots he bought. He wore them every day. It was the same. Some days worse.

We went back and he mentioned the cortisone shot. My husband did not want it. He'd read the stuff people say, that it hurts worse than anything and wears off and comes back angrier. He isn't scared of much and he was scared of that. But he was eight months in, and the doctor said it was the one thing that would get him relief fast, and he was worn down enough to say fine.

It helped for about three weeks. Then it wore off and the pain came back worse than before the shot.

Somewhere in there he tried to fix it himself, the way he fixes everything. He bought one of those percussion massage guns and drove it into the bottom of his foot one night to break up the pain. It hurt more, not less. He tried it a couple more times, it kept hurting, and he put it in a drawer.

By now we're a year and a half in. Third doctor, another podiatrist, hoping for something new.

That one said surgery. A fasciotomy. They go in and cut part of the fascia to release the tension. He said it plainly, like it was just the next step once everything else is used up.

And I sat in that room and something in me refused.

Because I'd watched two years of this. Three doctors, pills, a stretch sheet, three hundred dollars of inserts, a shot that made it worse, and now someone wanted to take a blade to my husband's foot. And under every visit was the same quiet thing. This is just how it is now. Manage it. Here's the next thing to try.

I was done being handed the next thing. That night I sat at the kitchen table after everyone was asleep and I read. Not shopping. Reading. Because I was starting to think none of them actually knew what was wrong with his foot.

It took a few nights, and then I found a study, and it broke the whole thing open.

It was published in 2003 in a podiatry medical journal, by a doctor named Lemont. They took tissue from fifty people with chronic plantar fasciitis, exactly what my husband had, and looked at it under a microscope.

There was no inflammation. None. In any of the fifty.

I read that line about five times. Because everything, all of it, every treatment for two years, was aimed at inflammation. The anti-inflammatory pills. The ice. The cortisone shot, which is an anti-inflammatory. We had spent two years fighting a fire that wasn't burning.

What the microscope actually showed was that the tissue was breaking down. Damaged, degenerating, the fibers dying off. Not inflamed. And the word for that isn't fasciitis. Itis means inflammation. This was fasciosis. A degeneration.

That's why the pills and the ice and the shot never worked. They weren't wrong because we did them wrong. They were aimed at a problem he didn't have.

Then I read why the tissue breaks down and can't climb back out, and that was the part that explained everything. The fascia barely gets any blood. It's the tissue at the bottom of your foot, farthest from the heart, and blood is what rebuilds damaged tissue. So it's a part of the body that tears from overload and then can't repair, because it can't get the blood to do the repair. And if you're a man standing and hauling on it ten hours a day, it never gets a rest from the tearing either.

That's the trap he was in. Torn, starved of the blood it needed to heal, and never off his feet. Tear, no repair, tear again, for two years.

And that's when the shoes finally made sense.

The reason those miracle shoes did nothing for him comes down to the arch. A shoe is built for one kind of foot. A flat foot needs the arch propped up. A high arch needs cushion, and if you put a high arch on a shoe with a big firm arch built into it, that shelf pushes straight up into the sore fascia and makes it worse. The same shoe that rescues one guy digs into the next. It was never that the shoes were fake. It's that a shoe off a shelf is built for an average foot, and it was fighting his.

But even the perfect shoe would've missed the real problem. Every shoe I bought worked from underneath. Cushioning the ground, holding the arch. Not one of them did anything about a tissue that was torn and couldn't get blood. They were all just softening the floor under a wound.

So now I knew the actual problem. He needed the load taken off that tissue so it could stop tearing, and blood pushed into it so it could finally rebuild. And he needed both while still working, because he was never going to stop working.

That's when I found the sleeve.

It's thin, goes on like a sock, open at the toe, a couple of straps across the middle, and it slides right into the boot he already wears. And it did the two exact things on my list. The straps hold the arch and take the load off that band, so it stops getting torn with every step, even while he's up on it. And the compression pushes blood down into the tissue that had been starving for it.

One line on there made it click. It said the point isn't to shut the foot down and rest it. The tissue still has to be worked to come back, like anything healing does. The sleeve just takes off the part of the load that overloads it. Like a spotter on a heavy lift. You're still doing the work, the bar's still in your hands, but something's there catching the weight that would crush you. He couldn't rest his foot and he wasn't supposed to. He just needed to use it without wrecking it every day.

I didn't say any of this to him. I'd promised him the shoes and the insoles would help and didn't want to disappoint him. I just ordered them and set them by his boots and told him to try the thing.

Three days in he came into the kitchen in the morning and I watched him cross the room to the coffee pot without that pause, without bracing. He didn't even notice he'd done it. I said nothing. I didn't want to jinx it.

A week later he took the dog out without a word. I watched him go down the driveway at a normal walk and I had to set my coffee down.

The mornings eased first. Then he stopped scaling back at work. Then one Saturday I went outside and he was down at the far end of our deck, the one he built, crouched on his heels replacing a couple of boards that had gone soft. Hauling the new ones from the truck himself. Nobody carrying them for him.

He looked up and saw me and neither of us said anything, because there was nothing to say. He was just back. The man who built the treehouse. The one who can't sit still.

I got my husband back. That's the whole thing. I didn't fix his foot with a shoe or a shot or a surgery. I sat at a table until I understood what was actually wrong, and then I got him the one thing aimed at it.

They're called Koprez Foot Sleeves.

If your husband's been limping for months, or some doctor's started saying surgery like it's the only thing left, here's what it took me two years to learn. His foot isn't inflamed. Turns out I don't have plantar fasciitis and you might not either.

I'm 52. I've had this in my right foot for two years and four months.

You know the mornings. That first step out of bed is the one that tells you what kind of day you're going to have. I used to sit on the edge of the mattress and just look at the floor. Actually look at it. Like it was a thing I had to negotiate with.

Then it stopped being just mornings.

It became the whole house.

I have not been barefoot in my own home in two years.

Not once. crocs on before my feet touch the carpet. crocs on to make coffee. crocs on to walk down my own hallway at eleven at night to check the back door. I keep a pair by the bed. I keep another pair by the couch so I don't have to cross the living room in socks. My husband walks around barefoot like it's nothing and I watch him do it the way you'd watch someone do a card trick.

And at night, the splint. That plastic boot strapped to my leg in my own bed.

That's the part nobody talks about. It's not that your foot hurts. It's that you are wearing footwear inside your own house at all hours except for when I'm sitting down. Always relying on something to soften the step even at the grocery store, I'm leaning on the cart. Not pushing it. Leaning.

I want to say what it takes from you and I don't know how to say it without sounding dramatic. So here's the plainest version.

I stopped planning things.

Not big things. I stopped planning the farmers market. I stopped saying yes to a hike because I didn't know what my foot would be in three weeks. My daughter asked me to come out for a long weekend and I said maybe. I said maybe to my own daughter because of my foot.

I did everything they told me.

Three podiatrists. Custom orthotics, the expensive ones. The cheap ones before that. Stretches every morning. The frozen water bottle. The spiky ball. Calf raises. Going up a shoe size. The night splint. A cortisone shot I was so scared of I nearly walked out of the office.

The shot worked. For about five weeks. Then it came back and it came back worse.

Two years of doing everything right and nothing moving.

The breaking point was a Tuesday in March. I was standing in my kitchen and I couldn't get to the sink. That's the whole story. It was nine feet away and I stood there and did the math on whether it was worth it. And I thought: this is my life now. This is just what it is.

My podiatrist had started using the word surgery. Not pushing it. Just letting it sit on the table between us.

I went home and I sat in the car in my own driveway for twenty minutes.

I got a second opinion. Not because I'm brave. Because I was out of moves.

The man I ended up in front of has been doing feet for twenty years. Older. Not slick. The kind who doesn't fill the silence while he's thinking.

He watched me walk. He asked me how long. I said two years and four months.

And he put his pen down and said, "Then you're being treated for the wrong thing."

I laughed at him.

The kind where I knew I was right, I'd had three podiatrists. I'd had an MRI. I had a diagnosis written on paper. I said, I have plantar fasciitis. Everyone agrees I have plantar fasciitis.

He said, "You did. Two years ago."

And I sat there in that chair and I could feel my ears getting hot. Because if that was true, then two years of my life were a mistake. And I would rather have been sick than have been wasting my time.

I looked at him with a confused but angry look, like I wasn’t sure if he was telling the truth or not

He saw the look on my face and explained it to me.

The word ends in "itis." Itis means inflammation. And when this starts, that's a fair description. You overload the fascia. You get tiny tears in it. Your body sends inflammation, because that's what a body does when something tears. That's not the disease. That's the repair crew showing up.

The trouble starts when the repair crew never gets to finish the job.

Because you cannot stop using your foot. You have to walk to the bathroom. You have to stand at the sink. So the tissue gets torn again before it's finished healing from the last time, and again before it finishes healing from that, and it never once completes a repair. 

And a tissue that never completes a repair does not stay the same. It changes.

He told me the fibers in there are supposed to lie down straight and tight, like the strands of a rope. When the healing keeps getting interrupted, they come back disorganized. Weak. The rope stops being a rope and starts being frayed cord.

That has a name. It's not fasciitis anymore. It's fasciosis.

Osis, not itis. Not inflammation. A degeneration.

I made him say it twice.

Degeneration. My foot wasn't sitting there inflamed and waiting for the swelling to go down. It was breaking down. The tissue itself was falling apart, getting structurally worse, month over month, for two years, while I iced it and stretched it and strapped it into a plastic boot at night.

He drew it on the back of a chart.

Overload. Tear. Start to heal. Overload again before it heals. Tear it worse. Start to heal. Overload again.

Every step you take rips open the thing that's trying to fix itself.

That's the whole disease. Not "my foot is inflamed." My foot was a rope that never got a single day to knit back together, and it was coming apart one strand at a time.

And once he said it, two years of failure rearranged themselves in front of me.

The mornings. I always thought the morning was bad because the foot got stiff overnight. It's worse than that. At night, off your feet, the fascia finally goes slack, and your body starts trying to patch it. That's the only window it gets all day.

But it's a bad window. That tissue sits at the end of the line, furthest from your heart, and lying still in bed you're barely moving any blood down there at all. So your body does the repair with almost nothing to build with. What it lays down overnight is thin. Weak. Half a patch.

Then you stand up. And your whole body weight goes down through that patch before it ever had a chance to harden.

That's what the first step is. That's the pain. It isn't stiffness. It's you tearing open the only repair your body managed all night, and it tears easy, because there was never enough blood down there to make it strong.

Every morning of my life. Ripping open the one thing my body tried to build while I slept.

Then the splint. Two years I slept in that thing. It holds your foot at a right angle so the fascia stays under a gentle stretch all night. And that does work, in a way. If the tissue is held taut, it can't go slack, and relax, so there's nothing there to tear in the morning and the first step doesn't hurt as much.

It buys you a quieter morning by taking away the one window your foot had. It parks that tissue in limbo all night, every night. Not stretched enough to tear. Not slack enough to heal.

All that splint ever bought me was a quieter first step. But as soon as it came off the rope kept fraying.

The stretches. I was pulling on a cord that was already coming apart and calling it treatment.

The orthotics. They cushioned the landing. They propped the arch from underneath. They did nothing about the tearing and nothing about the healing. A pillow under a wound.

The cortisone. That one hurts to say out loud. Cortisone is an anti-inflammatory. It goes after inflammation. It does not reorganize one collagen fiber and it does not stop one tear. It quieted the alarm for five weeks while the rope frayed on. And when it wore off I got the same foot back, five weeks worse, and I blamed my body.

Nothing I did failed because I did it wrong. Or it was a scam 

All of it failed because every last one of those things was aimed at the alarm and not at the fraying rope.

I asked him why nobody had told me this in two years.

He was honest with me. He said the first-line treatments are the first-line treatments. They get written down, they get handed out, and for most people they work. Most people get better and everybody feels good. The ones who don't get better keep coming back, and they get the next thing on the list, and then the shot, and then the conversation about surgery.

Then he said the quiet part. There's no money in telling you the tissue needs a chance to heal. There's money in the injection. There's money in the operation.

So I asked him what actually stops it.

He didn't hesitate. He said you have to break the cycle in two places at once. You have to take the load off it while you're on your feet, because you can't stop being on your feet. And you have to get blood down into it, because the fascia is at the very end of the line, furthest from your heart, and blood is what rebuilds a tissue.

Then he opened a drawer.

He took out a sleeve and put it in my hand.

It's like a compression sock with the toes open, and there are straps that wrap over the top and lock down underneath the arch. Thin. It disappears inside a shoe.

He told me he's been doing this twenty years and he didn't learn this in a classroom, he learned it watching people like me come back for a fourth and fifth visit. And that once he understood what was actually happening in there, he started sending patients to this instead of to the next injection.

He said the straps hold the arch so the tissue stops getting torn open with every step you take. And the compression drives blood down into a fascia that has been starved for months and can finally rebuild.

He said this is the only thing he's found that goes after both halves of that cycle at once.

I'll be honest, I still didn't believe it. I have a drawer at home full of things that didn't work.

I put it on that night the way you eat a salad you don't want.

It goes on like a sock. You pull the straps snug across the arch and you feel them take hold, like a hand cupping the bottom of your foot from underneath.

And I stood up. And I put my weight down wrong, the way you do when you're not thinking, and I braced for the thing that always happens.

It didn't happen. The pain wasn’t gone but it wasn’t unbearable, interrupting or the kind that has you reaching for a railing. 

That was the whole event. Nothing shot up through my heel. I stood in my kitchen at ten at night and put my weight on that foot again on purpose, just to check.

Two days later I walked to the bathroom in the morning without doing the thing I do, where I hold the doorframe and lower my heel down in stages.

I just walked.

I said "huh" out loud, to nobody.

Three weeks in, I made dinner and stood the entire time.

And then came the day I found out it was real.

My sleeve was in the wash. I had the whole day at home ahead of me and nothing to put on, and I remember thinking, fine. It's one day. I'm not going anywhere.

By the afternoon I felt it. Not the old thing. Nothing close to the old thing. A dull ache coming up through the arch, low and steady, the way a bruise reminds you where it is.

I sat down at my own kitchen table and I understood two things at once.

This dull ache used to be my good day. That was the best my foot ever felt for two years, and I used to be grateful for it.

And I hadn't thought about my feet in three weeks.

Not once. Not standing at the sink, not on the stairs, not getting out of bed. Three weeks of my life where my feet were just my feet. Until the one day my sleeve was in the wash

I sat there with my hand over my mouth.

That's when I believed him.

I went to the farmers market on a Saturday and I never once limped, I went to every stand I wanted to and not just the ones close to the parking lot. 

I did the whole grocery store, both sides, and I was pushing the cart. Pushing it. I got to the car and realized I hadn't leaned on a single thing, and I sat in the driver's seat and cried, which I'm not going to apologize for.

And a month ago I got up in the night for a glass of water, and I was halfway down the hall before I understood what I was doing.

Standing in my own hallway in the dark on my own two bare feet.

Two years. And I didn't even notice I was doing it.

And tomorrow night, while every beautiful she-wolf in the pack dressed in silk and waited for fate to choose her, I would attend the mating ball too, as the servant carrying their wine.
 
The night before the ball, I was summoned to Princess Marcy's chambers, the cruel pack princess, my greatest tormentor, cunning, beautiful, vicious. Hold still, mutt. She sneered, driving a dress pin into my wrist.
 
I bit the inside of my cheek and kept my eyes on the marble floor. Do not scream. Screaming only made it worse.
 
Marcy stood on a raised platform in front of three golden mirrors, her blonde hair shining down her back, her mouth painted rose pink, her eyes cold and pleased with themselves. Her expensive gown clung to her body like it had been bullied into submission. Silver silk, diamond beading, a long train, basically everything I would never touch unless I was being forced to bleed on it.
 
Nora, Marcy's best friend, knelt beside the hem with a handful of pins and a smile that made me believe she had been a hyena in a past life. She slid another pin through the fabric and into my forearm. I sucked in a breath.
 
Nora glanced up. Marcy smiled at me in the mirror. Careful, Nora.
 
If she yelps, we'll have to start over. Sorry. Not sounding sorry at all.

You look perfect. I know. Marcy's gaze slid to me.
 
Tauja. I swallowed. This was a trap.
 
You look beautiful, princess. Her hand cracked across my face. Pain burst across my cheek.

Marcy stepped off the platform and circled me slowly. Poor Tauja. The mating ball is tomorrow.

Hearts racing. Wolves howling. True love.
 
Destiny. Marcy leaned close. But not for you.
 
My throat tightened. No wolf, no bond, no mate. No one to ever look at you and say, mine.
