My heart slammed. The mating ball was upon us. One more night, I told myself.
 
I only had to hold on for one more night. What did fate have in store? What would happen at the full moon's peak? Downstairs, the mating ball had officially begun. Silver garlands draped from the chandeliers.
 
Moonflowers climbed the pillars. Crystal goblets sparkled on every table. The entire ballroom glowed beneath the solstice moonlight spilling through the glass ceiling above.
 
Tonight the silver moon will rise to weave our fate across the skies. A full heart will pray for destiny to find its way. Candles glow.
 
The violins sing. Moonflowers bloom as dancers spin. The grandest night the wolves have known to find the soul that's called their own.
 
Yet one small heart still dares to dream. Perhaps tonight fate waits for me. The ancient bond will soon ignite and every life will change tonight.
 
I moved through the crowd with a tray balanced on one hand, offering mushroom tarts, honeyed figs, and tiny lamb skewers to noble wolves who looked right through me. That was fine. Being ignored was one of my better talents.
 
Inside my chest, Liesli stirred. Barely. Her warmth had been fading all evening, thinning with every inch the moon climbed higher in the sky.
 
Liesli? I whispered, keeping my smile fixed as a she-wolf snatched two tarts without saying thank you. I'm here, she said softly. But she sounded far away.
 
Too far. My fingers tightened around the tray. You're fading.
 
I know. Above us, the solstice full moon rose higher and higher, bright and round. Everyone kept glancing up at it, waiting for the moment fate would pull mates together.
 
But what fate was waiting for me? What was supposed to happen when the moon finally peaked? Could I truly be more than the lowly runt everyone had always told me I was? And who was this mysterious man Liesli claimed would unlock it? I slipped outside to deliver a tray of drinks to the terrace, mostly because I needed one second where no one was sneering at me over a stuffed mushroom. The terrace overlooked the front drive, where black cars lined the courtyard. Dark howlers.
 
Even their cars looked daunting and expensive. Near the stone railing, a group of she-wolves huddled together, whispering and giggling. Nora was in the middle of them, of course.
 
She wore red silk and enough perfume to stun a battlefield. I heard he killed three rogues with his bare hands. One girl whispered, I heard he rejected an alpha's daughter because she smiled too much.
 
Another said, Nora fanned herself. I heard he's even more handsome up close. You saw him? Only for a second, Nora said.
 
But goddess, alpha daemon is... unreal. They all sighed. I tried to step around them, but Nora spotted me.
 
Her gaze flicked over my tray. Oh look, the kitchen rat is delivering refreshments. I lowered my eyes.
 
Would you like one? Not if your hands touched it. The rich girls laughed. I was used to it.
 
Then the air changed, and the girls went silent. A scent rolled across the terrace. Rich.
 
Dark. Warm. Coffee and chocolate and smoke after rain.
 
My breath caught. Liesli lifted her head inside me so sharply it hurt. Across the courtyard below, a tall figure stepped from the shadows.
 
Alpha daemon. I saw him only for a moment. Dark hair, broad shoulders, a black suit that hugged his muscled frame.
 
Even from far away, power clung to him like a storm about to break. The she-wolves around me practically melted into the stone. For one strange heartbeat, daemon turned his head toward the terrace.
 
The scent deepened. Chocolate. Coffee.
 
Danger. Then daemon disappeared back inside, and Liesli went quiet. Later, I stood along the side of the ballroom with a tray of bacon-wrapped dates and watched the wolves dance.
 
The moon was nearly at its peak now. Everyone could feel it. The air buzzed.
 
Couples kept pausing mid-step, glancing around as if their souls had started tugging on invisible strings. A girl near the musicians gasped and dropped her fan. Across the room, a young warrior froze.
 
Their eyes met. The whole room erupted into cheers as he crossed to her, shaking, and whispered something I couldn't hear. Another bond sparked near the punch table, then another by the balcony doors.
 
Wolves laughing, crying, embracing as fate handed them the one person made for them. I watched, smiling politely because that was my job. Inside, something ached because I knew I'd never have a maid of my own.
 
Someone who would see you once and know. Someone who would cross a room for you. Someone who would never let Marcy touch you again.
 
But who would ever choose a lowly Omega runt like myself? Liesli stirred faintly. Don't look so sad. I'm not sad, I whispered.
 
I'm holding bacon-wrapped dates. You are terrible at lying. Just then, a woman stepped beside me and plucked an appetizer from the tray.
 
Maya. I recognized her from reputation. The mate of Alpha Damon's beta.
 
Dark hair, sharp eyes, a rose and dagger tattoo on her forearm. She chewed thoughtfully, then brightened. Oh, this is delicious.
 
I blinked. Thank you, ma'am. What an amazing cook you are.
 
I was so unused to kindness that I almost looked behind me to see who she meant. Maya's gaze softened as she studied my face. What's your name? Talia.
 
Talia. She repeated. Are you always this small? I stiffened.
 
I try not to take up too much space. Her mouth tightened. That's not what I meant.
 
Her eyes moved over me, my thin wrists, my hollow cheeks. The faint bruising Liesli hadn't had enough strength to fully heal. Is this how Red Moon treats its Omegas? She asked quietly.
 
My stomach dropped. Before I could answer, a tall man stepped up beside her. Caden, Damon's beta.
 
He looked calmer than most of the Dark Howlers, which was to say he looked like he could politely remove someone's head if asked. He said, then glanced at me. His gaze sharpened for half a second.
 
I lowered my eyes. Maya touched his arm. Any sign of what's bothering Damon? Caden exhaled.
 
No, but he's been strange since we arrived. Restless, distracted, like something is driving him mad. My pulse picked up.
 
Or someone, Maya said. Caden's eyes flicked toward the moonlit ceiling. The Solstice can do strange things.
 
Do you think he found her? Maya asked softly. His mate? My fingers tightened around the tray. Could it be Marcy? She asked.
 
I shuddered at the thought. I don't know. Caden said.
 
But something is happening. Caden's eyes turned toward me, slow, assessing. Why was he staring at me? Before anyone could ask another question, a howl erupted through the ballroom, deep, primal, then another, and another.
 
The full moon had reached its peak. The ballroom exploded. Wolves cried out as bonds ignited.
 
Some laughed, some sobbed, some dropped to their knees. The mating ball had truly begun. Maya grabbed Caden's hand.
 
We need to find Damon. Caden nodded, but his gaze lingered on me one second too long. Then they disappeared into the crowd.
 
Inside my chest, Leasley flickered like a dying candle. Talia, she whispered. My throat tightened.
 
No. It's time. No.
 
You said soon. This isn't soon. This is now.
 
I will come back when you need me most. I need you now. Her warmth wrapped around my heart one last time.
 
Remember what I told you, my girl. You are more than we know. Trust me.
 
All will be revealed soon. Leasley. We will meet again.
 
Then she faded. The space inside me went quiet. Too quiet.
 
Like a room after the last candle goes out. I swallowed hard, blinking fast. No.
 
Not here. Not now. How could I go on without Leasley? What did fate have planned for me? And who was the mysterious man meant to unlock it? I looked across the ballroom, desperate to focus on anything else.
 
That was when I noticed Alpha Edward near the high table. His gaze was sharp and fixed directly on me. His earlier threat slammed back into my skull.
 
If Marcy did not end this night bonded to Damon, it would be my head. I scanned the ballroom, the dancers, the laughing she-wolves, the moonlit corners. Marcy was gone.
 
My blood turned cold. Oh, that was bad. That was very, very bad.
 
I set the tray down and ran. I checked the powder room, the dressing room, the side parlor. All empty.
 
My panic climbed with every door. Where was she? If Marcy was late to her own destiny, Alpha Edward would not blame Marcy. He would blame the disposable handmaiden.
 
Me. I raced upstairs to Marcy's chambers and pressed my ear to the door. Nothing.
 
No voices. No movement. Then I heard a sound from down the hall.
 
A low murmur. A breath. From the guest room.
 
I crept toward the sound and stopped outside the largest guest room, Alpha Damon's room. My body went cold. I knocked lightly.
 
No answer. I pushed the door open. I froze.
 
Marcy was on her knees in front of Alpha Damon. Her hands were on his belt. His expression was hard.
 
His jaw tight. His body rigid. I had just walked in on the most powerful Alpha in the realm, being seduced by the pack princess I was supposed to be supervising.
 
I gasped. Damon's head snapped toward me. His eyes locked onto mine.
 
Ice blue. Piercing. His scent hit me full force.
 
Coffee. Chocolate. Danger.
 
My knees nearly gave out. Marcy whipped around. Talia? I did the only thing I could.
 
I turned and ran. Wait! Damon barked. Oh, goddess.
 
He was going to kill me. I barely made it into the hall before a hand caught my wrist. The world spun.
 
My back hit the wall. Damon pinned me there. One hand braced beside my head.
 
The other locked around my wrist. He was huge. Warm.
 
Close. Too close. His scent wrapped around me until I could barely think.
 
Was this how I died? I wished for Lieselie so hard it hurt. Damon leaned closer. His eyes searched my face like he was trying to remember me from a dream.
 
You. He breathed. I swallowed.
 
Me? A low growl rumbled from his chest. Not angry. Hungry.
 
Possessive. Terrifying. Then Marcy stormed into the hall.
 
What the hell is this? Damon did not move away from me. Marcy's eyes went from his hand on my wrist to my body trapped against the wall. Her face twisted.
 
You little thief. I didn't. The dagger from before flashed in Marcy's hand before I saw it coming.
 
Pain tore through my side. I looked down. Marcy's blade was buried inside me.
 
For one second, I stared at it like it belonged to someone else. Then she yanked it free. Blood spilled hot over my dress.
 
I gasped, knees buckling. Damon's growl shook the hallway. The sound made the torches flicker.
 
He turned on Marcy, eyes blazing. Do not touch her. Why was he so angry? Why did he care that Marcy had hurt me? Why did he care about a wolfless runt? Damon grabbed Marcy's wrist, twisting it until she dropped the blade.
 
He threw her back against the wall. Then George appeared at the end of the hall. His eyes locked on Marcy.
 
On Damon. Something broken and furious twisted across his face. With a roar, he charged.
 
Damon moved fast. He caught George by the throat and threw him sideways into the wall like he was nothing. Stone cracked.
 
George collapsed. Guards shouted. Doors burst open.
 
Red moon warriors flooded the hallway. Protect the princess! Seize him! Help for Damon! Caden and Maya appeared from the stairwell, pushing through the chaos. Damon snarled as guards tackled him.
 
Three wolves hit him at once. He threw one off, then another. The hallway became a blur of bodies, growls, fists, and flashing claws.
 
No one looked at me. For once, being invisible helped. I pressed a hand to my bleeding side and slid down the wall.
 
Leasley, I whispered. Nothing. Leasley, please.
 
Blood soaked through my fingers. My head swam. I crawled.
 
One arm forward, then the other. Away from the shouting. Away from Marcy.
 
Away from Damon. My vision blurred. The floor tilted.
 
I left a trail of blood behind me. Too much blood. Then the world dimmed.
 
The last thing I saw was the moonlight stretching across the hallway floor. The last thing I felt was the hollow ache where Leasley used to be. And then, I passed out cold.
 
I didn't hear Damon throw off the guards. I didn't hear the roar that silenced the hall. I didn't hear his voice tear through the packhouse.
 
Where is she? Someone answered, trembling. Where is who, Alpha Damon? Damon's roar shook the walls. Where is my mate? Is it possible? Is Talia truly Damon's fated mate? What will Damon do to protect her? Will their bond ignite a war between the two most powerful packs in the order? Who is Talia really? What hidden power lies buried in her veins? And would any of them survive Red Moon territory long enough to find out?

bodyText:
I was told my neuropathy was permanent at 47. I'm 61 now. Turns out everything my nerves needed, I'd been swallowing for years.

It just never reached them.

For fourteen years, I "managed" a condition nobody ever actually explained to me.

Fourteen years of compression socks that helped for an hour during the day and did absolutely nothing when the burning woke me up at 2 AM.

Fourteen years of capsaicin creams that burned like fire for twenty minutes and wore off before I finished my morning coffee.

Fourteen years of B vitamins, B1, B6, B12, every combination the internet recommended, swallowed faithfully every single morning with no change.

Fourteen years of alpha lipoic acid capsules at the clinical dose, twice daily, for months at a time.

Fourteen years of expensive massage devices that felt nice for exactly as long as I used them and accomplished nothing the moment I put them down.

Fourteen years of doctors who looked at my feet, ran their tests, nodded slowly, and handed me printed handouts about "lifestyle modifications" that had nothing to do with what was actually happening inside my body.

I did everything they asked.

I cut out alcohol completely. Two full years with not a single drink, because every article said alcohol worsens neuropathy. I walked every day, even when my feet felt like they were filled with broken glass and thumbtacks at the same time.

I spent over $180 a month on supplements. Benfotiamine. Magnesium glycinate. Fish oil capsules I choked down every morning because someone on a forum swore by them. Expensive nerve formulas with fancy labels and long ingredient lists that added up to nothing.

When that didn't stop the progression, they sent me to a neurologist.

She ran a series of tests on the nerves in my feet and legs. Afterward she sat down across from me and said the damage was real, it was progressing, and it was consistent with everything I'd been describing for years.

More tests after that. Your nerves are thinning, they told me. Which sounded serious but still explained nothing about what to actually do about it.

Blood work ruled out the obvious causes. "We don't always find a clear reason for this," my neurologist said. "Sometimes the body just does this. Very common after 45."

She mentioned gabapentin. Said it was the standard of care. That it would help with the burning and the electric sensations.

I told her I'd think about it.

I'd done my research. I knew what gabapentin and Lyrica did to people over time. The brain fog that settled in and never fully lifted. The weight gain that crept up regardless of what you ate. The dizziness that made falls, already a real risk with numb feet, even more dangerous. I'd read it over and over in people's own words. Walking around like a zombie. And the dependence. The way doses climbed. The way stopping it became its own ordeal.

I wasn't ready for that. Not yet. Not if there was anything else.

So I kept trying.

I bought a TENS unit. Used it twice a day for six weeks. The stimulation distracted from the pain while the pads were on. The moment I took them off, everything came back.

I tried acupuncture. Eight sessions. My practitioner was kind and clearly believed in what she was doing. The tingling was unchanged.

I ordered infrared light therapy panels. Set them up in my bedroom. Used them every evening for three months. Spent $400 on equipment that now collects dust in my closet.

I tried cold water immersion for my feet. Ice baths, actually. Every morning. The cold would temporarily quiet the burning. Then I'd dry my feet off and within twenty minutes the electric buzzing would be back, angrier than before.

Nothing stopped the progression.

That's the part that broke me, more than the pain itself.

The burning, the buzzing, the electric shocks that fired up my calves without warning, those were bad enough. But I could have lived with a stable level of bad. What I couldn't live with was watching it spread.

It had started in my toes. Small patches of tingling that my first doctor waved off as circulation. By year three it had moved into the balls of my feet. By year six, my entire foot, sole to ankle, was involved. By year ten, it was creeping up my calves.

And I couldn't feel temperature anymore. Not reliably. Hot water that should have felt warm felt like nothing. I had to be careful in the shower, careful in the kitchen, because I couldn't trust my feet to tell me when something was dangerous.

I stopped walking barefoot anywhere. Even my own bathroom felt unsafe. I wore shoes all the time, soft soled, wide, nothing that put pressure on the parts that were most sensitive. I hadn't worn a normal shoe in four years.

Stairs had become something I thought about before I took them. I held railings everywhere. I scanned every floor I walked on for anything uneven, anything that could catch my foot, because I couldn't fully trust what my feet were telling me.

I stopped hiking. I'd loved hiking, trails, real trails, with rocks and roots and uneven ground. That was over. The liability of not trusting my footing on anything that wasn't flat and smooth was too high.

I stopped driving at night because my focus on managing the burning made everything else harder.

My husband watched all of this and didn't say much, because what was there to say. He just quietly started doing things I used to do. Taking out trash on icy mornings. Carrying things from the car. Standing close enough on stairs that he could catch me if something went wrong.

I hated that. I hated needing that. I hated becoming someone who needed to be caught.

And my next neurologist appointment was in eight weeks. And I knew what was going to happen. The tests would be worse. The damage would have moved further. And the prescription pad would come out and this time I wasn't going to have a good argument against it.

I had stopped believing anything would help. I had started doing the math on gabapentin, on what "managed but not fixed" looked like for the next thirty years. On whether that was just my life now.

Then I ran into a woman I used to know from my hiking group.

We'd drifted apart over the years. She'd had neuropathy too, diagnosed around the same time as me, which was how we'd originally connected. We ran into each other at a farmers market on a Saturday morning, and she was moving differently than I remembered. Light. Easy. No hesitation on the cobblestones.

I asked her how she was doing.

She looked at me for a second and said, "Honestly? Better than I've been in fifteen years. I was going to reach out to you."

We sat down at one of the outdoor tables. She got straight to it.

"I know you've been struggling," she said. "I know because I was exactly where you are. Awake all night, every night. Running out of things to try. Looking at the gabapentin prescription and wondering if I was out of options."

"What happened?" I asked.

"I found out why none of it was working. Not the nerves. The reason all those supplements I was taking never made a dent, even when I was doing everything right."

She paused.

"Has anyone ever explained to you where the pills you swallow actually end up?"

I looked at her blankly.

"Your nerves need a few specific things to stay calm and stay coated, magnesium to settle the overfiring, the active form of B12 to support the sheath around them, a couple of others. That part you probably know. Here's the part nobody told me. When you swallow a capsule, it has to survive your stomach acid, then squeeze through your gut wall, then get past your liver, which strips out a huge share of it on the first pass. Whatever's left gets watered down into your entire bloodstream. And your feet are the farthest point in your body from your heart. The very end of the line."

I was listening.

"So by the time anything reaches the nerves that actually hurt, there's almost nothing left. It's not that the magnesium doesn't work. It's that the magnesium never gets there. You're paying for the whole bottle and your feet are getting the last few drops at the bottom of the pipe."

"Okay," I said. "But why does it hit the feet the hardest?"

"Because they're last in line for everything in your blood. Always have been. So when delivery is poor, they're the first place to come up short. They feel it before anywhere else." She leaned forward. "And here's the flip side. When something finally gets delivered straight to them, they're the first place you feel it come back."

She let that sit.

"That's why the tingling starts in the toes. Then the burning. Then the spreading. Not because your nerves are uniquely broken. Because they're standing at the end of a line that was already running dry."

I stared at her.

"You're telling me the supplements weren't the wrong idea?"

"The supplements were the right idea delivered the wrong way. Magnesium calms overfiring nerves. That's real. The active form of B12 supports the coating around them. That's real. Alpha lipoic acid is an antioxidant. That's real. But if it never gets past your gut and down to your feet, your nerves can't use a single bit of it."

"But I've been taking all of that for years," I said. "B12. Magnesium. ALA. All of it."

She nodded like she'd been waiting for me to say that.

"I know. I did the same thing. For years. And here's what took me forever to understand."

She paused.

"It's like pouring water on the sidewalk next to the pot and wondering why the plant won't grow. The water was never the problem. It just never reached the roots."

That hit me harder than anything anyone had ever said about my condition.

"That's why the supplements didn't work. It was never that your body is different, or that you're unlucky. It was a delivery problem. The pills were arriving in your stomach and getting thrown away before they ever made it to your feet."

"So all those years," I said. "All those bottles. All that money."

"You weren't failing the treatment. The treatment was failing you. It never once got the nutrients to the place that actually needed them. Every one of those bottles just said 'nerve support' on the label while almost none of it ever reached a single nerve in your feet."

I sat there for a long time.

"So what actually gets it there?" I asked. "If not a pill?"

"You stop sending it through the gut at all. You put it through the skin."

"Through the skin?"

"For centuries, people with aching nerves and aching joints traveled to mineral hot springs and the Dead Sea to soak. They didn't have a word for why it helped. They just knew they went home moving easier. What they were actually doing was absorbing minerals straight through the skin, into the tissue underneath, without their gut ever touching it. They didn't understand it. They just watched it work, over and over, for generations."

"And now?"

"Now we understand exactly why. Certain minerals absorb directly through the skin into the area right beneath it, and skip the gut, the liver, the whole losing battle. So instead of one capsule fighting its way through your whole digestive system hoping a few drops reach your feet, you put it on the skin, right over where it hurts, and it goes in steady, for hours, exactly where it's needed."

She pulled out her phone.

"When researchers measured how much of a swallowed magnesium pill actually makes it into your bloodstream, the number was as low as 4 percent. Up to 96 percent of what you swallow can be gone before it does anything. That's not the magnesium failing. That's the delivery failing."

I looked at the screen. Then I looked at her.

"So this isn't just another supplement that claims to help nerves."

"No. This is the thing that finally gets what you've been taking for years to the place it was always supposed to go. It doesn't mask the burning. It doesn't fog you out the way the drugs do. It puts the support your nerves actually need right where the gut could never deliver it. That's why everything else fell short. And that's why this felt different when nothing else did."

I left that conversation and couldn't think about anything else.

That night I went looking for everything I could find on the subject. Why nerve symptoms keep going even when you're doing all the right things. Why swallowed supplements so often fall short. What I found kept pointing back to the same thing. Oral absorption is leaky and inconsistent, the feet sit at the far end of circulation, and what little survives the gut is spread so thin that the place that hurts most gets the least. And transdermal delivery sidesteps the entire problem.

I found people online who sounded exactly like me. Years of pills. Awake all night. Watching the numbness spread. Then they switched to getting it through the skin instead, and for the first time something landed.

I texted her that night: "Okay. I believe you. What patch do I actually get?"

She called me the next morning.

"Most patches on the market are junk. They use the cheap form of magnesium, the oxide kind, which can barely cross the skin at all. They use the cheap B12 that your body has to convert before it can do anything. So you stick on a patch that was never going to deliver in the first place."

One brand kept coming up consistently in everything I looked at. Avalaine NerVana+ Nerve Relief Patches. Magnesium chloride, the form actually prepared to absorb through the skin, not the oxide that sits on top of it. Methylcobalamin, the active B12 that needs no conversion. Alpha lipoic acid. L-methylfolate. Third-party tested, certificate of analysis available, pharmaceutical-grade, designed in the USA. One patch a day, eight hours of steady delivery, put right on the spot that hurts.

60 day money back guarantee. After fourteen years of things that didn't work, one more try wasn't going to break me.

I started the morning after the box arrived. Peeled one patch, put it on the worst spot, the top of my left foot.

I expected nothing. I had trained myself to expect nothing.

By the second night, I noticed the burning was slightly different going into sleep. Not gone. But quieter somehow. I fell asleep before midnight instead of fighting it past 1 AM like I had for years.

I'd fooled myself before. I didn't let myself think about it.

I kept using it.

One week: I slept close to seven hours straight. The burning that had been waking me four and five times a night woke me once. I woke up at 6:40 naturally, in the same position I'd fallen asleep in.

I was laying there for a moment before I moved, just taking that in.

I hadn't slept through the night in over three years.

Two weeks: My husband said something over breakfast. "You're moving differently." He wasn't trying to be kind. He looked almost confused. "Your face looks different when you walk."

The evenings that used to sit at an 8 out of 10 were landing closer to a 5. Not gone. But undeniably less.

Three weeks: I stepped into the shower and felt the temperature change when the hot water hit my feet. Felt it. Not perfectly, not the way I used to, but something was there that hadn't been there in years. That same afternoon I walked the full block, about fifteen minutes, without scanning every step.

I turned the water hot and cold, back and forth, standing there in my shower, just feeling my feet register the difference. I started crying and I couldn't have told you exactly why. It was just such a small thing. Such an ordinary thing.

Four weeks: My neurologist appointment.

She did the monofilament test, the one where they touch different spots on your feet and you say whether you can feel it. She started at my toes. Moved to the ball. The arch. The heel.

She stopped. Checked her notes. Went back to my toes.

"When did your sensation change?" she asked.

"About three weeks ago," I said. "Maybe four."

She did the test again, slower. Last visit I'd felt 3 of the 10 points she touched. This time I felt 7. Then she sat back and looked at me with an expression I hadn't seen on a neurologist's face before. Not concern. Something closer to genuine puzzlement.

"Your sensation scores are higher than your last visit," she said. "Not dramatically. But meaningfully."

I told her about the patches. About the gut, and how almost nothing in a swallowed pill ever reaches the feet, the farthest point in the body from the heart, the last in line for everything in the blood. About how getting it through the skin instead skips the whole losing battle and puts it right where it hurts. About magnesium chloride and methylcobalamin and the active forms that actually absorb.

She typed while I talked. Asked me to spell the brand twice. Asked which one.

Then she closed her laptop and looked at me.

"Whatever you're doing, keep doing it. No medication today."

That was eight months ago.

Most mornings now I have to remind myself I ever spent my nights awake at all.

And it isn't spreading anymore.

I check every week. I note where I can feel and where I can't. For eight months, that line hasn't moved forward. For eight months, the creep that had been marching steadily up my calves for fourteen years has simply held still.

I've been back on trails. Not the difficult ones yet. But real trails, with real terrain, with my husband walking next to me instead of behind me with his hands ready. I sleep six, seven hours most nights. I walk two, sometimes three miles without counting my steps, without scanning every surface for what might catch my foot.

Last month I wore a normal shoe. Just for an hour. To a dinner, nothing special. But I wore it and it wasn't agony and I drove home without thinking about my feet the entire way.

Here's what I need you to understand.

If you've tried nerve supplements and they didn't work, it wasn't a failure of natural ingredients.

It wasn't that your body is different, or that you're unlucky, or that you just have to accept the progression.

It was that you were swallowing those nutrients into a gut that threw most of them away before they ever reached your feet. And because your feet are last in line for everything in your blood, they kept coming up short no matter how much you took.

You weren't failing the treatment. The treatment was failing you. It never once got what your nerves needed to the place that actually needed it.

NerVana+ does it differently. Not by masking anything. Not by fogging you out. By skipping the gut entirely and absorbing through the skin, steady, for eight hours, right on the spot that hurts. When the delivery finally works, your feet, the first place to come up short, are the first place you feel it come back.

But only if the forms are right. And only if the delivery actually works.

NerVana+ is the patch I found that got both right.

Magnesium chloride prepared to absorb through the skin. Methylcobalamin, the active B12. Alpha lipoic acid. L-methylfolate. Third-party tested, certificate of analysis available, pharmaceutical-grade, designed in the USA. No pills, no powders, no creams. One patch a day.

Right now, they're running a promotion with significant savings. But Avalaine is a small company. They make everything in small batches to protect the actives. When they sell out, it's usually weeks before the next batch is ready.

60 days to try it. If nothing changes, full refund. No questions asked.

But if it works?

If by the second night the burning is a little quieter and you fall asleep before midnight instead of fighting it past 1 AM?

If by week one it stops waking you four and five times and you sleep close to seven hours straight?

If three weeks in you step into the shower and feel the temperature on your feet, and walk the block without scanning every step?

If a month from now your neurologist is running the filament test twice because you felt 7 of the points instead of 3?

If eight months from now you're walking trails again, wearing normal shoes, sleeping through the night instead of tracking the edge of the numbness every single day?

You'll wish you started fourteen years ago.

I know I do.

My doctor looked me straight in the eyes and said, "We need to start talking about a knee replacement."
I'm 67 years old. I've got grandkids I want to chase around. A garden I've been tending for 30 years. A life I'm not ready to give up.
But four weeks later, I'm back on my feet. Kneeling in the dirt planting tomatoes. And my surgeon is scratching his head wondering what happened.
If you or someone you love is dealing with knee pain, stiffness, or that awful bone on bone grinding, you need to hear what I discovered. Because it completely changed everything I thought I knew about aging knees.
Let me back up.
Six months ago, my knees were a mess. Osteoarthritis in both of them. The cartilage was practically gone. Every morning I'd sit on the edge of my bed for 30, sometimes 40 minutes, just waiting for my knees to "warm up" enough to walk to the bathroom.
Stairs? Forget it. I started sleeping in the guest room downstairs because I couldn't face those steps at night.
The grinding sound was the worst part. That crunching, popping noise every time I stood up. My wife said she could hear it from across the room.
My doctor tried everything. Pain pills that upset my stomach. Cortisone shots that helped for maybe two weeks. Physical therapy that I couldn't keep up with.
Then he brought up knee replacement surgery. Six weeks of recovery. Months of rehab. And here's the part that really got me: he said the artificial joint might only last 15 years. So if I got it done now, I'd probably need ANOTHER surgery in my 80s.
No thank you.
I tried every knee brace I could find. The drugstore ones. The copper ones my buddy swore by. The fancy one my doctor recommended.
They all ended up in the same place. The junk drawer.
One was so tight I could barely get it on. My fingers don't work so great in the morning either, you know? I'd be sitting there for ten minutes just wrestling with a knee brace before my day even started.
Another one was okay at first. But after an hour, my leg was hot and sweaty. By afternoon, I couldn't wait to rip it off.
And that expensive one from the medical supply store? It slid down to my ankle by lunchtime. I spent the whole day yanking it back up.
So I gave up. Started accepting that this was just my life now. Slow mornings. No more gardening. Watching from the porch while my grandkids played in the yard.
Then my wife found something.
She was up late one night, couldn't sleep, scrolling through Facebook. And she saw this article from a retired nurse talking about knee pain.
Now, I'll be honest. I almost didn't look at it. I figured it was just another gimmick.
But one thing the nurse said caught my attention.
She said, "Your body does most of its healing while you sleep. So why aren't you supporting your knees during those 8 hours?"
I'd never thought about it that way.
Think about it. You sleep 8 hours a night. That's a third of your life. And during that time, your body is working hard. Reducing inflammation. Repairing damaged tissue. Trying to heal what got beat up during the day.
But what are most people doing during those 8 crucial hours?
Nothing. Their knees just lay there. No support. No compression. No help at all.
It's like plugging in your phone every night but the charger's broken. You wake up and wonder why the battery's dead.
Here's the other thing I learned.
Almost every knee brace on the market is designed for young athletes. People who hurt their knee playing basketball. They wear it for an hour at practice, then take it off.
That's a completely different situation than mine.
I'm not recovering from a sports injury. I'm dealing with decades of wear and tear. And I need support I can actually live with. Not something I'm fighting against all day.
Those athletic braces are made from synthetic materials that trap heat. They use super high compression that's almost impossible to get on. And wearing them overnight? You'd be miserable. Trust me, I tried.
So the nurse in this article had worked with a company to design something different. A knee sleeve made specifically for older folks who need overnight support.
The material is bamboo. Yeah, like the plant. Sounds strange, I know. But bamboo is naturally softer than cotton. It breathes instead of trapping heat. And here's the wild part: it actually gets softer every time you wash it.
The weave has this 4 way stretch that lets it form to your leg instead of squeezing the life out of it. I can actually get it on by myself. Even at 6 in the morning when my fingers feel like sausages.
And because bamboo regulates temperature naturally, my knee stays comfortable all night. No more waking up at 3 AM in a pool of sweat.
I figured, what do I have to lose? They had a 60 day guarantee anyway.
So I ordered a pair.
First night, I honestly forgot I was wearing them. That's how comfortable they were. I kept reaching down to check if they were still there.
That first morning, something was different. I sat on the edge of the bed like always, waiting for my knees to cooperate. But after maybe 10 minutes, I was up and moving. Not 30. Not 40. Ten minutes.
I thought maybe it was a fluke.
But the next morning was the same. And the morning after that.
By the end of the first week, I was getting out of bed and walking straight to the kitchen. No sitting. No waiting. No dreading those first few steps.
By week two, I noticed the grinding wasn't as loud. Still there, but quieter. Like someone turned down the volume.
And somewhere around week three or four, I found myself standing in front of the stairs. The ones I'd been avoiding for months.
I grabbed the railing and went up. One step at a time. And you know what? It wasn't bad. It wasn't easy, but it wasn't the nightmare I'd been expecting.
My wife started crying. I didn't realize she'd been watching.
Now look. I want to be honest with you.
My knees aren't 25 years old again. The cartilage didn't magically grow back. I still have osteoarthritis and I probably always will.
But my mornings are different now. I'm not a prisoner waiting for my body to cooperate. I'm up and moving. Making coffee. Letting the dog out. Starting my day like a normal person.
I'm back in my garden. On my knees in the dirt, doing what I love. I couldn't do that six months ago.
Last week, I got down on the floor to play with my grandson. Actually got down there with him. And then I got back up again. He thought it was hilarious. I thought it was a miracle.
My doctor noticed too. At my last appointment, he looked at how I was moving and asked what I'd been doing differently.
I told him about the knee sleeves. About wearing them every night. About the 8 hours of support while my body does its repair work.
He just nodded and said, "Well, whatever you're doing, keep doing it."
We haven't talked about surgery since.
Here's what I've figured out.
8 hours a night, times 365 nights a year. That's almost 3,000 hours of gentle support. Almost 3,000 hours of helping your body do what it's already trying to do. Heal. Recover. Fight back against all that wear and tear.
None of those other braces could give me that. They weren't designed for it.
But this bamboo sleeve was built for exactly this. For people like me. Over 60. Dealing with real arthritis. Who need something they can actually wear. Actually sleep in. Actually stick with.
If your doctor is telling you that knee pain is just part of getting older, that surgery is your only option, that you should just learn to live with it?
That's not the whole story.
There IS something you can do. Something that doesn't involve pills or needles or going under the knife.
You see that garden out there? I thought I'd have to let it go to weeds. That I'd spend the rest of my life watching through the window instead of being out there with my hands in the soil.
Well, I was out there this morning. On my knees. Planting peppers.
The nurse who wrote that original article put together a whole page explaining how overnight knee support works. Why bamboo makes such a difference. And how to know if this might help you too.
It's free to read. No one's going to call you or pressure you. It's just information.
If you're tired of those worthless braces in your junk drawer. If you're sick of mornings that take forever to get started. If you want to get back to the things you love without surgery or endless pills.
Just click below and read what this nurse discovered.
It might change everything for you. It sure did for me.

Turns out I don't have plantar fasciitis and you might not either.

I'm 52. I've had this in my right foot for two years and four months.

You know the mornings. That first step out of bed is the one that tells you what kind of day you're going to have. I used to sit on the edge of the mattress and just look at the floor. Actually look at it. Like it was a thing I had to negotiate with.

Then it stopped being just mornings.

It became the whole house.

I have not been barefoot in my own home in two years.

Not once. crocs on before my feet touch the carpet. crocs on to make coffee. crocs on to walk down my own hallway at eleven at night to check the back door. I keep a pair by the bed. I keep another pair by the couch so I don't have to cross the living room in socks. My husband walks around barefoot like it's nothing and I watch him do it the way you'd watch someone do a card trick.

And at night, the splint. That plastic boot strapped to my leg in my own bed.

That's the part nobody talks about. It's not that your foot hurts. It's that you are wearing footwear inside your own house at all hours except for when I'm sitting down. Always relying on something to soften the step even at the grocery store, I'm leaning on the cart. Not pushing it. Leaning.

I want to say what it takes from you and I don't know how to say it without sounding dramatic. So here's the plainest version.

I stopped planning things.

Not big things. I stopped planning the farmers market. I stopped saying yes to a hike because I didn't know what my foot would be in three weeks. My daughter asked me to come out for a long weekend and I said maybe. I said maybe to my own daughter because of my foot.

I did everything they told me.

Three podiatrists. Custom orthotics, the expensive ones. The cheap ones before that. Stretches every morning. The frozen water bottle. The spiky ball. Calf raises. Going up a shoe size. The night splint. A cortisone shot I was so scared of I nearly walked out of the office.

The shot worked. For about five weeks. Then it came back and it came back worse.

Two years of doing everything right and nothing moving.

The breaking point was a Tuesday in March. I was standing in my kitchen and I couldn't get to the sink. That's the whole story. It was nine feet away and I stood there and did the math on whether it was worth it. And I thought: this is my life now. This is just what it is.

My podiatrist had started using the word surgery. Not pushing it. Just letting it sit on the table between us.

I went home and I sat in the car in my own driveway for twenty minutes.

I got a second opinion. Not because I'm brave. Because I was out of moves.

The man I ended up in front of has been doing feet for twenty years. Older. Not slick. The kind who doesn't fill the silence while he's thinking.

He watched me walk. He asked me how long. I said two years and four months.

And he put his pen down and said, "Then you're being treated for the wrong thing."

I laughed at him.

The kind where I knew I was right, I'd had three podiatrists. I'd had an MRI. I had a diagnosis written on paper. I said, I have plantar fasciitis. Everyone agrees I have plantar fasciitis.

He said, "You did. Two years ago."

And I sat there in that chair and I could feel my ears getting hot. Because if that was true, then two years of my life were a mistake. And I would rather have been sick than have been wasting my time.

I looked at him with a confused but angry look, like I wasn’t sure if he was telling the truth or not

He saw the look on my face and explained it to me.

The word ends in "itis." Itis means inflammation. And when this starts, that's a fair description. You overload the fascia. You get tiny tears in it. Your body sends inflammation, because that's what a body does when something tears. That's not the disease. That's the repair crew showing up.

The trouble starts when the repair crew never gets to finish the job.

Because you cannot stop using your foot. You have to walk to the bathroom. You have to stand at the sink. So the tissue gets torn again before it's finished healing from the last time, and again before it finishes healing from that, and it never once completes a repair. 

And a tissue that never completes a repair does not stay the same. It changes.

He told me the fibers in there are supposed to lie down straight and tight, like the strands of a rope. When the healing keeps getting interrupted, they come back disorganized. Weak. The rope stops being a rope and starts being frayed cord.

That has a name. It's not fasciitis anymore. It's fasciosis.

Osis, not itis. Not inflammation. A degeneration.

I made him say it twice.

Degeneration. My foot wasn't sitting there inflamed and waiting for the swelling to go down. It was breaking down. The tissue itself was falling apart, getting structurally worse, month over month, for two years, while I iced it and stretched it and strapped it into a plastic boot at night.

He drew it on the back of a chart.

Overload. Tear. Start to heal. Overload again before it heals. Tear it worse. Start to heal. Overload again.

Every step you take rips open the thing that's trying to fix itself.

That's the whole disease. Not "my foot is inflamed." My foot was a rope that never got a single day to knit back together, and it was coming apart one strand at a time.

And once he said it, two years of failure rearranged themselves in front of me.

The mornings. I always thought the morning was bad because the foot got stiff overnight. It's worse than that. At night, off your feet, the fascia finally goes slack, and your body starts trying to patch it. That's the only window it gets all day.

But it's a bad window. That tissue sits at the end of the line, furthest from your heart, and lying still in bed you're barely moving any blood down there at all. So your body does the repair with almost nothing to build with. What it lays down overnight is thin. Weak. Half a patch.

Then you stand up. And your whole body weight goes down through that patch before it ever had a chance to harden.

That's what the first step is. That's the pain. It isn't stiffness. It's you tearing open the only repair your body managed all night, and it tears easy, because there was never enough blood down there to make it strong.

Every morning of my life. Ripping open the one thing my body tried to build while I slept.

Then the splint. Two years I slept in that thing. It holds your foot at a right angle so the fascia stays under a gentle stretch all night. And that does work, in a way. If the tissue is held taut, it can't go slack, and relax, so there's nothing there to tear in the morning and the first step doesn't hurt as much.

It buys you a quieter morning by taking away the one window your foot had. It parks that tissue in limbo all night, every night. Not stretched enough to tear. Not slack enough to heal.

All that splint ever bought me was a quieter first step. But as soon as it came off the rope kept fraying.

The stretches. I was pulling on a cord that was already coming apart and calling it treatment.

The orthotics. They cushioned the landing. They propped the arch from underneath. They did nothing about the tearing and nothing about the healing. A pillow under a wound.

The cortisone. That one hurts to say out loud. Cortisone is an anti-inflammatory. It goes after inflammation. It does not reorganize one collagen fiber and it does not stop one tear. It quieted the alarm for five weeks while the rope frayed on. And when it wore off I got the same foot back, five weeks worse, and I blamed my body.

Nothing I did failed because I did it wrong. Or it was a scam 

All of it failed because every last one of those things was aimed at the alarm and not at the fraying rope.

I asked him why nobody had told me this in two years.

He was honest with me. He said the first-line treatments are the first-line treatments. They get written down, they get handed out, and for most people they work. Most people get better and everybody feels good. The ones who don't get better keep coming back, and they get the next thing on the list, and then the shot, and then the conversation about surgery.

Then he said the quiet part. There's no money in telling you the tissue needs a chance to heal. There's money in the injection. There's money in the operation.

So I asked him what actually stops it.

He didn't hesitate. He said you have to break the cycle in two places at once. You have to take the load off it while you're on your feet, because you can't stop being on your feet. And you have to get blood down into it, because the fascia is at the very end of the line, furthest from your heart, and blood is what rebuilds a tissue.

Then he opened a drawer.

He took out a sleeve and put it in my hand.

It's like a compression sock with the toes open, and there are straps that wrap over the top and lock down underneath the arch. Thin. It disappears inside a shoe.

He told me he's been doing this twenty years and he didn't learn this in a classroom, he learned it watching people like me come back for a fourth and fifth visit. And that once he understood what was actually happening in there, he started sending patients to this instead of to the next injection.

He said the straps hold the arch so the tissue stops getting torn open with every step you take. And the compression drives blood down into a fascia that has been starved for months and can finally rebuild.

He said this is the only thing he's found that goes after both halves of that cycle at once.

I'll be honest, I still didn't believe it. I have a drawer at home full of things that didn't work.

I put it on that night the way you eat a salad you don't want.

It goes on like a sock. You pull the straps snug across the arch and you feel them take hold, like a hand cupping the bottom of your foot from underneath.

And I stood up. And I put my weight down wrong, the way you do when you're not thinking, and I braced for the thing that always happens.

It didn't happen. The pain wasn’t gone but it wasn’t unbearable, interrupting or the kind that has you reaching for a railing. 

That was the whole event. Nothing shot up through my heel. I stood in my kitchen at ten at night and put my weight on that foot again on purpose, just to check.

Two days later I walked to the bathroom in the morning without doing the thing I do, where I hold the doorframe and lower my heel down in stages.

I just walked.

I said "huh" out loud, to nobody.

Three weeks in, I made dinner and stood the entire time.

And then came the day I found out it was real.

My sleeve was in the wash. I had the whole day at home ahead of me and nothing to put on, and I remember thinking, fine. It's one day. I'm not going anywhere.

By the afternoon I felt it. Not the old thing. Nothing close to the old thing. A dull ache coming up through the arch, low and steady, the way a bruise reminds you where it is.

I sat down at my own kitchen table and I understood two things at once.

This dull ache used to be my good day. That was the best my foot ever felt for two years, and I used to be grateful for it.

And I hadn't thought about my feet in three weeks.

Not once. Not standing at the sink, not on the stairs, not getting out of bed. Three weeks of my life where my feet were just my feet. Until the one day my sleeve was in the wash

I sat there with my hand over my mouth.

That's when I believed him.

I've been wearing them since April.

I went to the farmers market on a Saturday and I never once limped, I went to every stand I wanted to and not just the ones close to the parking lot. 

I did the whole grocery store, both sides, and I was pushing the cart. Pushing it. I got to the car and realized I hadn't leaned on a single thing, and I sat in the driver's seat and cried, which I'm not going to apologize for.

And a month ago I got up in the night for a glass of water, and I was halfway down the hall before I understood what I was doing.

I was barefoot.

Standing in my own hallway in the dark on my own two bare feet.

Two years. And I didn't even notice I was doing it.

That's the thing I would have paid anything for. Not "less pain." I wanted to stop thinking about my feet. I wanted my house back.

They're called Koprez Foot Sleeves.

If you've had this longer than a few months, hear the one part that matters. What's wrong with your foot now is that it’s never getting the chance to heal. The stretching and the icing and the inserts and the splint are not failing because you're doing them wrong. They're failing because they're aimed at the alarm bell. And that fascia is tearing open every morning before you've had your coffee and it is not being allowed to finish a single repair.

Every month you stay on the list, that rope frays a little further.

There's a 30-day guarantee, so if you wear them and nothing changes, you say so and they make it right. No trial that quietly turns into a subscription. Nothing to mail overseas.

You wear them for a month and you find out.

Put them on and go stand in your kitchen.

That's all I'd ask you to do.

I won't call it a miracle. I'll say I wore shoes in my own living room for two years, and I don't anymore.

bodyText:
“I want to make babies with you.”
A giant black wolf stood before Talia & transformed into Damon.
Talia shook her head. “No you can’t, You are an alpha”
“I’m just a slave”
“You are my mate.”
He saw the bruises on her neck and froze.
“Who touched the mother of my children?”
Talia’s eyes filled with tears.
“If I tell you, they’ll kill me.”
Damon pulled her into his arms.
“Not if I kill them first.”
“Tell me their name”
Before she could answer, The dream melts.

Damon wakes up, breath uneven, his body covered in sweat.
 
It always ends there. But night after night, the same girl returned. With the same wounds, fear, and the same desperate plea for help.
 
Please help me. Alpha Damon had never bowed to beauty or cared for desire. The most feared alpha in the realm stopped sleeping.
 
Stopped eating. Her screams followed him even after waking. At first, Damon believed the dreams were a curse.
 
Until one day, he was patrolling the woods and chanced upon a seer. Her white eyes locking onto him like she had been waiting. She told him the girl in his dreams was real.
 
Faded to be his mate and that she was suffering. Damon froze. For the first time in months, his heartbeat stumbled.
 
Who is she? Your fated mate. The words hit him like a blade to the chest. Damon had never cared for the idea of mates.
 
Never wanted one. Yet the girl haunted him more than war ever had. Tell me where she is.
 
You will recognize her by her violet glowing eyes. Eyes that hold divinity. Then, she vanished.
 
From that moment, Damon searched. He crossed territories. Questioned alphas.
 
Raided underground auctions believing she may have been sold. Followed every rumor about imprisoned omegas. Searched villages, yet found nothing.
 
Until he was summoned to the Red Moon Pack for an alliance marriage with Marcy, the daughter of Alpha Edward. Damon accepted because the moment he heard Red Moon Pack, his wolf stirred inside him. But the moment he entered the Grand Hall of the Red Moon Pack, everything changed.
 
The faint freezer scent lingered in the Grand Halls of the Red Moon Pack. But before he could isolate it, the scent vanished. Something felt wrong.
 
His wolf paced restlessly beneath his skin from the moment he entered the territory. His wolf stirred violently. Find her.
 
The Grand Hall of Red Moon overflowed with gold, silk, and false smiles. Marcy greeted him proudly beside her parents, draped in jewels like she was already Luna. Damon realized quickly the scent didn't belong to Marcy, but it belonged to someone in the pack, and he would have to play along and show interest in Marcy in order to get closer to his mate.
 
At that moment, Luna Layla, Marcy's mother, stepped in, her presence commanding the room. Alpha Damon. Your room is ready.
 
Please rest. Damon gave a brief nod, and walked away. But in the kitchen, a very different storm raged.
 
Marcy's jeweled hand cracked sharply against my face. Pfft, she hissed. Can't you handle a simple job of serving? Her pride wounded, her control slipping.
 
Blood spilled from my mouth and pooled onto the kitchen floor. Clean it up. Do you have any idea how disgusting your filthy face would look to Alpha Damon? Don't you dare ruin the alliance.
 
Stay out of sight. Stay invisible. And remember, one wrong move and you'll pay for it.
 
The princess had always been cruel, but this time, it was her wounded pride that burned hottest. I scrubbed the floor, bruises blooming across my knees, mirroring those already carved into my body. I was spared this time, only because Marcy was in a hurry to attend Alpha Damon.
 
But the relief was brief, fragile, because I knew what came next. Our next meeting already haunted me, fear curling tight in my chest. I had no way of knowing my fate was about to change, no way of knowing that Alpha Damon, the most powerful pack leader in the realm, had caught my scent.
 
They all sat down in the dining hall, its gaudy opulence a reflection of Red Moon's inflated ego. Marcy arrived fashionably late, every detail of her appearance sharpened like a blade. Shimmering blonde hair, a sculpted figure.
 
She was the type of girl who got what she wanted. Her friend Nora wasn't as restrained. She eyed Damon with hunger, her gaze sliding over him like a caress.
 
The rumors had reached her ears, about his appetite, his stamina, his size. She didn't care that Marcy was supposed to win the Alpha's hand, Nora wanted a taste for herself. Marcy's mother, Luna Layla, noticed the heat in Nora's stare, and the flicker of fury in her daughter's eyes.
 
Marcy, Layla said too sweetly, Why don't you show Alpha Damon to his room so you two can… talk? While the Red Moon pack celebrated Damon's arrival, elsewhere in the kitchens, Talia worked until the sweat stung her eyes. All she could dream of was the scraps she might scavenge when the feast was over. The other Omegas had different plans for her.
 
Anna, their cruel ringleader, stepped into Talia's path, towering over her. Listen up, slave! The other Omegas giggled behind her like hyenas. Anna's lips twisted into a cruel smirk.
 
You're going to deliver towels to Alpha Damon's room. Talia froze. Right now? But what if he's inside? Anna raised her hand, ready to strike.
 
Are you questioning me? Talia flinched, her heart pounding. Without her wolf, she was defenseless against the bullies. Without another word, she took the towels and hurried off, every step dragging her closer to the Alpha's quarters, and whatever fate awaited her behind that door.
 
When Talia entered the room, she froze. Damon was in his room, but he wasn't alone. There was Marcy, on her knees, between Damon's legs.
 
Marcy whipped around, her eyes blazing with fury as they locked onto Talia's. The insolence, a jolt of fear shot up Talia's spine. Retribution would be certain.
 
Damon's eyes snapped to Talia. Stop! He barked. But Talia was gone, bolting from the room, too terrified to look back.
 
What Talia didn't know, what she couldn't have known, is that in that moment, Damon's world had shifted. Her scent, it hit his veins like a spark of kindling, igniting something primal within him. Could it be? His inner wolf howled the truth within him again and again.
 
She, a lowly Omega, a serving girl without a friend, was his fated mate. Ignoring the mocking laughter of Anna and the others, Talia ran until she reached the attic, shoving the cabinet against the door before collapsing in the corner, struggling to quiet her frantic breathing. Is this it? Is this the day I die? Back in Damon's room, Marcy landed clumsily on her backside as Damon shoved her away, his expression thunderous and unreadable.
 
Who was that girl, he demanded, hastily buttoning his pants. Marcy knew exactly who she was. Talia, that wolfless bitch.
 
How dare she step into an alpha's chambers uninvited? And worse. If word got out that Marcy had been pleasuring Damon before he'd even proposed, she'd be humiliated. A laughingstock.
 
Her reputation would be in shreds. Marcy's jaw clenched with fury. She should have done more than just beat the girl this morning.
 
But Damon didn't notice Marcy's simmering rage. He was too distracted, his mind replaying the moment when she walked in. How that intoxicating scent, freesia and citrus, had struck him.
 
How his wolf had howled, wild and urgent. All he could think about was pulling her into his arms. Mate.
 
His wolf howled in confirmation. He had never expected to hear that word. Never wanted to.
 
And yet, the moment Talia entered the room, something inside him had shifted. Changed. His wolf growled inside him.
 
Find her! Damon clenched his jaw. Find her, he ordered. Now! Marcy hesitated.
 
She was confused. Why would an alpha give a shit about a slave? Damon's alpha energy radiated off of her, making her lower her head. Yes, alpha Damon.
 
But Marcy already knew. She'd be doing much more than just finding her. Meanwhile, Damon paced.
 
Running his tongue over his teeth. Irritated beyond reason. His body still ached with unfinished release.
 
But the thought of Marcy's coconut scent made him recoil. It wasn't her scent he wanted. It wasn't her body against his that he needed.
 
It was her. Talia. The girl with the smart doe eyes and copper-colored hair.
 
Damon prowled through the packhouse, inhaling deeply. Nothing. No trace of her scent.
 
His wolf snarled. Find her! If she was really my mate, why did she run? Why didn't she feel it too? You had another woman on her knees in front of you. His wolf sneered.

My name is Damon. He put on his best non-intimidating smile but she saw it like a beast showing teeth before devouring its prey. What's your name? Damon asked.
 
Talia's eyes darted to the door and then went back to him. Please, leave, she said in a shaky voice and his heart ached. He finally found her and there was no way he would leave just like that.
 
Damon was not sure what to do. Why was she so scared? Why was she chasing him away? I won't hurt you, he assured her. I'm here only to talk.
 
Say what you have to and leave, Talia said and gestured toward the door, her hand moving enough for the sleeve to hitch higher and expose her swollen wrist. Damon grabbed her hand and pulled it toward him. Delightful sparks formed upon contact, catching him by surprise.
 
The sensation was stronger than he remembered and he inhaled a shaky breath. He focused mightily on inspecting her injury. What happened? Don't tell me that you fell again, his expression darkened.
 
Is it Marcy? I will teach her a lesson. Talia panicked. Please, don't.
 
If you say anything, she will hit me more. Damon paused and observed her face which was now peeking up above her knees and he noticed a few more bruises compared to what he saw the previous night. Rage rippled through Damon at the thought of Talia getting hurt again and he was right here in this packhouse oblivious to her sufferings.
 
It happened on his watch. Damon was enraged and his wolf was as well. One fury amplified the other and Damon radiated inexplicable violence that was tangible.
 
At the sight of Talia shivering in fear, Damon forced his rage down. Settling scores will need to wait. Did Marcy hit you again? Damon asked Talia and the way she avoided him made him suspect another thing.
 
Was it because of me? Talia's eyes widened and that was enough for him to confirm how his intuition was right. He knew that Marcy was a white lotus. There was no way Marcy would forget that Talia saw her in a compromising position between Damon's legs and when Damon told Alpha Edward that Marcy was hitting Omega's Marcy probably knew that his comment was about Talia.
 
In a way, it was his fault that Talia got hurt. Twice. Another wave of rage swelled within him.
 
I will kill her. Don't, Talia pleaded. Can you just leave and pretend that you didn't see anything? Don't come here and everyone will leave me alone.
 
Damon's heart cracked. Even if everyone left her alone, how the hell was he supposed to do that? Didn't she know that he nearly went mad when he didn't know where she was? Without a word, Damon sat on the futon next to Talia and wrapped her in his arms, pulling her to lean on his chest. He let Damon's whole body hum in pleasure.
 
Delightful sparks overtook his senses and he was lost in a gaze. Talia froze. She was not used to physical contact of any kind.
 
It took her a moment to collect herself and start squirming to get out of his hold. Shh. Damon coaxed Talia to calm down, unwilling to let go of her.
 
He was not a hugger and he never cuddled with a woman, but this girl was different. He wanted to hold her and her resistance hurt. Can I hold you like this just for a minute? No, not a minute.
 
He wanted an hour, or at least until he became immune to these sparks that were making him crave devouring her. But if he said that aloud, she would definitely freak out. Talia stopped struggling, not because she agreed, but because she realized that he was too strong and her struggle made her injuries ache more.
 
Talia resigned herself to her fate. There was nothing she could do. Even if he wanted to harm her, she could only endure it.
 
She was too weak to fight for herself and if she shouted for help, no one would come. Damon smirked when he felt that Talia relaxed. He wished to move her to sit on his lap, but he feared that it might be too much.
 
With his arms around her, Talia appeared tiny and fragile and Damon was confident that he could carry her around with ease. Or maybe he should stuff her into his pocket so that she stays close to him all the time. Lost in the moment, Damon ran his fingers through Talia's coppery colored hair and inhaled the sweet citrusy scent of freesia and his world was at peace.
 
Damon closed his eyes, his enjoyment amplified by the sounds of yips and whimpers his wolf made in pleasure. Hey, Talia called after some time. When are you going to let me go? First, my name is Damon.
 
Not hey, Damon said with amusement in his voice. It had been a while since he heard someone speak to him this casually, but the lack of respect didn't bother him. And second, he wasn't thinking about it.
 
If it was up to him, never. To make his point clear, he tightened his hold on her, making sure he didn't crush her. Feeling that she was stiff again, he asked, am I hurting you? Talia was absolutely confused with this development.
 
Well, no, but... Then it's fine. Damon cut her off. He didn't want to hear any buts.
 
As much as Damon enjoyed this newfound feeling, he couldn't ignore Talia's injuries. The scent of dried blood disturbed the nasty scent of freesia, telling him that she was not okay. Damon took Talia's hand in his and observed a cut that was on top of a nasty bruise.
 
It was scabbing, but it still looked fresh. Mate's healing is slow because she doesn't have a wolf, Damon's wolf explained. Damon raised Talia's hand towards his lips and licked the cut.
 
Talia jerked her hand away, but Damon's reflexes were top-notch and he increased his grip, no one ever licked her before and this was a scary alpha. Would he eat her? Shush! Don't you know that our saliva has analeptic properties? I'm helping your wound heal. You should say thank you and not complain, Damon said and grimaced.
 
Considering her sweet scent, he assumed that she would taste sweet also, but why was it bitter? I applied an herbal paste so it didn't get infected, he touched her forehead, it was not warm but he still asked. Do you have a fever? No, Talia responded with urgency, she had no intention to admit she was flustered because a scary alpha came, hugged her and then he licked her hand. Damon guessed that she didn't see a doctor, it was obvious that she didn't get proper first aid.
 
Did you make the medicinal paste yourself? Talia confirmed with a nod. He was about to lick her hand again and paused. Is it poisonous? Talia was not sure if she should laugh or cry.
 
You should ask that before you put things into your mouth. I was treating your wound and I didn't see that there was medicine. He grumbled and then he licked her again.
 
Can you stop doing that? Talia protested. His coarse tongue touching her skin made her feel funny. Damon looked at Talia like he had no idea what she was talking about and then he licked her again.
 
Talia exhaled helplessly while wondering what game Damon was playing. He was an important guest, an alpha, yet instead of mingling with the elite of the red moon pack, he was huddled in the corner of the attic, holding her close to him and licking her hand. It didn't make sense no matter how she thought about it.
 
Is this the part where Marcy barged in and they all started laughing at her? Actually, if they only laughed that would be good. Maybe Damon would join Marcy and the two of them would give her another beating. Talia was anxious and she wanted this charade to be over.
 
When are you leaving? Damon was not sure if she asked him about leaving the attic or the red moon pack. In either case, his answer would be the same. Why are you eager to chase me away? Because this is where I stay.
 
You are in a fancy bedroom with Alpha and Luna and your future wife. My future wife? Damon asked in confusion like he heard about it for the first time. Princess Marcy told me that you would get married when she came here and she understood.
 
She will not be my wife in this lifetime or in any next one. Damon said grimly. Talia shook her head.
 
Maybe you should tell that to her and not to me. Your relationship with her is not my business. Can you please leave? Damon was lost in her big, honey-colored eyes that looked at him pleadingly and he wondered if he could leave.
 
Could he? Yes, but only in one case. Come with me. She asked him to leave the attic before anyone can see them in this inexplicable situation.
 
Yet he wants her to join him? What? Where? I am the Alpha of the Dark Howlers Pack. Come with me to my pack. Talia's brain paused.
 
She thought that Damon had invited her to his room to clean up or maybe to make fun of her. But now it seemed he was asking her to leave the Red Moon Pack with him. Why? I will get you clothes that fit and you can eat anytime you want and as much as you want.
 
For every scratch and bruise there will be a pack doctor to take care of you and if anyone gives you a hard time I will deal with them. No one will bully you in my pack. Our pack, his wolf added eagerly.
 
Unfortunately, only Damon heard him. Talia blinked. Now she was not wondering if her ears were tricking her and if this last beating messed with her brain or maybe something was wrong with him.
 
Maybe he was talking gibberish. There were some herbs that could make people say things they didn't mean or did he confuse her with Princess Marcy? It's not that Talia didn't think about leaving the Red Moon Pack. Every time Anna and her henchmen bullied Talia Talia thought about escaping but she didn't know where to go.
 
And here was an Alpha offering her a new home with all the luxury she ever dreamed of. Assuming that this was real and both of them were sane. Talia wondered if this was a prank containing this whole conversation or maybe she was sleeping and the Cinderella story mixed with her dreams because Damon definitely looked like a prince.
 
A handsome prince that smelled of the forest and dark chocolate. Will you come with me? Damon asked when his patience cracked. Why do you want me to come? Because... The words got stuck in his throat.
 
Could he tell her she was his mate and that when he sees her harmed his soul aches? No, that would only freak her out. Getting away from her was practically impossible. If she doesn't come willingly he would kidnap her or maybe move in with her into this attic.
 
Ah, he sounded like a creep to himself. Damon was exasperated. All this would be simpler if she could feel the bond and the delicious sparks that make him feel alive.
 
Because, he repeated I feel responsible. You got hurt because of me and it's not right. Let me help you, it will make me feel better.
 
This was the truth Do you think every girl who gets hurt back to your pack? Not really, but he is not the guy who would look away from injustice. However, he couldn't tell Talia that she was special either. When you come to the Dark Howlers pack you will see for yourself that we accept everyone who comes seeking help without bad intentions.
 
I promise that if you don't like it in the Dark Howlers pack I will help you resettle at the location of your choice. With his index finger his silent promise had an additional clause how he would make sure she was treated well and she never wanted to leave. Talia bit the inside of her cheek while considering her options.
 
Juan was staying at the Red Moon pack Anna's bullying was escalating and Marcy started picking on her also. Yesterday Marcy came to the attic and Talia got a beating for something she didn't do. The second option was to go to the Dark Howlers pack.
 
Alpha Damon said that in his pack people were accepted. Probably not. Of course there was also the third option for Talia to leave on her own somewhere but that option was scary and uncertain and it will exist even if she goes with Alpha Damon.
 
Damon saw that Talia was considering it and he spoke with urgency before she could decline his offer. Grab your things. You only need to say that you reject the Red Moon pack and Edward Redmayne as your Alpha and the mind link will break.
 
With that you are free to go and they can't find you. I love the mind link. Alpha Edward's father brought me here as a child and I never went through the ceremony.
 
Good. Damon exclaimed louder than intended. She doesn't belong anywhere and he was more than happy to give her a home.
 
With him. Get your things. Just like that.
 
Damon nodded. Just like that. Talia paused and decided to ask the question that was bothering her from the moment he came to the attic.
 
Her body separated from hers. He extended his hand toward Talia palm up. Let me prove it to you.
 
Now that Damon has found his fated mate how will he keep her safe? And what will Talia choose? Will she trust him? Stay a slave at the Red Moon estate? Will she attempt to escape from all of them? What will happen when Edward and Marcy discover Damon has found Talia?
