bodyText:
What the heck?

Able Monroe's trowel bit deep into the red desert and hit something with a clank.

It wasn't no darn space rock, and that's for sure.

"Ach!" the man winced as the shock of the impact ran up his arm. Whatever was down there was as solid as iron. He leaned in, peering into the gravel and dusty soil as the hot desert sun above battered mercilessly down on everything.

There was a glimmer of blue through the gravel. Silver-blue, like metal.

Metal? Old car bonnet? Water can?

But he was a good two meters below the surface. Someone would have gone to an awful lot of effort to bury something this deep, and this challenging a position.

"There shouldn't be anything much down at this level," the thirty-six year old prospector muttered out of the corner of his mouth. And if there was any man who should know, then it should be a man like Able Monroe.

He'd been all over the Red Rock formation, ever since he was old enough to spend a night on the prairies by himself. Added to his childhood camping under the stars was a degree in geology he'd earned from Nevada State, and so Able Monroe was fairly confident in saying he knew what should be out here.

Like space rocks, he considered. The fallen meteorites that Able made his living hunting, and selling on to private buyers. A good bit of iron chondrite hopefully, or a peridot-infused pallasite if he was really lucky.

His battered excavation gloves scraped away at the orange and red dirt, and came into contact with something hard, and smooth...and big.

Able rubbed the sweat out of his eyes, wondering if the sun had gotten to him. He was certain he could see a faint tracery of designs across the metal surface. They looked like lines and curves, almost like where different parts of the metal plate joined together.

"But I couldn't even put a fingernail between these plates," Able whispered to no one but himself and the condors.

For the next hour and a half, Able forgot all about the burning hot sun and the death cries of the circling birds far above. He dug out the scree, hauling it in buckets to the side of the dried up basin before transferring to one of the thick excavation brushes in his kit.

By the time that his back started to ache and his legs were starting to cramp, he had uncovered a four by four meter surface of curving metal, tapering to a thick edge on one side, and it was looking like the object only got bigger the further into the basin he could dig.

For the first time this morning, Able noticed his racing heartbeat, the excitement that shivered through his aching limbs.

This find was big. Really big.

And it shouldn't be here at all.

He sat back on the surface itself, finding that even despite the blazing hot sun, the silver-blue metal with its strange whorls and lines was still strangely cool to the touch, like it wouldn't allow the sun's waves to penetrate it.

He fumbled for his cell phone, dropped it, then picked it up again. He half dialed a number, then the man in the light checkered shirt and blue jeans jammed the phone back in his shirt pocket, and opted for the larger, CB mobile radio he had in his side holster instead. The thing was a brick, but it was worth it when he was out in the field.

There was one frequency Able knew this CB would reach, which only one other person kept a matching unit attuned to.

"Carl? Carl, please tell me you're getting this. It's me. I'm at the site I told you about. And I need you to get out here right now, with as much kit as you can lay your hands on," Able clicked off to send, to hear a crackle of static on the other end.

His eyes slid down to the cool silver-blue metal plates underneath him. The metal that shouldn't be there.

He added, "and keep your mouth shut about it. Don't tell anyone. Able out."

Able Monroe sat back against the red rock of the Nevada deserts, and tried to calm down.

Just what was a giant piece of curved metal doing embedded several feet down in the Nevada rock?

Able Monroe hadn't always been the kind of guy to do things on the sly, or to be so secretive about what he spent his days doing, but he guessed he had learned the hard way about that.

You couldn't trust everyone all the time, and some people none of the time.

That had been particularly true of his last partner, a two-bit worm of a man named Jamie Aviemore, who apparently, the rest of the meteor-hunting community thought was a geologist's version of Tom Cruise.

Right now, as he stood in the shadowed lee of the Red Rock formation and saw the puff of automobile dust approaching him over the location, Able did his best to try not to think about his old partner.

He failed.

Just being out in the field again brought back the same old bitter memories, the same way that the work awakened the ache in his shoulder, and reminded him he was not exactly a spring chicken any more.

Well, I'm not exactly middle aged, either! He thought. Thirty six was enough years to know just where he was going wrong in life, but not enough to tell him what he should do different...at least, that is what Able's late father had said about his thirties.

But his father was no more, passing a few years ago to a prolonged and thoroughly miserable illness, leaving Able with a mountain of debts and the need to work with 'wunderkinds' like Jamie Aviemore.

That was, until Jamie had goosed him, stealing Able's field reports and claiming that he had been the one to find a rare pallasite meteor.

Jamie had shot to fame, and a rather unwise decision involving a night at Callahan's Saloon, a bottle of cheap rye, a tub of paint and Jamie's Ford Pickup had left Able forever untouchable in the space-rock community.

"But all that is going to change now, isn't it?" Able stepped forward, smelling the dust of the desert, and feeling the wave of afternoon heat fall over him like a blanket.

Despite being burned by his ex-partner, there was still a couple of people that Able trusted, or more importantly, trusted him.

He raised his hand to wave, a grin splitting his stubble at the sight of his buddy Carl Jonson's modified Toyota pick-up. It was one of the flat-bed editions, but Carl had built out a large container box on the back, and reinforced the bed so it could handle a small hydraulic winch system. Carl was a mechanic, so he knew his stuff. He was also Able's oldest friend.

"Hey! You wanna not stand there grinning like a darn crazy person, will-ya..?" Carl swerved the white Toyota truck in a sharp arc, sending up a spray of red dust and making something rattle and hiss as it scuttled across the sands.

"You're scaring my wife, man," Carl laughed as he rolled down the window and beamed at him.

Carl was a mountain of a man, all of one-ninety, maybe two hundred pounds and most of it muscle. He'd played basketball at high school but although he had the reach he didn't like the speed, but then he took up wrestling and competed at state level...Able was sure he would have gone all the way, but Carl said he couldn't handle the leotards.

"Speak for yourself, hot-shot," snapped a second voice from the truck, as Yates, Yaz, or Yazmin Jonson to her students, popped the door and jumped down to the desert sand, to not look scared or phased at all.

They were both used to getting wild calls in the middle of the weekend from Able, convinced he had found something big out in the desert.

"What is it this time, champ?" Yates shot him a sharp look.

"I don't know for sure. Which is why I need you," Able greeted her with a hug, until Carl got out, complaining about missing the action and managed to lift them both of their feet for a second before he collapsed into laughter.

"Now what is this all about, man? You think I like having this thing hissing in my ear all day?" he waved the matching CB mobile radio he held in one hand.

Able checked the horizon. They still had a few hours of light left. Maybe it was enough to get an eye on what was really going on back there.

What that thing IS, he thought, as a shiver ran up his spine.

It could be anything, right?

Anything that was buried almost in the bedrock. And clearly constructed from some high-grade materials he'd never seen before.

"Thanks for keeping the radio on this time. Trust me, you're not going to want to miss this," Able wiped the sweat out of his eyes.

For a moment he looked at his two friends, and he almost felt sorry for them.

They had no idea what they were about to wander into. Maybe the find of their lives. The find that would make them all rich?

But then again, he had no idea what he was getting into either, not really.

"Grab your stuff, it's on the other side of Red Rocks," Able said. "And you're going to want to set up camp. We won't be going anywhere tonight."

"Wonderful," Yates groaned, tying up her mounds of dark, frizzy hair with a groan, as Able led them to the small fissure in the rocks that led to the inside of the basin.

"Well, you know I keep one eye on all news I can of potential meteor impacts," Able said as he waited at the top of the rocks for Carl and Yates to clamber up to the path.

Red Rock was well named, a buttress of bedrock and splintered boulders that stuck out of the desert, surrounded of thin, scratchy thorn bushes.

"I don't remember hearing anything?" Yates looked up with a frown.

Able knew that Yates, of any of them, would know exactly what he was looking at. He had first met her at Nevada State where she was a year ahead of him on the Geological Earth Sciences course. She'd been his route in to the career, in all honesty. And when he had introduced her to his high school friend of Carl, the pair had become instant sweethearts.

Yates now lectured at the same university where they had met, and somehow her reputation survived knowing the willful, wild, and 'dangerous' Able Monroe.

"There hasn't been any activity out here for years. But I was going over old survey reports of the area, and one of the early geophysics reports said that there was a spike in unusual rock density right here," Able said. "The signals are consistent with metals. Probably conductive materials…"

Yates nodded. "So you're thinking iron or stony-iron meteorite. A field no one has picked up on?"

Able grinned excitedly. "Exactly. I knew I needed you here. Thought maybe it was even a splash site, I mean, look at how Red Rocks form a natural basin?" He pointed at the semi-circle of buttresses, spearing several times larger than any of them above the desert floor.

"Could be a vein of normal mineral iron. Go down deep enough, and these rocks are full of it," Yates reached the path, turning to give her sweating husband a hand up.

Able thought of the shining, cool metal surface.

"Trust me, this isn't any vein of iron," Able said with absolute certainty. It wasn't even the splash site of a regular impact crater either, now he came to think about it.

They have no idea, he thought, his breath catching in his throat.

"Uh-huh. I think I see..." Yates murmured a little quieter behind him. "You're looking for a way back, aren't you?"

Able heard the tone in her words and it hurt like she had thrown daggers into his back.

It wasn't my fault my partner stiffed me! Or that I lost my temper! Able shook his head. In just a few more paces none of this would matter. Not what anyone thought of him. Not whether people thought he was too reckless to deal with.

He rounded the boulders to where it showed the side of the basin, and the collapsed side where he had dug his trench.

And there she was.

A large, curving edge of silver-blue. The last rays of the light could picked out the metal segments like plates but with no rivets visible, and the strange, whorled patterns.

"I get is, Able, you want your old life back. Maybe I could even make some inquiries at the university for you, maybe there's some student-aide work…" Yates was saying as she joined him overlooking the pit.

"Oh." Yates fell instantly silent.

"Sheesh, what is it guys, you got a Tyrannosaur skull down there or something?" Carl lumbered up beside them.

And then he fell silent for a moment, too.

"Riiight," the big man said. "What exactly am I looking at here, and exactly how much trouble are we about to get into, because to me that looks like a great big hunk of armored plate."

"Armored plate?" Able frowned, looking at him.

Of course, Able thought. Carl had been in the services before going full-time mechanic. That was where he earned his engineering chops, and why Able knew he could count on him. He didn't think there was a mechanical anything he couldn't drop in front of Carl and his buddy not be able to figure it out.

"Military for sure. That's gotta be some kind of graphene coating, right? Over a steel alloy?" Carl pointed out.

"Military." Able repeated.

Oh great. Had he just uncovered some military test thingie? Was it out here keeping watch on the skies? Or something that had crashed?

Was it radioactive!?

"You brought the Geiger counters I asked for?" Able said, leading the scramble down to the dig, as his heart plummeted.

If the thing was U. S. Military, then they'd be lucky if they could just back-fill it and hightail out of there. It was much more likely they would get prosecuted for messing with Federal Secrets.

"Sure thing boss, but I'm telling you, we're going to get men with very shiny shoes and black sunglasses swarming us if we mess with that thing," Carl said, heaving the large hiking pack on his shoulder to the ground, and taking out the handheld Geiger counter to start taking readings.

Able had reached the edge of the excavation pit, and looked down at his find.

It was clearly no meteorite. So no private museum or collector would be interested in buying it.

Carl called out that the readings were fine, and already Able was figuring where they would erect the floodlights and the tent.

"At least it's not radioactive," he thought as he stripped his glove and reached down to press a hand against the smooth surface. As if touch alone would tell him what this thing was.

Strange… From this angle it even looked like the edge was some kind of a grill, but one choked up with rock dust.

"Uh, Able?" Yates worried voice called down to him.

"Yup?" Able looked up to see Yates and Carl looking back between the rocky outcrops, back towards the dying sunlight.

"We got dust on the horizon. Looks to be three SUV's, incoming," Carl announced. He always slipped into military-speak when he was on a job.

Able froze where he was. "SUV's? Got insignia?"

Thoughts of Carl's men with shiny shoes and sunglasses filled Able's mind. Was it the spooks? Had his buddy been right and they'd discovered something they really shouldn't have?

Maybe this really was private land. Maybe this was one of those government test facilities that they had plausible deniability over. Some secret listening post or…

"I got eyes on it. Yellow and black. Looks like a...shield?" Carl squinted as he cupped his hands around his eyes.

"Yellow and black shield?"

Able's panic turned in a flash to a feeling of anger. He knew that insignia. He knew that logo only too well...he'd poured paint all over it just last year.

"That's Aviemore Excavations. Who told Jamie about this!? How did he get wind I was out here!" Able snapped. Pushing himself up from his crouch and turning to snarl at the fading light and approaching cars.

Jamie Aviemore. The little thief himself, come to steal what wasn't his again, no doubt…

"Not me, boss!" Carl said. "Maybe that little squirt has been listening into your radio chatter. I told you to get a decent satellite phone for out here."

"I'll talk to him. He still respects the university, at least. And there is clear public domain access rights here-" Yates sighed as she laid a restraining hand on her husbands massive shoulder, and looked back to where Able was standing on the craft.

"Uh, Able?" Yates suddenly sounded alarmed. Very alarmed, in fact.

"Don't worry, I haven't got any paint this time around. Or petrol." Able grumbled.

But Yazmin didn't appear to be angry about that. Her eyes were wide with surprise as she stared past him.

"Able! What in heavens name did you do?" she gasped.

"What? You know what I did. I threw paint on his car," Able muttered. "But that was a different me. I'm much calmer now…"

"To the find, you idiot!" Yates thrust a hand, pointing down to his feet. "Look!"

Able looked down, to see a green imprint of his hand, vivid against the silver-blue metal.

No...inside the silver-blue metal.

He snatched his hand back, just in time to see the glow fade into the metal as if it had never been there.

But in its place, faint green lines were running out from where the mark had been, racing along the whorls and joining seal marks between the plates.

Able felt something shift underfoot, and heard a deep, creaking groan like the very bones of the earth were cracking.

"What's happening?" Able stumbled as the metal surface shook once again.

Small rivers of sand and dirt were running down the side of the pit walls, puddling on the strange metal and dancing, as the metal itself...vibrated.

"I don't know, Able. But you did something to it," Carl said. The big man was already moving, scrabbling over the boulders towards him. "It must be some sort of alarm system. You must have activated it…"

"I activated what!?" Able shouted.

He reached for the edge of the excavated pit walls, just as there was an audible click, and the shaking metal instantly ceased, and Able fell into blackness.

"Hey!"

A dark oval shape had opened up out of nowhere, right under where Able had been standing.

Or not standing any more, as he fell into the dark, his arms flailing for a wild moment before he thumped onto something painful and hard.

"Abe!" He heard Carl and Yates shouting, and heard their scrabbling towards him as Able shook his head, and pushed himself up into a crouch.

The fall hadn't been deep. No more than seven or eight feet, actually, but he could tell that the surface beneath him was hard, grill-work metal.

Ouch. They didn't think to have crash-pads or something in this joint?

Able leaned back, peering through the dusty light to see he was in some kind of metal antechamber, a wide oval of the same blue-black metals with a bulkhead door at his back, and a large, open archway right in front of him.

"You hurt down there, buddy? Don't move, let me get a rope…" Carl's shadow eclipsed the light overhead, but Able was already entranced by the space around him.

The structure was mostly made of metal, and had a vague industrial look to it. He could see girders and panels, metal grills with the dark gleam of pipework behind them.

And then there was the electric green light again.

As Able watched, he saw the bottom of the walls around him start to glow with a faint green strip light, as the light raced to the open archway, as if inviting him forwards.

Click.

There was the small, grating sound of metal as a small panel beside the arch flashed with the same green light, and popped open.

It was a tiny containment box, and something that had been wedged inside of it spooled out, and fell with a clank to the metal floor below.

"You hurt, Able? Jamie will have a satellite phone won't he? I'll get him to call in 911…" Yates shouted down. There was the softer thump as a coil of thick nylon climbing rope loosed from the still open hatch behind him.

"Well what do you know, what's this?" Able didn't hear them as he moved over to reach toward the strange item that had popped out of the wall, and fallen onto the ground.

It was a bulky object, attached to a fine steel chain. He saw a gleam of something like gemstone in its center. Above his head, the green indicator light beside the containment box faded back into blackness, like it's job had been done.

It was an amulet by the looks of it, made of shining black metals. A large metal ring held smaller, more intricate disks inside of it, and in its very center was held a shard of gleaming green crystal.

"Holy Smokes, Boss. Is that emerald?" Carl thumped to the floor behind him and looked over his shoulder. "That thing has got to be worth thousands..."

"Tens of thousands," Able corrected. "If the crystal's genuine, that is."

He held it up before Carl's torch, seeing that the surface of the black metal had a fine tracery of engraves lines and curls and dots. It almost looked like a language, but it was no language he had ever seen before. The emerald...or emerald-like rock, anyway, had a faint, glassy surface that shone oddly in the light.

"You know what, I don't think this place is military," Carl was saying, as Able's hands holding the amulet tingled with expectation.

Whatever else came out of this dig, maybe this weird gemstone alone would put him in the history books.

"A military place wouldn't be so inviting," Carl murmured behind him. He should know, Able thought.

"And it would have way more gun turrets," Yates added, as she jumped down into the small antechamber beside them. "What's that through there?"

She shined her light through the arch, for Able to catch a reflection like a vast pane of glass, and a narrow, wedge-shaped room...

"Well, I'm glad no one has tried to shoot us yet," Able said, still holding the amulet up before his eyes. "Maybe this is some kind of high-tech emergency bunker, right? Some billionaire built it and forgot about it," he said, as, without fully understanding why, he slipped the strange palm-sized amulet over his neck.

And instantly, he felt a tingle of something like static electricity against his skin, but it wasn't painful at all.

What the..?

And it was at that exact moment, when the green light around the archway ahead flashed once more as if warning them of something...and a deep mechanical vibration tore through the nerd bunker.

At the same time, the perfect oval opening above that they had just dropped through closed with a sudden snap, as if the doorway had never been there at all.

bodyText:
My daughter-in-law put me on the shuttle bus in Pompeii while the family walked. She told the group it was for my knees. The knees weren't the problem.

I'm fifty-eight. My husband Robert died seven years ago.

My son David got married last year to a woman named Lauren. Lauren is thirty-four and runs the events team at a hotel group in Charlotte. She is, by every measurable standard, a wonderful person. Warm, competent, the kind of woman who remembers your birthday and your mother's birthday and the name of your hairdresser.

Lauren had been planning the Italy trip for ten months. Eight days. Rome, Florence, the Amalfi coast, Pompeii. Twelve of us — David and Lauren, Lauren's parents, her sister and brother-in-law, the kids, and me.

She'd built a spreadsheet. Color-coded. Each day mapped with timing, transport, meal reservations, optional excursions. She'd cc'd everyone.

At the bottom of the spreadsheet was a tab called Mom.

The note said: Mom — Pompeii: shuttle bus from parking lot to amphitheater area. Stairs and hills difficult. Will meet group for lunch at the café near the entrance.

Stairs and ruins difficult.

I read that twice.

She hadn't asked me. I'd told her, eighteen months ago at the Thanksgiving table, that I was nervous about doing the long walking days in Italy because of my knees — Robert had been the one who used to plan rest stops and pace the days and figure out the cobblestones for me, and I'd lost that. I said it as one comment in a longer conversation. She'd written it down.

She'd been writing things down for a year.

I didn't want a shuttle bus. I wanted to walk Pompeii with the kids. I wanted to figure it out.

I sat with the spreadsheet open at my kitchen island for the rest of the afternoon.

I called my sister Helen that night.

Helen is sixty. Two years ago she walked the Camino de Santiago. Five hundred miles across northern Spain. She'd lost twenty pounds doing it and come back tan and a little smug and obsessively interested in knees.

She's the only person in the family I let myself complain to.

I told her about the spreadsheet. The shuttle tab. The note. The thing I'd said eighteen months ago at the Thanksgiving table.

"Sarah. How are your knees."

"They're fine."

"Sarah."

"They're sixty-year-old knees. They ache by the end of a long day. They were not the reason I was nervous about Italy."

"What was."

I sat with that.

"I don't know. I think I just didn't know how to ask Robert to slow down anymore. And then he was gone. And I didn't know how to be the one who slowed down for myself."

"Right."

"So Lauren put me on a shuttle bus."

"Right."

She was quiet for a second.

"How many pairs of shoes were you planning to bring."

"For Italy. Three. Walking sandals for the cobblestones. A nicer pair for dinners. Some sneakers."

"Cancel all of them. One pair. The walking ones. You walk into that trip in one pair of shoes and you don't change them for eight days."

"Helen."

"I'm serious. The walking days are what you're afraid of. If the shoes are right, the walking days are not the problem. If the shoes are wrong, even the shuttle bus is the problem."

"What pair."

She sent me a link.

"This is what my whole Camino group switched to for the reunion walk next year. We did three weeks on stone in northern Spain and not one of us had knee pain in the evening. There's a knit version that looks like a normal slip-on — you could wear it to a museum and nobody would think that's a hiking shoe. The front is a lot wider than a normal sneaker. Your toes have room to spread when you push off — which is the whole reason your feet hurt after long days. They're being held together at the front."

"That's not what a podiatrist would tell me."

"It is what a podiatrist would tell you if he walked the Camino. Mine did. He sent me to these."

I looked at the link.

"And they're not orthopedic-looking."

"They're not. They're a lightweight slip-on. Breathable mesh. The kind of thing my mother would have called house shoes except they go anywhere."

She was quiet for a second.

"My group ordered together — they had something running, 50% off plus free shipping, so I grabbed the beige and the navy for the reunion. The beige sold out two days after we ordered. The colors sell out fast on these and once a color is gone it doesn't come back until next year, if at all."

I ordered the beige.

The box arrived four days later.

I opened it at the kitchen island. The shoes were lighter than I expected. The kind of light where you check the bottom of the box to make sure something hadn't been forgotten.

I put them on barefoot. Walked the length of the hallway and back.

The front of the shoe was not where my toes were. My toes had somewhere to go. I stood at the end of the hallway and spread them inside the shoe and felt them spread. The sole was completely flat — no tilt, no pitch forward. I felt level. Planted.

I had not been allowed to do that in any shoe I owned.

In the back of my closet, on the top shelf, was a small leather notebook.

Robert had bought it for me in 1998 on our first trip to Italy. We'd done Rome and Florence over ten days. He'd been forty-three. I'd been forty-two. He'd carried both our bags through Termini Station the day we arrived because mine wasn't going to fit through the turnstile, and he'd insisted.

I'd written sketches and notes in the notebook for the whole trip. The little café where we'd shared a pastry in Trastevere. The view from the dome of the Duomo. The night we'd walked back to the hotel along the river in Rome and I'd taken off my shoes and walked the last block barefoot because my knees were aching and Robert had not said anything, just slowed down to match my pace.

I'd kept the notebook on the top shelf for seven years. I had not opened it since the year he died.

I took it down. I held it. I did not open it. I put it in the inside zip pocket of my carry-on.

Before anything else.

The flight to Rome was overnight.

I landed at Fiumicino at 8 AM with one bag. Through customs in fifteen minutes.

Lauren and David and Lauren's family arrived an hour later on a connecting flight from Munich. They had eleven checked bags between them. I saw Lauren at the baggage claim through the window from where I was sitting at the café, sorting through luggage that had not all made the connection.

The first day in Rome was the Vatican.

Lauren had arranged a wheelchair for me at St. Peter's. Mom — wheelchair available at the entrance, request at the main desk, you don't need to do the lines.

I walked up to the main desk. I thanked the attendant. I told her I wouldn't be needing the wheelchair today.

I did the entire Vatican on my feet. Eleven thousand steps before lunch. The Sistine Chapel. The Pietà. The full route through the museums. The dome.

At the dome — the climb to the cupola, five hundred and fifty-one steps up a tight stone spiral staircase — Lauren's mother stopped halfway. Lauren stopped to be with her. David went the rest of the way up.

I went up too. I came back down. I didn't talk about it.

That night at dinner, Lauren said: "Mom, you've barely sat down all day. Are your knees okay."

"They're fine."

"You can take it easier tomorrow. Pompeii is the long one."

"I'm doing Pompeii."

She blinked.

"The shuttle is already booked, Mom."

"I'll cancel it in the morning."

She looked at David. David didn't say anything.

The next morning at the bus loop in Pompeii, the family was loading onto the walking-tour minibus. The shuttle that Lauren had booked for me was idling on the other side of the parking lot, two retirees from Wisconsin already inside.

I walked past it.

Lauren saw me at the gate of the ruins. She was holding her seven-year-old daughter Emma's hand.

"Mom. What are you doing."

"Walking Pompeii."

"The shuttle —"

"I cancelled it."

Emma looked up at me. "Are you walking with us, Grandma?"

"I'm walking with you, sweetie."

Lauren said nothing. She watched her daughter take my hand.

We walked four hours through the ruins. Emma and I. The whole grid of it — the Forum, the House of the Vettii, the amphitheater, the bath house. I lifted Emma to see over the wall at the amphitheater because she was too short.

At the lunch café, Lauren had reserved a table for the family. We arrived three minutes before everyone else. Lauren's mother was limping slightly. Lauren's brother-in-law was carrying his wife's sandals because the strap had broken on the cobblestones. Lauren was wearing a pair of brown leather sandals — pretty, expensive, the wrong shoe for the day — and her left heel was wrapped in a hotel napkin under the strap.

She looked at my feet.

"What are those."

I told her.

She didn't say anything else.

The next morning, the third day, Lauren's brother-in-law's wife stopped me at the breakfast buffet.

She was in her forties. She'd done her residency at Duke — Lauren had mentioned this once, in passing. I'd assumed she was a hospital doctor.

She said: "I'm a podiatrist."

I looked at her.

"I noticed your shoes yesterday at lunch. The way you were walking. I've been telling patients about these for eight months. Where did you order yours."

I told her. HF Stride. By Hike Footwear.

She nodded. "I bought a pair for my mother in May. Both knees had severe cartilage breakdown — two surgeons told her to prepare for replacement. These were the only shoes that let her walk without the rotational stress grinding her cartilage down. She cancelled the surgery four months later. They sold out of her size within a week of when I ordered."

She paused.

"I'd been wondering whether to recommend them on my practice's social. After watching you walk Pompeii yesterday, I think I'm going to."

She wrote down the name on a hotel notepad.

Florence. Day five. The hill up to Piazzale Michelangelo.

The path goes up four hundred stone steps from the river. It's a steady climb. Tourists do it for the view at sunset.

Lauren had arranged for the family to take a car up.

I walked it.

I walked the four hundred steps with Emma. Halfway up she got tired and I carried her on my hip for thirty steps and then she got off and we walked the rest hand in hand.

At the top, while we waited for the rest of the family to arrive by car, Emma sat on the wall with her legs swinging and watched the city go gold below us.

She said: "Grandma. Does your knee hurt?"

"A little."

"Mine does too. We did a lot today."

"We did."

She looked at my shoes.

"I want shoes like yours when I'm bigger."

Lauren came up the stairs from the parking lot a few minutes later, walking carefully because the heel of her sandal had come off completely on the ride up. She was carrying it in her hand.

She saw Emma on the wall. She saw me beside her.

She did not say anything.

The last night was on a rooftop in Rome. The family had a private dinner booked at a restaurant near the Pantheon. After dessert Lauren came out to where I was standing at the railing looking down at the lit-up dome of San Salvatore.

She stood next to me for a moment.

"Mom. About Pompeii."

"It's fine."

"It's not fine. I made a spreadsheet and I put you on a shuttle bus and I didn't ask you."

I didn't say anything.

"I thought I was being thoughtful."

"I know."

"And then I watched you walk for eight days."

I waited.

"The shoes, Mom. The ones the podiatrist asked about. Where did you get them. I need to know before we go home."

I looked at her.

"They're called HF Stride. By Hike Footwear. Helen ordered them when her Camino group switched."

"And they're still available."

"They do small drops. Helen's group had to move fast — a few sizes were already gone when I checked back this week. Once the stock is gone for the season, it doesn't come back for weeks"

She nodded slowly.

"I'd move sooner rather than later if there's one you want."

"Of course."

We stood at the railing for a while longer.

Then she said: "Emma told me she wants a pair like yours when she's bigger."

"I heard her."

Lauren laughed quietly.

"My daughter wants to be sixty-year-old you. I have to recalibrate everything."

I didn't say anything. I let her have that one.

Here's what I learned.

For seven years, since Robert died, I'd been waiting for someone to tell me what I could and couldn't do.

I hadn't realized I was waiting. I just thought I was being careful.

I thought Robert had been the one who knew. He'd handled the maps in Italy, the train tickets, the cobblestones, the slowing-down. After he was gone, I started believing that whoever I lived close to became the one who knew. My son. My daughter-in-law. The doctor at the annual visit who said some stiffness is normal at your age.

Lauren put me on a shuttle bus because she'd been listening for eighteen months. She wasn't being cruel. She was being careful, the way I'd taught everyone to be careful with me.

The shoes didn't change my knees.

They changed who got to decide what my knees could do.

If someone has been quietly redrawing your life around what they assume you can't —

If they've planned the shuttle bus and the wheelchair and the rest stop and the easier seat —

If you've started believing the long days are over —

Look at the shoe before you believe any of it.

Not because it solves everything. It doesn't. The stairs are still stairs. The dome of St. Peter's is still five hundred and fifty-one steps.

But because the moment you realize you've been getting on the shuttle bus on purpose — that's the moment your knees get a vote again.

Helen has the beige pair waiting in her closet for the Camino reunion next year. I'm bringing the navy — they're still running that sale where it’s 50% off plus free shipping, so I ordered a second pair for Emma's mother because she asked.

The beige was nearly gone the morning I ordered. A few sizes were already sold out when I checked back this week.

I'd move sooner rather than later if there's one you want.

I'm planning Greece next year. Emma wants to come.

Your move.
