I was diagnosed with cervicogenic headache at 34. I'm 46 now. Turns out I never had a neck-origin headache at all. I had something nobody screened me for, hiding in plain sight in the light sensitivity and nausea I had every time my "neck flared up."
For twelve years, I "managed" a condition I didn't actually have.

Twelve years of chiropractic adjustments. Weekly. Sometimes twice a week when I was in a bad round. I have had my neck manipulated approximately four hundred and eighty times.
Twelve years of physical therapy for cervical instability. Chin tucks. Prone Y-T-W exercises. Isometric neck strengthening. Deep-neck-flexor activation.
Twelve years of ergonomic setups. A standing desk. A monitor arm. A split keyboard. An expensive office chair. A car seat lumbar cushion. A driving neck pillow. A memory-foam pillow that cost $180 and was supposed to be "cervical-support optimized."
Twelve years of being handed a new modality — cervical traction, dry needling, cupping along the trapezius, radiofrequency ablation of the C2 medial branch, cervical facet injections, cervical epidural steroid injections — and told to "just give it time."
I did everything they asked.

I got a new mattress. Then a new pillow. Then another new pillow. Then a pillow that was specifically made for side sleepers. Then one specifically for people with cervical instability. My husband and I have five pillows in a closet from years of me trying to find the right one.
I gave up sleeping on my stomach in 2015. I gave up sleeping on my left side in 2018 because the pain radiated up to my temple when I did.
I got fitted for a soft cervical collar that I wore for six weeks in year seven when a particularly bad flare had me unable to turn my head.
I paid $1,400 out of pocket for a full cervical MRI in Boston, plus another $600 for a functional MRI that was supposed to show "dynamic instability." The scans showed mild degenerative changes at C5-C6 that my neurologist called "normal for your age" and could not explain my pain.
I saw a pain management doctor in Manhattan who charged $2,400 for a full cervical workup and put me through three rounds of cervical facet injections at $800 each. The first round gave me two weeks of relief. The second round gave me one week. The third round did nothing.
He recommended radiofrequency ablation next — burning the small nerves in the cervical joints to interrupt pain signaling. He warned me the effect would wear off in nine to twelve months and I would need to repeat it. He warned me the joints would eventually degenerate faster because of the repeated procedures. He said it was still my best option.
I said I would think about it.
I thought about it for two years.

I felt like I was crazy. The MRI showed nothing serious. The pain management doctor could not fix it. My chiropractor kept saying, "You're right on the edge, let me get in there." But every single day, my neck ached and my head throbbed and no amount of adjusting was making it stop.
By the time my alarm went off, my neck was already stiff. I could not turn my head to look at the clock without rotating my whole torso. I would spend the first ten minutes of every day doing the gentle stretches my PT had prescribed, then walk to the bathroom holding the base of my skull with one hand.
Getting through breakfast was a production. Chewing set off pain that traveled from the base of my skull up the back of my head to my right temple. Chewing hard bread made it worse. Chewing gum was out of the question.
By 10 a.m., if I had a morning of meetings, I would be doing what my husband called "the head-cradle." Sitting with my elbow on the desk and my hand supporting the base of my skull to take the pressure off.
By 2 p.m. the ache would migrate from the back of my neck up over the top of my scalp and settle behind my right eye. I would take an over-the-counter anti-inflammatory. I would put a warm compress on the back of my neck. I would try to push through.
By 4 p.m. I would be looking at the clock and calculating how much longer until I could go home and lie down flat.
And the math never stopped.

If I drive more than an hour, my neck will spasm halfway there and I will have to pull over. If I sit in a movie theater, the seat angle will hurt my neck within twenty minutes and I will not remember what I watched. If I look up at anything — a bookshelf, a menu board, my nephew's Little League game from the bleachers — I will pay for it for the next twenty-four hours.
I stopped saying yes to anything that involved sitting in an angled seat, driving distance, or looking up. My sister's beach house on Cape Cod, because the drive was three hours. My friend's wedding in Vermont, because it was four. My nephew's Little League tournament, because it was outdoors in the sun and involved looking up at the field.
I would be at a work dinner and my neck would spasm and I would have to reach up and press my hand against the base of my skull and pretend I was thinking. I got good at hiding it. My colleagues thought I was thoughtful. I was actually trying not to cry.
I also had what I called my "neck-flare headaches" about three or four times a month. Pressure behind my right eye. Sensitivity to light. Sometimes nausea. Usually within a day or two of a bad neck day. I would take another anti-inflammatory. Lie down in a dark room. Push through.
Nobody ever asked me about the light sensitivity in twelve years. I never thought to mention it. I had been told I had cervicogenic headache — pain from the cervical spine referring up into the head. The light sensitivity felt like a separate thing. Probably from the pain. Probably from being tense.
I looked fine on the outside. Inside my whole cervical spine was on fire and my head throbbed.

And every specialist just nodded. "That's cervicogenic. Keep the adjustments. Keep the exercises. Consider the ablation."
I tried acupuncture in year eight. I tried a $2,200 posture-correcting brace I wore under my clothes. I tried a cervical decompression device that lifted my head off my shoulders for twenty minutes a day. I tried a special water-pressure device you put in your bathtub that was supposed to give you a "clinical-grade cervical traction session."
Nothing worked.

I started to believe this was just my life now. That I would spend the rest of my life on the head-cradle at my desk and turning my whole body to look at things and skipping any event that involved a drive.
Then a woman I met in the waiting room of my chiropractor's office said something no cervicogenic-headache specialist ever had.
Her name is Yasmin. She is 51. She had been a Pilates studio owner for twenty years and had recently trained as a Migraine coach after her sister was diagnosed with chronic Migraine at 43. She was in the waiting room for her own neck adjustment. We started talking because we were both there for the third time that month.
She asked me a question I had never been asked.

"Rebecca. When your neck flares — do you notice anything with the light? Anything with your stomach?"
I said, without thinking about it, "Well, yes. Light bothers me on those days. And sometimes I get a bit nauseous. But that's just from the pain."
She nodded slowly.
"Do you also get pressure behind your right eye when it's really bad?"
"Yes. Behind the right eye. That's from where the neck refers up."
She looked at me for a long moment.
"Rebecca. Light sensitivity, nausea, and unilateral eye pressure is not a cervicogenic pattern. That is a Migraine pattern. Cervicogenic headache does not typically produce light sensitivity or nausea. Migraine does."
I stared at her.

We went to a coffee shop next door after our appointments and she walked me through it for an hour.
The trigeminal nerve is the largest cranial nerve in your face. It converges at the brainstem with the upper cervical nerves — C1, C2, and C3 — through a structure called the trigeminocervical complex. The two systems talk to each other. Constantly. In chronic Migraine, the trigeminal cascade activates the cervical nerves and produces neck stiffness, neck pain, and referred pain along the back of the head that looks and feels exactly like cervicogenic headache.
Which is why chiropractors get to feel like they are helping. When they adjust the neck, they are working downstream of a nerve that is firing upstream. The temporary relief is real. The problem is the cascade keeps re-firing at the trigeminal level, which keeps activating the cervical nerves, which keeps producing the neck pain.
The cascade happens in three phases. Phase 1: the prodrome. 20 to 40 minutes before any head pain. Neck stiffness intensifies here. Base-of-skull tension. What I had been calling "a bad neck day." Phase 2: the head pain phase. Behind the eye. Across the forehead. Light sensitivity. Nausea. What I had been calling "my neck flare-up headaches." Phase 3: the postdrome. 24 to 72 hours after. Continued cervical activation. Sore trapezius. Reduced neck range of motion. Which sent me back to my chiropractor.
I sat there with my hands wrapped around my coffee cup.
She kept going.

"If you have three or four Migraines a month, Rebecca, you have roughly twelve to twenty days in some phase of the cascade. Your cervical nerves are getting activated every single one of those days. Your chiropractor is treating the muscle spasm and the joint restriction downstream. He is not touching the trigeminal nerve that is causing the cervical activation upstream."
"You don't have cervicogenic headache. You have chronic Migraine that has been driving cervical nerve activation for twelve years and looking exactly like a neck-origin problem to any chiropractor who was not screening for Migraine."
She told me the "normal-ish" MRI I paid $1,400 for was probably showing age-related changes that appear in most people over thirty-five and mean almost nothing. The changes were not causing my pain. My trigeminal nerve was.
I drove home slowly. My neck felt like it always did. My head throbbed the way it always did. But something in my head had shifted.
Twelve years. Chiropractors. PTs. A pain management doctor. Cervical facet injections. Almost a $38,000 radiofrequency ablation. And nobody had ever asked me whether the light sensitivity and nausea I had during my "neck flares" might mean I was having Migraines and not neck-origin headaches.
I texted Yasmin the next morning.
"Okay. If you're right. What do I actually do?"
She called me back that afternoon.

"You need to interrupt the trigeminal cascade at the source. The trigeminocervical complex. If you calm the trigeminal, the cervical nerves stop being fed the sensitization signal, and the neck-pattern pain starts to fade."
She told me about a topical roll-on developed by a neurologist named Dr. Fiora Laurent, who suffers from Migraines herself. Five ingredients chosen for trigeminal calming. Magnesium glycinate for nerve relaxation. Wild peppermint and menthol crystals for TRPM8 activation. Chamomile and feverfew extract for chronic reactivity reduction.
Applied to the three points where the trigeminal nerve surfaces closest to the skin — including the base of the skull, which is exactly the anatomical junction where the trigeminal and cervical nerves converge.
The nerve sits 2 millimeters under the skin at those points. A topical reaches it in 90 seconds. No 45-minute oral absorption gap. No injection into the cervical joints. No radiofrequency burn.

It was called Florus.
"You have been trying to relax the muscles and adjust the joints for twelve years. The muscles and the joints are downstream. The nerve is upstream. If you can calm the nerve, the trigeminocervical complex quiets, and the cervical activation walks back on its own."
She had been working with cervicogenic headache patients for three years. She estimated that in her practice, about half of the "cervicogenic" cases she had seen were actually chronic Migraine driving cervical nerve activation, and had been misdiagnosed for years because the referring physicians did not screen for Migraine when the presenting complaint was neck pain.
I sat with that for two days. Then I ordered the bottle.
First time I used it was a Wednesday morning. My neck had been stiff since I woke up. Twelve years of muscle memory said reach for the warm compress and schedule the chiropractor.
I rolled Florus across my temples, behind both ears, and — most importantly — right along the base of my skull where the cervical and trigeminal nerves converge. Ten seconds total.
Within 90 seconds I felt the cooling reach somewhere deeper than skin. I sat at my kitchen table and waited for the ache to spread up over my scalp the way it always did.
It did not spread.
By 10 a.m. the base-of-skull tension had faded. By noon I turned my head to look at my husband without rotating my torso. My range of motion had come back for the first time in weeks.
I stood in the kitchen and I started crying because I had not turned my head without pain in three years.

Week 1: I caught two prodromes with Florus. Both stopped. Neither developed into the head pain I had been calling a "neck flare." Neither was followed by the 48-hour cervical soreness that had structured my life.
Week 2: I drove to my sister's house. Two hours each way. I did not pull over. I did not have to lie flat when I got there.
Week 3: I sat through a full movie in a movie theater. I could not remember the last time I had done that.
Week 5: I stopped my weekly chiropractor visits. My chiropractor asked what changed. I told him. He was polite about it.
Week 8: I drove to Vermont for a weekend. Four hours each way. I slept on my left side in the hotel bed. My left side had not touched a pillow in six years.
Week 12: I went back to my pain management doctor. I told him I was not going to do the ablation. I showed him my new symptom log. I told him about Yasmin. The trigeminocervical complex. The prodrome window. The three application points. The topical that reaches the nerve in 90 seconds.

He listened. He was quiet for a long time. Then he said, "I am going to start asking my cervicogenic-headache patients about light sensitivity and nausea. I should have been asking all along."
Six months in: I hiked Camel's Hump in Vermont with my sister and her husband. Six miles round trip. Elevation gain of two thousand feet. I looked up at the summit for a photograph. I did not pay for it for three days after.
My sister took a picture of me at the top. I sent it to my husband. He wrote back: "You looked up. You actually looked up."
I do not have cervicogenic headache. I never had cervicogenic headache. I had twelve years of an unrecognized trigeminal cascade firing low-grade three to four times a month, activating my cervical nerves through the trigeminocervical complex, producing a neck-pattern pain that everyone, including me, had been calling cervicogenic.
And not one person in a white coat had thought to ask me about the light sensitivity.

If you have been diagnosed with cervicogenic headache. If you have been to a chiropractor weekly for years. If you have done PT, cervical injections, or been offered radiofrequency ablation.

They call him worthless. A good-for-nothing live-in son-in-law.  For three years, Charlie Wade has lived under the roof of his wife’s family, cooking their meals, scrubbing their toilets, enduring every insult they throw his way. To the Willson family, he is nothing but a freeloader, a burden they can’t wait to kick out. Even his mother-in-law mocks him daily, telling her daughter Claire she deserves better than a man like him. And Claire—though kinder than the rest—can’t hide the shame of having a husband everyone calls useless. But Charlie is hiding something no one could imagine.
One ordinary day, a man from his past appears. Stephen Thompson—loyal servant to the Wade family—hands Charlie a sleek black card. “Young Master,” he says, bowing low, “this card holds ten billion dollars. And it’s just the beginning. You are the heir to the Wade family empire—a trillion-dollar fortune.”
In that moment, Charlie’s carefully built disguise threatens to shatter. For three years, he’s lived as a nobody, but the truth is he could buy and sell the very people who sneer at him. Still, he chooses silence. He doesn’t brag, doesn’t reveal his power. Instead, he tucks the card into his pocket, deciding to keep playing the role of the worthless son-in-law. Because revenge, Charlie knows, is best served cold.
That night, as Claire returns home exhausted from being humiliated by her relatives at work, Charlie quietly pays her aunt’s two-million-dollar hospital bill in secret. He doesn’t tell Claire. He doesn’t tell anyone. He lets her family believe what they want—that he’s penniless, that he’s incapable. Only Charlie knows the truth: every sneer, every insult, is a debt. And one day soon, they’ll all pay.
The turning point comes when Claire is chosen to pitch for the Willson family at the Emgrand Group, the most powerful corporation in Aurous Hill. Everyone expects her to fail. Her cousin Harold mocks her openly, saying she’ll be lucky to get past the lobby. Her grandmother, the matriarch of the family, threatens to strip her of any role in the company if she embarrasses them.
But behind the scenes, the truth is far more shocking. The Emgrand Group belongs to Charlie. He is the mysterious new chairman whose identity the entire city is desperate to uncover. And when Claire arrives nervously at the glittering headquarters, she’s ushered straight into the vice chairwoman’s office. Doris Young, the most respected businesswoman in the city, greets Claire with warmth and hands her a contract—sixty million dollars, double what the Willsons had hoped for.
When Claire walks back into the family’s boardroom clutching the signed contract, the room falls silent. Everyone who mocked her is stunned. Her cousin Harold accuses her of lying, until the Emgrand Group posts the news publicly. The Willson family erupts in chaos. And when Charlie calmly reminds Harold of the bet he lost—to kneel and bow if Claire succeeded—the arrogant cousin is forced to the floor in humiliation. But the victory is bittersweet.
At the Willson family’s grand banquet, Claire is promised the directorship for securing the deal. Yet at the last moment, her grandmother betrays her, naming Harold as director instead. Claire flees the room in tears, humiliated yet again. Charlie follows, wrapping his coat around her shoulders, whispering that the Willsons don’t deserve her. Minutes later, Doris Young returns to the stage with a shocking announcement: the Emgrand Group is terminating its cooperation with the Willsons—unless Claire is appointed director.
Suddenly, the balance of power shifts. The very family who mocked Charlie and crushed Claire’s spirit is now on their knees, begging her to accept the position they stole from her. For the first time, Claire sees a glimpse of hope—that she and Charlie might finally rise above the cruelty of her family. But the story is only beginning.
Because Charlie’s secret stretches far beyond the Emgrand Group. Beyond the black card. Beyond Aurous Hill itself. He is the heir to a trillion-dollar empire, a man whose power could change the fate of everyone around him. Yet he remains silent, choosing patience over pride, playing the long game while his enemies laugh.

Total Cholesterol 267 at Age 59. My Father Hit 264 at Age 57. His Doctor Started Atorvastatin. He Died at 68 With Liver Damage and Memory Loss. Yesterday My Doctor Pulled Out Her Prescription Pad.

My father died at 68.

I'm 59.

Three weeks ago, my doctor closed the exam room door.

The click echoed.

She sat down. Pulled up my chart without looking at me.

"James. We can't wait anymore. I'm prescribing Atorvastatin. 20 milligrams daily. You'll start today."

I sat there. Let her finish. Then I said what I'd been holding in since I walked through that door.

"My father was on Atorvastatin for eleven years. He developed muscle pain, memory loss, liver damage. He died at sixty-eight. Heart failure. The medication controlled his cholesterol. It didn't save him."

She barely looked up from her screen.

"James, your father's case was different. He had other comorbidities. Atorvastatin is the standard of care for your numbers. The benefits significantly outweigh the risks."

Different.

Eleven years of watching my father's body break down. Muscle cramping so bad he slept in his recliner. Names of grandchildren forgotten by month eight. The afternoon he stood up from the couch — dizzy — and his legs just buckled. Face-first into the coffee table. Blood streaming from where his forehead split open. Six stitches.

The liver function tests that got worse. And worse. And worse.

ALT climbing. AST rising. Year 8: Fatty liver disease. Year 10: Liver inflammation.

Year 11: Constant fatigue. His skin yellow-tinged. Swollen. Painful.

A man who used to run marathons couldn't walk to the mailbox without gasping for breath.

My mother's words at the funeral, barely audible over my own sobs: "The pills didn't save him. They just made him suffer longer."

Eleven years of medication.

Eleven years of side effects.

My father died anyway. Heart failure. In his sleep. The Atorvastatin controlled his cholesterol. Didn't save his liver. Didn't prevent his death.

And my doctor called it "different."

I sat in my car in the parking lot for twenty minutes. Couldn't turn the key. Just gripped the steering wheel and stared at the dashboard.

Twenty years I'd been going to that office. Twenty years of appointments. And her response to everything I watched my father go through was "your father's case was different."

Like I hadn't been there. Like I hadn't watched it happen. Like eleven years of decline was a footnote in someone else's chart.

The prescription crinkled in my jacket pocket. I pulled it out. Stared at it.

Atorvastatin 20mg. Take one tablet daily.

My hands shook.

My wife was unloading groceries when I walked through the door. "Hey. How was your checkup?"

The words stuck. I handed her the prescription without speaking.

Total cholesterol 267. LDL 189.

The grocery bag hit the floor. Eggs shattered. Milk carton split. She didn't notice. Both hands covered her mouth. Tears streaming down her face.

"No." Her voice broke. "James, I watched what that medication did to your father. I can't. I can't watch you go through that. I can't —"

She couldn't finish. Turned away. Shoulders shaking.

That night I lay awake. The ceiling fan rotated. Over. And over. And over.

Red numbers glowed on the clock: 11:52 PM.

Rolled over. 12:41 AM.

Again. 1:38 AM.

At 2:23 AM I gave up. Went downstairs. Sat at the kitchen table. Opened my laptop.

The screen's blue glow hurt my eyes.

I typed: atorvastatin side effects

The search results loaded.

My chest tightened.

"Statin-induced cognitive impairment affects 15-30% of patients. Memory loss is progressive, debilitating. Resolves only after discontinuation."

Thirty percent.

I kept reading. Liver damage. Rhabdomyolysis — muscle breakdown so severe it can destroy your kidneys. A forum post from a woman whose husband died at 41. No warning. Just gone.

My father's face flashed in my mind. The yellowed skin. The constant fatigue. The swollen abdomen.

I closed the laptop. Rubbed my face with both hands.

What do I do?

The prescription sat on the counter. Five feet away. Mocking me.

I didn't fill it.

Three days passed.

The doctor's office called. "Mr. Mitchell, you haven't picked up your prescription. Dr. Chen needs confirmation you're taking the medication."

"I need more time."

"Sir, your cholesterol is dangerously high. This is urgent. Dr. Chen was very clear —"

"I said I need more time."

I hung up.

Five days.

Seven.

My brother called on day eight. My wife had told him about the prescription.

"Jimmy. Come on. Just take the medication. You're scaring everyone."

"Did you forget what it did to Dad?"

"Dad had other issues. The doctor said —"

"The doctor said his case was 'different.' That's what my doctor said too. Word for word. Like they're reading from the same script."

Silence.

"Jimmy, you're turning into one of those people. You know that, right? The ones who think they know more than their doctors. Just take the damn pill."

One of those people.

My own brother. Who stood next to me at Dad's funeral. Who watched the same man I watched waste away for eleven years. And his advice was the same as the doctor's. Just take the pill.

Easy for him to say. His numbers were fine last year.

My wife found me in the garage that evening. "James. What are you doing out here?"

"Thinking."

"About?"

"Options."

"The doctor said you need medication."

"The doctor said my father needed medication too. Didn't save him. Just made his last eleven years unbearable."

Her chin trembled. "But what if she's right? What if you have a heart attack? What if I lose you?"

"What if the medication destroys my liver like it did his? What if I end up with muscle breakdown? What if I die anyway but only after years of suffering?"

She had no answer.

That weekend I sat back down at the kitchen table. Opened the laptop. And this time I wasn't looking up what could go wrong. I was looking for what else existed.

Because clearly nobody else was going to figure this out for me. Not my doctor, who looked at eleven years of my father's decline and called it "different." Not my brother, who watched the same thing I watched and still told me to just take the pill.

If there was something out there that could actually move my numbers without destroying my body, I was going to find it myself.

Oolong tea appeared everywhere. Polyphenols. Adiponectin production. Studies from Duke, Stanford, Johns Hopkins showing 30-50 point cholesterol reductions.

Real universities. Real science. Not fringe pseudoscience.

Monday morning I ordered generic oolong tea. Highest rated on Amazon. 4.2 stars. Over 6,000 reviews.

Seven weeks later: Still 264 total cholesterol.

I tried Twinings oolong next. The one from the grocery store. Nine weeks. Never missed a day.

261 total cholesterol. Still dangerously high.

My follow-up appointment was in three weeks. Then two. Then one.

Every time my chest tightened — reaching for something overhead, climbing stairs — I saw my father. The yellowed skin. The memory loss. The muscle pain that never stopped.

Ten days before my appointment, I stood in Whole Foods. Tea aisle. Thirty different oolong products.

All useless.

Two men talking one aisle over.

"—problem isn't oolong tea. Most brands destroy the polyphenols with over-processing. You need high-altitude, hand-picked leaves."

I walked over. "What did you say about processing destroying polyphenols?"

The older man turned. Name badge: "Clinical Nutritionist."

"Machine harvesting and high-heat drying — cheap and fast. Destroys 90% of the EGCG and catechins that actually lower cholesterol."

My chest tightened. "I've been drinking oolong for four months. Numbers haven't moved."

"The clinical studies used high-altitude, hand-picked oolong with verified polyphenol content. Most store brands contain less than 10% of the therapeutic compounds."

"The label doesn't say that."

"They don't have to disclose polyphenol content. Just 'oolong tea.'" He pulled out his phone. "Only one brand I recommend — PiPi Tea. High-altitude grown. Hand-picked at peak potency. Published test results. Made in the USA."

Certificate of Analysis. Lab testing. Exact EGCG and catechin content verified.

"How do I know it works? I'm out of time."

"Within 15-20 minutes you'll feel an energy lift. Proof it's hitting your bloodstream. Then over 3-4 weeks, cholesterol drops. You'll know immediately."

The science actually made sense. And it made me angry.

Because this information isn't hard to find. Polyphenols. Adiponectin. EGCG. It's in the research. It's in the clinical studies. My doctor never once mentioned that antioxidant compounds in tea could affect cholesterol metabolism. Not once in twenty years of appointments. She had time to write a prescription in under a minute but not thirty seconds to mention that the compounds I was missing had been studied at Duke and Stanford.

The entire system would rather put you on a pill and monitor your liver function for a decade than tell you about a category of compounds that's been in the research literature for years.

I pulled out my phone. Ordered PiPi Tea standing there.

The bag arrived two days later.

I took my first cup that evening. Sat on the deck. Waited.

Seventeen minutes.

Then —

A lift. Like someone turned up the oxygen in my blood. The fog in my head... cleared. The exhaustion that hit me every evening around 6 PM... didn't come.

I walked inside. Made a note to get cholesterol tested in two weeks.

Called my doctor's office the next morning. Scheduled lab work.

Two weeks later: Total cholesterol 247. LDL 168.

I stared. Asked them to check again.

247 total cholesterol. LDL 168.

Down from 267 total, 189 LDL.

It's working.

One week later: 241 total, 162 LDL.

I checked labs every two weeks. Numbers kept dropping consistently.

My wife noticed I stopped falling asleep in my chair after dinner. Didn't comment. Just watched me move around with energy I hadn't had in months.

Four weeks: 228 total, 151 LDL.

Six weeks: 214 total, 138 LDL.

The morning of my follow-up, I got fresh labs: 209 total, 132 LDL.

At the doctor's office, the nurse pulled up my results. Stared at the screen.

Frowned.

Checked the patient ID twice.

Pulled up my previous results for comparison.

"Total cholesterol 209. LDL 132."

Silence.

Dr. Chen pulled up my history. Same doctor who sat across from me three months ago and told me my father's case was "different." Who wrote a prescription in under a minute and didn't look up when I told her about eleven years of watching my father die.

She stared at the numbers. Looked at me.

"James. What happened?"

I told her. High-altitude oolong tea. Hand-picked at peak potency. Verified polyphenol content. Published test results. Made in the USA.

She typed notes. Nodding.

"Well." She closed the laptop. "Whatever you're doing, continue. These numbers are excellent. No Atorvastatin necessary at this time."

No Atorvastatin necessary.

I just sat there for a second. Didn't say anything. I didn't need her to apologize. I didn't need her to admit she should have mentioned alternatives. I just needed to hear her say what I already knew — that I was right to keep looking.

I walked to my car. Got in. Sat there. Then called my wife.

"209 total, 132 LDL."

bodyText:
I almost lost my husband to kidney failure, and the only reason he’s still alive is that I gave a grieving widow in Walgreens 5 minutes of my time.

It was a Thursday morning in November. I was at the Walgreens on Piedmont Avenue, where I've been picking up Raymond's Lisinopril every ninety days for twelve years.

The woman in front of me was small, put-together, holding her purse with both hands.

She slid a bottle across the counter and asked the pharmacist, real quiet, to please take her husband out of the system.

The girl behind the counter didn't understand at first. Asked if she wanted to switch pharmacies.

"No, baby," the woman said. "He passed. Two weeks ago. And your system keeps texting his phone that his refill is ready. I need it to stop."

The pharmacist went quiet. The whole line went quiet.

And I stood there holding my ticket for a 90-day supply of the same little pills she was handing back.

She got her paperwork sorted and walked out. And I don't know what got into me, because I am not a woman who talks to strangers, but I left my spot in that line and went after her.

I caught her by the bench outside, near the sliding doors.

"Ma'am, I couldn't help but overhear. I'm so sorry about your husband."

She looked at me a long second. Then her eyes went down to the white bag in my hand, the one with the prescription stapled to it.

"Lisinopril?" she asked.

I said yes. My husband's.

"For his pressure or his kidneys?"

Both, I told her. His kidneys had been slipping a few years now.

Her name was Kendra. We ended up on a bench outside the Walgreens. We talked for the better part of twenty minutes with people wheeling their carts past us like her world hadn't ended two weeks ago.

Her husband Curtis started dialysis in July. He did everything his doctor told him. Cut the salt. Drank more water. Gave up the oxtail. Walked 3 miles a day. Took every single pill they handed him. He died of kidney failure on October 19th at 4:09 AM.

“He was 63. He'd gone in for a regular checkup back in May of 2023, feeling fine. Better than fine.” said Kendra. "The man thought he was unbreakable, and honestly, so did I."

Two days later the doctor called. Creatinine 2.1. eGFR 33.

"That man came home and emptied out the whole refrigerator. The ribs. The ground beef. The brisket from Sunday. The hot sauce he put on everything. He said, 'Whatever I gotta do, I'm doing it.' And Lord, he meant it."

She counted it off for me on her fingers. He gave up the red meat entirely. He weighed his food on a little scale. He stopped going out with his brothers on Friday nights because he couldn't sit there with a glass of water while everybody else got loose. He lost 22 pounds. He bought a juicer.

"Curtis, with a juicer," she said, and for one second there was almost a smile on her face. "I still can't picture it."

"The follow-up labs came back. Creatinine 2.9. eGFR 22. Worse. He did everything right and his numbers got worse."

The doctor told them these things take time. Added a medication and kept monitoring. More Lisinopril, and that dry, violent cough that wouldn't quit. Then Prednisone for the swelling in his ankles.

And every three months, the exact same visit. Same chair. Same screen turned toward them with numbers on it. They'd read his labs back to him and send him home.

"‘We're managing the progression,’ the doctor would say.”

Her hands tightened around her purse.

“I will hate that phrase until the day I die. ‘Managing the progression.’ Managed it right out of stage 3 and into stage 4.”

She took a slow breath.

"Then the office called. Said they wanted Curtis to come in for a preparatory consultation. We both knew what that meant. The machine."

He started dialysis that July. And she watched her husband disappear one session at a time. He'd come home gray in the face. Too weak to climb the stairs to their own bedroom. He slept down in the recliner because the climb was too much.

Her voice stayed steady. She'd told this part to herself a thousand nights.

Three months in, he woke up at 2 AM with his whole body swollen and heavy, red dots scattered up his legs and feet. 

“I drove him to the ER. Curtis spent 11 days in the ICU. His kidneys were failing. I learned things in that hospital about kidney failure that I will never be able to un-know.”

“I learned that when your kidneys give out, the fluid your body can't release has nowhere to go, so it backs up into your lungs until you feel like you’re drowning. I watched my husband fight for every single breath.”

“I learned that the poison the kidneys are supposed to clear builds up in the blood and crosses into the brain. By the second day, Curtis looked right at me and called me by his first wife's name. A woman he'd divorced back in 1984.”

Kendra let out a shaky breath.

"Day 11 — October 19th — I was in the family room down the hall. They'd asked me to step out while they intubated him. At 4:09 AM I heard the long beep. A doctor walked out to give me the news. I already knew."

The hospital bills came to $71,000. The funeral, another $9,000.

"His grill is still out back under the cover," she said. "I can't bring myself to uncover it. If I uncover it, then he's really gone."

I didn't say anything. What is there to say.

"He gave up everything he loved. Everything. And it didn't save him. And to this day, not one doctor has been able to tell me why."

"Why does a man do everything right and get worse anyway? Why did his numbers never improve? Not once?"

I had no answer for her. Nobody had ever given me one either.

She stood up. Straightened her coat.

"Whatever pills are in that bag, honey, they were in Curtis's bag too. Don't you sleep on this thing. It moves faster than they tell you."

She pulled a grocery receipt out of her purse, wrote her number on the back of it, and pressed it into my hand.

"If you ever need to talk to somebody who's been down this road, you call me."

And she walked to her car.

I drove home with Raymond's Lisinopril on the passenger seat and that receipt folded in my purse.

When I walked in, Raymond was asleep in his recliner. Four in the afternoon. TV on, remote still in his hand.

And I just stood there in the doorway looking at my husband like I was seeing him for the first time.

Raymond is 66. A car man. Thirty years turning wrenches at Goodyear, and even after he retired, that garage of ours never went quiet. Somebody's brakes, somebody's alternator, half the church bringing their cars to him instead of the dealer. And under the tarp in the corner, the '72 Chevelle he'd been restoring for years, the one he promised our grandson Marcus would be his when he turned sixteen.

Then his creatinine came back 1.9 on a routine panel three years ago. Then 2.4. Then 2.8. Last visit it was 3.3, with his eGFR down at 24.

And the doctor said what he always says. Watch the sodium. Watch the protein. Come back in three months. We're monitoring it.

Monitoring. That's all anybody ever did. I can read the man's labs to him myself, for free.

Meanwhile I watched my husband shrink into somebody I didn't recognize.

The tiredness was the worst of it. By two in the afternoon he was asleep in his chair, every single day. This is a man who used to spend whole Saturdays under a hood in July heat. Now he'd lift the hood, stand there a minute, and have to come inside and sit down.

By evening his ankles swelled up so tight I had to help him pull his socks off.

He was up three times a night to the bathroom. And one morning I heard him go quiet in there, too long, and when I asked, he finally told me about the foam. Sitting in the toilet like somebody poured dish soap in it. He looked at me like he'd done something wrong.

His lower back ached on both sides, months on end. The doctor told him kidneys don't usually hurt. Raymond told me, "I live in this body. It's not hurting for no reason."

And the eating. Lord, the eating. Everything on his plate got measured and weighed and worried over. No salt, no red meat, no this, no that. He ate like he was being punished. 

He did all of it. Every rule, every pill, every glass of water.

And the numbers kept climbing anyway.

By spring, the garage had gone silent. The church folks started taking their cars to the dealer. And the Chevelle sat under that tarp with the driver's door still off its hinges, right where he'd stopped. Marcus turns sixteen in the fall. Raymond stopped talking about it.

That night after the pharmacy, I lay next to Raymond and listened to him breathe.

Same Lisinopril Curtis was on. Same cough. Same swollen ankles. Same foam he went quiet about. Numbers a step or two behind where Curtis's were when they called him in for that preparatory consultation.

My husband was walking a dead man's road, and every doctor we had was telling him to keep walking.

I didn't sleep that night. Or the next.

Kendra's question wouldn't leave me alone.

Why does a man do everything right and get worse anyway?

So I did something I have never done in my life. I started researching.

I read for weeks. Medical articles I could barely make sense of. Kidney forums at two in the morning. Studies out of Japan, out of Germany. And one thing kept coming up over and over, that no doctor had said to us once in three years of appointments.

The reason the numbers never come down is that doctors only care about what goes IN.

Nobody had ever stopped to think about what can't get OUT.

Your kidneys have their own lymphatic system. A network of tiny drainage vessels that carry waste out of your kidney tissue every single day.

When those vessels are clear, your kidneys filter clean.

When they're clogged, the waste backs up inside the tissue.

That's the creatinine climbing. That's the eGFR dropping. That's the foam sitting in the toilet every single morning.

Think about it…

Your kidneys filter a whopping 50 GALLONS of blood every day.

And every single day, a little bit of the waste that gets left behind builds up inside your renal lymphatic vessels.

One day is nothing. One month is nothing. But ten, twenty, thirty years of buildup?

Decades of accumulated toxic sludge.

Sludge that hardens. Calcifies. Coats the inside of your kidney's drainage…

Until the waste backs up inside your kidneys the same way sewage backs up behind a blocked drain.

No ACE inhibitor dissolves that buildup.

Low-protein diets control what goes in, but they cannot clear what's blocking the way out.

Dialysis manages the backup. It never touches the source.

So your creatinine sits at 1.9, then 2.4, then 2.8, then 3.3.

And one day the doctor's office calls about a "preparatory consultation."

You already know what that means.

The machine. Three mornings a week, for the rest of your life.

This is why Black folk end up on dialysis at 3 times the rate of white people with the very same diagnosis.

Not because of our genetics.

Because we're handed treatments that were never designed to touch the real problem.

And the worst part is...

Almost no doctor talks about this. They don't even teach it in medical school.

Mainly because clogged kidney drainage is something that disproportionately affects Black folk...

And the American medical system DOES NOT care about you.

That's why so many Black folk die after spending years confined to a dialysis machine.

The system just isn't set up to cater to you.

I sat with that for three days straight.

Then I called my cousin's daughter, who's a doctor up in Charlotte. Somebody with a medical degree I actually trusted.

I told her everything. Kendra, Curtis, Raymond's numbers, the drainage vessels, all of it. I told her Raymond had been taking a cranberry supplement every morning for a year, the one his doctor "wasn't against."

She laughed. Not mean. But she laughed.

"Auntie, cranberry supplements help reduce inflammation, but they don't do anything to clear out what's blocking the drainage."

Then she said something I'll never forget.

"If that man Curtis had been on something that actually reactivated his renal lymphatic drainage, the picture might have been very different."

I stopped breathing for a second.

"Then why didn't his doctor prescribe that? Why hasn't Raymond's?"

She was quiet a long time.

"Because we don't prescribe supplements. And the version that works isn't a prescription."

The next morning I was back at that same Walgreens. Standing in the supplement aisle for a solid forty minutes, three counters down from where I'd met Kendra.

Found a bottle that said Lymphatic Drainage Support. Capsules. Twenty-some dollars.

Raymond took them for two weeks. Nothing moved.

So I went back to researching, and what I found made me throw that whole bottle in the trash.

A kidney that's already backed up can't absorb a capsule properly. The capsule has to pass through a body that's already struggling before the active ingredients ever reach the bloodstream. Most of what you paid for, you flush right back out.

Liquid bypasses this entirely. Liquid hits the bloodstream directly.

I had been doing the right thing in the wrong form.

And that wasn't the only problem with that bottle.

Because the deeper I read, the clearer it got that a real lymphatic formula has to contain six specific ingredients that work together, or it's a waste of your money.

Astragalus Root. Chinese emperors used it for 2,000 years to extend their lives, and modern science has finally shown how. A 2019 study found astragalus goes after the toxic buildup smothering the drainage vessels, breaking it down so waste can finally move again.

Burdock Root. Traditional medicine called it "the blood purifier." It flips on a process called autophagy, your body recycling its own dead and damaged cells, while flushing years of backed-up waste straight out of the kidney tissue.

Echinacea. Most folks know it for colds. Almost nobody knows it supercharges your NK cells, your body's "Natural Killer" cells, helping break up the blanket of buildup clogging the drain.

And the last three work together as a lymphatic flush. Cleavers acts like a power wash for the drainage vessels. Red Clover reactivates the circulation that pumps the waste through. And Calendula calms the inflammation in the vessel walls so the drainage can finally hold open instead of closing right back up.

Together, all six target the actual problem.

Not what's going in.

What can't get out.

I went back through every bottle in that drugstore aisle. Not one of them did all six. Most did one. The expensive ones did two. And not a single one of them was liquid.

That's when I found Flow+ by Elavyn.

All six ingredients. A liquid dropper you take under the tongue, morning and night. Tastes like honey. Formulated in the US. And a 30-day money-back guarantee. If your numbers don't move, you get every penny back, no questions asked.

I ordered it before I could talk myself out of it.

Raymond took it because I asked him to. Stubborn as a mule, but he listened. 

"Tastes like honey," he said, surprised.

Week two, he slept the whole night through for the first time in a year. Woke up and asked me if he'd really not gotten up at all. He sat on the edge of that bed a long minute, just thinking.

Week four, the socks came off easy. The skin around his ankles wasn't shiny and stretched tight anymore. And the two o'clock nap started losing its grip on him.

Week six, I heard something I hadn't heard in over a year. The garage radio, and a ratchet working under it. He was out there past ten that night with the tarp pulled back, hanging that driver's door back on the Chevelle. Came in with grease on his hands and more himself than I'd seen him in two years.

Every morning and every night, the same. A few drops under the tongue.

Week eleven, Raymond had his labs pulled, and then his appointment.

The doctor came in, pulled up the chart, frowned, and looked again.

"Creatinine 2.2. eGFR 38, Mr. Hayes."

Then he pulled up the numbers from three months back, 3.3 and 24, and read them side by side twice, like he was checking his own eyes.

"Mr. Hayes, your kidney function is the best it's been in three years. Whatever you've been doing, don't stop. I'll see you in three months."

I made it as far as the hallway outside that exam room before I started crying. Raymond put his arm around me and the nurse asked if I was alright, and I laughed and cried at the same time and couldn't get a single word out.

In the car, Raymond didn't start the engine. He reached over, took my hand, and said, "You still got that woman's number?"

I did. Folded in my purse, right where it had been since November.

I called Kendra that same afternoon.

She came to the house that Saturday. I put two bottles in her hands on my front porch. One for her, because her own labs had come back borderline at her last physical. One for her brother Frank, who'd just called her with a creatinine of 2.6 and no clue what to do.

She held those bottles a long time.

"I'm going to take it," she finally said. "And I'm going to mail this one to Frank today with a note that says if he doesn't take it every single morning I will never speak to him again."

She did, too.

A few months later, it was Frank's turn at the doctor. Creatinine 1.5. Down from 2.6. He hadn't changed his diet. Hadn't started exercising. The only thing he changed was those drops he took every morning.

He called Kendra crying. Her big brother. 64 years old. Crying on the phone like a child.

He said, "Kendra, I think Curtis died because nobody ever told him about this."

She had to hang up.

This past Sunday, Raymond backed that Chevelle down the driveway, finished. First time it's run in two years. Marcus rode shotgun with a grin you could see from the porch, and Kendra stood next to me watching them roll off down the street, and I had to look away so she wouldn't see my face.

I keep thinking about how close it came.

If Kendra had picked a different pharmacy to cancel those refills.

If I'd minded my business and stayed in that line.

If she hadn't looked at the white bag in my hand and asked me one question.

Every one of those was a hinge. My Raymond would be sitting in a dialysis chair three mornings a week, and I'd be the one walking up to a counter one day asking them to stop texting a dead man's phone.

I'm telling you all of this because I think you might be standing right where I was standing a year ago.

Watching yourself or somebody you love slip away in little pieces. The naps getting longer. The ankles puffing up by evening. The foam in the toilet bowl. The back that aches on both sides while the doctor swears it’s nothing.

Doing everything right, and getting worse anyway.

I'm not a doctor. I'm not a scientist. I'm not selling you a thing and I don't get one dime from any of this. I'm a 63-year-old woman who almost lost her husband, and the only reason I didn't is that a grieving widow in a pharmacy line took five minutes to tell me her story.

That's the line that finally made all of it make sense to me.

Not now.

"What's going on?" she asked the driver.
"Morning rush," he said. "We'll get there."
Susan nodded, but her chest felt tight. What if she was late? What if he had already come and gone? She hadn't asked Ethan how long he would wait. She had simply assumed he would be there, because he said he would.

"We're here," the driver said.

She hesitated.
Oh God. What if he's not there anymore? What if he didn't wait?
She looked down at herself. Rumpled clothes. Red eyes. No bouquet. No witnesses.
Would he even recognize her as his bride?
Susan pushed the thought aside and walked in.
Inside, footsteps echoed off the floor. Papers shuffled. Clerks spoke in low voices. Everyone else seemed prepared. Certain.
Susan wasn't.
She moved through the hall quickly, scanning faces she didn't know, her heartbeat loud in her ears. Near the registration counter, she stopped and took a breath.
Is he here?

Then the taxi slowed.
Susan leaned forward, fingers tightening around the strap of her bag. Cars inched along, horns sounding somewhere behind her. She glanced out the window, then at the road ahead.
Not now.
She checked the time once, then forced herself to stop. Checking again wouldn't make the cars move.
"What's going on?" she asked the driver.
"Morning rush," he said. "We'll get there."
Susan nodded, but her chest felt tight. What if she was late? What if he had already come and gone? She hadn't asked Ethan how long he would wait. She had simply assumed he would be there, because he said he would.
The taxi picked up speed.
Susan exhaled slowly. She had already chosen this. Turning back wasn't an option.
Then the car slowed again and stopped.
"We're here," the driver said.
Susan got out quickly and paid, barely waiting for her change. The Recorder's Office loomed ahead, people moving in and out calmly, as if it were just another ordinary morning.
She hesitated.
Oh God. What if he's not there anymore? What if he didn't wait?
She looked down at herself. Rumpled clothes. Red eyes. No bouquet. No witnesses.
Would he even recognize her as his bride?
Susan pushed the thought aside and walked in.
Inside, footsteps echoed off the floor. Papers shuffled. Clerks spoke in low voices. Everyone else seemed prepared. Certain.
Susan wasn't.
She moved through the hall quickly, scanning faces she didn't know, her heartbeat loud in her ears. Near the registration counter, she stopped and took a breath.
Is he here?
Is Susan running out of time? Will Ethan be waiting, or was she holding on to a hope that was never real?

The entire Red Moon Pack exploded with excitement.
Marcy spent weeks preparing for his arrival while I scrubbed floors like a ghost nobody noticed.
Then one day, the gates of the Red Moon opened.
A convoy of black armoured wolves from the Dark Howler’s pack entered the kingdom.
And at the center of them stood Alpha Damon.
Powerful.
Terrifying.
Beautiful.
The entire kingdom bowed before him.
And little did Talia know…
the Alpha King standing in front of her—
was the same stranger who once saved her in that parking lot years ago.
And the craziest part?
Nobody knew.
Not Marcy.
Not Talia.
Not even Damon himself. 
Will they recognise each other?
Will Damon save Talia… like he did years ago?

 He was the most powerful Alpha in all of North America. Women threw themselves at him. Rulers feared him. He could seduce a she-wolf with a glance, or tear out a man’s throat just as easily.
Damon was untouchable. 
He scorned the idea of love. Rejected every political match. Not a single potential bride, despite the many presented, could win his affection. None were worthy of being his Luna, the proud she-wolf to rule by his side.
Love was a distraction, an attempt to tame him. And Damon would never be tamed. 
Still, there were those who tried. 

Alpha Edward, leader of the Red Moon pack, was desperate to secure his political power. He invited Damon to meet his daughter, Princess Marcy, beautiful, cunning, cruel. She intended to make him hers.

Talia feared their union. Would Marcy succeed where so many others had failed? Would Marcy’s cruelty only intensify as Luna to such a powerful Alpha? 

The moment Alpha Damon stepped onto Red Moon Pack grounds with his mated Betas, Caden and Maya, something felt off. His wolf stirred uneasily beneath the surface. Damon didn’t need confirmation; he already knew: no one in the Red Moon Pack could be trusted.

They all sat down in the dining hall, its gaudy opulence a reflection of Red Moon’s inflated ego.

Marcy arrived fashionably late, every detail of her appearance sharpened like a blade. Shimmering blond hair, a sculpted figure. She was the type of girl who got what she wanted.
Her friend, Nora, wasn’t as restrained. She eyed Damon with hunger, her gaze sliding over him like a caress. The rumors had reached her ears: about his appetite, his stamina, his size. She didn’t care that Marcy was supposed to win the Alpha’s hand. Nora wanted a taste for herself.
Marcy’s mother, Luna Layla, noticed the heat in Nora’s stare… and the flicker of fury in her daughter’s eyes.
“Marcy,” Layla said, too sweetly, “Why don’t you show Alpha Damon to his room so you two can… talk?”

While the Red Moon Pack celebrated Damon’s arrival, elsewhere in the kitchens, Talia worked until the sweat stung her eyes. All she could dream of was the scraps she might scavenge when the feast was over.
The other Omegas had different plans for her.
Anna, their cruel ringleader, stepped into Talia’s path, towering over her, “Listen up, slave.” The other Omegas giggled behind her like hyenas. 
Anna’s lips twisted into a cruel smirk. “You’re going to deliver towels to Alpha Damon’s room.”
Talia froze. “Right now? But... what if he’s inside?”
Anna raised her hand, ready to strike. “Are you questioning me?”
Talia flinched, her heart pounding. Without her wolf, she was defenseless against the bullies. 
Without another word, she took the towels and hurried off, every step dragging her closer to the Alpha’s quarters and whatever fate awaited her behind that door.

When Talia entered the room, she froze. Damon was in his room. But he wasn’t alone. 
There was Marcy. On her knees. Between Damon’s legs. 
Marcy whipped around, her eyes blazing with fury as they locked onto Talia’s. The insolence! 
A jolt of fear shot up Talia’s spine. Retribution would be certain.
Damon’s eyes snapped to Talia.
“Stop!” he barked.
But Talia was gone, bolting from the room, too terrified to look back.
What Talia didn’t know, what she couldn’t have known, is that in that moment, Damon’s world had shifted.
Her scent. It hit his veins like a spark of kindling, igniting something primal within him.
Could it be? His inner wolf howled the truth within him, again and again. She, a lowly omega, a serving girl without a friend, was his fated mate?

Ignoring the mocking laughter of Anna and the others, Talia ran until she reached the attic, shoving the cabinet against the door before collapsing in the corner, struggling to quiet her frantic breathing.
'Is this it? Is this the day I die?'
Back in Damon’s room, Marcy landed clumsily on her backside as Damon shoved her away, his expression thunderous and unreadable.
"Who was that girl?" he demanded, hastily buttoning his pants.
Marcy knew exactly who she was. Talia. That wolf-less bitch. How dare she step into an Alpha’s chambers uninvited? And worse, if word got out that Marcy had been pleasuring Damon before he’d even proposed... she’d be humiliated. A laughingstock. Her reputation would be in shreds.
Marcy’s jaw clenched with fury. She should’ve done more than just beat the girl this morning.
But Damon didn’t notice Marcy’s simmering rage. He was too distracted, his mind replaying the moment when she walked in. How that intoxicating scent, freesia and citrus, had struck him. How his wolf had howled, wild and urgent. All he could think about was pulling her into his arms.
'Mate.' His wolf howled in confirmation. 
He had never expected to hear that word. Never wanted to. And yet, the moment Talia entered the room, something inside him had shifted, changed.
His wolf growled inside him. 'Find her!'
Damon clenched his jaw. "Find her,” He ordered. “Now."
Marcy hesitated, she was confused. Why would an Alpha give a shit about a slave? Damon’s Alpha energy radiated off of her, making her lower her head. "Yes, Alpha Damon."
But Marcy already knew. She’d be doing much more than just finding her… 
Meanwhile, Damon paced, running his tongue over his teeth, irritated beyond reason. His body still ached with unfinished release, but the thought of Marcy’s coconut scent made him recoil. It wasn’t her scent he wanted, it wasn’t her body against his that he needed.
It was her. Talia.
The girl with the smart doe eyes and copper-colored hair.
[SFX: HEAVY FOOTSTEPS ECHOING DOWN THE HALLWAY]
Damon prowled through the packhouse, inhaling deeply. Nothing. No trace of her scent.
His wolf snarled. 'Find her!'
'If she was really my mate, why did she run? Why didn’t she feel it too?'
'You had another woman on her knees in front of you,' his wolf sneered. 'What did you expect? That she’d throw herself into your arms?'
Damon scowled. His instincts screamed at him to chase, but logic held him back. He needed to stay in control. If he lost control and Marcy found out the truth, there was no telling what they would do to her! 
For now, he would wait.
[SFX: KNOCKS ON THE DOOR]
Later that night, Marcy returned to Damon’s chambers. She couldn't wait to tell him how she put the girl in her place, that wretched, wolf-less slave. But when she saw Damon standing there, Marcy forgot all about the girl.
And she would make him forget all about her too.
But Damon barely acknowledged her, his mind consumed by the memory of that freesia scent.
Marcy advanced, “Hello, Damon.”
Damon swiftly turned toward the door to see Marcy peeking in. He wondered if she even knocked, but even if she did, he probably wouldn't have noticed.
He never felt this distracted!
What if that was an enemy? That copper-haired girl already caused him to be weak, and he didn't even acknowledge their mate bond.
"Why are you here?" Damon asked.
"You look tense..." Marcy said while reluctantly putting her palms on Damon's firm chest. 
"I can help you relax."
Damon's lips lifted into a half-smirk. "And how would you do that?"
"I know that nothing is confirmed, but technically, we are engaged,"
Damon observed her fingers as they moved slightly. 
She felt him out over the thin fabric of his shirt.
He noticed a big ring on her right middle finger, an oval-shaped ruby with small diamonds surrounding it. 
Damon looked at her almond-shaped blue eyes, straight nose, and full lips, and he confirmed that she objectively appeared attractive.
Damon felt his wolf's anger and dejection, but he decided to ignore it.
Unaware of the conversation Damon had with his wolf, Marcy inched closer to Damon and she smiled seductively.
"I can..."
Before Marcy could finish her sentence, Damon's hand landed at the back of her head, and he pulled her closer for a kiss, pulling her toward the bed.
“Wait,” Marcy breathed.
"Wait?” Damon replied, “What happened to were technically engaged? Get out."
Marcy didn't understand.
"What?"
"I said... GET OUT!"
The clock struck two. Damon lay restless, tension coiled in his muscles, his thoughts tangled in a torment he refused to name. The oppressive stillness of the Red Moon packhouse suffocated him. He needed air. Control. Escape.
He moved silently, intent on a midnight run—until it hit him. Freesia.
That intoxicating scent. Sweet citrus and wild temptation. His pulse pounded, his body moving before his mind caught up, drawn to the scent like a predator to prey. His hunt led him to the kitchen, shadow pooling in the corner, the hum of the refrigerator filling the quiet.
And there she was.
A small figure bathed in the cold glow of the open fridge, unaware of the danger lurking just behind her.
Damon closed the distance. Too close. Close enough that his heat ghosted over her nape, close enough that he could imagine how she’d feel beneath him. Soft. His.
"Mhm." His voice came unbidden, dark, possessive.
Talia gasped, jerking back—right into him.
[SFX: SHARP INHALE, HEAD THUDDING AGAINST SHELF]
She spun, eyes wide, body trembling. Fear. A scent he despised on her.
"Aw," she whimpered, rubbing the back of her head, shrinking under his gaze. Wrong move, little one. You’re not leaving.
She scurried sideways, but Damon was faster, his arm blocking her escape.
"What are you sorry for?" he murmured, his voice low, dangerous.
She stammered, refusing to meet his eye, her lip caught between her teeth—a sight that shouldn’t send heat curling in his gut, but damn it, it did.
He cupped her chin, tilting her face toward the light. Sparks. A wildfire licked up his arm, searing through his vein. His wolf howled, triumphant. Mate.
But that momentary euphoria crashed when he saw her bruise.
His grip tightened. Rage.
"What happened?" His voice was no longer smooth. It was a blade, sharp with violence.
She flinched. "I—I fell."
"Lies." His thumb ghosted over the mark on her cheek. It was shaped like—a ring.
Marcy.
His wolf roared inside him, demanding blood. Demanding vengeance.
"Who did this?" he growled.
Talia shuddered. "No one."
A lie. A plea. A desperate attempt to protect the monster who hurt her.
Damon inhaled deeply, trying to rein in the storm inside him, but her scent—the sweetness, the fragility—it wrecked him.
"I will not hurt you," he swore, his tone softer now, but she didn't believe him. He could see it in the way her body coiled, ready to run.
Then, she did.
Gone. Vanished.
She had run from him AGAIN, Damon couldn’t believe it.
[SFX: DOOR SWINGING SHUT, FOOTSTEP FLEEING]
Damon stood frozen for a second. Then—"Damn it!"
His wolf snarled. Find her.
Damon’s body moved on instinct, chasing the fading scent of freesia into the night.
Damon halted in the middle of the garden, nostrils flaring as he inhaled deeply, searching for her scent. 
The freesia and citrus still lingered in the air, but it was interwoven with the overpowering fragrance of hydrangeas and roses, scattered wildly by the wind.
"Shit!" he cursed, his fists clenching. "I lost her. Why did she run?"
'Maybe because you scared the soul out of her.' His wolf growled.
Damon frowned. 'I scared her?'
'You grabbed her, cornered her, demanded answers... You think she’s not used to being mistreated? 
And let’s not forget, the first time she saw you, another she-wolf was on her knees for you, and you barked at her to stop. Hardly a warm introduction, if I may say.'
Damon cursed under his breath. He hadn’t considered it from that angle.
The girl haunted him. Her wide, fearful eyes. The bruises marring her delicate face. The way she shrank when he spoke. It made something primal inside him snap.
'If she’s my mate, why didn’t she feel it? She should have wanted to be near me, not running for her life.'
'Maybe she doesn’t know you’re her mate.'
'Is she too young?'
'No, she’s small and malnourished, but she’s definitely over eighteen.' His wolf hesitated. 'The problem is... I can’t sense her wolf.'
Damon’s body stiffened. 'She’s a human?'
That thought made him recoil. A human? The Moon Goddess paired a fragile human with an Alpha like him? That was insanity.
'No,' his wolf corrected. 'She’s a she-wolf. But for some reason, her inner wolf hasn’t awakened. It could be abuse. Starvation. Or something darker. Maybe… her wolf has been silenced.”
Silenced? Who would do such a thing? What reason could they possibly have to justify such  cruelty? Ripping a wolf from her other half, severing the sacred bond between soul and beast.  Damon couldn’t imagine a fate more brutal. More inhumane.
Damon raked a hand through his hair, his frustration mounting. He’d frightened her. He let her leave without food. And now, she was out there—alone, vulnerable.
'How do I fix this?'
His wolf growled. 'Fix what? 
You came here to seduce Marcy, ruin Alpha Edward’s plans, and leave. 
What changed? You want to apologize for being an ass and take her out for dinner?'
Damon scowled, staring at the darkened tree line in the distance.
[SFX: TREES RUSTLING IN THE WIND]
He wasn’t the kind of man to coddle or chase after anyone. He told himself to forget her, to move on. 
But the truth was, he wasn’t sure if he could.
Damon stormed up the stairs, each step heavier than the last. His blood ran hot, his chest tight with frustration he couldn’t shake.
She ran from him.
The copper-haired girl with those wide, frightened eyes and the scent that still clung to his skin. Like she wanted nothing to do with him.
Fine. Let her go.
He threw the bedroom door open without thinking—and froze.
Nora was already there, draped across his bed like she belonged, wearing nothing but a wicked smirk.
“I figured you’d need company,” she purred, stretching, letting her fingers trail across his pillow. Marking her territory. "Rough night?"
Damon exhaled hard, his fists clenching at his sides. The girl’s scent was still in his head, citrus and freesia, clinging like a curse.
But Nora smelled of want. Willing. Available.
A distraction.
That’s all he needed. That’s all this was.
He closed the door with a snap and stepped toward the bed, gaze dark and unreadable.
“Shut up,” he growled.

Talia jerked her hand away, but Damon's reflexes were top-notch, and he increased his grip, preventing her from doing so.
"What are you doing?" Talia asked in panic.
No one ever licked her before, and this was a scary Alpha! Would he eat her?
"Shush! Don't you know that our saliva has analeptic properties? I'm helping your wound heal. You should say, thank you, and not complain." Damon said and grimaced. Considering her sweet scent, he assumed that she would taste sweet also, but… "Why was it bitter?"
"I applied an herbal paste, so it didn't get infected," Talia said in a small voice.
Damon observed her face and noticed that she was beet red. Is she sick?
He touched her forehead. It was not warm, but he still asked, "Do you have a fever?"
"No," Talia responded with urgency. She had no intention to admit she was flustered because a scary Alpha came, hugged her (and was still hugging her!), and then he licked her hand.
Damon guessed that she didn't see a doctor. It was obvious that she didn't get proper first aid.
"Did you make the medicinal paste yourself?"
Talia confirmed with a nod.
He was about to lick her hand again and paused. "Is it poisonous?"
Talia was not sure if she should laugh or cry. "You should ask that before you put things into your mouth."
"I was treating your wound and I didn't see that there was medicine…" He grumbled, and then he licked her again.
"Can you stop doing that?" Talia protested. His coarse tongue touching her skin made her feel funny.
Damon looked at Talia like he had no idea what she was talking about, and then he licked her again.
Talia exhaled helplessly while wondering what game Damon was playing.
He was an important guest, an Alpha, yet instead of mingling with the elite of the Red Moon pack, he was huddled in the corner of the attic, holding her close to him, and licking her hand.
It didn't make sense no matter how she thought about it.
Is this the part where Marcy barged in and they all started laughing at her? Actually, if they only laughed, that would be good. Maybe Damon would join Marcy and the two of them would give her another beating?
Talia was anxious and she wanted this charade to be over.
"When are you leaving?"
Damon was not sure if she asked him about leaving the attic or the Red Moon pack. In either case, his answer would be the same. "Why are you eager to chase me away?"
"Because this is where I stay. You are in a fancy bedroom, with Alpha and Luna, and your future wife."
"My future wife?" Damon asked in confusion, like he heard about it for the first time.
"Princess Marcy told me that you would get married when she came here and…" Talia didn't finish, but Damon understood.
"She will NOT be my wife in this lifetime or in any next one." Damon said grimly.
Talia shook her head. "Maybe you should tell that to her, and not to me. Your relationship with her is not my business. Can you, please, leave?"
Damon was lost in her big honey-colored eyes that looked at him pleadingly and he wondered if he could leave. Could he? Yes, but only in one case.
"Come with me."
Talia was sure that her ears malfunctioned. She asked him to leave the attic before anyone can see them in this inexplicable situation, yet he wants her to join him? "What? Where?"
"I am the Alpha of the Dark Howlers pack. Come with me to my pack."
Talia's brain paused.
She thought that Damon had invited her to his room, to clean up or maybe to make fun of her, but now it seemed he was asking her to leave the Red Moon pack. With him. "Why?"

"I will make sure you have a room, better than the ones downstairs. I will get you clothes that fit, and you can eat anytime you want and as much as you want. For every scratch and bruise, there will be a pack doctor to take care of you and if anyone gives you a hard time, I will deal with them. No one will bully you in my pack."'Our pack!', his wolf added eagerly. Unfortunately, only Damon heard him.
Talia blinked. Now she was not wondering if her ears were tricking her, and if this last beating messed with her brain.

Or maybe something was wrong with him. Did he eat a funny fruit and was talking gibberish? There were some herbs that could make people say things they didn't mean. Or did he confuse her with princess Marcy?
It's not that Talia didn't think about leaving the Red Moon pack. Every time Anna and her henchmen bullied Talia, Talia thought about escaping, but she didn't know where to go. And here was an Alpha, offering her a new home with all the luxuries she ever dreamed of. Assuming that this was real and both of them were sane.
Talia wondered if this was a prank, or if she was imagining this whole conversation, or maybe she was sleeping and the Cinderella story mixed with her dreams because Damon definitely looked like a prince. A handsome prince that smelled of the forest and dark chocolate.
"Will you come with me?" Damon asked when his patience cracked.
"Why do you want me to come?"
"Because…" the words got stuck in his throat.
Could he tell her she was his mate and that when he sees her harmed, his soul aches? No. That would only freak her out.
Could he tell her that staying away from her was practically impossible? If she doesn't come willingly, he would kidnap her or maybe move in with her into this attic. Ah! He sounded like a creep to himself!
Damon was exasperated. All this would be simpler if she could feel the bond and the delicious sparks that make him feel alive.

"Because…" he repeated. "I feel responsible. You got hurt because of me, and it's not right. Let me help you. It will make me feel better." This was the truth. Part of the truth, at least.
"Do you take every girl who gets hurt back to your pack?"
Not really. But he is not the guy who would look away from injustice. However, he couldn't tell Talia that she was special either.
"When you come to the Dark Howlers pack, you will see for yourself that we accept everyone who comes seeking help without bad intentions. I promise that if you don't like it in the Dark Howlers pack, I will help you resettle at the location of your choice."
With his index finger, Damon made a cross over his chest where the heart was, to confirm his sincerity, but his silent promise had an additional clause how he would make sure she was treated well and she never wanted to leave.

Talia bit the inside of her cheek while considering her options.
One was staying at the Red Moon pack. Anna's bullying was escalating, and Marcy started picking on her also. Yesterday Marcy came to the attic and Talia got a beating for something she didn't do.
The second option was to go to the Dark Howlers pack. Alpha Damon said that in his pack people were accepted. Could it be worse than here? Probably not.
Of course, there was also the third option for Talia to leave on her own somewhere, but that option was scary and uncertain, and it will exist even if she goes with Alpha Damon.
Damon saw that Talia was considering it and he spoke with urgency before she could decline his offer. "Grab your things. You only need to say that you reject the Red Moon pack and Edward Redmayne as your Alpha, and the mind link will break. With that, you are free to go, and they can't find you."Talia shook her head. "I don't have the mind link. Alpha Edward's father brought me here as a child, and I never went through the ceremony."
"Good!" Damon exclaimed louder than intended. She doesn't belong anywhere, and he was more than happy to give her a home. With him. "Get your things."
"Just like that?"
Damon nodded. "Just like that."
Talia paused and decided to ask the question that was bothering her from the moment he came to the attic. "How do I know that you are not tricking me?"
Damon stood up and Talia felt chills surround her when his body separated from hers.
He extended his hand toward Talia, palm up. "Let me prove it to you."

  
Now that Damon has found his fated mate, how will he keep her safe?! Will Talia recognise Damon?! Will she trust Damon and escape the red moon pack with him? What will happen when Edward and Marcy discover Damon has found Talia?!
