A tornado took our house on a Saturday in March. The men who came to rebuild it are the reason my husband is still alive.

I know how that sounds. It sounds like they pulled him out of the wreckage.

They didn't. Curtis made it out of the storm cut up, but alive.

By the time those men first set foot on our property, everybody we knew was saying the same thing. Thank God. The worst is behind you.

We were all wrong. The close call hadn't happened yet.

They came the next morning, without being asked. Eleven men I had never met, standing in my yard at half past six with their tools, looking at the pile that used to be my kitchen.

Nobody sent for them. Nobody paid them. To this day, not one of them will take so much as gas money.

They stayed six weeks. They put a house up.

And about halfway through those six weeks, one of them, a man older than my husband, sat down across from Curtis and asked him a question nobody had thought to ask in 9 years.

That question is the reason he's still alive.

When the tornado came, I was forty miles away, at my sister's kitchen table with a cup of coffee.

Curtis had stayed home with Gus, our old brindle catahoula.

Mid-afternoon my phone started going off. Watch first, then warning. Then my sister's TV put up the radar, and the red was sitting just west of us, moving east.

I called Curtis. He answered on the second ring, and I could hear the wind behind him.

"I see it," he said. "Sky's a color I don't much care for. Gus has gone and crawled under the camper bunk again. Dog knows before the radio does. If it turns ugly I'll grab him and we'll get down cellar."

Twenty minutes later I called back. It rang through to nothing.

I called again. And again. My sister stood behind me with her hand on my shoulder, and neither of us said anything.

The call that finally came, a little after 5, was from a number I didn't know. Wayne Purdy, who farms the piece across the road from us.

"Marlene. He's out and he's talking. That's the first thing. He's cut up and they're running him in to get sewed up, but he's out and he's talking."

Then I asked how bad the house was, and for a second he didn't say anything. That was my answer.

"You'll want to come on home."

My sister drove. The rain quit like somebody shut a tap, and the sun came out before we were halfway there. That sun felt wrong the whole way.

They took me back to him behind a curtain at the county hospital. He was sitting up, holding a wad of red gauze to his arm, black dirt ground into every crease of his face.

Gus was the reason he never made it down cellar.

The dog was under the camper bunk and wouldn't come out, and Curtis is not a man who leaves his dog.

He says the rain stopped dead while he was still in there wrestling him, and his ears popped, and that's when he knew they weren't making it back across the yard.

So he got down in the aisle of the camper, put himself over the dog, grabbed the dinette leg where it bolts to the floor, and waited.

He guesses it lasted ten seconds.

The camper came off its blocks, rolled twice, and landed on its side eighty feet away, up against the trees. Curtis rode it the whole way wrapped around sixty pounds of shaking dog.

He says it sounded like standing under a tailgate while the whole world came out of it.

Then it was over. Rain on bare metal, and Gus licking his chin.

Wayne Purdy and his boy were in our yard before it quit raining. The camper door was against the ground, so they broke out the big side window and hauled him up through it.

He never felt the glass cut him. He saw blood all over the dog's side and thought Gus was hurt. It was his own arm.

19 stitches, elbow to palm.

Wayne's boy ran him in with a shop towel pressed to his arm, and the Purdys kept the dog.

They were still sewing his arm when a nurse came in to take his blood pressure. Routine, she said. They do it on everybody who comes through.

She pumped up the cuff, watched it, and frowned. Then she moved it to Curtis's other arm and took it again.

178 over 104.

She stepped out, and a few minutes later a doctor came in. Young. Polite. Tired around the eyes.

He asked if Curtis had high blood pressure.

"Nine years," I said, because Curtis was busy being sewed. "He takes lisinopril and amlodipine. Every morning. He never misses."

The doctor nodded like he'd heard that before.

"A day like he's had will spike anybody," he said. "I'm not worried about tonight. Tonight has a reason."

Then he looked at the chart again.

"The nine years is what I'd want looked at. High pressure doesn't hurt. It sits quiet. And then one day it takes the part of you that talks, or the part that walks."

He said it kindly.

Curtis allowed that it had been a day. The doctor didn't laugh.

"Follow up with his regular doctor this week," he said, and moved on to the next curtain.

Curtis heard all of it and none of it. He had a house in a pile, a dog at the neighbors', and a fresh row of stitches.

If you'd asked him that night what the doctor said, he'd have told you: follow up this week.

I heard the other part.

They let him go a little before midnight, and we stayed at my sister's. Curtis slept. I didn't.

We drove back out in the morning.

Half the road in looked like nothing had happened. Mailboxes standing. Daffodils up.

Then you came around the bend by the creek, and it looked like somebody had drug a harrow through everything, a quarter mile wide.

Our place sat at the end of it.

The house was a slab and a pile.

The chest freezer was out in the bean stubble, sitting upright with the lid thrown back. A bedsheet was wound around the top of the hackberry like somebody had tied it there on purpose. And there was a church bulletin lying in the yard from a town on the far side of the county.

The cellar we'd counted on was still there. Steps going down under open sky.

Curtis walked the slab once around and didn't say anything. There wasn't anything to say.

People stopped all day. Neighbors, church people, men Curtis had graded driveways for.

They brought coffee and gloves and chainsaws, and every one of them said some version of the same thing. Thank God. It's just a house. The worst is behind you.

I said it back to them. I believed it.

We picked at the pile till dark and made no dent you could see. Three boxes of things worth keeping, and a slab.

Curtis stood looking at it a long time before he got in the truck. Sixty-four years old, and starting from dirt.

Monday morning we drove out at first light.

We came around the bend by the creek, and the lane was full.

Buggies. Five of them, pulled off in a line along the fence, horses tied. Two flat wagons. And men all over our property.

I counted eleven.

Their settlement sits seven miles from us. I'd been waving at those buggies my whole life and had never once had a conversation with anybody in one.

They'd been at it a while. The pile that used to be my kitchen was already three piles. Lumber, metal, burn.

Two men were up in the split maple with a crosscut saw. A boy was hitching a team of draft horses to the trunk of it.

Curtis stopped the truck in the middle of our own lane, and we just sat there.

"Who are they?" I said.

He didn't know either. And Curtis knows everybody in this county.

The oldest of them came across the yard to meet us. A man older than Curtis, white in his beard, built like a gate post.

"You'd be the Tarrs," he said. "We heard. We'll get it cleared off, and then we'll see about a house."

Curtis asked who sent them.

"Nobody sends us. Word carries."

Curtis stood there with his arm wrapped elbow to palm and didn't know what to say. I'd never seen that before, not in forty-one years.

I hadn't cried yet. Not at the hospital. Not standing on the slab.

I cried then, in my own lane, with both hands over my mouth, watching eleven strangers pick up my life.

By afternoon there were more people. Neighbors, church folks, women from town carrying food. I couldn't even offer anybody a cup of coffee.

They worked until the light went. By dark you could see the whole slab, swept clean as a floor.

Then they loaded their tools, and the oldest one told Curtis they'd be back at half past six.

That was Abram.

They came back at half past six, like he said. More of them, even. Some days that spring we had eighteen on the place.

Abram Wiebe is seventy-three years old. He farms, and he's been framing houses since he was a boy. He ran that job the way Curtis used to run his own grading crews. Few words, none wasted.

Curtis tried to pay him the second morning. Abram said no.

So Curtis tried the long way around and offered to cover the lumber, the diesel, feed for the horses. Abram said no to all of it, and never once explained himself.

The most Curtis ever got out of him was three words: "You'd do it."

The sill plates went down that same week. Then the walls, one at a time, and the smell of cut pine over the whole place.

Curtis worked alongside them every day the stitches allowed. One-handed at first, holding and fetching, then more.

I did the thing I could do, which was feed people. The Purdys' kitchen across the road, two borrowed camp stoves, dinner rolls by the hundred. We ate off sawhorse tables in the yard, eighteen at a time.

Our granddaughter Nora, eight years old, our oldest boy's girl, came after school and appointed herself nail girl. Nobody argued with her.

And in the middle of all that, one of the young ones came across the yard one evening holding something little.

Nora's hospital bracelet, from the day she was born. It had lived in a cedar box in our bedroom, and the bedroom was scattered over half the county.

He'd found it out in the beans, thirty yards past the slab.

I carried it in my coat pocket the rest of the spring.

Somewhere in those weeks, I started seeing my husband the way eleven strangers must have been seeing him.

Around two every afternoon, Curtis would find a reason to come down off the ladder. Check the lumber. Study the plans. Sit a minute.

Abram is nine years older than my husband. Abram never came down.

I told myself it was the stitches.

And there was the cough. I'd quit hearing it years ago, the way you quit hearing a clock. That spring I heard it fresh, because eleven other men could hear it too.

It came out on a Friday evening after supper. The young one who'd found Nora's bracelet asked Curtis how long he'd had that cough.

Curtis gives everybody the short version of everything. That night he gave the whole thing.

Nine years, he told them. The cough came with his blood pressure pill. Doc says it does that to some people. Curtis figured it was a fair trade for staying ahead of the pressure.

They doubled that pill when the number crept back up. They added a second one three years ago when the first wasn't enough.

That's where I set the coffee pot down and said my piece. Salt has been gone from my cooking for nine years. He walks two miles every morning, rain or shine. He has never missed a pill. Not one.

You know where all of it got him?

158 over 96 the day they found it. 152 over 94 last week.

Nine years, two pills, three thousand mornings of doing everything right, and the number moved six points.

"We'll find the right combination," Doc keeps telling him. Nine years of finding it.

Then he told them the part I'd only heard once.

He'd been back to his own doctor that first week, like the ER doctor said. Doc didn't care about the storm spike. It was the nine stuck years he didn't like. He wants a third pill on top of the two.

Curtis asked for the summer first. Let me get my house up, he said.

So now there's an appointment the second week of July, a cuff in the truck to log every morning, and if the log hasn't come down by then, the third pill starts.

In nine years, it has never once come down.

Nobody said anything for a minute. Then somebody asked what was for dessert, and the table moved on.

Except Abram.

Abram was looking at my husband the way Curtis looks at a bad road.

He didn't say a word that night.

Saturday the crew knocked off early, and Abram didn't leave with them. He poured himself the last of the coffee, came over, and sat down across from Curtis at the sawhorse table.

I went on scraping plates, because men don't talk with a woman standing over them. But I can hear just fine.

"I'd like to ask you one thing about the pills," Abram said. "If you'll let me."

"Ask it."

"How long do they mean to keep adding to it?"

Curtis opened his mouth, and then he closed it.

Because there's no answer to that one. Doctors ask if you're taking it. They ask about dizzy spells. They see you in six months.

Nine years of waiting rooms, and I never once heard anybody ask where it ends.

"I don't know," Curtis said. It took him a while to say it.

Abram nodded, slow, like a man getting something confirmed he'd rather not have confirmed.

"I ask," he said, "because I watched it go start to finish, once."

"My brother," he said. "Isaak."

Abram said the fair part first. "I'm not going to sit at your table and tell you medicine does nothing. It does what it's built to do. I'm only going to tell you what I watched."

Isaak was the youngest of them, seven years behind Abram. At twenty-two he left the colony and went English. No falling-out, Abram said. Some men just go.

He drove a truck out of Fort Wayne and married a girl named Nettie. Came back for harvests his whole life.

"Same house, same table, same food, same blood," Abram said. "Right up to twenty-two."

At fifty-two, a company physical caught his pressure high, and they started him on a pill.

The pill got doubled. A second got added. Isaak took every one of them, and Nettie will tell you he never missed. The numbers came down some. Never enough. Never stayed.

The third pill came when Isaak was sixty.

The stroke came when he was sixty-one. He didn't live through it.

Abram went down and brought him home, and they buried him with their people.

I did the arithmetic where I stood, with a dish towel in my hand.

Isaak never saw sixty-two. Curtis is sixty-four.

After the funeral, Isaak's widow Nettie gave Abram a folder thick as a seed catalog. Nine years of it. Every reading, every dose change, every note from every visit.

"I read that folder more times than I can tell you," Abram said. "I couldn't make it add up. More medicine every year, and the number never following. I wanted to know why."

Then he said the thing I'd been half-thinking all spring.

"People figure we keep some old secret about health. We don't. We eat what our grandfathers ate and we work like they worked, and that's the whole of it. But none of that tells you why your brother's medicine couldn't hold him. That part, I had to go ask about."

So he took the folder to Dr. Hoeppner, who has doctored the families in their settlement for thirty years.

"It took me five years of asking to understand the answer. I'm not a doctor. I'm a man who buried his brother and wanted to know why."

Curtis sat there a while.

"So what killed him?"

"The stroke was the end of it," Abram said. "Not the start of it."

"Then what was the start of it?"

"Tell me what the cuff measures," Abram said.

"Blood pressure," Curtis said.

"It measures how hard the blood is shoving against the wall of the pipe it's moving through," Abram said. "That's all it knows. It's a gauge. And for nine years, everybody's been working on the gauge."

"I always figured it like scale building up in a pipe," Curtis said. "Old pipe, less room."

"Everybody figures pipes. That's the trouble. A pipe is a dead thing. Water pushes, pipe holds. A blood vessel is muscle. A mile of soft muscle, and it tightens and loosens all day long, on command. Room for the blood when the blood needs room."

He said Dr. Hoeppner had to tell him that three times before it took.

"The command to loosen up is a real thing. A molecule. Your body has made it your whole life, out of a lining on the inside of every pipe in you no thicker than a skin. And past forty that lining is worn, and it makes less of the command every year. The food that used to help top it up doesn't anymore.

"So year by year, the signal gets quieter. And a muscle that quits hearing it does the only thing muscle knows how to do on its own."

He made a fist and set it on the table.

"It does that. Now hold that fist till July."

Curtis looked at the fist a long time.

"And the cuff reads the squeeze, faithful as a scale," Abram said. "Tighter muscle, less room, heart shoves harder, number climbs. The gauge isn't lying. It's reading the top of the thing, is all."

Then Abram asked if anybody had ever told him what kind of high blood pressure he had.

"The regular kind, I guess."

"There's a word in Isaak's file. It'll be in yours too. Essential hypertension. I asked Hoeppner what it meant, because I figured it meant something. It means we don't know why.

No bad kidney, no tumor, no cause anybody can point at. Pressure that's just there. Essential, as in, it just is.

"That's the word they've been writing on men like Isaak for sixty years. It's medical speak for: we can't tell you why this is happening, so here's something to push the number down."

It got quiet.

"It's not essential. Nothing about it just is. It's a missing signal."

Nobody said anything for a while after that, either.

Then he looked at Curtis.

"So understand me. Your wife told us what those nine years looked like. The salt. The walking. Not one missed pill. So hear me: it was never the salt. It wasn't the walking. It wasn't your discipline.

"Three thousand mornings didn't fail, Curtis. They were aimed at a gauge. You've been fighting the wrong problem."

Curtis sat with his fist still on the table. Then he asked the only question left.

"So how does a man get the signal back?"

"First you need to see what the pills have been doing," Abram said. "Or the answer won't make sense."

"The two you take push through different doors, but it's the same move. They shove the muscle open from the outside, and the reading comes down some. That's the whole job.

The muscle isn't loosening, Curtis. It's being overruled.

"And understand, nobody's doing anything wrong. The pills can only force. There's nothing in them that was ever built to restore. Nothing in them ever goes and asks why the muscle quit loosening on its own. They don't know. It's not their job."

Curtis was quiet a long time.

"Here's the part that took me longest," Abram said.

"Your muscle and those pills are in a contest of strength. The pill pries. The muscle grips. And the muscle is not tired. Add a second pill, you've added a second pry-bar to the same grip.

The third one's a third pry-bar. That's all the ladder ever was.

"That's what they mean when they say a man's pressure is resistant. It doesn't mean his body is fighting the medicine. It means the medicine is fighting his body, and his body is winning.

"Isaak was on three pry-bars. In nine years, his grip never got tired once."

Curtis didn't say anything to that.

"The signal is different," Abram said. "It doesn't join the contest. It doesn't out-pull anything. It goes to the muscle and gives the order, and a muscle that gets the order lets go on its own.

A thing that lets go isn't being held open. It's just open.

"Force fights the clench. The signal ends it. And when the vessel opens on its own, the number comes down on its own. Same reading. Opposite reason."

"And the signal comes from where?" Curtis said.

"A plant," Abram said. "The makings of it ride in on what you eat, and the deep red ones carry the most of it. Hoeppner has proper names for all of it. Nitric oxide, and the red is anthocyanins. I just call it the signal and the color."

He was quiet a second.

"That's when my brother finally made sense to me," he said. "Same blood. Different tables."

Curtis asked what a man ought to be drinking, then.

"I'll show you tomorrow," Abram said, and put his hat on.

Sunday afternoon he came up the lane in the buggy, alone, with a flour sack on the seat beside him.

Flowers.

Dried whole, deep ruby red going on black, grown on high ground from seed his mother's family carried to the colony longer than anybody now living can remember.

"Jamaica," he said. "Hibiscus, they call it here. Every house had a jar of it. Nobody ever called it medicine. It was what was on the table."

"This is where the signal comes from?" Curtis said.

"This is the plant it comes from," Abram said. "The red in it is the whole of the point. That color is the compound. Drink it steady your whole life, a cup at a time, and the signal stays topped up. That's what our grandfathers were doing without knowing they were doing it."

Then he asked me for a white saucer.

I brought him one and he reached into the sack and spilled a small handful out on it. The dish went dark underneath them before he'd put a kettle anywhere near it. Deep ruby red, near black down in the folds.

"That's what it looks like when it's alive," he said. "Take a good look at it. You'll want to know that color."

I looked. Then he brushed them back into the sack and folded the top over.

"But starting at sixty-four, with nine years of clench to undo, that's a different job. Hoeppner showed me the studies, and then he showed me what's actually in a store box. A cup a day was always the right amount. That was never the trouble. The trouble is what's in the cup."

"They cook it down to nothing before it ever reaches the shelf. You steep it and you get pale pink water. That's the signal at a whisper. You need it at full voice."

He turned the sack over in his hands.

"And here's what it costs a man, and this is the part I'd want you to hear. He buys the pale kind. He drinks it every morning for a year, faithful. His log never moves a point. And he decides hibiscus doesn't work and he never comes back to it. It worked fine. He never had any."

"So where does a man get it at full voice?" Curtis asked him.

"Whole flowers, picked by hand, grown high, dried slow. There are people who still do it that way."

Then he said the part I should have listened to harder.

"Finding one that's real, that's the hard part. It took Hoeppner and me the better part of two years just to work out how to tell a real one from sweepings."

That night I did what anybody my age with a phone and a worry does. I looked it up.

I won't pretend I read medical journals. I didn't have to dig, either. Hibiscus, blood pressure, anthocyanins. It was sitting right out in the open, with university names on it.

Studies where they gave people hibiscus and the pressure came down. Real ones. More than I could count.

Abram hadn't been telling us a secret. He'd been telling us something with receipts that nobody had once mentioned in nine years of waiting rooms.

And the same search that showed me the studies showed me the other thing. Boxes. Hibiscus tea bags, pages of them, $8.49 and up, two-day shipping.

I ordered one before I went to bed. I figured one hibiscus was as good as another. I didn't even tell Curtis.

It came two days later. Red box, a flower drawn on it, "hibiscus herbal tea" in big letters.

I had it sitting on the table when Abram came in at noon. He read the box, front and back. Then he asked for the same white saucer.

He tore one bag open over it and tapped it out.

Pale. Pink going on gray, and fine as face powder. Nothing at all like what had been sitting on that same dish two days before.

I knew before he said a word. That was the point of the first saucer, I think. He'd wanted me to have something to compare it to.

"The color is the tell," he said. "The color is the medicine. If the color's dead, everything else in it is dead too. This was cooked before it ever saw the box."

He wasn't scolding me. "This is the hard part I spoke of," is all he said.

Then he told me what happens to a flower on its way to a box like that.

"Two things. First, that isn't the flower. That's what's left after the flower. The whole ones go to people who know what they're buying. A machine strips the rest, and the broken bits and the dust get swept up and bagged. Second, they flash-dry it with heat, because fast is cheap. Heat takes the color out. What you're holding is pale pink dust with a picture of a flower on the box."

So I asked him what wouldn't be pale pink dust. What I should have asked before I spent the $8.49.

He put up four fingers. Two years of asking, in four fingers.

"Whole flowers, picked by hand, and it says so on the label. Not 'hibiscus tea.' Not 'herbal blend.' If a machine stripped it, you're buying pieces of it.

Grown high. Above forty-five hundred feet, and they tell you where. A plant only builds that color when the sun and the cold make it defend itself.

Dried slow in the sun, never flash-dried. And if they won't say how they dry it, flash is how.

And tested for heavy metals, batch by batch, with the sheet posted where anybody can read it. Most of what comes in from overseas would not pass that test. If nobody will show you a lab sheet, there's a reason."

That night I went back to the phone with those four things written on the back of a receipt.

It went quicker than you'd think, because nearly everything fell at the first fence. Boxes that wouldn't say whole flower. Blends that wouldn't say how much hibiscus was even in them. Pretty labels with no lab sheet anywhere.

By the second evening, I had exactly one left standing.

Pipi Tea.

Whole flowers, hand-picked, said right on the label. Grown above forty-five hundred feet and they name the ground. Sun-dried slow, never flash-dried. Triple-tested for heavy metals, with the report posted batch by batch.

I read all four of those out loud to Abram the next day.

He nodded, slow, the way he does.

"I know that flower," he said. "High ground, whole, dried the slow way. That's how it was done in the colony. Some still do."

That was enough for me. I ordered it before supper.

When the bags came, I did the saucer myself, before anybody could ask.

Whole flowers, deep red ruby, and they marked the dish dry, the same way Abram's had. I put the kettle on and poured, and the water ran red. Not pink. Red. It kept going darker the whole time it sat, and when I rinsed the cup out it left a ring.

The next morning Curtis swallowed his two pills, same as always, and drank a cup of it alongside them. Then he went up his ladder.

I drank one myself.

At my physical last fall, my own number had come back 144 over 88.

"We'll keep an eye on it," they said.

I'd spent the whole winter not thinking about it. A woman who watches her husband get cuffed in an emergency room quits not thinking about it.

About twenty minutes on, something let go behind my eyes. That's the only way I know to put it. Like a hand I hadn't known was there came off the back of my neck.

Curtis felt it too. He didn't say much. He set the cup down and looked at it a second, then went back to work.

Now, I'm not going to sit here and tell you a hot drink makes your hands warm and call that proof. Of course it does. Anything hot does.

But that wasn't hands. That was behind the eyes, and it came a good twenty minutes after the cup was empty, and it came again the next morning, and the one after.

We still knew better than to make too much of it. Feeling steady isn't a blood pressure reading. The number would take weeks to move, if it moved at all.

I got into a way of doing it. I put the flowers in while the coffee was going, because it wants five or seven minutes and that's about how long I'm standing at that counter anyway. You can watch the color come up in the pot the whole time it sits. Then it's poured and waiting at his place when he comes down.

He said it was sour. I put a spoon of honey in it and he quit saying so. Before long he was asking me to fill a thermos before he left.

So we logged the cuff every morning, and we let the house go up around us.

The July appointment was twelve weeks out. We started counting.

The first week, the log read 150s, same as always.

Week three, Curtis wrote down 146 over 90 and stood looking at it. "Cuff's acting up," he said. It read near the same the next morning, and the morning after.

That same week, the mornings changed shape. He quit coming down off the ladder at two. The men noticed. Nobody said anything.

By week six he was writing numbers that started with 14 more days than not. Once, a 139. He circled it.

My own log crept too. 130s, sliding toward the 120s by June.

The house got done ahead of us. Roof by the third week of April, trim and porch railings behind it, and the first week of May the last of the crew drove out with the place standing painted behind them.

Abram went last. Tipped his hat to me, shook Curtis's hand, and told him he'd see him at the July telling.

The second week of July, we drove in to the telling.

Curtis handed over the log, twelve weeks of mornings in his square handwriting. Doc went down it a page at a time, not saying a word.

Then he cuffed him. Watched the dial. Moved the cuff to the other arm and took it again.

128 over 82.

Six points in nine years. Twenty-four in twelve weeks.

"What changed?" Doc said.

Curtis told him the whole of it. Abram, the brother, the signal, the flowers. And he set the bag on the desk.

Doc turned it over and read the label.

"What's in it?"

Curtis pulled a paper towel off the roll by the sink and tipped a few of the flowers out on it. Doc looked at the color a while. Then he looked back down at the log. Then at the color again.

He didn't endorse it, and he didn't wave it off.

"Numbers don't care how they got here," he said. "And this is a good log. Keep the pills exactly as they are, keep this if you're keeping it, and keep writing the mornings down."

It was Curtis who brought up the third pill.

"There's a prescription from March still sitting in the computer," Doc said. "It never got sent. Come back in October, and we'll see if it ever does."

My own recheck came first, in August. 124 over 78.

Nobody told me we'd keep an eye on it. There wasn't anything to keep an eye on.

In September, word came around that a family at the settlement was putting up a dairy barn. Curtis was there at half past six with his tools. Nobody had asked him. Abram had that right too.

Abram was up on the frame, seventy-three years old. Curtis worked beside him to quitting time and drove home in the dark, and I heard about every hour of it at supper.

October, Doc's office. The log had run 120s all summer.

Doc looked at the log, then looked at Curtis.

"That prescription from March," he said. "I deleted it this morning."

Then he said the thing we hadn't asked for and didn't see coming.

"And I'd like to try taking the lisinopril down. Half. Keep the amlodipine, keep the tea, keep the log. If the mornings hold through winter, we'll talk again in spring."

Curtis, being Curtis, asked him if he was sure.

"Bring me the log in March," Doc said. "The log will tell us."

So that's where we are. Two pills still, one of them half what it was. A red cup beside them. Every morning, same as always.

The house still smells like cut pine when the mornings get cold.

Nora's bracelet sits in the top drawer of a dresser that didn't exist last March.

And Gus sleeps on a porch that didn't either.

It's been almost a year since the sirens.

People still say the tornado was our close call. I let them say it.

But you know better now. The tornado was ten seconds. The close call was nine years long, and we called it staying ahead.

A man seven miles up the road had watched that same close call go all the way to the end, once. That's why he asked his question. And that question is the reason my husband is still alive.

I wrote all this down for one person. I don't know her name.

She's married to a man who's been on the pills for years. Maybe two of them. Maybe three.

He takes them faithful, and the number came down some, and then it quit coming down, and the doctor keeps talking about finding the right combination.

She quit salting anything years ago. He walks. He does everything right, and every year there's more medicine, and the number sits where it sits.

If that's your table, hear the thing nobody said at ours for nine years.

It was never the salt. It was never the walking. It was never his discipline, and it wasn't yours either. You've been fighting the wrong problem.

There are two roads from here. One you already know. The same contest, another pry-bar, we'll see in six months. That was Isaak's road.

The other one doesn't ask him to quit anything. It goes underneath. You put the signal back where it's gone missing, alongside every pill his doctor wants kept, and you let the log do the talking.

And if it's your own arm the cuff goes on every morning, this is for you too. Same road, same signal.

And hear this part like I'm sitting across from you: you do not stop the pills. You don't skip one, you don't halve one. Not on your own, not ever, and not because some woman on Facebook told you her story. And tell your doctor you're adding it, the first morning you add it, so it's in the chart in his handwriting and not just yours.

Curtis never stopped his. Every change in this story was his doctor's idea, made off a log, in an office. That's the only way it's done.

What we drink is called Pipi Tea. One cup every morning, alongside whatever the doctor has him on. Whole flowers, picked by hand, grown high, sun-dried slow, and the lab sheet posted where anybody can read it.

bodyText:
My husband has never once asked me for help in 38 years of marriage. 

Not once. 

So when he reached for my hand in the dark last February and said, "I don't know what to do anymore," I didn't know what to say back.

George has had type 2 diabetes for eleven years. 

He manages it well enough, takes his medications, checks his numbers every morning, does what the doctors tell him to. 

For a long time that was enough. 

But about three years ago his feet started giving him trouble at night. 

Burning, mostly. 

Sometimes what he calls the "electric zaps," little shocks that shoot through his toes without warning. 

And a deep numbness that he says is somehow worse than the pain because at least pain means something is still working.

At first it was just bad nights here and there. 

He'd get up quietly so as not to wake me, and I'd hear him in the kitchen at 2am, walking slow circles because standing hurt less than lying still. 

I'd lie there and pretend to be asleep because I knew he didn't want me to make a thing of it.

We lost a lot of things slowly, without ever deciding to lose them. 

The evening walks we used to take after dinner, just down to the park and back, nothing long, maybe twenty minutes. 

He stopped suggesting them and I didn't push. 

Saturday mornings George used to spend two or three hours in the garage. 

He called it his thinking time. 

One day the garage door just stopped going up on Saturdays and neither of us said anything. 

And the thing that hurt me most, every Sunday after church we'd stop at the little diner on Route 9, same booth in the back, same order every time, just two hours of talking. 

He stopped wanting to go because the walk from the parking lot had become something he couldnt trust his feet with anymore.

I tried to say something once. 

I asked whether maybe we should see a specialist, someone who deals specifically with this. 

He looked at me like I'd said something insulting. 

"I'm fine," he said, and walked out of the room. 

I didn't bring it up again.

So I carried it by myself. 

Watched him from across the room and worried and didn't say a word, because that's what you do when you love someone who's proud. 

You carry your worry somewhere they can't see it. 

I had never felt so alone in 38 years of marriage and I couldn't tell him that either.

A woman from my church mentioned a Facebook group for wives whose husbands had diabetes. 

I joined mostly out of desperation. 

And it became the only place I could say what was really going on, because those women had the same husbands. 

The same 2am kitchen sounds. 

The same careful silence they maintained around men who refused to be helped.

One night, after George had three bad nights in a row, I posted in the group. 

I said I didn't know wether to cry or scream, that I felt useless, that I kept buying things that didn't help and watching him suffer anyway. 

And a woman named Patrice, someone I'd never talked to before, sent me a private message.

She said her husband had the same thing. 

Same burning, same shocks, same stubbornness. 

And she said their podiatrist had told them something nobody else ever had. 

The reason foot neuropathy gets so much worse at night isn't just the nerves acting up randomly. 

Its a circulation problem. 

During the day, movement and gravity help push blood through the feet. 

When you lie down that stops, and fluid that's built up through the day redistributes, and that redistribution agitates nerves that are already hypersensitive. 

The burning spikes at night because the body's circulation system, which is already compromised in diabetic feet, loses its daytime assist.

She said what finally helped her husband was wearing soft compression sleeves on his feet overnight. 

Not medical-grade, not tight, but gentle consistent pressure to keep the circulation moving while he slept so the fluid didn't have a chance to pool and set off the nerves. 

Bamboo ones, she said, because his skin was too sensitive for anything else.

I ordered them that same night. 

I didn't explain what they were. 

I just left them on the nightstand with a glass of water and said they were something I'd read about. 

George put them on without asking questions, which is maybe the most he's ever trusted me without making me justify myself first.

I did not sleep that night. 

I watched the clock.

He slept five hours straight. 

I woke up and it was quiet and I checked the time and then I just lay there because I didn't know what to do with the silence except feel grateful for it.

Its been four months. 

He still wears them every night. 

The WORST nights, the ones where he'd be in the kitchen by 2am, have almost stopped entirely. 

Last week he asked if I wanted to go to the diner on Sunday. 

Just like that. 

Like we'd been going all along.

If your where I was, I put the link below. No pressure. Just in case it helps someone the way Patrice helped me.

P.S. They have a 60-day guarantee, so if it doesn't help, you're not out anything.

bodyText:
The night I caught my Alpha boyfriend cheating with my stepsister, I gave my virginity to a stranger with an intoxicating scent in the forest.
By morning, his mark was burning on my neck. I lay fully sated against his chest, still unaware of who he really was.
At that same moment, the Alpha King's palace went into a frenzy.
Servants scrambled through the halls after receiving a shocking mind-link command from their King himself—
"Prepare the Luna coronation immediately! I found HER!"
Tonight was supposed to be the night I finally gave my virginity to my boyfriend Alpha Ryan. On our first Mating Day, I wanted to reward the only man who didn't treat me like trash for being wolfless.
My heart was racing as I flung his bedroom door open. He was looking all hot and unclothed like I imagined.
But with another woman on top of him.
My younger half sister, Zara.
"What the-" I froze in his doorway.
Zara was straddling Ryan, facing me. When she spotted me, she smirked and moaned, dipping her head to nip at Ryan's neck.
"Oh yes. Just like that!" she breathed in his ear. Ryan grunted and lifted her up to roll over on top of her.
My stomach flipped. I felt like I was going to throw up.
Then Ryan noticed me and froze. "Avery," he breathed.
Guilt flushed across his face, but his hands didn't leave Zara's body. The room was silent for a moment.
"Zara and I just found out we were fated mates," Ryan's words hammered into my heart.
Fated Mate.
On Mating Days, werewolves over 19 could smell and recognize their fated mates.
The attraction between fated mates is irresistible. Once they marked each other, the bond would last lifelong. The only way to resist a fated mate was to mark a chosen mate before you met your fated one. That's what Ryan and I wanted to do tonight on our first Mating Day.
I knew I would never get a fated mate because my wolf seemed dormant. I could feel her there back in my mind. But no one believed what I said, and it became a joke amongst my bullies, especially from my sister Zara's little group.
"Wolfless freak."
"Pathetic human liar."
They would say these words to my face, believing that I was too weak to fight back without a wolf within.
And yet, I was with Ryan, the Alpha heir. He did his best to protect me; we both believed we were meant to be together. He had been the only light in my life.
But now he was taken by Zara.
How could Moon Goddess treat me like this?
"You choose Zara? Knowing she has been my bully for so long?" A sob was lodged in my throat, but I refused to let it out.
I hated that my voice shook as I stared into his eyes.
A flash of regret crossed Ryan's handsome face.
Zara snaked one arm around his neck and yanked him closer to her, smirking at me from the bed.
Ryan clenched his jaw, "Fated mates make each other stronger, Avery."
"So I was nothing to you?" The sob tore loose.
"Ave--" Ryan's face softened, and he started to rise away from Zara, reaching one hand towards me.
Zara reached up and intertwined her fingers with his, stopping his gesture. Her eyes gleamed at me from under her dark lashes.
"Ryan, Mating Day is the best time to have the strongest Alpha heir with your fated one…" She arched her bare body up into him.
Ryan swallowed, leaning back down to nuzzle at Zara's neck.
I could see the yellow flash of wolf in his eyes. When he looked back up at me, the man I had known was gone. Only coldness remained.
"Get lost now, human," Ryan's wolf growled past me.
Tears streamed down my face. I suppressed my sobs as I ran out and darted down the hidden trails into the old forest.
Where could I go?
There was only one spot I knew was safe, the place I always turned to when I needed to heal myself.
A quiet little pond hidden in the woods.
The water shimmered faintly under the moonlight. I settled at the edge, knees pulled to my chest, letting the cool moss beneath me soften the weight I carried.
I could hear the rasp of my breathing, thick with the tears in my throat.
Slowly, the sounds of the night filtered in. The breeze in the trees, and the rustling of leaves across the ground.
Then I heard a different, most sinister sound. The distant howl of wolves.
Of course. Tonight was the Full Mating Moon. The rogue hordes of unruly, unmated wolves would be more agitated on this night.
While it was unlikely anyone would find me here, it also wasn't safe. I needed to get back to the pack town.
I wiped my tears on my sleeve and was about to rise to my feet to head back when I smelled something, delicious and intoxicating.
A ripple of heat rushed through my body from the base of my spine to my fingertips. Desire slammed into my body, washing over me and leaving me breathless.
What was this?
I breathed deeply again. I needed more of whatever that was. My body craved it with every nerve and fiber.
While I was lost in the hazy, distracting sensation, I suddenly realized that this might be…the mating heat?
How is that possible? I thought my wolf was dormant.
No matter what it is, I need to go home now.
There was danger nearby, and I had no mate - not even a chosen one anymore - to share this heat with.
I shook my head, trying to clear the dizzying sensation. I managed to rise to my feet and started to make my way home, but the intoxicating smell kept coming towards me and getting stronger, as if it was coming from someone running towards me.
Was this what was triggering me into heat?
"Lads, look what we've found," a low voice suddenly spoke from the tree-line. "A female wolf in heat."
I whirled to face the man who stepped into the clearing. He was tall and lean. His face bore the stubble of a few days unshaven.
More strangers stepped from the trees. They wore rough denim and leather. Knives and nets hung from their belts.
They smelled sweaty, almost blocking the delightful smell from earlier.
They must be Rogues! I realized with horror.
"Looking for something, pretty?" a flash of teeth in the dark beneath dark, shadowed pits for eyes.
"No, I was just leaving," I could hear my voice shaking.
"Why leave? If you're looking for a mate-" the man inhaled a shuddering breath, sniffing the air pointedly, "and it certainly smells like you are… then I'm sure we have several young bucks who would be willing to help, right lads?"
Murmured approval rose. They were fanning out behind me now, cutting off my escape.
"G-Get away from m-me," I tried to growl. "I don't w-want you!"
Another man laughed. "Looks like we got ourselves a feisty one, lads."
The man lunged forward. I felt his fingers snatch at the hem of my coat, yanking me backwards towards him.
Tears started to well in my eyes as he grabbed at me.
"LEAVE HER ALONE!"
A voice cracked through the air like thunder. That intoxicating scent that had triggered my heat immediately enveloped me.
One of the rogues scoffed without even looking at who was behind him. "Back off, lad. Go find your own girl—"
"Wait. He's not…" another stammered.
The rogues all turned their attention to the man behind them.
I saw a figure, all in black, standing there. His height and broad shoulders emanated strength and power.
He looked even stronger than Ryan, who was already a strong Alpha, but I couldn't see his face in the dark.
"I said, leave her alone. Don't make me say it a third time," the man warned the rogues again.
"Heck, let's go-," The rogues stumbled back, muttering curses, and then fled away.
And then there was silence.
Now I was alone with him. From here, I could sense that he was in heat as well. I felt drawn to him like a moth to flame.
For one second, warning bells blared in my mind. Had I traded one pack of predators for an even more dangerous one?
Then he started walking towards me. With every step, the intoxicating smell became heavier, luring me in as we drew closer to each other.
"Mine," the stranger growled, his arms slamming me flush against his hard chest, sending jolts of electric heat down my spine.
Before I could react, his fangs sank into the skin at the nape of my neck...
Time stuttered past in gasps of breath and heat.
His lips and hands dragged wildfire across my skin, and lower.
I squirmed as his hands parted my clothing, and then moaned as he sank his fingers between my legs.
Already we had leaped past anything I had ever done with Ryan.
I found I didn't care. There was only this man. Only he mattered now.
The moon above danced in my vision as I lost myself in the haze of pleasure and sensation.
I couldn't get enough of him. Nothing had ever felt better. No one had ever touched me like this…
I was liquid moonlight in his arms as he undressed me in the darkness.
I unbuttoned his clothing, wanting his skin against mine.
His mouth ran across my body like he was worshipping me. The sounds he made as he touched me everywhere was lavish praise.
"Mine." He repeated in a growl, stroking my skin and listening to my pleasured cries as he moved behind me.
His hands were all over me, and I felt him pushing at my entrance. I spread myself further for him, I needed him so badly. The mating heat had set me aflame.
Pleasure crescendoed within me, somewhere a wolf howled.
We rested against each other after our first joining. He was strong and searingly hot as I leaned back on his chest and he slowly continued to move, our bodies locked together.
He pressed soft kisses to the top of my head, and then we found our rhythm again, mating again and again.
When we finally separated, it was only so that I could mount him from the top this time.
He kissed along my jaw as his hands grasped my waist and lifted me onto his lap. I rocked my body against him, feeling him in me.
His nails scratched down my back as he made sounds of approval beneath me.
He leaned up so his mouth claimed mine while his hands caressed every part of me, and he murmured sweet, prayerful praises into my skin.
I felt treasured and beautiful under his admiration.
When his head sank to my neck again, there was a sudden stinging of pain, followed by more pleasure.
I felt like I was going to explode with sensation. We moved together, crying out in dual, synchronous pleasure.
I didn't know who he was, but in the throes of heat, I didn't care. He was perfect.
I was his. He was mine. We fit together perfectly.
That was all that mattered.
I woke in the dewy grass in pre-dawn darkness.
My stranger lay behind me, cradling me in his strong arms.
I couldn't see his face in the shadows, but I traced the contours of his jaw with my fingers, gently.
Who are you? I wondered. Whoever he is, he's massively strong.
I couldn't believe my first mating had been with a rogue in the forest. It was hard to feel regret when it had felt so good.
"Thank you for protecting me." I whispered against his sleeping cheek, "And thank you for showing me pleasure."
I slowly pulled myself away from him and dressed, wincing at sore muscles and other places that were tender after what we'd done. I blushed a bit at the memory. It had been lovely, but now it would be a secret treasure I kept for myself, forever.
As dawn rose over the forest, I carefully left without waking him up.
I returned home as quickly as possible.
I could hear my family chatting loudly in the living room as I tried to slink silently down the hallway to my room.
"The Alpha's heir is quite the catch, Zara," my father was saying with a pride he never showed for me.
"Think of the prestige this will bring to our daughter!" my step-mom exalted. She had been the one who had called me a liar, accusing me of pretending to have a wolf and encouraging others to bully me.
You would think my father as Gamma, the military coordinator for our pack, would have seen this as an affront to his family.
Instead, he had loathed me for bringing that negative attention home. He blamed me for what he saw as the loss of our family's prestige.
While they all seemed distracted by celebrating Zara's mating with Ryan, I snuck up the stairs to my room.
Thankfully, no one seemed to have noticed that I'd been gone all night.
I was a mess from spending the night messing around on the forest floor, and I needed a shower badly.
When I undressed, I gasped at the sight of a bite-mark on my neck.
How could he mark me?
If anyone saw this mark, I would be ruined.
To be marked by a strange rogue from outside our pack without our Alpha's consent was considered treason. I needed to hide it.
With a bang, the door to the bathroom flew open.
"Didn't know you got home already, human." Zara stepped into the room with glee.
I tried desperately to hide the mark on my neck with my hand, but she noticed the movement.
"What are you hiding?" Zara strode across the room and pulled my arm down roughly.
"A mating mark!" She laughed cruelly.
"Dad! Mom!" Zara shouted to the living room downstairs.
"Please Zara, no!" I pleaded.
"The pathetic human got marked by someone, and she dared to hide it from us!"
Chapter 3
Avery's POV
"What the heck-" my father cursed as he stomped up the stairs.
My father and stepmother burst into the room. I tried to back away as they advanced on me in the small space.
Zara snatched at my arm and whirled me around so that the bite was more visible in the light.
My father took a look at the bite mark, stunned.
"This mark looks like it was left by a strong wolf," he muttered incredulously. "Who marked you?"
When Zara and her mother heard the word ‘strong', they stared at me with stunned and dirty looks.
I didn't want to answer, could barely believe it myself, but I had learned to speak when spoken to in this house.
"I don't know." I whispered.
"Where is he then?" His voice rose to a bellow.
"Probably still by the pond in the forest, but I'm not sure…."
"I bet he just ran off," Zara sneered, "I told you, a human like you would never be wanted by anyone."
The first kick from my father caught me off guard. My father was quite a strong Gamma, and I immediately fell to the ground on the other side of the room.
"How dare you say you know nothing after being marked!" my father bellowed. "I should've never accepted you into my family. I knew you're just destined to be a lowly scum like your mom!"
The second kick descended swiftly as I yelped and curled like a worm on the ground.
"This is the gratitude I get for raising you!"
I teared up thinking about my mother.
My mother is just a normal servant in my pack. She accidentally slept with my father while he was drunk and conceived me.
My father, as the gamma of the pack, never wanted a servant like her. So he angrily announced that she'd seduced him, and she was demoted to work as an omega slave in our pack.
The old Alpha, out of mercy, asked him to at least keep me and raise me in his family.
I was almost never permitted to see my mother, but I remembered her kindness when I sneaked a few chances to visit.
"Avery should be demoted to a slave too, just like her mom, since she is a scum who got herself marked and abandoned." Zara suggested to her father.
Zara had long hated that I was Ryan's girlfriend, wanting him instead for herself. Now I suppose she had gotten what she'd wished for.
"No daughter of mine will be a slave!" my father hissed. "First wolf-less, now this! I can't let you tread on my honor as the pack's Gamma anymore."
I flinched away from his kicks, but had long ago learned not to run. It would only make him angrier. I could feel my back welting under his blows.
Finally, he slowed down, breathing heavily. He leaned towards me, roughly gripping my jaw in his hand and stared for a long moment at the mark on my neck.
Then a cunning and cruel expression crept over his face.
"At the mating ball, find a man who will accept you, marked scum," my father growled. His fingers bruised my face with the force of his grip, "and if you do not, then it will be my duty to remove you from this world."
He had threatened to kill me before, but this time I could see in his flat stare that he meant it.
A knot of ice formed at the base of my spine. Fear and panic warred with outrage and anger within me.
I could not outrun him. I could not fight him. I had nowhere to go.
And the mating ball……
Our Silvermoon Pack had a tradition of intermarriage with Nightwolf Pack.
The Nightwolf Alpha must pick a wife from Silvermoon in every three generations and vice versa.
This particular mating ceremony was to be held for the young and unmated Nightwolf Alpha, Gideon, to choose a wife.
The rest of werewolves from both packs would participate and mingle to see if they too could find suitable matches.
It should be a fun time, but everyone was nervous about it instead.
Because Alpha Gideon was a cold-blooded murderer.
It was said that he had wiped a dozen packs from the face of the earth, their survivors scattered and packless.
In contrast, Silvermoon's Alpha was old and weakening.
I didn't think anyone in a strong and cold-blooded pack like his would want me. A dormant and marked wolf.
"You will leave this house for a husband, or you will leave it on a slab." my father punctuated his final statement with a backhand across my cheek that sent me reeling into the wall, and then left the room.
Gideon's POV
I woke from the best dream of my life to find my mate was gone.
At first, I didn't worry. I had marked her, she couldn't get too far.
But when I tried to reach out to her through our bond, all I got was a muted dead-end.
How is that possible?
My memories of the night before were so vivid. It hadn't been a dream.
Mate. My wolf had said. We'd caught the delicious scent of her, drifting to me on the forest breeze.
The joy I'd felt at knowing I was about to meet my mate. Nothing could have kept me from her!
I had run miles through that forest to get to where she was.
Then I saw her surrounded by rogue filth, and they were trying to take her from me!
The frenzy that awoke in me when my wolf realized our fated mate was in danger was lethal.
I had chased them away, which was better than they'd deserved. They had offered no real challenge to my wolf's dominance.
I had found her. Claimed her. Mated her.
The wolf-sense had overwhelmed all others. Every fiber of my being demanded I mark her properly. Make her mine, forever.
I sunk my fangs into her neck when my wolf released enough pheromones to make sure she couldn't feel the pain.
That mark should have been indelible. I should have been able to follow it for miles.
Now the bond connection dissipated as though it had never existed, and so had her intoxicating scent.
The worst thing was that we'd mated in the darkness, and I didn't even know what she looked like yet.
My wolf had been pacing impatiently at the back of my mind. Restless and concerned.
I searched the area for a while longer, then went home and recalled my Beta, Tegan, to my office immediately.
I explained the situation and asked him to find my marked fated mate.
Tegan was surprised to find out I'd marked someone last night.
My Beta cleared his throat, "What will you do if you find her? This mating ball with Silvermoon is an unbreakable tradition."
Knowing he was right only made his words more distasteful to my ears.
"I'll just pick a woman who wants to be my Luna nominally, but I will only mark, want, and love my true mate. I will make that clear before anyone dares to volunteer."
I would never honor an arranged marriage while the woman who was my fate mate remained a mystery.
Chapter 4
Avery's POV
A few days later I stood in front of my mirror. I pulled my nightshirt away from where my shoulder met my neck.
My bite mark was already healed.
That was remarkably fast.
I touched the smooth skin in disbelief.
There was now no visible indication of what had happened under the Mating Moon. I knew the mark was still there, but it was sealed inside and invisible to others.
If only I could reach out and find the man who had mated with me! However, since my wolf was dormant, I also could not sense my mate through the bond.
I had no way to find him, or communicate with him. I didn't even know what he looked like!
Today was the Mating Ball where the Nightwolf Alpha would choose his mate.
I needed to find someone to accept me by the end of today, or my father would kill me to save face.
It felt like an impossible task.
A commotion rose from down below, and I lifted my head from my knees, listening.
"Alpha Gideon is about to arrive!" I heard my step-mother snap.
"Finish the preparations." Zara's tone was tense and fearful.
Alpha Gideon was not someone anyone would mess with.
I pressed my hand over my heart, feeling it thud against my palm. I could hear it clearly in the silence of my dusty, still, bedroom.
It was time for me to leave, but when I stood and tried to leave my room, the door lock clicked loudly.
From the other side, I heard Zara laughing.
"No one want you anyway. You might as well just wait for death, dear sister!"
Gideon's POV
Being Alpha of Nightwolf pack means dealing with a large amount of bureaucratic nonsense.
Tradition was a venerable word that sometimes felt more like a venomous curse. I had long ago learned to face uncomfortable duties head-on.
Still, there were few obligations I despised more than this one to which I was headed.
It was the day of the mate selection.
I had done my best to distract myself from the distasteful task to come. Spread across the leather seat next to me were thick dossiers detailing the most recent reports on attacks throughout my territory. The ledger in my hands detailed my commands for troop movements, and where to place our scouts as the dangerous time of the dark moon approached.
Paperwork, unfortunately, was not enough to occupy my mind these days.
As my driver guided the sleek sedan through the dense woods, I watched swirls of mist rise above the trees. Thick bands of vapor arced up towards the distant sun and shattered into smaller puffs, drifting down the valley into which we were descending.
The motion reminded me of a woman, arching her back in pleasure off of the forest floor beneath me. She too, had shattered and disappeared.
"Still no sign of that girl from that night?" I snapped. It came out more harshly than I intended, and my Beta sitting across from me widened his eyes in surprise.
"Apologies, Alpha." Tegan replied carefully, "No new marked women have been reported in any pack I searched."
I tapped my fingers on the seat and frowned. Within me, my wolf was pacing in aggravation.
"Keep finding her. At all cost."
Tegan flinched at my response but said nothing as the car rolled to a stop at the Silvermoon ceremony hall. Behind us in the drive, more vehicles from my pack parked behind us.
I stepped out of the car, and straightened my jacket. There was a group of women standing near the door, eying me appreciatively.
Their scents were all shouting a mix of curiosity and fear. I saw a few dive out of my line of sight to avoid attracting my attention. Didn't they know that motion is what attracts predators' attention?
Foolish.
I knew why they were running though. I had heard what the other packs said about me, and the things I had done.
I couldn't care less.
But with my scary reputation, it was more difficult to believe that some of their cheeks were flushing already. I guess there were always lunatics who would take any risk if it meant a chance at power and status.
I spared no more attention to any of them while I strode towards where the old Alpha of Silvermoon was waiting.
"Alpha Gideon." the old Alpha nodded his head in greeting over our clasped forearms. "I am honored to welcome you to this hall."
"Alpha Leon." I nodded brusquely in return, suddenly weary of these formalities. "I understand there was a rogue incursion here a few nights ago. I encountered some of them as well. Have you been able to make any way into locating them? It seems to be originating somewhere near your borders."
The old man's face took on a distant, wary expression.
"Oh, well now, let's see." Alpha Leon cast his rheumy gaze around the room, as though the answers were written on the far wall. "No, we haven't located that. We've had some other incidents that have required our focus."
Something in his tone gave me the distinct impression the rogue issue hadn't featured in his attention at all, much less been the center of his focus.
Irritation bubbled up within me with all the subtlety of a geyser.
"Then I suggest you focus on that," I ground out, "and stop causing trouble that I will have to clean up."
Silence fell over the ceremony hall. To the side, I saw Tegan's lips twitch. He knew how much I was leaving unsaid. Alpha Leon was lucky he'd only gotten a taste of my temper.
Even if I caused him to lose face in his pack, I couldn't bring myself to feel sorry about it.
If his pack had been patrolling properly, my mate would not have been almost attacked. My wolf might be less angry, and I might not need to claim her right there in the forest to calm my wolf.
If my wolf was patient enough to take her back to my packhouse, I wouldn't have let her just run away the next morning.
The awkward moment passed, and formalities resumed, but I had already checked out. I moved through the greetings and hospitality traditions - my mind miles away. The sooner I got out of here, the sooner I could resume my search for her.
In the middle of what felt like an endless parade of Silvermoon's eligible mates, one of the men in the crowd approached.
"I'm Cohen, the Gamma of the pack, Alpha Gideon," He said. "I am responsible for organizing this mating ball. You have been shown all the daughters of our highest ranking families. Which matches are you most interested in so far?"
Everyone went quiet in the room. I could sense expectation, fear and curiosity bubbling from the crowd.
I glanced at all the girls in the room and crossed my arms. No big difference.
"I don't really care. Anyone will do. Before I take volunteers, however, you need to know-" I paused. "I won't mark anyone I choose today. Prepared for that..."
"But the tradition-" Alpha Leon hesitated.
"The tradition doesn't force me to mark anyone. Just marriage," I cut his words before he could finish. "I have a marked mate already."
Now the room was filled with apprehension and wary glances.
I guess no one wanted to be picked under these conditions, by an Alpha known to be ruthless and a mistress to compete with in the future.
I was glad. It was better if no one volunteered anyways.
"So anyone will do," I turned to the Gamma who spoke to me earlier. "Maybe your daughter?"
"Oh-, She-uh-she's mated to Ryan already. So-" The gamma clearly panicked and stuttered.
"Father, how could you forget about Avery?" One of the girls walked to the front and turned around to face me. "Alpha Gideon, I'm Zara, the Gamma daughter of the pack. Forgive my father for neglecting to mention that I also have a sister."
"She admires you a lot, but she isn't here because she hasn't been feeling well lately. Maybe you'd like to meet her?" she continued, but there was something to her smile that made me feel like she was scheming something vicious.
Still, all women except my fated mate were all the same to me.
"Fine. Bring her to me."
Chapter 5
Avery's POV
The key turning in my door seemed obscenely loud.
When Zara stepped in, her face bore a haughty and pleased expression. My stomach sank. This wouldn't be good.
"Lucky you. You get to live a little longer." She informed me, dumping a pile of clothing onto the bed. "Your marriage has been decided."
So. They had found some unlucky but obliging wolf to foist me onto.
I tried to stir up an emotion, but all I felt was relief that I wasn't going to die.
Until she told me who it was.
"You will marry Alpha Gideon." Zara crowed triumphantly.
A flare of panic raced through me. My fingers trembled where they gripped the blankets.
It can't be! The man is ruthless! I might as well die anyways!
Zara looked at my pale face and laughed.
"Oh yes, you're the only woman he would agree to marry." She stepped to the bed where I sat and pulled me to my feet. "Get up, Bride-to-be! It's your lucky day!" she sneered.
I clutched at Zara's arm frantically as she hauled me up.
"Zara, if he discovers that I was marked, he will kill me," I pleaded.
"Actually, he won't mark you because he has a marked mate already. Who knows what happened to her! I bet you will enjoy all the drama." My stepsister laughed in my face, "And if he still finds out you were marked, just kill yourself before he tortures you to death."
Zara snatched my hairbrush from my dresser and began attacking the knots in my hair. She twisted my hair up into a pile on top of my head and secured it with a clip. Then she held out a formal dress from the pile of clothing she'd brought.
"Get dressed. Your fiancé is waiting, and he doesn't look like a patient man."
When she was done preparing me I didn't recognize the woman staring at me in the mirror. The draped shot silk of the dress clung to my body suggestively and the flashy beading and high neck of the collar sent the whole outfit into "trying too hard" territory.
I had always preferred simple styles that weren't so flashy. A dress like this was not something I would ever have chosen for myself.
None of this was.
You can feel sorry for yourself later. If you survive.
Zara surveyed her handiwork with satisfaction.
"Well, no one will mistake who you're intended for." She smirked, "Let's go."
I blinked at the sunshine as we stepped out of the house. Already it felt like ages since I'd felt the sun on my face and the breeze on my skin. I would have rejoiced more in my freedom if it didn't feel like I was headed to my funeral.
The path to the ceremony hall was lined with members of the pack. They milled about nervously, anticipation thick in the air. I saw Lillian, a friend of mine, staring at me worriedly.
"Avery!" Lillian rushed to my side as we passed, "Are you sure you want to do this?" she whispered.
I was touched by her concern. Lillian was one of the few packmates who'd never judged me for not being able to summon my wolf. She had been kind, and also brought me news about my mother when she could.
I wished I could tell her everything but that would only put her in danger as well. Although it felt like I had no true choice at all, I could choose not to endanger anyone else.
I hugged her tightly instead, trying to put all of my gratitude and friendship into the embrace and then kept walking. She dropped back, her eyes full of questions, but she didn't pursue me any further.
"Smart human " Zara laughed at me under her breath as we continued on, "keeping your mouth shut. Let the wolves do the talking, hmm?"
A familiar man stepped into our path. Seeing his handsome figure sent a pang of ice through my heart. Maybe one day it wouldn't hurt to look at him and remember how foolishly I'd loved and believed him.
Ryan squared his shoulders and stared at me with disdain as we approached.
"How quickly you've changed, Avery." He said in a snide, cold voice. "It took no time at all for you to cling to another Alpha."
There had been a time when Ryan had claimed to care about my well being. How quickly the man I thought I knew had changed.
And now he accused me of being false? Anger boiled under my skin at the double standard.
"Well you would know all about betrayal." I snapped back, "If anyone's trust was misplaced, it was clearly mine."
I glanced between him and Zara, "Congratulations, you two really are perfect for each other."
Ryan's jaw clenched and he looked away guiltily. I hoped he was remembering now all the times I'd shown him my loyalty. He would be lucky to get half as good from his new mate.
Zara snorted, "Oh don't let her fool you with that innocent pretense. She's no helpless victim."
She ran her fingers underneath the lapels of Ryan's jacket and leaned into him to whisper, "She was so desperate to get back at you that she allowed someone else to mark her!"
"WHAT?!" Ryan roared and reached for me. I tried to pivot away but he snatched at the high collar of my dress and yanked it roughly.
The delicate silk and bead work was no match at all for the Alpha heir's strength. My dress tore to my collarbone, exposing my neck.
"Wait-, the mark is gone-" Ryan questioned. "She healed this fast?"
Zara seemed to be surprised too, grasping my neck even harder.
Suddenly, the pain abated, and Zara's grip loosened. I looked up to see a large, dark form looming over us, silhouetted by the setting sun.
Something familiar about him.
I could not see his face at first, but his Alpha aura was menacingly palpable as he pushed Ryan and Zara away with a casual shove.
The stranger turned to face me, and I was struck by his handsome appearance.
I should thank him.
"Thank yo-" I started to say, but the man cut me off.
"So you are my chosen bride - " His eyes narrowed. "But why did I hear something about you being marked?"
