bodyText:
A tornado took our house on a Saturday in March. The men who came to rebuild it are the reason my husband is still alive.

I know how that sounds. It sounds like they pulled him out of the wreckage.

They didn't. Curtis made it out of the storm cut up, but alive.

By the time those men first set foot on our property, everybody we knew was saying the same thing. Thank God. The worst is behind you.

We were all wrong. The close call hadn't happened yet.

They came the next morning, without being asked. Eleven men I had never met, standing in my yard at half past six with their tools, looking at the pile that used to be my kitchen.

Nobody sent for them. Nobody paid them. To this day, not one of them will take so much as gas money.

They stayed six weeks. They put a house up.

And about halfway through those six weeks, one of them, a man older than my husband, sat down across from Curtis and asked him a question nobody had thought to ask in 9 years.

That question is the reason he's still alive.

When the tornado came, I was forty miles away, at my sister's kitchen table with a cup of coffee.

Curtis had stayed home with Gus, our old brindle catahoula.

Mid-afternoon my phone started going off. Watch first, then warning. Then my sister's TV put up the radar, and the red was sitting just west of us, moving east.

I called Curtis. He answered on the second ring, and I could hear the wind behind him.

"I see it," he said. "Sky's a color I don't much care for. Gus has gone and crawled under the camper bunk again. Dog knows before the radio does. If it turns ugly I'll grab him and we'll get down cellar."

Twenty minutes later I called back. It rang through to nothing.

I called again. And again. My sister stood behind me with her hand on my shoulder, and neither of us said anything.

The call that finally came, a little after 5, was from a number I didn't know. Wayne Purdy, who farms the piece across the road from us.

"Marlene. He's out and he's talking. That's the first thing. He's cut up and they're running him in to get sewed up, but he's out and he's talking."

Then I asked how bad the house was, and for a second he didn't say anything. That was my answer.

"You'll want to come on home."

My sister drove. The rain quit like somebody shut a tap, and the sun came out before we were halfway there. That sun felt wrong the whole way.

They took me back to him behind a curtain at the county hospital. He was sitting up, holding a wad of red gauze to his arm, black dirt ground into every crease of his face.

Gus was the reason he never made it down cellar.

The dog was under the camper bunk and wouldn't come out, and Curtis is not a man who leaves his dog.

He says the rain stopped dead while he was still in there wrestling him, and his ears popped, and that's when he knew they weren't making it back across the yard.

So he got down in the aisle of the camper, put himself over the dog, grabbed the dinette leg where it bolts to the floor, and waited.

He guesses it lasted ten seconds.

The camper came off its blocks, rolled twice, and landed on its side eighty feet away, up against the trees. Curtis rode it the whole way wrapped around sixty pounds of shaking dog.

He says it sounded like standing under a tailgate while the whole world came out of it.

Then it was over. Rain on bare metal, and Gus licking his chin.

Wayne Purdy and his boy were in our yard before it quit raining. The camper door was against the ground, so they broke out the big side window and hauled him up through it.

He never felt the glass cut him. He saw blood all over the dog's side and thought Gus was hurt. It was his own arm.

19 stitches, elbow to palm.

Wayne's boy ran him in with a shop towel pressed to his arm, and the Purdys kept the dog.

They were still sewing his arm when a nurse came in to take his blood pressure. Routine, she said. They do it on everybody who comes through.

She pumped up the cuff, watched it, and frowned. Then she moved it to Curtis's other arm and took it again.

178 over 104.

She stepped out, and a few minutes later a doctor came in. Young. Polite. Tired around the eyes.

He asked if Curtis had high blood pressure.

"Nine years," I said, because Curtis was busy being sewed. "He takes lisinopril and amlodipine. Every morning. He never misses."

The doctor nodded like he'd heard that before.

"A day like he's had will spike anybody," he said. "I'm not worried about tonight. Tonight has a reason."

Then he looked at the chart again.

"The nine years is what I'd want looked at. High pressure doesn't hurt. It sits quiet. And then one day it takes the part of you that talks, or the part that walks."

He said it kindly.

Curtis allowed that it had been a day. The doctor didn't laugh.

"Follow up with his regular doctor this week," he said, and moved on to the next curtain.

Curtis heard all of it and none of it. He had a house in a pile, a dog at the neighbors', and a fresh row of stitches.

If you'd asked him that night what the doctor said, he'd have told you: follow up this week.

I heard the other part.

They let him go a little before midnight, and we stayed at my sister's. Curtis slept. I didn't.

We drove back out in the morning.

Half the road in looked like nothing had happened. Mailboxes standing. Daffodils up.

Then you came around the bend by the creek, and it looked like somebody had drug a harrow through everything, a quarter mile wide.

Our place sat at the end of it.

The house was a slab and a pile.

The chest freezer was out in the bean stubble, sitting upright with the lid thrown back. A bedsheet was wound around the top of the hackberry like somebody had tied it there on purpose. And there was a church bulletin lying in the yard from a town on the far side of the county.

The cellar we'd counted on was still there. Steps going down under open sky.

Curtis walked the slab once around and didn't say anything. There wasn't anything to say.

People stopped all day. Neighbors, church people, men Curtis had graded driveways for.

They brought coffee and gloves and chainsaws, and every one of them said some version of the same thing. Thank God. It's just a house. The worst is behind you.

I said it back to them. I believed it.

We picked at the pile till dark and made no dent you could see. Three boxes of things worth keeping, and a slab.

Curtis stood looking at it a long time before he got in the truck. Sixty-four years old, and starting from dirt.

Monday morning we drove out at first light.

We came around the bend by the creek, and the lane was full.

Buggies. Five of them, pulled off in a line along the fence, horses tied. Two flat wagons. And men all over our property.

I counted eleven.

Their settlement sits seven miles from us. I'd been waving at those buggies my whole life and had never once had a conversation with anybody in one.

They'd been at it a while. The pile that used to be my kitchen was already three piles. Lumber, metal, burn.

Two men were up in the split maple with a crosscut saw. A boy was hitching a team of draft horses to the trunk of it.

Curtis stopped the truck in the middle of our own lane, and we just sat there.

"Who are they?" I said.

He didn't know either. And Curtis knows everybody in this county.

The oldest of them came across the yard to meet us. A man older than Curtis, white in his beard, built like a gate post.

"You'd be the Tarrs," he said. "We heard. We'll get it cleared off, and then we'll see about a house."

Curtis asked who sent them.

"Nobody sends us. Word carries."

Curtis stood there with his arm wrapped elbow to palm and didn't know what to say. I'd never seen that before, not in forty-one years.

I hadn't cried yet. Not at the hospital. Not standing on the slab.

I cried then, in my own lane, with both hands over my mouth, watching eleven strangers pick up my life.

By afternoon there were more people. Neighbors, church folks, women from town carrying food. I couldn't even offer anybody a cup of coffee.

They worked until the light went. By dark you could see the whole slab, swept clean as a floor.

Then they loaded their tools, and the oldest one told Curtis they'd be back at half past six.

That was Abram.

They came back at half past six, like he said. More of them, even. Some days that spring we had eighteen on the place.

Abram Wiebe is seventy-three years old. He farms, and he's been framing houses since he was a boy. He ran that job the way Curtis used to run his own grading crews. Few words, none wasted.

Curtis tried to pay him the second morning. Abram said no.

So Curtis tried the long way around and offered to cover the lumber, the diesel, feed for the horses. Abram said no to all of it, and never once explained himself.

The most Curtis ever got out of him was three words: "You'd do it."

The sill plates went down that same week. Then the walls, one at a time, and the smell of cut pine over the whole place.

Curtis worked alongside them every day the stitches allowed. One-handed at first, holding and fetching, then more.

I did the thing I could do, which was feed people. The Purdys' kitchen across the road, two borrowed camp stoves, dinner rolls by the hundred. We ate off sawhorse tables in the yard, eighteen at a time.

Our granddaughter Nora, eight years old, our oldest boy's girl, came after school and appointed herself nail girl. Nobody argued with her.

And in the middle of all that, one of the young ones came across the yard one evening holding something little.

Nora's hospital bracelet, from the day she was born. It had lived in a cedar box in our bedroom, and the bedroom was scattered over half the county.

He'd found it out in the beans, thirty yards past the slab.

I carried it in my coat pocket the rest of the spring.

Somewhere in those weeks, I started seeing my husband the way eleven strangers must have been seeing him.

Around two every afternoon, Curtis would find a reason to come down off the ladder. Check the lumber. Study the plans. Sit a minute.

Abram is nine years older than my husband. Abram never came down.

I told myself it was the stitches.

And there was the cough. I'd quit hearing it years ago, the way you quit hearing a clock. That spring I heard it fresh, because eleven other men could hear it too.

It came out on a Friday evening after supper. The young one who'd found Nora's bracelet asked Curtis how long he'd had that cough.

Curtis gives everybody the short version of everything. That night he gave the whole thing.

Nine years, he told them. The cough came with his blood pressure pill. Doc says it does that to some people. Curtis figured it was a fair trade for staying ahead of the pressure.

They doubled that pill when the number crept back up. They added a second one three years ago when the first wasn't enough.

That's where I set the coffee pot down and said my piece. Salt has been gone from my cooking for nine years. He walks two miles every morning, rain or shine. He has never missed a pill. Not one.

You know where all of it got him?

158 over 96 the day they found it. 152 over 94 last week.

Nine years, two pills, three thousand mornings of doing everything right, and the number moved six points.

"We'll find the right combination," Doc keeps telling him. Nine years of finding it.

Then he told them the part I'd only heard once.

He'd been back to his own doctor that first week, like the ER doctor said. Doc didn't care about the storm spike. It was the nine stuck years he didn't like. He wants a third pill on top of the two.

Curtis asked for the summer first. Let me get my house up, he said.

So now there's an appointment the second week of July, a cuff in the truck to log every morning, and if the log hasn't come down by then, the third pill starts.

In nine years, it has never once come down.

Nobody said anything for a minute. Then somebody asked what was for dessert, and the table moved on.

Except Abram.

Abram was looking at my husband the way Curtis looks at a bad road.

He didn't say a word that night.

Saturday the crew knocked off early, and Abram didn't leave with them. He poured himself the last of the coffee, came over, and sat down across from Curtis at the sawhorse table.

I went on scraping plates, because men don't talk with a woman standing over them. But I can hear just fine.

"I'd like to ask you one thing about the pills," Abram said. "If you'll let me."

"Ask it."

"How long do they mean to keep adding to it?"

Curtis opened his mouth, and then he closed it.

Because there's no answer to that one. Doctors ask if you're taking it. They ask about dizzy spells. They see you in six months.

Nine years of waiting rooms, and I never once heard anybody ask where it ends.

"I don't know," Curtis said. It took him a while to say it.

Abram nodded, slow, like a man getting something confirmed he'd rather not have confirmed.

"I ask," he said, "because I watched it go start to finish, once."

"My brother," he said. "Isaak."

Abram said the fair part first. "I'm not going to sit at your table and tell you medicine does nothing. It does what it's built to do. I'm only going to tell you what I watched."

Isaak was the youngest of them, seven years behind Abram. At twenty-two he left the colony and went English. No falling-out, Abram said. Some men just go.

He drove a truck out of Fort Wayne and married a girl named Nettie. Came back for harvests his whole life.

"Same house, same table, same food, same blood," Abram said. "Right up to twenty-two."

At fifty-two, a company physical caught his pressure high, and they started him on a pill.

The pill got doubled. A second got added. Isaak took every one of them, and Nettie will tell you he never missed. The numbers came down some. Never enough. Never stayed.

The third pill came when Isaak was sixty.

The stroke came when he was sixty-one. He didn't live through it.

Abram went down and brought him home, and they buried him with their people.

I did the arithmetic where I stood, with a dish towel in my hand.

Isaak never saw sixty-two. Curtis is sixty-four.

After the funeral, Isaak's widow Nettie gave Abram a folder thick as a seed catalog. Nine years of it. Every reading, every dose change, every note from every visit.

"I read that folder more times than I can tell you," Abram said. "I couldn't make it add up. More medicine every year, and the number never following. I wanted to know why."

Then he said the thing I'd been half-thinking all spring.

"People figure we keep some old secret about health. We don't. We eat what our grandfathers ate and we work like they worked, and that's the whole of it. But none of that tells you why your brother's medicine couldn't hold him. That part, I had to go ask about."

So he took the folder to Dr. Hoeppner, who has doctored the families in their settlement for thirty years.

"It took me five years of asking to understand the answer. I'm not a doctor. I'm a man who buried his brother and wanted to know why."

Curtis sat there a while.

"So what killed him?"

"The stroke was the end of it," Abram said. "Not the start of it."

"Then what was the start of it?"

"Tell me what the cuff measures," Abram said.

"Blood pressure," Curtis said.

"It measures how hard the blood is shoving against the wall of the pipe it's moving through," Abram said. "That's all it knows. It's a gauge. And for nine years, everybody's been working on the gauge."

"I always figured it like scale building up in a pipe," Curtis said. "Old pipe, less room."

"Everybody figures pipes. That's the trouble. A pipe is a dead thing. Water pushes, pipe holds. A blood vessel is muscle. A mile of soft muscle, and it tightens and loosens all day long, on command. Room for the blood when the blood needs room."

He said Dr. Hoeppner had to tell him that three times before it took.

"The command to loosen up is a real thing. A molecule. Your body has made it your whole life, out of a lining on the inside of every pipe in you no thicker than a skin. And past forty that lining is worn, and it makes less of the command every year. The food that used to help top it up doesn't anymore.

"So year by year, the signal gets quieter. And a muscle that quits hearing it does the only thing muscle knows how to do on its own."

He made a fist and set it on the table.

"It does that. Now hold that fist till July."

Curtis looked at the fist a long time.

"And the cuff reads the squeeze, faithful as a scale," Abram said. "Tighter muscle, less room, heart shoves harder, number climbs. The gauge isn't lying. It's reading the top of the thing, is all."

Then Abram asked if anybody had ever told him what kind of high blood pressure he had.

"The regular kind, I guess."

"There's a word in Isaak's file. It'll be in yours too. Essential hypertension. I asked Hoeppner what it meant, because I figured it meant something. It means we don't know why.

No bad kidney, no tumor, no cause anybody can point at. Pressure that's just there. Essential, as in, it just is.

"That's the word they've been writing on men like Isaak for sixty years. It's medical speak for: we can't tell you why this is happening, so here's something to push the number down."

It got quiet.

"It's not essential. Nothing about it just is. It's a missing signal."

Nobody said anything for a while after that, either.

Then he looked at Curtis.

"So understand me. Your wife told us what those nine years looked like. The salt. The walking. Not one missed pill. So hear me: it was never the salt. It wasn't the walking. It wasn't your discipline.

"Three thousand mornings didn't fail, Curtis. They were aimed at a gauge. You've been fighting the wrong problem."

Curtis sat with his fist still on the table. Then he asked the only question left.

"So how does a man get the signal back?"

"First you need to see what the pills have been doing," Abram said. "Or the answer won't make sense."

"The two you take push through different doors, but it's the same move. They shove the muscle open from the outside, and the reading comes down some. That's the whole job.

The muscle isn't loosening, Curtis. It's being overruled.

"And understand, nobody's doing anything wrong. The pills can only force. There's nothing in them that was ever built to restore. Nothing in them ever goes and asks why the muscle quit loosening on its own. They don't know. It's not their job."

Curtis was quiet a long time.

"Here's the part that took me longest," Abram said.

"Your muscle and those pills are in a contest of strength. The pill pries. The muscle grips. And the muscle is not tired. Add a second pill, you've added a second pry-bar to the same grip.

The third one's a third pry-bar. That's all the ladder ever was.

"That's what they mean when they say a man's pressure is resistant. It doesn't mean his body is fighting the medicine. It means the medicine is fighting his body, and his body is winning.

"Isaak was on three pry-bars. In nine years, his grip never got tired once."

Curtis didn't say anything to that.

"The signal is different," Abram said. "It doesn't join the contest. It doesn't out-pull anything. It goes to the muscle and gives the order, and a muscle that gets the order lets go on its own.

A thing that lets go isn't being held open. It's just open.

"Force fights the clench. The signal ends it. And when the vessel opens on its own, the number comes down on its own. Same reading. Opposite reason."

"And the signal comes from where?" Curtis said.

"A plant," Abram said. "The makings of it ride in on what you eat, and the deep red ones carry the most of it. Hoeppner has proper names for all of it. Nitric oxide, and the red is anthocyanins. I just call it the signal and the color."

He was quiet a second.

"That's when my brother finally made sense to me," he said. "Same blood. Different tables."

Curtis asked what a man ought to be drinking, then.

"I'll show you tomorrow," Abram said, and put his hat on.

Sunday afternoon he came up the lane in the buggy, alone, with a flour sack on the seat beside him.

Flowers.

Dried whole, deep ruby red going on black, grown on high ground from seed his mother's family carried to the colony longer than anybody now living can remember.

"Jamaica," he said. "Hibiscus, they call it here. Every house had a jar of it. Nobody ever called it medicine. It was what was on the table."

"This is where the signal comes from?" Curtis said.

"This is the plant it comes from," Abram said. "The red in it is the whole of the point. That color is the compound. Drink it steady your whole life, a cup at a time, and the signal stays topped up. That's what our grandfathers were doing without knowing they were doing it."

Then he asked me for a white saucer.

I brought him one and he reached into the sack and spilled a small handful out on it. The dish went dark underneath them before he'd put a kettle anywhere near it. Deep ruby red, near black down in the folds.

"That's what it looks like when it's alive," he said. "Take a good look at it. You'll want to know that color."

I looked. Then he brushed them back into the sack and folded the top over.

"But starting at sixty-four, with nine years of clench to undo, that's a different job. Hoeppner showed me the studies, and then he showed me what's actually in a store box. A cup a day was always the right amount. That was never the trouble. The trouble is what's in the cup."

"They cook it down to nothing before it ever reaches the shelf. You steep it and you get pale pink water. That's the signal at a whisper. You need it at full voice."

He turned the sack over in his hands.

"And here's what it costs a man, and this is the part I'd want you to hear. He buys the pale kind. He drinks it every morning for a year, faithful. His log never moves a point. And he decides hibiscus doesn't work and he never comes back to it. It worked fine. He never had any."

"So where does a man get it at full voice?" Curtis asked him.

"Whole flowers, picked by hand, grown high, dried slow. There are people who still do it that way."

Then he said the part I should have listened to harder.

"Finding one that's real, that's the hard part. It took Hoeppner and me the better part of two years just to work out how to tell a real one from sweepings."

That night I did what anybody my age with a phone and a worry does. I looked it up.

I won't pretend I read medical journals. I didn't have to dig, either. Hibiscus, blood pressure, anthocyanins. It was sitting right out in the open, with university names on it.

Studies where they gave people hibiscus and the pressure came down. Real ones. More than I could count.

Abram hadn't been telling us a secret. He'd been telling us something with receipts that nobody had once mentioned in nine years of waiting rooms.

And the same search that showed me the studies showed me the other thing. Boxes. Hibiscus tea bags, pages of them, $8.49 and up, two-day shipping.

I ordered one before I went to bed. I figured one hibiscus was as good as another. I didn't even tell Curtis.

It came two days later. Red box, a flower drawn on it, "hibiscus herbal tea" in big letters.

I had it sitting on the table when Abram came in at noon. He read the box, front and back. Then he asked for the same white saucer.

He tore one bag open over it and tapped it out.

Pale. Pink going on gray, and fine as face powder. Nothing at all like what had been sitting on that same dish two days before.

I knew before he said a word. That was the point of the first saucer, I think. He'd wanted me to have something to compare it to.

"The color is the tell," he said. "The color is the medicine. If the color's dead, everything else in it is dead too. This was cooked before it ever saw the box."

He wasn't scolding me. "This is the hard part I spoke of," is all he said.

Then he told me what happens to a flower on its way to a box like that.

"Two things. First, that isn't the flower. That's what's left after the flower. The whole ones go to people who know what they're buying. A machine strips the rest, and the broken bits and the dust get swept up and bagged. Second, they flash-dry it with heat, because fast is cheap. Heat takes the color out. What you're holding is pale pink dust with a picture of a flower on the box."

So I asked him what wouldn't be pale pink dust. What I should have asked before I spent the $8.49.

He put up four fingers. Two years of asking, in four fingers.

"Whole flowers, picked by hand, and it says so on the label. Not 'hibiscus tea.' Not 'herbal blend.' If a machine stripped it, you're buying pieces of it.

Grown high. Above forty-five hundred feet, and they tell you where. A plant only builds that color when the sun and the cold make it defend itself.

Dried slow in the sun, never flash-dried. And if they won't say how they dry it, flash is how.

And tested for heavy metals, batch by batch, with the sheet posted where anybody can read it. Most of what comes in from overseas would not pass that test. If nobody will show you a lab sheet, there's a reason."

That night I went back to the phone with those four things written on the back of a receipt.

It went quicker than you'd think, because nearly everything fell at the first fence. Boxes that wouldn't say whole flower. Blends that wouldn't say how much hibiscus was even in them. Pretty labels with no lab sheet anywhere.

By the second evening, I had exactly one left standing.

Pipi Tea.

Whole flowers, hand-picked, said right on the label. Grown above forty-five hundred feet and they name the ground. Sun-dried slow, never flash-dried. Triple-tested for heavy metals, with the report posted batch by batch.

I read all four of those out loud to Abram the next day.

He nodded, slow, the way he does.

"I know that flower," he said. "High ground, whole, dried the slow way. That's how it was done in the colony. Some still do."

That was enough for me. I ordered it before supper.

When the bags came, I did the saucer myself, before anybody could ask.

Whole flowers, deep red ruby, and they marked the dish dry, the same way Abram's had. I put the kettle on and poured, and the water ran red. Not pink. Red. It kept going darker the whole time it sat, and when I rinsed the cup out it left a ring.

The next morning Curtis swallowed his two pills, same as always, and drank a cup of it alongside them. Then he went up his ladder.

I drank one myself.

At my physical last fall, my own number had come back 144 over 88.

"We'll keep an eye on it," they said.

I'd spent the whole winter not thinking about it. A woman who watches her husband get cuffed in an emergency room quits not thinking about it.

About twenty minutes on, something let go behind my eyes. That's the only way I know to put it. Like a hand I hadn't known was there came off the back of my neck.

Curtis felt it too. He didn't say much. He set the cup down and looked at it a second, then went back to work.

Now, I'm not going to sit here and tell you a hot drink makes your hands warm and call that proof. Of course it does. Anything hot does.

But that wasn't hands. That was behind the eyes, and it came a good twenty minutes after the cup was empty, and it came again the next morning, and the one after.

We still knew better than to make too much of it. Feeling steady isn't a blood pressure reading. The number would take weeks to move, if it moved at all.

I got into a way of doing it. I put the flowers in while the coffee was going, because it wants five or seven minutes and that's about how long I'm standing at that counter anyway. You can watch the color come up in the pot the whole time it sits. Then it's poured and waiting at his place when he comes down.

He said it was sour. I put a spoon of honey in it and he quit saying so. Before long he was asking me to fill a thermos before he left.

So we logged the cuff every morning, and we let the house go up around us.

The July appointment was twelve weeks out. We started counting.

The first week, the log read 150s, same as always.

Week three, Curtis wrote down 146 over 90 and stood looking at it. "Cuff's acting up," he said. It read near the same the next morning, and the morning after.

That same week, the mornings changed shape. He quit coming down off the ladder at two. The men noticed. Nobody said anything.

By week six he was writing numbers that started with 14 more days than not. Once, a 139. He circled it.

My own log crept too. 130s, sliding toward the 120s by June.

The house got done ahead of us. Roof by the third week of April, trim and porch railings behind it, and the first week of May the last of the crew drove out with the place standing painted behind them.

Abram went last. Tipped his hat to me, shook Curtis's hand, and told him he'd see him at the July telling.

The second week of July, we drove in to the telling.

Curtis handed over the log, twelve weeks of mornings in his square handwriting. Doc went down it a page at a time, not saying a word.

Then he cuffed him. Watched the dial. Moved the cuff to the other arm and took it again.

128 over 82.

Six points in nine years. Twenty-four in twelve weeks.

"What changed?" Doc said.

Curtis told him the whole of it. Abram, the brother, the signal, the flowers. And he set the bag on the desk.

Doc turned it over and read the label.

"What's in it?"

Curtis pulled a paper towel off the roll by the sink and tipped a few of the flowers out on it. Doc looked at the color a while. Then he looked back down at the log. Then at the color again.

He didn't endorse it, and he didn't wave it off.

"Numbers don't care how they got here," he said. "And this is a good log. Keep the pills exactly as they are, keep this if you're keeping it, and keep writing the mornings down."

It was Curtis who brought up the third pill.

"There's a prescription from March still sitting in the computer," Doc said. "It never got sent. Come back in October, and we'll see if it ever does."

My own recheck came first, in August. 124 over 78.

Nobody told me we'd keep an eye on it. There wasn't anything to keep an eye on.

In September, word came around that a family at the settlement was putting up a dairy barn. Curtis was there at half past six with his tools. Nobody had asked him. Abram had that right too.

Abram was up on the frame, seventy-three years old. Curtis worked beside him to quitting time and drove home in the dark, and I heard about every hour of it at supper.

October, Doc's office. The log had run 120s all summer.

Doc looked at the log, then looked at Curtis.

"That prescription from March," he said. "I deleted it this morning."

Then he said the thing we hadn't asked for and didn't see coming.

"And I'd like to try taking the lisinopril down. Half. Keep the amlodipine, keep the tea, keep the log. If the mornings hold through winter, we'll talk again in spring."

Curtis, being Curtis, asked him if he was sure.

"Bring me the log in March," Doc said. "The log will tell us."

So that's where we are. Two pills still, one of them half what it was. A red cup beside them. Every morning, same as always.

The house still smells like cut pine when the mornings get cold.

Nora's bracelet sits in the top drawer of a dresser that didn't exist last March.

And Gus sleeps on a porch that didn't either.

It's been almost a year since the sirens.

People still say the tornado was our close call. I let them say it.

But you know better now. The tornado was ten seconds. The close call was nine years long, and we called it staying ahead.

A man seven miles up the road had watched that same close call go all the way to the end, once. That's why he asked his question. And that question is the reason my husband is still alive.

I wrote all this down for one person. I don't know her name.

She's married to a man who's been on the pills for years. Maybe two of them. Maybe three.

He takes them faithful, and the number came down some, and then it quit coming down, and the doctor keeps talking about finding the right combination.

She quit salting anything years ago. He walks. He does everything right, and every year there's more medicine, and the number sits where it sits.

If that's your table, hear the thing nobody said at ours for nine years.

It was never the salt. It was never the walking. It was never his discipline, and it wasn't yours either. You've been fighting the wrong problem.

There are two roads from here. One you already know. The same contest, another pry-bar, we'll see in six months. That was Isaak's road.

The other one doesn't ask him to quit anything. It goes underneath. You put the signal back where it's gone missing, alongside every pill his doctor wants kept, and you let the log do the talking.

The night Aiden stopped being invisible began with a mop and a neon flicker. He was supposed to be nothing more than background noise at the strip club—sweeping glitter and sweat into the drains while the world in designer clothes passed him by—until a single spin of his father’s old ring caught a light and changed everything.
He had twenty-four hours to save his life. His landlord had just slammed the door in his face. His car had been repossessed. His pockets were empty, and Vanessa’s birthday was tomorrow. The ring on his finger was the only thing that still belonged to him, and when he took it off to pawn it, the pawnbroker’s reaction told him the ring was never meant to be a scrap of metal. It was a name. A history. A trigger. The man pointed a gun at him and whispered a single sentence into a trembling phone call: “The Tiger is back.”
The word sent a jolt through the city’s underbelly more powerful than any siren. From the alley where his father died to the private booths of the Sapphire Club, the name carried weight. It pulled Cyrus Shaw into Aiden’s life like a tide. Cyrus was a man who moved pieces on maps Aiden had never seen, and when he asked to see the ring, Aiden handed it over because he didn’t yet know how to say no to what his blood demanded. Cyrus’s face shifted from curiosity to reverence. “Tiger,” he breathed. “It’s you.”
In a single evening, Aiden was invited into rooms that had no doors for people like him. Ben Jameson, the kind of real estate titan who could buy a city block and not look back, scoffed at him, then challenged him to fight. Aiden accepted. It wasn’t pride that pushed him into the ring in Cyrus’s basement—it was proof. If he could stand toe-to-toe with a man like Ben and win, he could stake a claim to the name sewn into his palm. The fight was brutal, old rules and newer hunger clashing in concrete light. Aiden moved like the kid who learned to fight to survive; his fists remembered a promise his father made in a dying voice. He walked out of that ring with a bruised jaw and Ben’s respect, and with people who would now answer when he spoke.
Cyrus gave him money, a car, and a job offer that came wrapped in warnings. “Keep your head down,” Cyrus said, but the city has a way of stripping secrecy. News travels on whispers and guns. The Tiger’s return rippled through Dominic Grayson’s world the moment Aiden’s BMW rolled past Club Cain. Dominic’s smile was a promise of violence; his poolside loungers were the throne of a man who measured conquest in bodies and brands.
Aiden was reckless by necessity. He wanted a look, a feel, a map of his enemies. Club Cain should have been a place to gather intelligence. Instead, it became a place where the past and present crashed into one another. He followed a woman he recognized—Rachel, Cyrus’s cool, unreadable assistant—into a back corridor and watched her move through Dominic’s den with an ease that didn’t belong to a secretary. She greeted Dominic like someone who belonged behind his arm; she passed like someone with keys to rooms Aiden couldn’t imagine. Then, as if the city wanted to spit him straight into his nightmares, Raymond Caster stepped into the frame.
The scar across Raymond’s cheek was a cut Aiden had seen in nightmares for eighteen years. It was the face his father asked him to remember while he bled in the rain. It was the man who had turned Aiden’s childhood into an echo. Seeing Raymond alive and laughing beside Dominic felt like the world had lied to him. Cyrus had told him Raymond was dead. Cyrus had said there were bigger plans. Somewhere in the flash of the scar and the curl of a cigar, all of Aiden’s promises collided—vengeance, identity, destiny.
Aiden moved. It was not a calculated step so much as the only motion left in a body that had been waiting its whole life to close that distance. Rage sharpened his focus. He thought, for one frantic second, that he would finally pull the ghost from memory into the now and claw his way to the answer he’d been denied. He pictured the ring catching sunlight on Raymond’s fingers as he ripped it off like a trophy and all the years of silence collapsing into the sound of his own hands.
Then a small sound made him freeze: the faint, unmistakable click of a gun being cocked.
He didn’t turn. The gun pressed cold and merciless into the back of his skull like the hands of the city itself. A voice, low and unfamiliar, whispered instructions he could not refuse. The threat was polite and final at once: Don’t move. Don’t make a scene. Don’t be a hero. The man behind him was not Dominic, not Cyrus, not Ben, and certainly not the boy who had once watched his father die. He was something else—an unknown with a trigger temperament and access to the exact moment Aiden had been about to ruin.
All the threads pulled tight at once. Rachel stood a breath away from Raymond, smiling like a woman who knew how to take advantage of being underestimated. Cyrus’s offices and promises hummed like a machine with hidden cogs. Dominic’s world smelled of power and rot. Aiden had a ring in his pocket and a dead father in his head, and the city had just closed the noose.
He could feel the cliff-edge of a choice: attack and die with a kind of honor, or stay and survive to fight another, smarter day. The Tiger inside him throbbed, an animal starved of justice and close to breaking free. But the muzzle at his temple was a cold, inconvenient reminder that some battles are won with patience, and others are lost with impulse.
For a moment, time sharpened into a single, thin line: the sound of a match striking somewhere down the corridor, a laugh from Dominic’s camp, the muffled clink of a bartender’s glass in an empty room. The man behind Aiden’s head tightened his grip just enough to make the point plain. “Don’t even think about it,” he said.
Aiden didn’t breathe. He didn’t blink. He didn’t move. The ring burned a secret promise into his palm: someday, this would be settled. Not with luck. Not with chance. With everything he had left.
The corridor held its breath. The city outside kept spinning. Spinal stenosis is not a bone problem. It's a lock. No injection opens it. No laminectomy opens it. I'm an anesthesiologist, and too many of the patients I put to sleep came back with the same burning legs.

My name is Dr. Harry Smith. Board-certified anesthesiologist, thirty-one years in the operating rooms of a major teaching hospital in Columbus, Ohio.

People ask what an anesthesiologist knows about backs. Fair question. The surgeon sees your canal once, on a screen. I was the last voice thousands of patients heard before the knife, and the face hundreds of them saw again, eighteen months later, in pre-op for the second operation. Different gown. Same burning legs. Nobody else in that building watches them come back. I do.

So let me show you the lock. Because spinal stenosis is not one problem. It's four, running in a loop. Surgery treats one. Here are all four, in the order they actually happen. An order nobody laid out for me in thirty-one years.

Step 1. The canal narrows. Bone spurs. A thickened ligament. This is what your MRI shows. This is the only step anyone ever operates on.

Step 2. Deep in your back, two to three inches down, the multifidus muscle locks into permanent spasm to guard the narrowing. But a locked muscle pulls the vertebrae closer together. The guard tightens the very tunnel it's protecting.

Step 3. That clamped muscle strangles its own blood supply. Oxygen can't get in. Inflammatory waste can't get out. The nerve root sits in acid. That's your burning legs. That's the numbness by noon.

Step 4. Starved of oxygen, the energy factories inside that muscle run their batteries to zero. And a dead battery cannot let go. It can't release the muscle. It can't calm the nerve. The loop feeds itself.

Now look at your own history through those four steps, the way I finally looked at my brother's.

That's why the gabapentin never fixed anything. It muffles step 3 for a few hours, and fogs you in front of your grandchildren. It never reaches the battery.

That's why they handed you a photocopied sheet of stretches. A sheet of paper, for legs that go numb by lunchtime.

I know what your house looks like right now. The cane by the door. The pillow behind your back in the recliner. Every room measured by where you can sit down.

That's why every injection faded faster than the last. Six weeks. Three. One. Fourteen hundred dollars each. It shrinks the swelling at step 1 while the lock keeps tightening underneath.

And that's why surgery disappoints so many. It removes bone from step 1 and leaves steps 2, 3 and 4 locked in the dark. The canal was wider. The patient still hurt. I know, because I met them again in pre-op.

You wouldn't fix a dead phone battery by tightening the case around it. You'd charge it.

You wouldn't widen a hallway while someone keeps pushing the walls in. You'd stop the walls.

So why does the system keep treating steps 1 and 3, and never the lock?

Because a laminectomy bills Medicare thirty to fifty thousand dollars. The surgeon bills. The facility bills. I bill. A fifteen-minute session at your kitchen table has no billing code. It generates zero revenue. So it will never be offered to you. Nobody in that room is a villain. I wasn't. But the machine is built to bill, and it will never hand you the thing it can't invoice.

I learned this from the last man I expected. A retired spine surgeon, thirty-two years, three thousand operations. No clinic. No staff. Just a folding table and a notepad. He drew me one diagram and said the sentence that ended my career as I knew it.

"Everyone in that room treats the space. Nobody treats the lock."

Then he showed me the part that made my stomach drop. The research is public. NASA published the mitochondrial science decades ago. A specific wavelength of red and near-infrared light, absorbed inside the cell, switches those dead batteries back on. The FDA cleared the technology for muscle spasm and pain years ago. It sat there my entire career. No rep ever walked it into our hospital, because there was nothing to prescribe and nothing to bill.

But here's the critical piece.

Massage alone breaks the spasm for hours, then the muscle clamps right back down. The cells are still drained.

Heat alone warms the surface but never reaches the multifidus two inches down.

Red light alone recharges the cells but can't get through a locked, blood-starved muscle.

All three together? Deep heat floods the strangled muscle with blood and oxygen. Pulsing massage mechanically breaks the spasm cycle. And that exact wavelength of red and near-infrared light recharges the dead cells. Simultaneously. One device. Fifteen minutes a day. At home.

That's the device he and his son, a biomedical engineer, spent years building. The Revornyn ThermaPro. A cordless belt. I examined it the way I examine monitors. Two to three inches of penetration, exactly where the multifidus lives. They understood the lock. They built the key.

I gave it to my brother Frank first. Sixty-nine years old. Forty years at a lathe outside Akron. The cane by his door had become a walker.

Week two, he walked to the end of his driveway and back without the cane.

Week ten, he was standing at his workbench rebuilding a carburetor. Three hours on his feet. The narrowing on his scan was identical. The bone never changed. He just couldn't feel it anymore, because the muscle finally let go.

Then Ruth. The woman who grabbed my wrist in pre-op before her second laminectomy and said, "Doctor, level with me. Will this fix me?" I said the words I was paid to say that day. Eight weeks on the belt, she walked into her follow-up without the walker. "I wish someone had told me about the muscle before they cut me the first time."

Now, the part I owe you as a physician.

If you've lost bladder or bowel control, or your legs are getting weak fast, that's not what I'm describing. That's an emergency. Hospital tonight, not this page.

And not everyone responds the same. Some feel changes in days. Others take weeks. The ones who've been locked for years take the longest, because there's more damage to undo. That's not my opinion. That's the pattern, over and over.

But here's what I need you to understand about timing.

A starved nerve doesn't complain forever. There is a point where the wiring changes, where this stops being a compression problem at all. It has a name in the research. It has a point of no return. I don't have room to explain it here, because I watched my own brother walk right up to that line.

So I asked a colleague to write it all down. An MRI technologist. The man who slides people like you into the scanner, sixteen years, over three thousand stenotic spines. He can show you what your scan shows, and what it can never show. The four steps. The NASA research. The exact protocol. And what it looks like when someone crosses that line.

Read his article before you do one more thing to your spine.

Luna Layla and Marcy desperately pushed Talia’s carriage to end her life once and for all.
“What if it doesn’t go over?”
“Then we push harder.”
“Push.”
“It’s moving.”
Talia was fast asleep when the carriage reached the edge of the cliff, while Marcy and Luna Layla watched in satisfaction as the carriage fell.
“She’s dead?”
“She has to be.”
“Now, the game is over.”
“Goodbye, worthless servant.”
“Take the carriage. We were never here.”
They believed Talia was dead, but as her carriage slipped off the road, it came into Alpha Damon’s view.
And seeing her in danger, he immediately rushed to rescue her.
“Stop the carriage.”
“Hold on.”
“Please, somebody help me.”
“I can’t reach you.”
“You’ve got to try.”
“I can’t reach any further, and you can’t stay there forever.”
“What happened?”
“I… I don’t know. I remember being in the carriage. Then everything went dark.”
Damon looked around.
The evidence suggested that it was not an accident.
Someone pushed that carriage.
“You think someone tried to kill me?”
“I don’t think. I just know.”
“You don’t look so good. Come. I’ll take you home.”
Talia did not realize that the man who saved her was Alpha Damon.
He offered her a ride in his own carriage, determined to get her to safety.
“I’m never supposed to leave the house. But today, Luna Layla suddenly granted my wish to go. I should have known. Something was wrong right then.”
“I don’t have any proof. But I truly believe they did this on purpose, because the Red Moon Pack always wanted to kill me.”
“It’s the coachman jumping off the carriage. It’s the crash. Everything.”
“And even if I told my pack members, they would never believe me.”
The moment Talia spoke about her pain, Damon’s wolf
Damon didn’t need confirmation.
He already knew.
No one in the Red Moon Pack could be trusted.
They all sat down in the dining hall, its gaudy opulence a reflection of Red Moon’s inflated ego.
Marcy arrived fashionably late.
Every detail of her appearance sharpened like a blade — shimmering blonde hair, a sculpted figure.
She was the type of girl who got what she wanted.
He was the most powerful Alpha in all of North America. Women threw themselves at him. Rulers feared him. He could seduce a she-wolf with a glance, or tear out a man’s throat just as easily.
Damon was untouchable.
He scorned the idea of love. Rejected every political match. Not a single potential bride, despite the many presented, could win his affection. None were worthy of being his Luna, the proud she-wolf to rule by his side.
Love was a distraction, an attempt to tame him. And Damon would never be tamed.
Still, there were those who tried.
Alpha Edward, leader of the Red Moon pack, was desperate to secure his political power. He invited Damon to meet his daughter, Princess Marcy, beautiful, cunning, cruel. She intended to make him hers.
Talia feared their union. Would Marcy succeed where so many others had failed? Would Marcy’s cruelty only intensify as Luna to such a powerful Alpha?
The moment Alpha Damon stepped onto Red Moon Pack grounds with his mated Betas, Caden and Maya, something felt off. His wolf stirred uneasily beneath the surface. Damon didn’t need confirmation; he already knew: no one in the Red Moon Pack could be trusted.
They all sat down in the dining hall,
Its gaudy opulence a reflection of Red Moon’s inflated ego.
Marcy arrived fashionably late, every detail of her appearance sharpened like a blade. Shimmering blond hair, a sculpted figure. She was the type of girl who got what she wanted.
Her friend, Nora, wasn’t as restrained. She eyed Damon with hunger, her gaze sliding over him like a caress. The rumors had reached her ears: about his appetite, his stamina, his size. She didn’t care that Marcy was supposed to win the Alpha’s hand. Nora wanted a taste for herself.
Marcy’s mother, Luna Layla, noticed the heat in Nora’s stare… and the flicker of fury in her daughter’s eyes.
“Marcy,” Layla said, too sweetly, “Why don’t you show Alpha Damon to his room so you two can… talk?”
While the Red Moon Pack celebrated Damon’s arrival, elsewhere in the kitchens, Talia worked until the sweat stung her eyes. All she could dream of was the scraps she might scavenge when the feast was over.
The other Omegas had different plans for her.
Anna, their cruel ringleader, stepped into Talia’s path, towering over her, “Listen up, slave.” The other Omegas giggled behind her like hyenas.
Anna’s lips twisted into a cruel smirk. “You’re going to deliver towels to Alpha Damon’s room.”
Talia froze. “Right now? But... what if he’s inside?”
Anna raised her hand, ready to strike. “Are you questioning me?”
Talia flinched, her heart pounding. Without her wolf, she was defenseless against the bullies.
Without another word, she took the towels and hurried off, every step dragging her closer to the Alpha’s quarters and whatever fate awaited her behind that door.
When Talia entered the room, she froze. Damon was in his room. But he wasn’t alone.
There was Marcy. On her knees. Between Damon’s legs.
Marcy whipped around, her eyes blazing with fury as they locked onto Talia’s. The insolence!
A jolt of fear shot up Talia’s spine. Retribution would be certain.
Damon’s eyes snapped to Talia.
“Stop!” he barked.
But Talia was gone, bolting from the room, too terrified to look back.
What Talia didn’t know, what she couldn’t have known, is that in that moment, Damon’s world had shifted.
Her scent. It hit his veins like a spark of kindling, igniting something primal within him.
Could it be? His inner wolf howled the truth within him, again and again. She, a lowly omega, a serving girl without a friend, was his fated mate?
Ignoring the mocking laughter of Anna and the others, Talia ran until she reached the attic, shoving the cabinet against the door before collapsing in the corner, struggling to quiet her frantic breathing.
'Is this it? Is this the day I die?'
Back in Damon’s room, Marcy landed clumsily on her backside as Damon shoved her away, his expression thunderous and unreadable.
"Who was that girl?" he demanded, hastily buttoning his pants.
Marcy knew exactly who she was. Talia. That wolf-less bitch. How dare she step into an Alpha’s chambers uninvited? And worse, if word got out that Marcy had been pleasuring Damon before he’d even proposed... she’d be humiliated. A laughingstock. Her reputation would be in shreds.
Marcy’s jaw clenched with fury. She should’ve done more than just beat the girl this morning.
But Damon didn’t notice Marcy’s simmering rage. He was too distracted, his mind replaying the moment when she walked in. How that intoxicating scent, freesia and citrus, had struck him. How his wolf had howled, wild and urgent. All he could think about was pulling her into his arms.
'Mate.' His wolf howled in confirmation.
He had never expected to hear that word. Never wanted to. And yet, the moment Talia entered the room, something inside him had shifted, changed.
His wolf growled inside him. 'Find her!'
Damon clenched his jaw. "Find her,” He ordered. “Now."
Marcy hesitated, she was confused. Why would an Alpha give a shit about a slave? Damon’s Alpha energy radiated off of her, making her lower her head. "Yes, Alpha Damon."
But Marcy already knew. She’d be doing much more than just finding her…
Meanwhile, Damon paced, running his tongue over his teeth, irritated beyond reason. His body still ached with unfinished release, but the thought of Marcy’s coconut scent made him recoil. It wasn’t her scent he wanted, it wasn’t her body against his that he needed.
It was her. Talia.
The girl with the smart doe eyes and copper-colored hair.
Damon prowled through the packhouse, inhaling deeply. Nothing. No trace of her scent.
His wolf snarled. 'Find her!'
'If she was really my mate, why did she run? Why didn’t she feel it too?'
'You had another woman on her knees in front of you,' his wolf sneered. 'What did you expect? That she’d throw herself into your arms?'
Damon scowled. His instincts screamed at him to chase, but logic held him back. He needed to stay in control. If he lost control and Marcy found out the truth, there was no telling what they would do to her!
For now, he would wait.
Later that night, Marcy returned to Damon’s chambers. She couldn't wait to tell him how she put the girl in her place, that wretched, wolf-less slave. But when she saw Damon standing there, Marcy forgot all about the girl.
And she would make him forget all about her too.
But Damon barely acknowledged her, his mind consumed by the memory of that freesia scent.
Marcy advanced, “Hello, Damon.”
Damon swiftly turned toward the door to see Marcy peeking in. He wondered if she even knocked, but even if she did, he probably wouldn't have noticed.
He never felt this distracted!
What if that was an enemy? That copper-haired girl already caused him to be weak, and he didn't even acknowledge their mate bond.
"Why are you here?" Damon asked.
"You look tense..." Marcy said while reluctantly putting her palms on Damon's firm chest.
"I can help you relax."
Damon's lips lifted into a half-smirk. "And how would you do that?"
"I know that nothing is confirmed, but technically, we are engaged,"
Damon observed her fingers as they moved slightly.
She felt him out over the thin fabric of his shirt.
He noticed a big ring on her right middle finger, an oval-shaped ruby with small diamonds surrounding it.
Damon looked at her almond-shaped blue eyes, straight nose, and full lips, and he confirmed that she objectively appeared attractive.
Damon felt his wolf's anger and dejection, but he decided to ignore it.
Unaware of the conversation Damon had with his wolf, Marcy inched closer to Damon and she smiled seductively.
"I can..."
Before Marcy could finish her sentence, Damon's hand landed at the back of her head, and he pulled her closer for a kiss, pulling her toward the bed.
“Wait,” Marcy breathed.
"Wait?” Damon replied, “What happened to were technically engaged? Get out."
Marcy didn't understand.
"What?"
"I said... GET OUT!"
The clock struck two. Damon lay restless, tension coiled in his muscles, his thoughts tangled in a torment he refused to name. The oppressive stillness of the Red Moon packhouse suffocated him. He needed air. Control. Escape.
He moved silently, intent on a midnight run—until it hit him. Freesia.
That intoxicating scent. Sweet citrus and wild temptation. His pulse pounded, his body moving before his mind caught up, drawn to the scent like a predator to prey. His hunt led him to the kitchen, shadow pooling in the corner, the hum of the refrigerator filling the quiet.
And there she was.
A small figure bathed in the cold glow of the open fridge, unaware of the danger lurking just behind her.
Damon closed the distance. Too close. Close enough that his heat ghosted over her nape, close enough that he could imagine how she’d feel beneath him. Soft. His.
"Mhm." His voice came unbidden, dark, possessive.
Talia gasped, jerking back—right into him.
She spun, eyes wide, body trembling. Fear. A scent he despised on her.
"Aw," she whimpered, rubbing the back of her head, shrinking under his gaze. Wrong move, little one. You’re not leaving.
She scurried sideways, but Damon was faster, his arm blocking her escape.
"What are you sorry for?" he murmured, his voice low, dangerous.
She stammered, refusing to meet his eye, her lip caught between her teeth—a sight that shouldn’t send heat curling in his gut, but damn it, it did.
He cupped her chin, tilting her face toward the light. Sparks. A wildfire licked up his arm, searing through his vein. His wolf howled, triumphant. Mate.
But that momentary euphoria crashed when he saw her bruise.
His grip tightened. Rage.
"What happened?" His voice was no longer smooth. It was a blade, sharp with violence.
She flinched. "I—I fell."
"Lies." His thumb ghosted over the mark on her cheek. It was shaped like—a ring.
Marcy.
His wolf roared inside him, demanding blood. Demanding vengeance.
"Who did this?" he growled.
Talia shuddered. "No one."
A lie. A plea. A desperate attempt to protect the monster who hurt her.
Damon inhaled deeply, trying to rein in the storm inside him, but her scent—the sweetness, the fragility—it wrecked him.
"I will not hurt you," he swore, his tone softer now, but she didn't believe him. He could see it in the way her body coiled, ready to run.
Then, she did.
Gone. Vanished.
She had run from him AGAIN, Damon couldn’t believe it.
Damon stood frozen for a second. Then—"Damn it!"
His wolf snarled. Find her.
Damon’s body moved on instinct, chasing the fading scent of freesia into the night.
Damon halted in the middle of the garden, nostrils flaring as he inhaled deeply, searching for her scent.
The freesia and citrus still lingered in the air, but it was interwoven with the overpowering fragrance of hydrangeas and roses, scattered wildly by the wind.
"Shit!" he cursed, his fists clenching. "I lost her. Why did she run?"
'Maybe because you scared the soul out of her.' His wolf growled.
Damon frowned. 'I scared her?'
'You grabbed her, cornered her, demanded answers... You think she’s not used to being mistreated?
And let’s not forget, the first time she saw you, another she-wolf was on her knees for you, and you barked at her to stop. Hardly a warm introduction, if I may say.'
Damon cursed under his breath. He hadn’t considered it from that angle.
The girl haunted him. Her wide, fearful eyes. The bruises marring her delicate face. The way she shrank when he spoke. It made something primal inside him snap.
'If she’s my mate, why didn’t she feel it? She should have wanted to be near me, not running for her life.'
'Maybe she doesn’t know you’re her mate.'
'Is she too young?'
'No, she’s small and malnourished, but she’s definitely over eighteen.' His wolf hesitated. 'The problem is... I can’t sense her wolf.'
Damon’s body stiffened. 'She’s a human?'
That thought made him recoil. A human? The Moon Goddess paired a fragile human with an Alpha like him? That was insanity.
'No,' his wolf corrected. 'She’s a she-wolf. But for some reason, her inner wolf hasn’t awakened. It could be abuse. Starvation. Or something darker. Maybe… her wolf has been silenced.”
Silenced? Who would do such a thing? What reason could they possibly have to justify such cruelty? Ripping a wolf from her other half, severing the sacred bond between soul and beast. Damon couldn’t imagine a fate more brutal. More inhumane.
Damon raked a hand through his hair, his frustration mounting. He’d frightened her. He let her leave without food. And now, she was out there—alone, vulnerable.
'How do I fix this?'
His wolf growled. 'Fix what?
You came here to seduce Marcy, ruin Alpha Edward’s plans, and leave.
What changed? You want to apologize for being an ass and take her out for dinner?'
Damon scowled, staring at the darkened tree line in the distance.
He wasn’t the kind of man to coddle or chase after anyone. He told himself to forget her, to move on.
But the truth was, he wasn’t sure if he could.
Damon stormed up the stairs, each step heavier than the last. His blood ran hot, his chest tight with frustration he couldn’t shake.
She ran from him.
The copper-haired girl with those wide, frightened eyes and the scent that still clung to his skin. Like she wanted nothing to do with him.
Fine. Let her go.
He threw the bedroom door open without thinking—and froze.
Nora was already there, draped across his bed like she belonged, wearing nothing but a wicked smirk.
“I figured you’d need company,” she purred, stretching, letting her fingers trail across his pillow. Marking her territory. "Rough night?"
Damon exhaled hard, his fists clenching at his sides. The girl’s scent was still in his head, citrus and freesia, clinging like a curse.
But Nora smelled of want. Willing. Available.
A distraction.
That’s all he needed. That’s all this was.
He closed the door with a snap and stepped toward the bed, gaze dark and unreadable.
“Shut up,” he growled.
Then he grabbed her.
Damon sat on the edge of the bed later, running a hand through his damp hair. The shower hadn’t washed away the frustration, nor the bitter aftertaste of what just happened. Nora was already gone.
He glanced down and saw a pair of torn panties near the foot of the bed.
Not Marcy’s.
Nora’s.
His lip curled. Perfect. Just another mess to clean up.
"You’re a damn fool." His wolf's voice slithered into his mind, thick with disgust. "Did that make you forget her? Did she feel like our mate?"
Damon clenched his jaw. No.
Nora had been warm, willing—everything he should’ve wanted. But it had been empty. Pointless. The moment his release faded, the hunger in his chest only grew sharper.
His wolf sneered. "I warned you. She is the only one who can satisfy us."
Damon growled under his breath. He didn’t want this to be true. He didn’t want to need the girl with the copper-colored hair.
And yet… he did.
If he was ever going to find peace again, he needed to find her.
His frail, elusive mate.
The Omega who kept slipping through his fingers.
The next morning, Damon contacted Caden and Maya through their mind link.
'Are you guys up?'
'We are now,' Caden grumbled.
They had an agreement—nights were private between him and Maya, and Damon only disturbed them if something urgent came up.
Maya’s voice grew alert. 'Did something happen?'
'Caden, come to my room.'
There was a pause before Caden responded. 'On my way.'
When Caden arrived, he gave the room a once-over before raising a brow at Damon. "You look like shit. Were you attacked?"
His gaze fell on the shredded panties discarded on the floor. "Oh. Never mind. Guess you had a long night."
Damon wasn’t in the mood for jokes.
He tossed and turned the entire night, plagued by nightmares. He saw the copper-haired girl trapped in darkness, shadowy hands choking her, bruising her skin. He clawed at an invisible barrier, screaming her name.
Except he didn’t even know her name.
"How did you feel when you met Maya?" Damon asked abruptly.
Caden’s grin faded. "Why? Is Marcy your mate?"
Damon rolled his eyes. "Just answer the damn question."
"Attraction, sparks, happiness. I needed Maya to be happy so I could be happy. I thought I knew what happiness was before, but after meeting her, I realized I’d been clueless."
Damon clenched his jaw. That wasn’t what he felt. He felt restless, furious, out of control.
"Did you ever think about resisting it?"
Caden looked appalled. "Why the hell would I? She’s the best thing that ever happened to me. I waited my whole life for her. Why would I reject her?"
Damon’s stomach twisted. "What if Maya was in danger because of you? Would you pick her safety over your happiness? What if the only way to protect her was to reject her?"
Caden frowned. "What kind of twisted scenario is that? I wouldn’t be happy if she suffered. Rejection would break us both, so I’d rather face danger together."
He eyed Damon sharply. "What’s going on? Did last night fry your brain?"
Damon exhaled harshly. "I don’t know what’s going on."
Caden shrugged. "Alright. We’re still leaving after breakfast, right?"
Damon hesitated. Could he really leave without seeing her again? Just one more time—to make sure she was okay, to confirm that the sparks weren’t in his head?
"Let me think about it.”
Caden studied his Alpha, his oldest friend. There was something Damon wasn’t saying. He could feel it. But he didn’t press. Damon would talk when he was ready, and when he did, Caden would be there. He always was.
He couldn’t have known Damon’s mind was consumed by the copper-haired girl, his true fated mate. Or that beneath his calm exterior, he was seething over the bruise Marcy had left on her skin. That cruel woman. His so-called betrothed. He could tear her apart if it wouldn't start a damn war. Though maybe there were other ways to destroy her…
Caden turned toward the door when Damon’s voice stopped him. “Could you look into Marcy for me? Anything we can use to discredit her: past scandals, secrets, whatever you can find.”
Caden nodded without hesitation. “Anything, Damon.” He slipped out, closing the door softly behind him.
'Are you thinking about rejecting her?' his wolf asked.
Damon sighed. 'I need to protect her.'
'Then keep her close. Don’t reject her.'
His wolf had explained that, without her wolf, Talia didn’t feel the bond. She wasn’t drawn to him the way he was to her. To win her, he’d have to do it the human way; court her, earn her trust.
But without the bond, nothing guaranteed she would stay and that terrified Damon the most!
Damon didn’t know the first thing about romance, but he knew one thing—no one could know she was his mate.
If Alpha Edward learned, he’d use her against him. She’d become leverage, a hostage. Damon couldn’t allow that.
After breakfast, Damon met with Alpha Edward in his office.
"I wonder if you’re aware of how your Omegas are treated," Damon said.
Alpha Edward frowned. "Elaborate."
"Do they get paid? Fed? Protected?"
Edward bristled. “We provide accommodations, three meals a day. They have access to the kitchen. We train them, discipline them if necessary, but no one is mistreated."
Damon leaned forward. "Then why did I see one yesterday, perfectly fine—and hours later, covered in bruises?"
Alpha Edward’s jaw tightened. "Disputes happen."
Damon smirked. "Then maybe you should have a chat with your daughter."
Edward’s eyes sharpened. "Marcy?"
"A Luna should protect her people—not beat them to a pulp. If my mate was ever treated like that—" Damon cut himself off, clenching his fists.
Edward narrowed his eyes. "I’ll speak with her."
Damon smirked. "I’m counting on it."
Later when Marcy entered Edward’s study, he cut straight to the point.
"How is your relationship with Damon?"
Marcy smiled. "We’re getting along well. I think he plans on making me his Luna."
Edward’s voice darkened. "Then explain why he thinks you beat Omegas half to death."
Marcy paled.
"What were you thinking?!" he roared. "You don’t beat an Omega when an Alpha you’re trying to impress is watching!"

"Do whatever it takes. Do you understand me?"
Alpha Edward’s voice was razor-sharp, slicing through the thick air between them. His hand slammed against the desk, the loud crack making Marcy jump.
Marcy swallowed hard, nodding fervently. "Yes, Father."

Marcy’s breath hitched. "I—I can fix it. I promise."
Edward’s jaw clenched. "You’d better. Find Damon. Make him yours. By any means necessary."
Marcy rushed to her room, slamming the door shut behind her. Her hands trembled as she braced herself against the vanity. That was close.
And it was all her fault. That lowly mutt, Talia. A constant thorn in Marcy’s side. Why would Alpha Damon, of all people, care so much about such a useless little omega? It made no sense.
After a deep breath, Marcy steeled herself. She wouldn’t fail.
She stripped off her dress, selected something more daring—plunging neckline, fabric that clung in all the right places—and touched up her makeup before making her way to find Damon.
She found him outside his room, speaking with his mated betas Caden and Maya.
"Are you guys going out?" she asked, feigning casual interest.
Caden nodded. "James offered to show us around the warrior training grounds."
Marcy barely suppressed her grimace. The training grounds reeked of sweat and desperation, two things she had no interest in.
Damon’s eyes were cold as they landed on her. "Can I help you, Marcy?"
She nearly flinched. His tone was ice. It was worse than anger—he was indifferent.
He found out.
The bruised little rat had reached his ears. Her father had been right. She needed to fix this—fast.
She smiled sweetly. "I was hoping we could talk. Just the two of us."
Damon glanced at Caden, who gave him a knowing nod before leading an eye rolling Maya away.
Once they were alone, Marcy stepped forward and, without hesitation, wrapped her arms around Damon’s waist.
He didn’t return the embrace.
Instead, his hands gripped her wrists and peeled her off him as if she were something repugnant.
"What are you doing?"
"I’m sorry," Marcy said quickly.
Damon arched a brow. "For what?"
She hesitated. Did she mean last night? Or the Omega? Or both?
"My behavior yesterday was… unacceptable."
Damon leaned back against the chair, his arms folding over his chest. "You came here to apologize. Do it without touching me."
Marcy took a breath. "I also want to fix things."
His brow lifted. "Fix what, exactly?"
She clenched her hands at her sides. Just do it. Give him what he wants. You can control him once you’re Luna.
"I wasn’t thinking straight last night," she admitted. "I said things I didn’t mean."
Damon smirked. "You didn’t mean what you said? About your limits? What you’d do?"
Marcy’s cheeks burned. "I mean… I said we needed to know we were heading toward marriage first. And we are. So… I’m fine with whatever you want to do."
Damon leaned forward, his smirk darkening. "Whatever I want?"
Marcy swallowed. "Yes."
"Undress."
She blinked. He’s serious.
With slightly trembling fingers, she unbuttoned the front of her dress, letting the fabric pool around her ankles. She stood before him in lace lingerie, heart hammering.
Damon’s gaze swept over her body, unreadable.
"All of it."
She hesitated for only a second before obeying. The bra slid from her shoulders, the panties kicked to the side. She stood bare, feeling powerful and vulnerable all at once.
Damon’s smirk remained. "Turn around."
She did. Slowly.
Gritting her teeth, she obeyed. Damon circled her slowly.
And then—
Marcy jolted as his palm connected with her bare skin, leaving a bright pink imprint on her skin. The sting melted into pleasure, making her whimper.
She arched her hips, offering more. But Damon stepped away.
She turned, confused, just in time to see him buttoning his cuffs.
"What?" she gasped. "What are you doing?"
Damon smirked, voice dripping amusement. "Parting is such sweet sorrow."
And with that, he walked to the bathroom, washed his hands as if cleansing himself of her, and left without looking back.
Marcy stood there, naked, humiliated.
He. Just. Left.
"That was fast," Caden teased as Damon joined them.
"Shut up," Damon replied.
Maya crossed her arms. "Did you get anything we can use against Marcy?"
Damon exhaled. "No."
Caden and Maya exchanged a look.
"She’s been careful," Caden admitted. "No photos. No proof of her messing around. Just whispers."
Damon’s jaw tightened. "Keep digging. Someone has something."
“We did find something else,” Maya said, holding up a sealed envelope.
Damon’s eyes narrowed. “About Marcy?”
“No,” Caden shook his head. “Another girl from the Red Moon Pack. A servant girl. With copper hair.”
Damon’s eyes widened, his entire body stilled. He snatched the envelope from Maya’s hand and tore it open. He couldn't believe his eyes.
His grip tightened, voice low and urgent. “We need to find her. The copper-haired girl. Now.”
"You don’t even know her name," Maya pointed out.
Damon clenched his fists. But I know her scent.
He turned abruptly. "I’ll be back in ten minutes."
Maya and Caden exchanged another look as he strode off.
"What’s gotten into him?" Maya asked.
Caden sighed. "Hell if I know. But I think we just found his weakness."
As Damon searched the grounds more desperately, he hatched an idea. Damon knew that as a guest he couldn't go anywhere he wanted, so he asked Alpha Edward to assign him an escort.
"Can Marcy accompany you?" Alpha Edward asked. He obviously wanted to increase the time that Damon and Marcy spent together.
He immediately contacted Marcy through the mind link and after a brief pause, he said, "Oh, sorry. She's busy right now. Can you wait a little bit?"
Damon guessed that Marcy sulked after he left her hanging in his room. That made him feel good.
Damon didn't care who accompanied him. He had no clear goal in mind and as long as that person didn't get in his way, it seemed fine. "I'd like to start now if it's OK with you. You can tell Marcy to join me whenever she's ready."
Alpha Edward wondered why Damon seemed in a rush, but he didn't question it. Damon wanted to walk around, and he even acted considerate enough to ask for someone to escort him.
It took Alpha Edward two seconds to find his next candidate. A person who knew what went on and wouldn't embarrass him.
Nora waited for Damon in front of the study with a big smile on her face. "Alpha Edward asked me to escort you and to answer any questions you might have."
Damon hummed in understanding. "Take me to where Omegas stay."
"Sure."
Damon eyed Nora. If she was surprised by this demand, she didn't show it.
Damon observed the two-story high building. The bottom floor had a kitchen, a common area that doubled as a lounge and dining room, and four bedrooms. The upper floor had ten bedrooms.
Based on the information they received about the Red Moon pack, each room housed six to eight people, so Damon estimated about one hundred people in each building.
Nora didn't understand why Damon asked to visit this place, but other than walking through the hallways, he didn't stop.
"Do you want to see inside rooms?"
Damon refused. "That's not necessary. Is this the only building for Omegas?"
"No, there are three more," Nora responded.
"I want to visit them."
Three buildings later, Damon lost hope that he would find the mysterious copper haired girl.
Not a single whiff of freesia appeared, no matter how much he searched.
After four buildings without any hints of the copper haired girl., Damon was frustrated.
"Are you looking for anything in particular?", Nora asked when she saw Damon spacing out in the middle of the hallway.
Damon shrugged and shook his head. He was not sure himself.
Nora stepped closer to him and spoke in a sultry voice, "Whatever you want, I can give you…"
Damon frowned. "Keep your distance, Miss Nora, or people might get the wrong idea." She didn't move and his expression darkened.
"Do you want to start the rumors about us? I wonder, what would Alpha Edward say if he thinks there is something going on between us? I'm sure you are aware of my reputation. One more girl won't make a difference, but for you who tried to ruin Marcy's chances of becoming the Luna of the Dark Howlers pack..." Damon clicked his tongue.
Nora gave him a tight smile and increased the distance between them. She got the message to stay away. For now.
Damon became immersed in his thoughts, completely ignoring Nora who fidgeted by his side. He was recollecting everything he knew about the copper haired girl and trying to come up with something that makes sense. Damon assumed that she was an Omega because she brought towels into his bathroom, and because of the poor treatment she received.
If she had any standing, Alpha Edward wouldn't be oblivious that she was mistreated. Of course, there was a possibility that Alpha Edward knew about it, and he was pretending to be oblivious. However, if he was concealing the issue, he would deny it and not tell Damon that he would talk to Marcy.
Damon spent the last decade among Alphas, and he learned a thing or two about reading them. He was confident that Alpha Edward didn't know that Marcy (and maybe someone else) was physically punishing Omegas.
Damon wanted to ask Nora if she knew something about beatings or the girl with copper-colored hair, but he quickly decided not to. He didn't want to appear to be snooping into something that was not his business and if anyone suspected that he was specifically interested in one girl with poor standing, that could backfire big time.
The last thing he wanted was to jeopardize her in any way. He had to connect the dots on his own.
Anyone with such injuries would probably stay in bed, either in the pack hospital or in her room, and an Omega would help her out. Hell, even if she was an Omega, someone should take care of her and not let her search for food in the middle of the night.
The fact that she was looking for food in the middle of the night while injured, meant that she didn't have dinner, and her skinny appearance told Damon that she skipped many other meals as well. His heart ached.
He thought that maybe she committed some crime and was being punished, but if she was imprisoned or tortured, she wouldn't be able to come to the kitchen, so he crossed off that as a possibility.
If she truly was an Omega, she would live in one of these common buildings, and Damon could pick up her scent. Another mystery was, why would she look for food in the packhouse when there was a kitchen in each of these buildings?
The more Damon thought about it, the less sense it made. It all felt like he was trapped in a game of hide-and-seek. He was exasperated and his mind was a mess.
His life was so much simpler before he saw that girl sneaking out of his room while Marcy was pleasuring him.
Damon didn't want to think about the copper haired girl, and he couldn't believe that he spent so much time searching for her. The girl ran away, and she probably didn't care about him.
The smartest thing to do was leave this pack and return to his routine. Eventually, her addictive scent would fade from his mind, and he would be normal again.
Damon wanted to leave the Red Moon pack and go home. He really did. But as time passed, Damon realized that he couldn't leave without seeing the girl with the copper-colored hair again. Just one more time.
He wanted to ensure that she was fine. At least that's what he told himself. Damon hoped that if he could inhale her sweet citrusy scent of freesia a few more times, he might get sated, or maybe he would find out that it didn't affect him anymore. And then there were those sparks that felt divine. Yes, he needed to feel those again also.
Just once and then he would leave. Definitely.
Damon came up with a million reasons to see the girl he couldn't get out of his mind, and he roamed around the packhouse and community buildings, but with no luck.
It was like the girl simply disappeared.
Damon was desperate. Was she a ghost who came to torture him? He was never this anxious.

Damon was irritable and he said more than once that they were leaving, only to turn around and tell them they were staying longer.
To say that Maya and Caden were confused, was an understatement.
