Damon was never indecisive, and he never refused a naked woman and this was enough proof for Caden and Maya that Damon was losing it.

Damon sat in the kitchen of the packhouse with the lights off and waited. That's where he saw the copper-haired girl, so he hoped that she would show up again.
Damon didn't sleep the previous night, and he was not in his best shape, but every one of his muscles was tense, and he didn't feel like sleeping.
His mind was going through numerous scenarios of what he would say when the mysterious girl showed up, and how she would respond.
Would he play it cool and ask casually how she was doing?
Or maybe he should show a stern expression and demand an explanation to why she disappeared last night without a goodbye?
Or maybe he should make a pitiful expression and say how she hurt his feelings? Based on the internet, girls liked it when a man exposed his vulnerable side.
Damon was still not sure if he should embrace this madness or reject her, but he knew that he had to see her.
His wolf would growl in displeasure whenever Damon thought about rejecting her as his mate, and whimper sadly when Damon worried why she was not there yet.
What if she is hurt? Did she leave? Was she hungry? Damon shoved his hand into his hair. Maybe the girl was fine and sleeping and he was an idiot for spending the night in the kitchen.
Seconds ticked into minutes that turned to hours, painfully slow, and Damon was exasperated when he saw dawn cracking through the window. She didn't come.
Damon was about to give up and head to his room when footsteps from the hallway got his attention.
He impatiently jumped to his feet, in the hope that it was the copper haired girl.
Damon's handsome eyebrows came together when he saw a woman with a duster in her hand. A blonde Omega in her late-twenties.
Her eyes widened in surprise, and she stuttered. "Can… can I help you, Alpha Damon?"

"Can I ask you something, but you make sure it stays between us?"

Damon remembered one more detail. "She wore old clothes that were oversized for her."
The woman made a thoughtful expression.
"You know her?", Damon asked in an urgent whisper while inching closer to the Omega who was now blushing profusely.
"I… I…" The words were stuck in her throat. He was too handsome and too close, and all this was too sudden. "She… maybe…"
"Yes? Yes!?" He asked impatiently.
She blinked rapidly. "The attic. There is a girl living in the attic."
Damon climbed to the attic faster than the wind and his lips curved into a smile when he inhaled the scent of freesia he was craving for.
The girl was there.
He stared at the closed door in front of him and took a moment to compose himself.
Damon thought about how he went all around the Red Moon pack's properties in search of the girl. Why didn't he think of checking the packhouse thoroughly?
He already knew that the girl was not in the common buildings because she came to the kitchen in the packhouse.

Nothing. He knocked again, this time with a bit more force.

He gave it another knock and then turned the door handle.
The dawn gave barely any light through the small windows, but Damon's Alpha sight was enough for him to see the scarce furniture and the girl sitting on the edge of the futon, in the corner, hugging her knees and looking at him with her big doe-like eyes.
Damon stood at the door frozen, locked in some kind of a staring contest with Talia, overwhelmed by his emotions that were amplified by the joy of his wolf.

That's the scary Alpha who was the reason she got beaten twice. The first time because she looked in when Princess Marcy was between Alpha Damon's legs, and the second time because she complained how Princess Marcy hit her the first time.

And now he was here, in the attic, bringing more misfortune with him.
With every next second of Damon's presence in the attic, Talia sensed a calamity approaching, a calamity in the form of princess Marcy wanting to kill her.
Talia didn't say anything and Damon stepped inside.
She pushed with her legs, getting further into the corner while trying to increase the distance between them.'You are scaring the girl again…', his wolf growled in his head.
Damon lifted his hands, palms facing Talia. "I won't hurt you."'Yeah, you won't hurt me, but others will because of you.', Talia thought.
In slow movements, he closed the door behind him and approached her carefully until his feet touched the edge of the futon.
He went down into a squat so that they were on the same level, but she was still much smaller than he was.
"My name is Damon." He put on his best non-intimidating smile, but she saw it like a beast showing teeth before devouring its prey.
"What's your name?" Damon asked.
Talia's eyes darted to the door and then went back to him.
"Please, leave." She said in a shaky voice, and his heart ached. He finally found her and there was no way he would leave just like that.
Damon was not sure what to do. Why was she so scared? Why was she chasing him away?
"I won't hurt you." He assured her. "I'm here only to talk."
"Say what you have to and leave," Talia said and gestured toward the door, her hand moving enough for the sleeve to hitch higher and expose her swollen wrist.
Damon grabbed her hand and pulled it toward him.
Delightful sparks formed upon contact, catching him by surprise. The sensation was stronger than he remembered, and he inhaled a shaky breath.
He focused mightily on inspecting her injury.
"What happened? Don't tell me that you fell again." His expression darkened. "Is it Marcy? I will teach her a lesson."
Talia panicked. "Please, don't. If you say anything, she will hit me more."
Damon paused and observed her face which was now peeking up above her knees, and he noticed a few more bruises compared to what he saw the previous night.
Rage rippled through Damon at the thought of Talia getting hurt again, and he was right here, in this packhouse, oblivious to her sufferings. It happened on his watch!
Damon was enraged, and his wolf was as well. One fury amplified the other and Damon radiated inexplicable violence that was tangible.
At the sight of Talia shivering in fear, Damon forced his rage down. Settling scores will need to wait.
"Did Marcy hit you again?" Damon asked Talia, and the way she avoided him made him suspect another thing. "Was it because of me?"
Talia's eyes widened and that was enough for him to confirm how his intuition was right.
He knew that Marcy was a white lotus. There was no way Marcy would forget that Talia saw her in a compromising position – between Damon's legs – and when Damon told Alpha Edward that Marcy was hitting Omegas, Marcy probably knew that his comment was about Talia.
In a way, it was his fault that Talia got hurt. Twice.
He clenched his teeth as another wave of rage swelled within him. "I will kill her."
"Don't," Talia pleaded. "Can you just leave and pretend that you didn't see anything? Don't come here and everyone will leave me alone."
Damon's heart cracked. Even if everyone left her alone, how the hell was he supposed to do that?
Didn't she know that he nearly went mad when he didn't know where she was?
Without a word, Damon sat on the futon next to Talia and wrapped her in his arms, pulling her to lean on his chest.
The feeling of Talia against him made Damon's whole body hum in pleasure. Delightful sparks overtook his senses, and he was lost in a daze.
Talia froze. She was not used to physical contact of any kind. It took her a moment to collect herself and start squirming to get out of his hold.
"Shh…" Damon coaxed Talia to calm down, unwilling to let go of her. He was not a hugger, and he never cuddled with a woman, but this girl was different. He wanted to hold her, and her resistance hurt. "I won't harm you. Can I hold you like this, just for a minute?"
No, not a minute. He wanted an hour, or at least until he became immune to these sparks that were making him crave devouring her. But if he said that aloud, she would definitely freak out.
Talia stopped struggling. Not because she agreed, but because she realized that he was too strong, and her struggle made her injuries ache more.
Talia resigned herself to her fate. There was nothing she could do. Even if he wanted to harm her, she could only endure it. She was too weak to fight for herself and if she shouted for help, no one would come.
Damon smirked when he felt that Talia relaxed. He wished to move her to sit on his lap, but he feared that it might be too much.
With his arms around her, Talia appeared tiny and fragile, and Damon was confident that he could carry her around with ease. Or maybe he should stuff her into his pocket, so that she stays close to him all the time.
Lost in the moment, Damon ran his fingers through Talia's coppery-colored hair and inhaled the sweet citrusy scent of freesia, and his world was at peace.
Damon closed his eyes, his enjoyment amplified by the sounds of yips and whimpers his wolf made in pleasure.
"Hey…" Talia called after some time. "When are you going to let me go?"
"First, my name is Damon. Not, hey," Damon said with amusement in his voice. It'd been a while since he heard someone speak to him this casually (other than Caden), but the lack of respect didn't bother him.
"And second…" he drawled, "I'm thinking about it."
If it was up to him, never. To make his point clear, he tightened his hold on her, making sure he didn't crush her. Feeling that she was stiff again, he asked, "Am I hurting you?"
Talia was absolutely confused with this development. "Well… no… but…"
"Then, it's fine." Damon cut her off. He didn't want to hear any buts.
As much as Damon enjoyed this newfound feeling, he couldn't ignore Talia's injuries. The scent of dried blood disturbed the sweet citrusy scent of freesia, telling him that she was not OK.
Damon took Talia's hand in his and observed a cut that was on top of a nasty bruise. It was scabbing, but it still looked fresh.'Mate's healing is slow because she doesn't have her wolf,' Damon's wolf explained.
Damon raised Talia's hand toward his lips and licked the cut.
Talia jerked her hand away, but Damon's reflexes were top-notch, and he increased his grip, preventing her from doing so.
"What are you doing?" Talia asked in panic.
No one ever licked her before, and this was a scary Alpha! Would he eat her?
"Shush! Don't you know that our saliva has analeptic properties? I'm helping your wound heal. You should say, thank you, and not complain." Damon said and grimaced. Considering her sweet scent, he assumed that she would taste sweet also, but… "Why was it bitter?"
"I applied an herbal paste, so it didn't get infected," Talia said in a small voice.
Damon observed her face and noticed that she was beet red. Is she sick?
He touched her forehead. It was not warm, but he still asked, "Do you have a fever?"
"No," Talia responded with urgency. She had no intention to admit she was flustered because a scary Alpha came, hugged her (and was still hugging her!), and then he licked her hand.
Damon guessed that she didn't see a doctor. It was obvious that she didn't get proper first aid.
"Did you make the medicinal paste yourself?"
Talia confirmed with a nod.
He was about to lick her hand again and paused. "Is it poisonous?"
Talia was not sure if she should laugh or cry. "You should ask that before you put things into your mouth."
"I was treating your wound and I didn't see that there was medicine…" He grumbled, and then he licked her again.
"Can you stop doing that?" Talia protested. His coarse tongue touching her skin made her feel funny.
Damon looked at Talia like he had no idea what she was talking about, and then he licked her again.
Talia exhaled helplessly while wondering what game Damon was playing.
He was an important guest, an Alpha, yet instead of mingling with the elite of the Red Moon pack, he was huddled in the corner of the attic, holding her close to him, and licking her hand.
It didn't make sense no matter how she thought about it.
Is this the part where Marcy barged in and they all started laughing at her? Actually, if they only laughed, that would be good. Maybe Damon would join Marcy and the two of them would give her another beating?
Talia was anxious and she wanted this charade to be over.
"When are you leaving?"
Damon was not sure if she asked him about leaving the attic or the Red Moon pack. In either case, his answer would be the same. "Why are you eager to chase me away?"
"Because this is where I stay. You are in a fancy bedroom, with Alpha and Luna, and your future wife."
"My future wife?" Damon asked in confusion, like he heard about it for the first time.
"Princess Marcy told me that you would get married when she came here and…" Talia didn't finish, but Damon understood.
"She will NOT be my wife in this lifetime or in any next one." Damon said grimly.
Talia shook her head. "Maybe you should tell that to her, and not to me. Your relationship with her is not my business. Can you, please, leave?"
Damon was lost in her big honey-colored eyes that looked at him pleadingly and he wondered if he could leave. Could he? Yes, but only in one case.
"Come with me."
Talia was sure that her ears malfunctioned. She asked him to leave the attic before anyone can see them in this inexplicable situation, yet he wants her to join him? "What? Where?"
"I am the Alpha of the Dark Howlers pack. Come with me to my pack."
Talia's brain paused.
She thought that Damon had invited her to his room, to clean up or maybe to make fun of her, but now it seemed he was asking her to leave the Red Moon pack. With him. "Why?"
"I will make sure you have a room, better than the ones downstairs. I will get you clothes that fit, and you can eat anytime you want and as much as you want. For every scratch and bruise, there will be a pack doctor to take care of you and if anyone gives you a hard time, I will deal with them. No one will bully you in my pack."'Our pack!', his wolf added eagerly. Unfortunately, only Damon heard him.
Talia blinked. Now she was not wondering if her ears were tricking her, and if this last beating messed with her brain.
Or maybe something was wrong with him. Did he eat a funny fruit and was talking gibberish? There were some herbs that could make people say things they didn't mean. Or did he confuse her with princess Marcy?
It's not that Talia didn't think about leaving the Red Moon pack. Every time Anna and her henchmen bullied Talia, Talia thought about escaping, but she didn't know where to go. And here was an Alpha, offering her a new home with all the luxuries she ever dreamed of. Assuming that this was real and both of them were sane.
Talia wondered if this was a prank, or if she was imagining this whole conversation, or maybe she was sleeping and the Cinderella story mixed with her dreams because Damon definitely looked like a prince. A handsome prince that smelled of the forest and dark chocolate.
"Will you come with me?" Damon asked when his patience cracked.
"Why do you want me to come?"
"Because…" the words got stuck in his throat.
Could he tell her she was his mate and that when he sees her harmed, his soul aches? No. That would only freak her out.
Could he tell her that staying away from her was practically impossible? If she doesn't come willingly, he would kidnap her or maybe move in with her into this attic. Ah! He sounded like a creep to himself!
Damon was exasperated. All this would be simpler if she could feel the bond and the delicious sparks that make him feel alive.
"Because…" he repeated. "I feel responsible. You got hurt because of me, and it's not right. Let me help you. It will make me feel better." This was the truth. Part of the truth, at least.
"Do you take every girl who gets hurt back to your pack?"
Not really. But he is not the guy who would look away from injustice. However, he couldn't tell Talia that she was special either.
"When you come to the Dark Howlers pack, you will see for yourself that we accept everyone who comes seeking help without bad intentions. I promise that if you don't like it in the Dark Howlers pack, I will help you resettle at the location of your choice."
With his index finger, Damon made a cross over his chest where the heart was, to confirm his sincerity, but his silent promise had an additional clause how he would make sure she was treated well and she never wanted to leave.
Talia bit the inside of her cheek while considering her options.
One was staying at the Red Moon pack. Anna's bullying was escalating, and Marcy started picking on her also. Yesterday Marcy came to the attic and Talia got a beating for something she didn't do.
The second option was to go to the Dark Howlers pack. Alpha Damon said that in his pack people were accepted. Could it be worse than here? Probably not.
Of course, there was also the third option for Talia to leave on her own somewhere, but that option was scary and uncertain, and it will exist even if she goes with Alpha Damon.
Damon saw that Talia was considering it and he spoke with urgency before she could decline his offer. "Grab your things. You only need to say that you reject the Red Moon pack and Edward Redmayne as your Alpha, and the mind link will break. With that, you are free to go, and they can't find you."Talia shook her head. "I don't have the mind link. Alpha Edward's father brought me here as a child, and I never went through the ceremony."
"Good!" Damon exclaimed louder than intended. She doesn't belong anywhere, and he was more than happy to give her a home. With him. "Get your things."
"Just like that?"
Damon nodded. "Just like that."
Talia paused and decided to ask the question that was bothering her from the moment he came to the attic. "How do I know that you are not tricking me?"
Damon stood up and Talia felt chills surround her when his body separated from hers.
He extended his hand toward Talia, palm up. "Let me prove it to you."

bodyText:
"Why can't you be more like your sister?"
Susan's fiancé asked her that question every chance he got.
At dinner.
At parties.
Even in bed.
Jacob: "You know I love you... but you're just not enough."
Susan thought he wanted her to be better.
She had no idea...
Jacob wanted Sophia.
Even Susan's best friend begged her.
Friend: "Leave him, Susan. He's toxic."
Susan smiled.
Susan: "He loves me."
So she changed.
She dressed like Sophia.
She wore a wig like Sophia.
She copied the way she laughed.
She became everything Jacob asked for.
It still wasn't enough.
Jacob "You look pathetic"
So Susan walked into a sex shop.
She wanted to surprise the love of her life.
She rushed home.
Heart racing.
And hid under the bed.

Susan hid under the bed while her fiancé made another woman scream in delight.
“Yes! Jacob! Don’t stop!”
Susan silently cried, covering her mouth so her sobs wouldn’t alert them.
Not that they would hear – the springs were squeaking too loudly.
This betrayal would’ve been life-ruining on any old day. 
What made this even more excruciating was that Susan and Jacob were getting married…this fall.
When the woman cried out in crescendo, Susan’s stomach dropped.
Is that Sophia? Susan wondered. It sounds like her voice. But Jacob would surely not cheat on me with my own sister?
“Hurry and get dressed, Sophia. We need to leave before Susan comes home.”
How could he betray me with her of all people? Out of all the people in the world… My sister?
How could she do this? Sophia. The one I love more than anyone. The one I’ve always protected.
I worked nonstop so she wouldn’t have to. I made sure she could live freely, happily. I gave her everything. And this… this is how she pays me back?
She ruined everything.
Sophia laughed and rolled over. “What? Are you scared she'll find out about us? It’s been years and poor naive Susan doesn’t have a clue. Pathetic.”
They both cackled at Susan’s expense.
Years? He’s been cheating for years? This couldn’t get any worse...
Susan watched their ankles as they slid on their clothes. She imagined herself slicing their Achilles tendons so they could never walk again.
“Are you coming to the party tomorrow?” Jacob asked with a chuckle. “It’s your sister’s homecoming party, after all. She’s coming back after a year.”
Sophia let out a small, knowing laugh. “Of course I’m coming. But you need to stop calling it her homecoming party. You know very well what it’s really being organized for.”
What did she mean by that?
Jacob rolled his eyes.
“Let’s not talk about your father transferring eighty percent of the company shares to you until it’s finalized,” he said quickly. Almost nervously. “Please.”
The words didn’t make sense at first. Then they did.
Sophia… is getting the majority stake? Susan felt the air leave her lungs.
While I worked day and night to grow that company? I was the one flying overseas. I was the one staying up all night finishing projects. And she’s the one getting it? Susan gasped.
“Did you hear that?” Sophia asked. 
Susan held her breath. The only thing more humiliating than spying on them having sex was getting caught spying.
“It sounded like Susan. Maybe she’s downstairs. Quick, we will sneak you out the back!”
Jacob and Sophia scurried out of the room, giving Susan time to slide out from under the bed.
What was she supposed to do? Confront Jacob? Expose him? Call off the wedding? Run away?
Very quickly, her heartache turned to rage. How dare he put her in this predicament a few months before their wedding? After everything she sacrificed for him?! This was a fate worse than death.
Then it dawned on her. Jacob once said being poor is a fate worse than death.
The memory echoed clearly in her mind, and her stomach dropped. So that’s what this is about. That’s why he chose Sophia.
He chose her because she will own more shares in the Drew Corporation. He chose her because she will be richer. Because I am no longer the better option.
Fine, Susan thought. I will show you what is worse than death. My revenge.
A faint, dangerous smile formed on her lips.
You think I’m pathetic? Watch me burn your world! Susan thought maniacally.
She wiped off her tears and smiled. Just then, Jacob walked into the bedroom. He jumped when he saw her.
“Ah! Susan! I didn’t hear you come in! I was…just taking out the trash.” 
He’s not lying, Sophia is trash, Susan thought. Both Jacob and my bitch sister are trash.
“Come here, give your bride-to-be a kiss,” Susan said. 
Jacob got visibly nervous. He still had the taste of Sophia’s tender kisses on his mouth. He eyed the dirty sheets, too. How was he going to get out of this?
Susan knew he was slimy. He would find a way.
“Let me shower first, I was just napping and had a nightmare. I’m all sweaty!” Jacob ripped the bedsheets off the mattress and went down the hallway.
“Coward,” Susan whispered under her breath.
The next morning, Susan got dressed for the party. It was a dress that Jacob had bought for her. As angry and devastated as she was, when she slipped it on, she felt an intense love for Jacob.
She had just come back after a year away. Tonight, she had planned to announce their wedding to the world. This was supposed to be the happiest day of their lives. Was she making a mistake by sabotaging their relationship? Maybe he had a good explanation for his affair with Sophia?
Then her expression hardened. No. My revenge starts with telling Dad everything.
She would expose Sophia. She would reveal the affair. And then she would see how Sophia managed to keep the majority stakes after a scandal like that.
She would lose it all. Everything that had been handed to her would be taken away.
A small, cold smile crept onto Susan’s face as she pictured Jacob’s reaction. What would he look like when Sophia was left with nothing?
Susan stood in the corner of the party in her beautiful white dress, waiting for Jacob to show up. She decided when he arrived, she would tell her parents the truth.
But Jacob didn’t show up alone. He strode in, hand in hand with Sophia, and accompanied by none other than... Susan and Sophia’s parents.

Susan’s breath caught. She thought she might die right there at that moment. 

My parents knew this was going on, and they did nothing to stop it. 

She watched as her own father clapped Jacob on the back and called him “son.” Her mother and Sophia shared hushed whispers and smiles. It looked like a picture-perfect family scene, like Susan had never existed at all.
She stood frozen in the corner, feeling foolish, and completely alone, as her world…and her planned revenge…began to crumble right in front of her.
Tears rolled down Susan’s cheeks, What? They all knew about this? My entire family betrayed me!
She smoothed her dress, wiped the sting from her eyes, and stepped away from the party.
Her mind replayed what she had seen and heard, like she had never existed at all.
That's when a familiar voice cut through the noise.
"Susan Drew?"
Susan turned. It was Helen. Her best friend.
Helen stopped in front of her and studied her face.
“Something’s wrong,” Helen said without hesitation. “I can see it in your eyes.”
Susan tried to smile, but the moment she did, tears spilled down her face.
“I saw Jacob,” she said.
Helen frowned. “Where?”
“With Sophia,” Susan answered, her voice barely steady. “naked in bed, being intimate.”
"And the shares, my father transferred everything to Sophia. The company I spent years building. It's all in her name now."
Helen was very still.
Then she exhaled slowly, shaking her head.
"That man never deserved a single day of you," she said. "Not one."
Susan gave a hollow laugh. "In one afternoon I lost everything."
"No," Helen said firmly, leaning forward. "You didn't lose anything. You just finally saw the truth." She held Susan's gaze. "And that is worth more than all of it."
Susan looked away. But just then she felt like something in the party had shifted. The air in the garden bar had changed. The voices around her grew softer. Laughter faded. Even the music suddenly felt distant.
Susan frowned slightly. “What is…”
Then she saw a man in a perfectly tailored gray suit had just walked in. He didn’t make a dramatic entrance. But Susan noticed the powerful, arrogant businessmen. The ones who barely acknowledged anyone and carried their egos like crowns…were standing up.
“They’re… standing?” she whispered under her breath.
The man didn’t even look at them. He just kept walking straight ahead, his phone pressed to his ear.
At that moment it felt like he was the center of the party without even trying. A couple of the big-shot businessmen quickly stepped forward, forcing polite smiles as they extended their hands.
“Good evening, sir…”
But the man walked right past them as if they weren’t there.
Susan sucked in a sharp breath. If anyone else did that, they’d be finished in this city…
But no one got angry. There was no offense. Just acceptance. Almost desperation.
Susan tilted her head slightly, listening. One of the businessmen let out a small, awkward chuckle as he lowered his rejected hand. “Well… it was worth the try at least,” he muttered to the man beside him.
The other man nodded. “One handshake with him,” he said quietly, “could change my life… and my company’s future.”
Susan’s gaze snapped back to the man. And for the first time that night, Susan forgot about Jacob.
The man walked a little farther off, listening carefully to whoever was on the other end of the call.
“What do you want me to do?” he snapped. “Marry some random woman off the street?”
Susan kept looking in his direction.
“You think just because you’re my grandfather you get to tell me who to marry and when to do it?”
There was something sharp in his voice, pure frustration, mixed with anger. Susan couldn’t help but take note of that.
In a daze, she mumbled, “Who is he?”
Helen’s gaze followed. "He's Jacob's cousin."
Susan froze, the wine glass trembling slightly in her hand.
"Jacob’s cousin?" she whispered, her eyes widening in surprise. "Are you sure?"
Helen looked back at him. For a brief moment, a trace of uncertainty crossed her face, but it disappeared almost instantly. She gave a firm nod and said, "Yes, I’m sure."
But her eyes didn’t fully agree.
"He owns twenty-five percent of the Smith family company," Helen continued, lowering her voice. "On top of that, he runs his own company overseas. He built everything himself, with no help and no handouts." She paused for a moment to let her words sink in. "Jacob always acted like he was the powerful one, but compared to his cousin..." She slowly shook her head. "Jacob does not even come close. He is just a shadow next to him."
Susan turned her eyes back to the man.  He was now sitting there with a drink in his hand, calm and perfectly composed, like a man who had never once needed anyone else’s approval to know his own worth.
Jacob had chosen Sophia for power. But the man sitting alone at the end of the bar had more power than Jacob ever would. A thought slowly settled into Susan’s mind, quiet but sharp.
"What if I married him?" she said.
Helen blinked in surprise. "Wait... are you serious?"
Susan kept her eyes fixed on the man. "Just imagine their faces. Jacob’s. Sophia’s. The moment they find out."
Helen stared at her for a long moment. Then, little by little, something fierce and certain lit up in her eyes.
"You know what?" she said. "Do it. Any man would be lucky to have you."
"Alright," Susan said. "I’m not just going to convince him to marry me."
Her eyes hardened with determination.
"I deserve love, and I’m going to make him fall in love with me."
Once the decision was made, Susan quickly fixed her makeup. Her face had been ruined by all the crying from earlier. There was no way she could hope to win over a man while looking like such a mess.
But within minutes, her delicate features were restored, and she looked effortlessly captivating. She then walked straight toward him 
The handsome stranger, Ethan.
Ethan looked up as Susan walked toward him.
He didn’t seem surprised to see her.
He just watched her quietly, calm and unhurried, the same way he seemed to do everything.
Susan came to a stop beside him.
“I hope I’m not interrupting,” she said.
Ethan looked at her for a moment, studying her face, but his expression gave nothing away.
“My name is Susan,” she said, holding his gaze without looking away. “And I have a proposal for you.”
“Why did you approach me?" Ethan asked, “Do you know who I am?”

 "You are Jacob’s cousin, if I’m not wrong?" 
The man smiled like a Devil, and spoke only a word, “Ethan,”
Susan's eyes widened.
“So, are you here looking for a bride, Ethan?” she asked, her eyes tracing his striking features. “Or have you already found someone interesting?”
Ethan scoffed, "None of the young women in here shall be my wife. They are all like matching dolls in a set."
 Susan said, “I am unlike any of them. You can make me your trophy wife since I’m no longer with Jacob.”
 “Jacob Smith?” Ethan repeated, “You better be careful. He's not the man he pretends to be.”
 Susan wasn’t shocked at the revelation. “I know, I just found that out." What choice do I have, Ethan? I can’t escape my fate unless…” She paused.
 “Unless what?” Ethan questioned, but he wasn’t ready for what Susan was about to propose.
 “Unless you were to marry me instead,” Susan replied.
 “What?” Ethan raised an eyebrow, intrigued. “It’s only been ten minutes, and you already think I’m in love with you?”
 "I am not looking for love, Ethan,” Susan said, her voice steady, “I am looking for a way out. But so are you.”
Ethan was surprised. “You think you know me that well?”
 Susan added, "See, I know your grandfather wants you to marry soon. For a man with no interest in romance, I might be your best option. I’ll live like a shadow in your home, silent, unseen, tending to your needs, and I promise, I’ll never love you."
 Ethan chuckled. “No strings attached? How can I trust you?”
 "What about a contract?" Susan proposed. She was desperate to convince him; it would be the perfect way to get revenge on her evil sister and Jacob.
 “A contract marriage?” Ethan repeated as he considered Susan's proposal. "Did your father set this up?" he asked, his tone skeptical.
 "My father has no idea that I am out here speaking to you, Ethan. He won't be pleased to see you here with me," Susan replied honestly.
 Ethan studied her for a moment. Susan continued, "I am not interested in marrying anyone for love. I only wish to leave this place and never look back."
 “Why don’t you just run away?” Ethan suggested.
 Susan said, “How long can a woman remain alone without the protection of a strong man? The world respects power, not independence."
 “Well, Susan, I am spoken of as the most eligible Bachelor in town,” Ethan said mockingly, his words dripping with pride. “Why should I marry you?”
 Susan's lips curled as she replied, “I do not care for your looks, Ethan, nor your money or anything else others might want. Frankly, I only see you as an escape." She explained. “This will be your way out of your problem with your grandfather. A win-win situation for both of us.”
 "Is that so?" Ethan said, intrigued. "It isn't hard for me to find an actress to play the role of my wife."
 "If it were so easy, you would have done so already," Susan countered, seeing through his bluff. "Your grandfather is toying with you. Present me to him as your bride, and the tables would turn.”
 Ethan smirked. "I can't wait to see my grandfather’s reaction when he has to bless you by kissing your forehead. He knows everything about what’s happening in Drew Corporation and your fallen status in the company. It'll be priceless to watch him squirm like that."
 “So?” Susan said, “Should I consider it a deal?”
 Ethan watched her for a moment before responding. "Meet me at a restaurant tomorrow. I’ll text you the details. We will further discuss this there, and then I will give you my answer."
Not long after Susan sat with Helen in a quieter corner of the venue.
Helen pushed two glasses across the table, the ice clinking softly.
 “Drink,” she said firmly. “Doctor’s orders.”
Susan stared at the amber liquid like it might bite her.
 “I don’t need alcohol.”
“That’s what everyone says right before they do,” Helen replied, already lifting her own glass. “
Susan gave a weak smile and took a sip. The burn slid down her throat, warm and sharp.
Helen leaned back, crossing her arms. “So Jacob’s Cousin?.”
Susan nearly choked.
“What about him?” she asked, too quickly.
Helen squinted. “You didn’t even deny it. Interesting.”
“There’s nothing to deny,” Susan said, setting the glass down carefully. “We just… talked.”
“Uh-huh. People don’t look like they’re about to flee a crime scene after ‘just talking.’” Helen tilted her head. “Also, he has the kind of face men are born with when the universe is unfair.”
Susan snorted despite herself.
“He’s not that handsome.”
“Oh, come on,” Helen scoffed. “He’s tall, broad-shouldered, and looks like he hasn’t smiled since childhood trauma. That’s prime market value.”
Susan laughed softly, then fell quiet.
Helen noticed immediately.
Helen sighed sympathetically.
 “Don’t think about him. Honestly, now that I’ve seen him properly, he’s not even that handsome. And he’s way too tall.”
She rambled on, trying to distract her.
Suddenly, Susan shook her head
“No,” she said softly. “He wants to meet me tomorrow. He wants to talk about the terms of our marriage.”
Helen froze—then burst into laughter.
 “Congratulations! You’ll be Jacob’s cousin-in-law.”
Susan blinked, finally snapping back to reality.
 “Do you… do you think he’ll really marry me?” she asked softly.
Helen pinched her cheek.
 “Why wouldn’t he? If I were a man, I’d fall in love with you at first sight. Come on—let’s go to my place and escape from here 
The following morning, at Helen's house.
Susan, who was deep asleep, was woken by the noise outside.
Just as she opened her eyes, she saw Jacob opening the door and striding into her room.
Helen, who followed him into the room, roared. “This is my house! You’re basically invading my home!”
“Sure enough, you’re here.” Jacob stared keenly at Susan, who had bloodshot eyes and slightly messy hair.
Susan became wide awake at that moment, her eyes expressing dejection.
“The two of you should have a good chat. It hasn’t been easy being together for so many years.” After some thought, Helen turned around and left, closing the door behind her.
The room was silent. Sitting on the edge of the bed, Jacob stretched out his hand to touch her hair.
With a scornful look, Susan dodged away from his hand. “Does Sophia know that you’re here?”
Jacob’s handsome face froze, then he clenched his fist. . “Susan, you know that the Drew family has decided to give Sophia 80 percent of the company’s shares.”
Susan stiffened, remembering those words from Jacob's mouth the night before. Hearing it again angered her so much that her lips turned pale. 
She lifted her head and looked at her childhood sweetheart, whom she loved back then. Tears began to gush from her eyes. “So that’s why you abandoned me, and chose Sophia, right?”
Jacob gripped her hands. “This is just temporary. As you know, my dad has an illegitimate son. If I don’t do this, I wouldn’t even be able to compete. Susan, I just want to provide you with a good life.”
“Bullshit.”
Susan snatched her hand out of his grasp and threw insults at him. “You’re only 25 years old. Even if you don’t get any inheritance from your family, can’t you just start your own business?”
“You’re too naive.”
Jacob stood up slowly, hiding the emotions in his eyes. He said helplessly, “It’s not in our power to choose certain things due to our background.”
Susan looked cold without uttering a word as she found it unreasonable.
Amid the silence, Jacob sighed softly. “Give me a few years, Susan. You’re still young. You can afford to wait.”
Susan nearly went mad.
How dare he say such things in a self-righteous manner, when he only wanted to make her keep her youth for him?
“You’re treating me as a fool, aren’t you? You’ve chosen to be engaged to Sophia for the ‘sake’ of your career. Who knows whether you’ll marry ‘me’ a few years later? Please get out of my face. I don’t want to see you anymore!”Jacob’s expression remained calm, but his eyes revealed a deep affection and an unmistakable longing.
“Time will show my love for you. You can be upset with me, but don’t go out and drown your sorrows with alcohol. It’s not good for your health.”
Since Susan was not going along with what he said, he merely advised her before he turned around and left.
Upon hearing the door shut, Susan flung a pillow to the wall with reddened eyes, and spent a few seconds sitting still. After that, she frantically put on her shirt and dashed out.
“He’s left. What’s the point of going after him?” Helen quickly stopped her.
Susan took a deep breath, then gnashed her teeth. “I agreed to meet Ethan at 10 a.m. “You actually believe him?” Helen asked.
“Didn’t you say you believed him last night?” Susan was confused at Helen’s question.Susan shot her a frustrated look. “
Helen laughed awkwardly and scratched the back of her head. “That’s just because I drank too much last night.”
“What if he’s serious about it?” Susan snapped, pushing Helen aside as she bolted out of the apartment.
Susan flagged down a taxi, her heart pounding as she climbed in. “The Drew family mansion,” she told the driver, her voice firm but tense.

Back at Drew Mansion, Susan rushed inside her room, brimming with anticipation as she got ready to meet Ethan. Suddenly, her eyes fell on the many documents her father had prepared for her after she came back from her business meeting in Paris.
 She didn’t feel the urge to open them until now.
A sudden wave of curiosity hit her, and she quickly opened one. Inside were documents like voting proxies for her company shares.
 "Why would my father prepare such documents for me to sign?" she muttered, confused.
 With growing unease, she ripped open the remaining packages, only to find documents she never could have imagined, not even in her darkest dreams: an agreement that strips her of all assets, contracts giving Sophia power of attorney over her affairs, and papers removing her from her father's company board.
"Perhaps this was their plan after grandpa died," she whispered to herself. 
Her thoughts drifted to the things he had quietly given her—never loudly, never for show. He had sent her abroad for her first independent project when no one else trusted her. He had insisted she attend negotiations instead of being kept on the sidelines. And on her twenty-first birthday, he had gifted her a small but decisive share in the company, telling her it was “for when you need to stand on your own.”
As long as he was alive, she had never felt expendable.
Now he’s gone.
Susan’s father was hinting at his perversions, making her sign these documents without offering an explanation.

 “Till now, I was blindly signing the documents offered by him, thinking that he was only building a safe nest for me.” She gulped down the sorrow.
 “He’s planning to hurt me, rip me off my powers in the company. All for Sophia?” She sighed deeply. “I must get a marriage contract with Ethan done soon. He is my only way out of this impending misery.”
Once they sign the marriage contract, Susan would automatically gain the power to compete with Drew Corporation head-on and take revenge. She couldn’t wait for her life to change.
At the same time, Ethan waited at the restaurant, seated in a private room he had reserved. His gaze lingered on the door, expecting Susan.
Instead, Felix, his secretary, walked in.
 "Sir, your drink is here."
 Ethan turned.
 "Should I place an order for your guests?" Felix asked.
 "I'm honestly not sure. I hope a woman won't turn down my invitation," Ethan said anxiously.
 "A woman visiting?" Felix said, surprised.
 Ethan frowned. "Not any random woman. She might become my wife."
 "W-What?" Felix said, surprised.
 Ethan stared at him unamused. "Why are you acting like it's such a surprise I would get a wife?"
Felix recollected himself. "Your exact words when your grandfather suggested you marry were, 'I am never fucking getting married. I would rather jump from the roof and die.' Maybe I misinterpreted those words. I apologize."
"Felix, I am not interested in marriage, but the woman I met last night was intriguing. A perfect way to piss off my grandfather and ward off some people from around me."
"I do not understand," Felix said.

"It will be self-explanatory if she arrives today. Check at the entrance if a Drew steps in, bring her to me," Ethan added.
"Drew? Please tell me it’s not Sophia!" Felix asked softly.
"No, the other daughter. Sophia Drew is the elder one," Ethan said.
"Thank goodness," Felix sighed in relief. 
"You are aware of the rumors concerning Susan, right?" Ethan asked.
"Anyone is better than Sophia in my book. If Sophia were to become your wife, I would jump out of the window and die.”
Ethan chuckled on hearing this.
 Felix added, “I have never seen her approach men except for business pursuits. I am not so sure she will arrive for such an arrangement.”
“Felix,” Ethan said coldly, “Start preparing to bankrupt the Drew Corporation. If that woman doesn’t show up… I want them to bleed in the market.”
“Understood, Sir,” Felix replied calmly. “I’ll deploy our finance team to California. They won’t even see it coming.”
Back at the Drew Mansion, just as Susan was about to leave, she was stopped by her father, Noah Drew.
"Susan," Noah said, inching closer. "Can you tell me what happened between you and Ethan last night? I saw you two talking.
 You know you shouldn’t talk about our company matters with him. That man is not to be trusted."
 "What did you talk about?"
 Susan kept her head down.” Nothing much, he was just offering me a drink.”
 "Still, you shouldn’t have interacted with him. What if you leaked some details about our business in the process?" Noah scolded.
 "I'm sorry, Father," Susan replied.
Then she remembered that she needed to meet Ethan. She said, “Dad, I have to meet someone for our next project. I’m leaving.”
 “Okay, Susan,” Noah agreed, “Promise me that you will help your sister sail through company processes easily. She has already been through a lot."
 "I promise," Susan rolled her eyes, frustration bubbling up.
Susan excitedly drove the car to the restaurant that Ethan had mentioned in a message. She entered the restaurant and scanned through it, awestruck by its grandeur. 
"Good morning. I have a reservation under the name, um, Ethan?," she asked the restaurant manager at the entrance.
The restaurant manager checked his book of reservations and said, "Please follow me, Miss." 
After a moment, she came in front of a private room where Felix stood waiting for her.
 "Welcome, Miss Susan Drew. Mr. Ethan is expecting you," Felix greeted her.
 "Good morning. It's nice to meet you," Susan said, offering a handshake.
 Felix shook her hand happily. "Please enter this door."
 "He is waiting for you," Felix said, knocking on the door and opening it for Susan.
The door closed behind her, and she felt her heart skip a beat.
 "I wasn't expecting you to show up, but now that you did, please have a seat," Ethan said, sitting at his desk, watching her every move.
 "I don't make false promises in business. I show up when I say I will." Susan responded without thinking.
Ethan raised an eyebrow, a flicker of surprise crossing his face before amusement settled in.
His next question stunned her, "Did you inform Mr. Drew about our meeting?”
Susan sat down, carefully considering her words. "I am not working with my father. He would never let me meet with a man like you, whether in private or public. He'd call me a traitor for even striking a deal with another family."
 "Does your father hate you?" Ethan asked bluntly.
 Susan hesitated before answering. "I don’t think he hates me. He is just more protective of Sophia than me."
 "It’s a parent’s job to love and protect all their children equally, no matter what. It’s a shame you were born a Drews’ daughter," Ethan remarked.
“Tell me something, I know you have conquered the world. But how the hell did you end up so powerless in your own family business? Whatever you’re hiding, it’s because you’re a Drews’ daughter, right? High society is quite competitive," Ethan interrupted.
 "Yes," Susan admitted.
 "Someone must have been really jealous of your success, Susan. Anyway, let’s get to the point now! Let’s say I believe this marriage is all your planning, and your father isn’t involved. Why would someone like me, who’s lived in hiding, want to marry someone like you in the spotlight?"
 "Truthfully, I never pictured someone as grand as you to come across when I was thinking about an escape plan. I thought we’d be a good match considering your family status and the connection to my family. I’ve considered two things about you: First, you’re private, so I wouldn’t need to mingle much; and second, given your status, you can control my family," Susan explained.
 Ethan raised an eyebrow. "I like to keep to myself, but there are parties I must attend. Am I to show up without my wife? It would be boring if you hid all the time."
"You misunderstand, Ethan. I never hide because I want to. My priorities have been business meetings rather than socialising with the fishwives of friction. I’d love to go out, attend parties, and dance. I have a lot of experience and confidence to mingle with the who’s who of town," Susan said earnestly.
 Ethan hummed thoughtfully. "A week ago, I wouldn’t have entertained this conversation, but now, I’m in the mood to play games." He placed a piece of paper on the table.

“What is this?” 
Susan asked as she looked at the paper with a large W Corporation logo in the corner. W? Susan thought, “What does that stand for?”
“A contract marriage needs to have rules and conditions, right?” Ethan pushed the paper and a pen toward her.
"No love shall be the first condition. It won’t be a problem on my end." Susan spoke first.
 "I hope you stay like this until the end," Ethan replied.
 "You’re not my type, Ethan," Susan said bluntly.
 "Oh, so there is a type?" Ethan mused.
 "Of course! I was quite in demand back then. I’ve seen rich and handsome men lurking around me. What should the second condition be?" Susan asked.
"My second condition: Speak of this to no one besides my secretary, Felix. He’ll be a shield for you in dangerous times.
"I must ask that I keep working in Drew Corporation till I can," Susan said. 
 "That’s your business. Do as you wish,” Ethan said.
Susan continued with the next condition, “Third, we must sleep in the same room.”
He paused and looked at Susan’s face. “Why are you surprised? Did you think I wouldn’t sleep with my husband?" she asked.
Ethan rolled his eyes. "I don’t think that’s necessary."
"Everyone does it. Young or old," Susan said brazenly.
"How young?" Ethan asked, misunderstanding.
Susan smirked. "Sleeping, Ethan. I was referring to just sleeping. But if you wish for something more."
"No! We will sleep in separate bedrooms," Ethan said quickly, embarrassed.
Susan asked, "Fine! Is there anything else?"
 "No, we’ve covered the basics. Anything else can be handled with communication. Sign it," Ethan said.
 "Don’t you want to add a punishment for breaking the contract? We haven’t set a timeline either," Susan pointed out.
 "The main thing is not to tell others about it. If it gets out, it’ll hurt you more than me. Lastly, we’ll be married for a few years. Add that to the contract," Ethan said. A thought popped into his mind; a few years might be enough to destroy everything the Drews have.
"For a few years?" Susan muttered in disbelief.
 "This is nothing more than a contract marriage. We’ll stay together for a few years, and if it doesn’t work out, we'll part ways. Don’t worry, I’ll make sure you’re well compensated. You’ll have more than enough to live comfortably for the rest of your life," Ethan said with a grin.
"At some point, you’ll need an heir," Susan said, doubt creeping in.
 "No, I don’t need one and if at all I need one, we will prepare a separate contract for that. All the conditions will be different then." Ethan was stunned at how bold her demands were.
 "Do you mind me having your child?" Susan asked with a smirk.
 "That's not what either of us signed up for. Let's stay focused on what this partnership actually is." Ethan said.
Susan nodded. "Cool, we can carry on with the contract, Ethan." She started to sign her name.
Susan was finally relieved that she was in safe hands.
“Sure, he’s cold and mean, but he’s not heartless,” Susan thought. A flicker of determination crossed her face. “I can definitely make him fall for me.”
Her dreamland was interrupted by Ethan’s cold voice. "I’ll hide the contract somewhere safe. And, your father, mother, and sister won’t gain entry to my home or my company after we’re married," Ethan said bluntly.
"Done. I look forward to being married to you," Susan replied. "I must leave now."
 "Okay. See you tomorrow at the wedding hall at 10 a.m.. Don’t forget to carry your birth certificate," Ethan said, standing.
Susan turned to face Ethan one last time. "Thank you," she said softly, her voice barely steady.
Ethan gave a curt nod, his expression unreadable.
As Susan stepped out of the private room, she felt a mix of fear and determination flooding through her. ‘Tomorrow. I'm really doing this. I am marrying Jacob’s Cousin! Yes! I am getting out of that hell! That gloomy Drew mansion! 

Susan sped off in her car, her mind still spinning. She was going to be the daughter-in-law of one of the most powerful families in California's elite business circles and when her family found out, they’d be furious! 
Especially Sophia, who wanted everything she owned!
 And then there was the abominable Jacob Smith.
“He is probably already making plans to torment me, ripping me off of all the powers from the Drew Corporation and snatching the percentage of whatever shares I hold in that company,” she thought. “They might retaliate once they learn about this new development with Ethan."
She could not help but feel anxious about the next day. Her life was in the hands of the powerful Ethan, and she hoped he would free her from her home and help her get her revenge. One thing was sure, after tomorrow, nothing would ever be the same!
 The next morning, Susan was jolted awake from a deep sleep by the sound of violent banging on her door.
 "Open the door, you bitch! Vile creature! Shameless slut!"

She froze, shocked by the words hurled from outside.
 It was her mother and sister.
 “Why are they shouting at me?” Susan wondered in alarm. “Did they find out about the contract?”
Before she could move, the door burst open. They stormed inside.
 "How dare you roam around in this mansion like a desperate bitch!" Sophia shouted.
 "Sophia, what are you talking about?" Susan asked, panicked.
Her mother swung her arm. A loud slap cracked across Susan’s left cheek, making her stumble back, lightheaded.
 “Don't ever call me your mother.”
Her mother yanked her by the hair and dragged her out of bed, still in her nightdress. Then, she slapped and shouted at her as she stood there, confused and trying to defend herself.
Maids gathered outside the door, drawn by the noise. Noah arrived last.
 “What is going on here?” he demanded.
“This daughter of yours is nothing but a walking scandal,” her mother hissed. “I warned you to get rid of her before she drags this family through more shame!”
“How could you speak of me like that, Mom!” Susan shouted. “Stop spreading lies and rumors!”
 “Rumors?” her mother shouted. “Don’t play innocent. The maid saw you sneaking into Jacob’s room at night.”
 Susan’s face froze. “What? That’s not true! I would never…”
Her mother motioned to the side, and a nervous maid stepped forward.
 Sophia gently said, “Go on. Tell them what you saw.”
 “I saw Ms. Susan going in and out of Mr. Jacob’s room… several nights.”
 "Liar! She's lying, Dad!" Susan, now on her knees, crawled closer to her father.
Noah turned toward the corner of the room. Susan and the others followed his gaze.
There stood Jacob.
With a sorrowful, whimpering voice, Jacob said, “Forgive me, Mr. Drew… but she forced me to be her sex slave since she returned from Paris. I tried to refuse her, but she threatened to ruin my engagement with Sophia if I didn't comply. I had no choice but to submit to her demands.”
“Dad, they’re lying. This is all fabricated!”
 Her mother stepped forward and slapped Susan hard across the face, sending her crashing to the floor, numb with shock.
“Enough,” her father finally shouted.
 “You can’t stay here anymore. You’ve proven to be a shame. You are a threat to our family before your sister’s marriage.”
 “Dad, please, don’t.” Susan pleaded to deaf ears.
At Noah’s command, everyone retreated from the room.
Her mother and her sister were the last to leave, their eyes cold as they stared at Susan, who was struggling to stay on her feet.
“Where will I go?” Susan pleaded, her voice shaking.
Sophia smirked. “You think this is the worst thing that could happen to you? Oh, darling, I have far worse planned.”
With that, she turned and walked out with her mother.
Susan sank to her knees.
“I knew no one would believe me,” She thought. “And I don’t have much time to argue with these idiots. The wedding. Ethan must be on his way. I will deal with my family later. Ethan is the most important person to me today. He’ll be waiting for me at the entrance of the wedding hall. I should not be late!”
Susan quickly hid her birth certificate in her purse and changed into a decent outfit. Then, she called for a cab and left for the wedding hall. 
On the way, Susan thought about everything she had left behind, and when things had begun to change.
After her grandfather passed, the house was never the same. The warmth disappeared. The people inside it changed. He had been the only one who made her feel safe there, and without him, it stopped feeling like home.
She decided not to look back. Instead, she fixed her eyes on the life she was about to begin with Ethan.
He was still a stranger. She didn't know his habits, his past, or what kind of husband he would be. But something about him felt familiar. Steady. Unexpectedly reassuring.
Then the taxi slowed.
Susan leaned forward, fingers tightening around the strap of her bag. Cars inched along, horns sounding somewhere behind her. She glanced out the window, then at the road ahead.
Not now.
She checked the time once, then forced herself to stop. Checking again wouldn't make the cars move.
"What's going on?" she asked the driver.
"Morning rush," he said. "We'll get there."
Susan nodded, but her chest felt tight. What if she was late? What if he had already come and gone? She hadn't asked Ethan how long he would wait. She had simply assumed he would be there, because he said he would.
The taxi picked up speed.
Susan exhaled slowly. She had already chosen this. Turning back wasn't an option.
Then the car slowed again and stopped.
"We're here," the driver said.
Susan got out quickly and paid, barely waiting for her change. The Recorder's Office loomed ahead, people moving in and out calmly, as if it were just another ordinary morning.
She hesitated.
Oh God. What if he's not there anymore? What if he didn't wait?
She looked down at herself. Rumpled clothes. Red eyes. No bouquet. No witnesses.
Would he even recognize her as his bride?
Susan pushed the thought aside and walked in.
Inside, footsteps echoed off the floor. Papers shuffled. Clerks spoke in low voices. Everyone else seemed prepared. Certain.
Susan wasn't.
She moved through the hall quickly, scanning faces she didn't know, her heartbeat loud in her ears. Near the registration counter, she stopped and took a breath.
Is he here?
Is Susan running out of time? Will Ethan be waiting, or was she holding on to a hope that was never real?

bodyText:
I used to set an alarm 20 minutes early just so I could sit on the edge of my bed and wait for my feet to stop screaming! 

That was my morning routine for almost two years. Not coffee. Not a shower. Just sitting there rubbing the bottoms of my feet, trying to talk myself into standing up. The first few steps to the bathroom were always the worst. Like walking on a bruise that never heals. 

My podiatrist said plantar fasciitis. Gave me a cortisone shot that worked for about three weeks, then the pain came back worse. Custom orthotics that cost me $400 and honestly didn't do much. A night splint that was so uncomfortable I lasted four nights before it ended up in the closet. 

I tried the frozen water bottle thing. The tennis ball thing. Stretching exercises from YouTube that I actually did religiously for three months because I was that desperate. Some of it helped during the day, I'll give it that. But every single morning I'd wake up and it was like my feet had reset to zero overnight. 

That's the part nobody tells you about plantar fasciitis. You can do everything right all day and your feet still betray you every morning. My physical therapist explained it like this: when your foot relaxes at night, the fascia tissue shortens up. Then your first step basically re-tears it. Every single morning. Like ripping a scab off before it's had time to heal. 

She's the one who mentioned these bamboo compression sleeves. Said a lot of her patients couldn't tolerate the night splints (apparently that's most people, which made me feel less like a quitter). She wasn't making any big promises. Just said some of her plantar fasciitis patients wear them to bed and the mornings seem to go better. 

I ordered a pair and then honestly forgot about them for a few days. I think I'd just stopped expecting anything to work at that point. But I put them on one Tuesday night and they actually felt... nice? Soft. Nothing like that rigid boot. More like a snug sock that just holds everything in place.

Next morning I did my usual thing. Sat on the bed. Braced myself. Stood up. And the pain was there but it was maybe a 4 instead of the usual 8. I told myself it was a fluke.

It wasn't. After about a week of wearing them every night, the morning hobble went from 20 minutes to maybe 5. After three weeks, most mornings I can just get up and walk to the bathroom like a normal person. Not perfectly. Not pain-free. But I don't need that alarm anymore.

They're not going to cure plantar fasciitis. My PT was very clear about that and I want to be clear about it too. The fascia still needs to heal on its own timeline and that takes time no matter what. But something about the gentle compression keeping things supported overnight, keeping blood moving while I sleep, it's making the mornings so much more livable. That's all I can tell you.

I'm four months in now. Still wear them every night. My husband asked me last week if my feet were getting better because he noticed I was already in the kitchen making coffee when he woke up. I almost cried. That used to be impossible. 

If you're dealing with that horrible first-step-of-the-morning pain, the kind where you dread getting out of bed, these might be worth trying. I'm not a doctor and I can't promise they'll work the same for you. But they gave me my mornings back and I honestly didn't think that was possible anymore.

bodyText:
Turns out I don't have plantar fasciitis and you might not either.

I'm 52. I've had this in my right foot for two years and four months.

You know the mornings. That first step out of bed is the one that tells you what kind of day you're going to have. I used to sit on the edge of the mattress and just look at the floor. Actually look at it. Like it was a thing I had to negotiate with.

Then it stopped being just mornings.

It became the whole house.

I have not been barefoot in my own home in two years.

Not once. crocs on before my feet touch the carpet. crocs on to make coffee. crocs on to walk down my own hallway at eleven at night to check the back door. I keep a pair by the bed. I keep another pair by the couch so I don't have to cross the living room in socks. My husband walks around barefoot like it's nothing and I watch him do it the way you'd watch someone do a card trick.

And at night, the splint. That plastic boot strapped to my leg in my own bed.

That's the part nobody talks about. It's not that your foot hurts. It's that you are wearing footwear inside your own house at all hours except for when I'm sitting down. Always relying on something to soften the step even at the grocery store, I'm leaning on the cart. Not pushing it. Leaning.

I want to say what it takes from you and I don't know how to say it without sounding dramatic. So here's the plainest version.

I stopped planning things.

Not big things. I stopped planning the farmers market. I stopped saying yes to a hike because I didn't know what my foot would be in three weeks. My daughter asked me to come out for a long weekend and I said maybe. I said maybe to my own daughter because of my foot.

I did everything they told me.

Three podiatrists. Custom orthotics, the expensive ones. The cheap ones before that. Stretches every morning. The frozen water bottle. The spiky ball. Calf raises. Going up a shoe size. The night splint. A cortisone shot I was so scared of I nearly walked out of the office.

The shot worked. For about five weeks. Then it came back and it came back worse.

Two years of doing everything right and nothing moving.

The breaking point was a Tuesday in March. I was standing in my kitchen and I couldn't get to the sink. That's the whole story. It was nine feet away and I stood there and did the math on whether it was worth it. And I thought: this is my life now. This is just what it is.

My podiatrist had started using the word surgery. Not pushing it. Just letting it sit on the table between us.

I went home and I sat in the car in my own driveway for twenty minutes.

I got a second opinion. Not because I'm brave. Because I was out of moves.

The man I ended up in front of has been doing feet for twenty years. Older. Not slick. The kind who doesn't fill the silence while he's thinking.

He watched me walk. He asked me how long. I said two years and four months.

And he put his pen down and said, "Then you're being treated for the wrong thing."

I laughed at him.

The kind where I knew I was right, I'd had three podiatrists. I'd had an MRI. I had a diagnosis written on paper. I said, I have plantar fasciitis. Everyone agrees I have plantar fasciitis.

He said, "You did. Two years ago."

And I sat there in that chair and I could feel my ears getting hot. Because if that was true, then two years of my life were a mistake. And I would rather have been sick than have been wasting my time.

I looked at him with a confused but angry look, like I wasn’t sure if he was telling the truth or not

He saw the look on my face and explained it to me.

The word ends in "itis." Itis means inflammation. And when this starts, that's a fair description. You overload the fascia. You get tiny tears in it. Your body sends inflammation, because that's what a body does when something tears. That's not the disease. That's the repair crew showing up.

The trouble starts when the repair crew never gets to finish the job.

Because you cannot stop using your foot. You have to walk to the bathroom. You have to stand at the sink. So the tissue gets torn again before it's finished healing from the last time, and again before it finishes healing from that, and it never once completes a repair. 

And a tissue that never completes a repair does not stay the same. It changes.

He told me the fibers in there are supposed to lie down straight and tight, like the strands of a rope. When the healing keeps getting interrupted, they come back disorganized. Weak. The rope stops being a rope and starts being frayed cord.

That has a name. It's not fasciitis anymore. It's fasciosis.

Osis, not itis. Not inflammation. A degeneration.

I made him say it twice.

Degeneration. My foot wasn't sitting there inflamed and waiting for the swelling to go down. It was breaking down. The tissue itself was falling apart, getting structurally worse, month over month, for two years, while I iced it and stretched it and strapped it into a plastic boot at night.

He drew it on the back of a chart.

Overload. Tear. Start to heal. Overload again before it heals. Tear it worse. Start to heal. Overload again.

Every step you take rips open the thing that's trying to fix itself.

That's the whole disease. Not "my foot is inflamed." My foot was a rope that never got a single day to knit back together, and it was coming apart one strand at a time.

And once he said it, two years of failure rearranged themselves in front of me.

The mornings. I always thought the morning was bad because the foot got stiff overnight. It's worse than that. At night, off your feet, the fascia finally goes slack, and your body starts trying to patch it. That's the only window it gets all day.

But it's a bad window. That tissue sits at the end of the line, furthest from your heart, and lying still in bed you're barely moving any blood down there at all. So your body does the repair with almost nothing to build with. What it lays down overnight is thin. Weak. Half a patch.

Then you stand up. And your whole body weight goes down through that patch before it ever had a chance to harden.

That's what the first step is. That's the pain. It isn't stiffness. It's you tearing open the only repair your body managed all night, and it tears easy, because there was never enough blood down there to make it strong.

Every morning of my life. Ripping open the one thing my body tried to build while I slept.

Then the splint. Two years I slept in that thing. It holds your foot at a right angle so the fascia stays under a gentle stretch all night. And that does work, in a way. If the tissue is held taut, it can't go slack, and relax, so there's nothing there to tear in the morning and the first step doesn't hurt as much.

It buys you a quieter morning by taking away the one window your foot had. It parks that tissue in limbo all night, every night. Not stretched enough to tear. Not slack enough to heal.

All that splint ever bought me was a quieter first step. But as soon as it came off the rope kept fraying.

The stretches. I was pulling on a cord that was already coming apart and calling it treatment.

The orthotics. They cushioned the landing. They propped the arch from underneath. They did nothing about the tearing and nothing about the healing. A pillow under a wound.

The cortisone. That one hurts to say out loud. Cortisone is an anti-inflammatory. It goes after inflammation. It does not reorganize one collagen fiber and it does not stop one tear. It quieted the alarm for five weeks while the rope frayed on. And when it wore off I got the same foot back, five weeks worse, and I blamed my body.

Nothing I did failed because I did it wrong. Or it was a scam 

All of it failed because every last one of those things was aimed at the alarm and not at the fraying rope.

I asked him why nobody had told me this in two years.

He was honest with me. He said the first-line treatments are the first-line treatments. They get written down, they get handed out, and for most people they work. Most people get better and everybody feels good. The ones who don't get better keep coming back, and they get the next thing on the list, and then the shot, and then the conversation about surgery.

Then he said the quiet part. There's no money in telling you the tissue needs a chance to heal. There's money in the injection. There's money in the operation.

So I asked him what actually stops it.

He didn't hesitate. He said you have to break the cycle in two places at once. You have to take the load off it while you're on your feet, because you can't stop being on your feet. And you have to get blood down into it, because the fascia is at the very end of the line, furthest from your heart, and blood is what rebuilds a tissue.

Then he opened a drawer.

He took out a sleeve and put it in my hand.

It's like a compression sock with the toes open, and there are straps that wrap over the top and lock down underneath the arch. Thin. It disappears inside a shoe.

He told me he's been doing this twenty years and he didn't learn this in a classroom, he learned it watching people like me come back for a fourth and fifth visit. And that once he understood what was actually happening in there, he started sending patients to this instead of to the next injection.

He said the straps hold the arch so the tissue stops getting torn open with every step you take. And the compression drives blood down into a fascia that has been starved for months and can finally rebuild.

He said this is the only thing he's found that goes after both halves of that cycle at once.

I'll be honest, I still didn't believe it. I have a drawer at home full of things that didn't work.

I put it on that night the way you eat a salad you don't want.

It goes on like a sock. You pull the straps snug across the arch and you feel them take hold, like a hand cupping the bottom of your foot from underneath.

And I stood up. And I put my weight down wrong, the way you do when you're not thinking, and I braced for the thing that always happens.

It didn't happen. The pain wasn’t gone but it wasn’t unbearable, interrupting or the kind that has you reaching for a railing. 

That was the whole event. Nothing shot up through my heel. I stood in my kitchen at ten at night and put my weight on that foot again on purpose, just to check.

Two days later I walked to the bathroom in the morning without doing the thing I do, where I hold the doorframe and lower my heel down in stages.

I just walked.

I said "huh" out loud, to nobody.

Three weeks in, I made dinner and stood the entire time.

And then came the day I found out it was real.

My sleeve was in the wash. I had the whole day at home ahead of me and nothing to put on, and I remember thinking, fine. It's one day. I'm not going anywhere.

By the afternoon I felt it. Not the old thing. Nothing close to the old thing. A dull ache coming up through the arch, low and steady, the way a bruise reminds you where it is.

I sat down at my own kitchen table and I understood two things at once.

This dull ache used to be my good day. That was the best my foot ever felt for two years, and I used to be grateful for it.

And I hadn't thought about my feet in three weeks.

Not once. Not standing at the sink, not on the stairs, not getting out of bed. Three weeks of my life where my feet were just my feet. Until the one day my sleeve was in the wash

I sat there with my hand over my mouth.

That's when I believed him.

I've been wearing them since April.

I went to the farmers market on a Saturday and I never once limped, I went to every stand I wanted to and not just the ones close to the parking lot. 

I did the whole grocery store, both sides, and I was pushing the cart. Pushing it. I got to the car and realized I hadn't leaned on a single thing, and I sat in the driver's seat and cried, which I'm not going to apologize for.

And a month ago I got up in the night for a glass of water, and I was halfway down the hall before I understood what I was doing.

I was barefoot.

Standing in my own hallway in the dark on my own two bare feet.

Two years. And I didn't even notice I was doing it.

That's the thing I would have paid anything for. Not "less pain." I wanted to stop thinking about my feet. I wanted my house back.

They're called Koprez Foot Sleeves.

The stretching and the icing and the inserts and the splint are not failing because you're doing them wrong. They're failing because they're aimed at the alarm bell. And that fascia is tearing open every morning before you've had your coffee and it is not being allowed to finish a single repair.

Every month you stay on the list, that rope frays a little further.
