bodyText:
What if the reason your plantar fasciitis never goes away is because it was never actually plantar fasciitis to begin with?

My name is Anabelen. I've been a physical therapist for over twenty years.

When I first started asking that question, my colleagues laughed at me.

What I found when digging into this, later gave them no choice but to apologize.

If you've had this stabbing heel pain for more than a few months, you already know the pattern.

The first steps out of bed are the worst. Some mornings it feels like stepping on glass.

It eases up once you're moving, then creeps back by the end of the day.

Standing at the sink. Standing in a checkout line. Standing anywhere long enough.

You've probably already tried the standard advice. Rest. Ice. Stretching every morning. Insoles. Supportive shoes. Maybe a night splint. Maybe a cortisone shot.

And still, months or years later, it's not gone.

Maybe you've started avoiding certain shoes. Or planning routes around where you'll be able to sit down.

Maybe you turned down a weekend trip because you weren't sure how much walking it would involve. Or told a friend you'd skip their birthday party, and blamed it on being tired.

Maybe you've quietly stopped doing the things that put you on your feet for long stretches, without really announcing it to anyone.

That's the part that gets to people the most.

Not just the pain, but the confusion. And the quiet way it started shrinking their life, one skipped plan at a time.

You did what you were told. You followed the plan. But the pain still remained.

Friends and family mean well, but "have you tried stretching" only lands so many times before it stops feeling helpful.

Some people start to wonder if this is just what their foot is like now. If this is just how the rest of their life looks.

That fear, more than the pain itself, is usually what brings someone into my office.

I remember the week I finally looked into why the condition is even called what it's called.

I'd just watched a patient cry in my treatment room. Not from the pain. From exhaustion. She'd done everything right for a year and had nothing to show for it.

That night I went home and started reading.

Plantar means sole of the foot. Fascia is the band of tissue underneath it.

Both are old medical Latin, the language doctors used to name almost everything in the body for centuries.

Then there's the ending, "itis," added by a doctor writing in that same old medical Latin back in the late 1800s.

It means inflammation.

Inflammation is supposed to be temporary. Redness, swelling, heat, pain, then it resolves, usually within a couple of weeks.

If your ankle is inflamed after a sprain, it calms down in ten to fourteen days.

So if "fasciitis" literally means inflammation, why does the pain still show up eight months, a year, sometimes years later?

Inflammation doesn't behave that way. Nothing about it lasts for years.

In 2014, researchers looked at tissue samples taken from patients with long-standing plantar fasciitis. They didn't find active inflammation.

They found degeneration. Collagen fibers that had become disorganized and frayed.

Structure breaking down, not swelling up.

Some researchers now call it "plantar fasciosis" instead of fasciitis, since "osis" refers to a degenerative process, not an inflammatory one.

Here's why that distinction matters. Inflamed tissue needs calming down. Degenerated tissue needs to be rebuilt. Those are two different jobs, and they call for two completely different approaches.

Treat inflammation and you reduce swelling. Treat degeneration the same way, and you're not actually doing anything for the torn, disorganized fibers underneath.

Most people are never told this distinction exists. Not because anyone is hiding it. Because the name "fasciitis" got locked in back in the 1800s, long before anyone looked at the tissue up close, and the treatment protocols built around that name never caught up.

So people get told they have fasciitis, and they get handed the same plan every time. Rest. Ice. Anti-inflammatories. Insoles. Supportive shoes. Stretching. Sometimes a cortisone shot. All of it built for inflammation that, in a lot of these cases, isn't actually there anymore.

Once you understand that the tissue itself has changed, from inflamed to degenerated, a lot of things stop making sense the way they used to. Namely, why the treatment stopped working months ago even though you never stopped following it.

It's a bit like being told your dashboard light is on because you're low on oil, then spending months topping off the coolant instead.

The light stays on. Not because the advice was bad advice in general, but because it was never aimed at what was actually wrong under the hood.

Ice, anti-inflammatory medication, cortisone injections, all of it is built to fight inflammation.

If what you actually have has moved past the inflammatory stage into a degenerative one, none of that is aimed at your actual problem anymore.

That's why these treatments tend to help a little at first, then plateau, then stop working altogether.

It's not that you did anything wrong.

It's that the treatment and the actual problem stopped matching months ago.

Here's the part that made my colleagues apologize to me.

Degenerated tissue doesn't need less swelling. It needs help rebuilding.

That means circulation. Delivering oxygen and nutrients to an area of the body that already has famously poor blood flow.

The fascia isn't like a muscle. It doesn't have a rich blood supply to begin with. It's also about as far from your heart as tissue gets, which makes it one of the last places circulation reaches and one of the slowest to heal, even under good conditions.

And it means something else too. Every step you take presses the fascia flat against the ground and stretches it out, right in the middle of trying to knit itself back together. Tissue that keeps getting re-torn by the next step never actually rebuilds. It just keeps tearing at the same rate it's trying to heal.

So the fascia needs two things at once. More blood moving into it. And relief from the constant pounding that keeps re-injuring it before it can recover.

That's not what ice does. That's not what a cortisone shot does. Neither one touches circulation, and neither one takes the daily pounding off the tissue.

Once I started paying closer attention to those two things instead of only inflammation, I started recommending something different to patients whose pain had gone on far longer than it should have.

And what I've found, after years of looking, is that almost nothing addresses both of those things at once. Most solutions pick one. An insole supports the foot but does nothing for circulation. A massage gun works the blood flow but does nothing to take the pressure off the fascia while you're standing on it.

The one thing I found that does both is a compression sleeve, worn around the foot, arch, and calf, during the day or overnight.

Not to numb the pain. To keep blood moving into the area consistently, while a set of built-in straps lift and support the arch, taking the fascia off the ground it keeps getting slammed against with every step.

The compression is graduated, meaning it's tightest at the foot and gradually loosens up toward the calf. That gradient is what pushes blood back up through the leg instead of letting it pool at the bottom, the same principle circulation stockings use for people who stand all day.

Not everyone reacts the same way. But after years of seeing results from this sleeve, the vast majority of my patients feel some relief the moment they put it on. Enough to go for a longer walk. Enough to stop turning down invitations.

That said, it isn't meant to be worn every once in a while. After tracking patients over time, we see a clear pattern: the ones who wear it consistently for 60 days get the most sustained relief, and eventually don't need it at all, because the fascia has had real time to rebuild.

If you've been dealing with this for months, maybe longer, here's what stood out to me most, watching patient after patient go through it.

Skipping the morning walk because you don't trust how your foot will feel.

Making excuses for why you can't stand at the sink long enough to finish the dishes.

Turning down invitations because you don't know if you'll be able to stay on your feet.

Refusing to garden. Refusing to play with your grandkids in the yard.

Timing your whole day around when you know the pain will be worst.

Refusing to just live the way you did before this started.

If you've tried the ice, the anti-inflammatories, maybe even a cortisone shot, and nothing has stuck for more than a few weeks, now you know why.

Almost everything on that list is built to fight inflammation.

If what you actually have has moved into degeneration, the treatments built for inflammation were never going to fix it, no matter how carefully you followed the routine. They were solving a problem you didn't have anymore.

It's a small company, and they make these in limited batches, so they sell out faster than most people expect. They've had a lot more attention on this lately, likely because patients keep telling each other about it.

And I know a couple of people who've had to check back more than once to catch it in stock.

Anabelen, PT

There's a money-back guarantee, so trying it doesn't have to be a leap of faith.

I wish I'd known that before a few of my patients spent months on things that did nothing for them.

I dropped 72 pounds and my plantar fasciitis stayed. What I added next made it disappear.

I've been a big girl my whole life.

I've never been a lazy one.

I teach fourth grade, and I walk all day in class.

Before any of this started, I was walking 10 to 15 thousand steps a day.

I used to be the one who planned every trip. My sister and I did New Orleans every spring…

We walked everywhere: the Quarter, the Garden District, Magazine Street until our shopping bags cut into our fingers.

I never once thought about my feet.

Four years ago, on our spring trip, my feet hurt so bad by the last night I was in tears. I assumed it was my shoes.

It wasn't.

When I got home, it didn't go away.

It started as a stiffness at the end of the workday.

Then it was there every morning, those first steps out of bed.

Then it was limping every time I stood up.

Getting up from my desk, from the couch, from the car.

Walking across a parking lot felt like walking on glass.

The doctor that finally diagnosed me with plantar fasciitis looked me up and down when he mentioned weight is a contributing factor.

Like, yes, I know, my guy.

Just tell me what insoles to get and let me live.

He didn't.

He told me to lose weight.

So did the next one.

And the podiatrist after that.

I swear every question I asked, weight loss was the solution.

I'm not stupid.

I know what I weigh.

People just love pointing out our weight and need to lose it, as if we don't look in mirrors or walk around in it all day every day.

What none of them could tell me was how.

Walking was how I'd always stayed active.

Walking was now the thing that hurt.

When one doctor told me to stay off my feet for six weeks and lose weight at the same time, I said it to his face:

"I can't stay off my feet for 6 weeks and continue to lose weight."

He assured me I was capable of that.

So I did what every woman in my position does.

I sat up at 1 AM and typed "best otc insoles for plantar fasciitis overweight heavy women" into Google.

The first thing it suggested was that I lose weight.

I laughed out loud, alone in my kitchen.

I didn't know what else to do.

Meanwhile the pain was taking my life apart one piece at a time.

The New Orleans trip that spring, my feet hurt so bad I was in tears.

I blamed my shoes. The next spring, I didn't go.

I stopped walking after dinner.

I stopped saying yes to anything that involved standing.

And, like everyone warned me, I gained weight, because the pain limited my steps.

There is only so much you can do to lose weight when you suddenly lose mobility.

So I tried everything that didn't involve walking.

Power Step insoles, then orthopedic shoes.

No relief.

Custom inserts from the podiatrist.

$500, and they never really helped at all.

A night splint.

The boots never fit comfortably on my calves, and I gave up on it.

A cortisone shot.

The pain was worse than the plantar fasciitis itself.

A frozen water bottle rolled under my feet every night on the kitchen floor.

And then I decided I was going to take away their favorite excuse.

Weight loss happens in the kitchen, not the gym.

So that's where I did it.

I cooked at home.

I measured everything.

I stopped eating after dinner.

It took me the better part of two years.

And I lost the weight.

I went back to that same doctor.

I stood in his office on the same two feet that had hurt the whole time, and I said:

"I lost the weight, but my foot still hurts. Are we going to do anything about this, or will you blame it on my hormones this time since you can't blame it on my weight?"

He told me to keep stretching.

I sat in my car in the parking lot afterward, and one thought kept running through my head.

All I want is to get my life back.

It was my friend Tasha who finally asked me the right question.

Tasha had PF a few years before me.

She's tiny.

Always has been.

When I told her about the doctor and the hormones comment, she didn't even look surprised.

She said her physical therapist told her it's not a weight-related injury.

Lots of very fit people have the exact same pain.

Then she said, "I know someone who lost 50 pounds and all that happened was she developed it in the other foot too."

I don't think I realized until that moment how much of the last four years I'd spent believing this was my fault.

Then Tasha asked me something no doctor ever had.

What had actually helped me, even for an hour?

I had to think about it.

A hot bath.

The heating pad.

Rubbing my own feet on the couch at night.

"It takes a long time," she said, "because of the small amount of blood flow to that area."

She told me someone had once told her you shouldn't ice it, because ice cuts down blood flow, and you should use heat instead.

And I sat there doing the math.

Every single thing that had ever helped me brought warmth and blood into my feet.

But nobody had ever given me something that did it on purpose.

That's when Tasha told me about her physical therapist.

After two podiatrists, she'd found a PT who works with Olympic athletes and is on the cutting edge of plantar fasciitis research.

Part of every session was a machine at the PT's office.

Red and infrared light, right on her feet.

"It helped a lot," she said. "I was trying to afford it again."

Because that was the catch.

It was $200 a session, a couple of times a week, and insurance wouldn't touch it.

So her PT recommended a version she could use at home.

A boot.

Same tech she used on the athletes at her practice.

I actually groaned.

I'd seen the red light pads all over my feed.

After four years, I didn't trust anything that lit up.

That night I did what I always do.

I sat up at my kitchen table and looked it up.

The first thing I found wasn't an ad.

It was on NASA's website.

Back in the late 1980s, NASA was funding red LED lights to grow plants in space.

The scientists working under those lights noticed the scrapes on their hands seemed to get better faster than normal.

So for years, NASA funded research on red and near-infrared LED light, because in space, injuries recover slowly.

The part that stopped me was what they did next.

NASA's team gave LED devices to U.S. Navy crews for their training injuries.

NASA reported "more than a 40 percent greater improvement in musculoskeletal injuries and a 50 percent faster healing time for lacerations, compared to control groups."

Physical therapists still use these kinds of devices today, just like Tasha's.

I kept thinking about every single thing that ever helped me. The warm bath. The heating pad. My own hands.

And it finally clicked.

Every one of them brought blood into my feet.

Fresh blood carries oxygen, and that's what damaged tissue needs for repair and recovery.

You need blood to flow to recover.

That's why it takes forever.

Tasha said it herself: there's only a small amount of blood flow to that area.

I told her what I'd already spent. Over $4,000 on shoes, inserts, shots, and appointments.

She said, "So what's one more, if you can send it back?"

They have a lifetime money back guarantee.

If it doesn't do anything for your plantar fasciitis just send it back.

No questions asked.

It's called the True Naturals Red Light Therapy Boot.

You slip it on and it wraps your entire foot: sole, heel, arch, top, and ankle.

It's lined with red and near-infrared lights, with adjustable warmth you can turn up or down.

It's cordless, so I can wear it on the couch without being stuck next to an outlet.

You set the timer for 10, 20, or 30 minutes and it shuts itself off.

It fits US shoe sizes 4 through 12 and closes with adjustable Velcro straps.

After the night splint, I needed to know the thing would actually fit me.

What made me order was the guarantee.

True Naturals backs it for life.

After four years of buying things that ended up in the back of my closet, that was the only reason I was willing to try one more.

It came on a Thursday.

I put it on during my show that night and fell asleep with it on.

The timer turned it off.

I wore it every night after that.

Both feet.

Twenty minutes on the couch.

Two weeks in, I stood up from my desk at work and walked to the printer before I realized I hadn't braced myself first.

A month in, I walked 3 miles after dinner for the first time in three years.

Last week I texted my sister a booking link to a hotel on Magazine Street.

She texted back: Are you serious?

I am.

I'm not writing this to tell anyone what to do with their body.

I spent four years being told that.

I'm writing it because important medical care is withheld all too often based on weight, especially for women.

I lost the weight, and it turned out that wasn't the whole story.

If you've done everything they told you, bought the inserts, gotten the shots, maybe even lost the weight…

and your feet still hurt…

it might not be the part of the story everyone keeps pointing at.

Here's the boot I use:

https://trytruenaturals.com/pages/li11rw2

It's $159.95 and backed for life. If it doesn't work, you send it back.

P.S. My sister booked the hotel. Magazine Street, second week of April.

bodyText:
𝐈 𝐡𝐚𝐯𝐞 𝐛𝐞𝐞𝐧 𝐚 𝐩𝐨𝐝𝐢𝐚𝐭𝐫𝐢𝐬𝐭 𝐟𝐨𝐫 𝟐𝟐 𝐲𝐞𝐚𝐫𝐬. 𝐀𝐧𝐝 𝐢𝐟 𝐲𝐨𝐮𝐫 𝐟𝐢𝐫𝐬𝐭 𝐬𝐭𝐞𝐩 𝐨𝐮𝐭 𝐨𝐟 𝐛𝐞𝐝 𝐢𝐧 𝐭𝐡𝐞 𝐦𝐨𝐫𝐧𝐢𝐧𝐠 𝐦𝐚𝐤𝐞𝐬 𝐲𝐨𝐮 𝐠𝐫𝐚𝐛 𝐭𝐡𝐞 𝐰𝐚𝐥𝐥...

I am about to tell you exactly what we have been getting wrong about plantar fasciitis. And why that mistake almost guarantees you stay in pain.

By the end of this, you are going to be furious.

My name is Dr. Hayes. Board-certified podiatrist. Twenty-two years treating heel pain.

And I am about to contradict nearly everything my profession has been telling you.

Because there are three things happening right now.

One. Your plantar fasciitis is not what your doctor told you it is.

Two. Every treatment they gave you was built on that wrong diagnosis.

And three. There is an entire system that profits every single time you come back in pain, because nothing they prescribed was designed to fix the actual problem.

So let me tell you what happened with one of my patients. Because her story is going to change how you see every appointment you have ever had.

Her name was Barbara. 64 years old.

She had spent thirty years on her feet. School secretary for most of her career. Grandmother who prided herself on never slowing down. Morning walks before the neighborhood woke up. Saturday farmer's markets with her husband. Gardening before the heat got too bad.

Then one morning she stepped out of bed and grabbed the wall.

She thought it was a cramp. By the end of the week she was sitting on the edge of the mattress every morning, bracing herself before the first step.

The pain was worst in those first fifteen steps. A sharp, stabbing sensation right at the base of her heel. It would ease to a dull ache by mid-morning. Then come back the moment she sat down and stood up again.

She stopped her morning walks. Stopped gardening. Started wearing thick-soled slippers before she made it to the bathroom.

And the identity of it. This woman had been moving her whole life. Suddenly she was timing her trips to the kitchen.

And here is what makes me genuinely ashamed of my profession.

She came through my office. Before me she had seen her GP and an orthopedic specialist. Thousands of dollars in appointments, X-rays, and imaging.

And every single one of us told her some version of the same thing.

"Rest it."

"Stretch your calf every morning. Roll a frozen water bottle under your foot."

"Try custom orthotics." Six hundred dollars.

"Let's do a cortisone shot."

She did the shot. Worked for about eight weeks. Then she was back.

We gave her a second one. Same result.

"Try the night splint."

Three nights in she woke up with it twisted, threw it in the closet.

And her heel? Still tearing every single morning.

I watched this woman do everything I told her, spend over two thousand dollars, follow every protocol exactly, and get worse. Not better. Worse.

And I kept telling her the same things because I did not have anything else to offer.

Until a researcher at a podiatry conference said one sentence that stopped me cold.

"Plantar fasciitis is the wrong name for what most of your patients have. It is not inflammation. It is degeneration. The tissue has stopped rebuilding. And you are treating a fire that is not there."

He showed slides. Tissue samples from actual chronic plantar fasciitis patients.

No inflammation. Almost none.

Just broken-down tissue that had stopped repairing itself.

After the session I walked up to him. Dr. Nathan Cole. Spent his career studying how the body heals tissue and what happens when it stops.

I told him about Barbara.

"I know exactly who she is," he said. "She is in every practice in this country. And we keep failing her because we are treating the wrong problem."

He found a quiet corner. Said it would take thirty minutes.

I gave him an hour.

He drew a diagram on the back of a program.

"The plantar fascia has almost no blood supply at the heel. That is the exact spot where the pain lives. The tissue tears every day under your weight, and it cannot repair itself the way a muscle would, because it is barely getting any blood to begin with."

He tapped the paper.

"So every night your body tries to fix the damage. Sends what little blood it can. Starts laying down new tissue. And every morning you stand up and tear straight back through it before it sets. It never fully heals. Not because your body is not trying. Because your cells do not have the fuel to finish the job."

"What fuel?" I asked.

He looked at me like the answer was obvious.

"ATP. It is what every cell in your body runs on. Think of it as the gas in the tank. Muscles have good blood flow, so they get plenty of it. The fascia at your heel does not. Those cells are running on empty. They are trying to repair. They just cannot."

Here is what he said next.

Every treatment you have tried addresses something other than the fuel problem.

Stretching? Takes mechanical pressure off the tissue. Does not refill the tank.

Orthotics? Spreads the load differently. Does not refill the tank.

Cortisone? Quiets the inflammation signal in tissue that is barely inflamed anyway. Does not refill the tank.

Rest? Stops the tearing input temporarily. Still does not refill the tank.

I sat there going through every tool I had used for twenty-two years.

Every single one worked around the problem. Not one of them put fuel into the cells that needed it to heal.

"So what does?" I asked.

He pulled up a study on his phone. Then three more.

Near-infrared light at 850nm penetrates through the skin and through the heel pad, all the way down to the fascia itself. At that depth, the light is absorbed by the mitochondria, the part of each cell that makes energy. It tells the mitochondria to produce more ATP. Faster than they would on their own. Significantly more.

And when those cells finally have the fuel they have been missing, the repair process that has been stuck in a loop for months, sometimes years, can actually complete.

"Before you say it sounds like something from a crystal shop," he said, "this is forty years of peer-reviewed research. The mechanism is real. The problem is nobody is connecting it to plantar fasciitis in a clinical setting. Because there is no money in connecting it."

He put his phone away.

"Not masking the pain. Not redistributing the load. Giving the cells the fuel they need to actually heal."

Here is what kept me up after that conversation.

The research exists. Has existed for decades.

But you cannot build a practice around a device someone uses at home. You cannot charge for cortisone injections if patients are healing themselves. You cannot sell orthotics on a recurring basis to someone whose heel has actually repaired.

The money is in management. Repeat visits. Ongoing symptom control. Not in resolution.

Every return visit I had from a chronic plantar fasciitis patient was a failure I was profiting from.

I did not see it that way at the time.

I went home and looked for a device that could deliver 850nm near-infrared light directly to the heel, with consistent contact on the sole of the foot.

Most of what I found was general wellness product. No real wavelength data. No indication it could actually reach the fascia.

Then I found FootRevive.

It was built by Dr. Michael James, an orthopedic specialist, in partnership with Kovaria, a US-based health company. They designed it with one specific goal: get near-infrared light at the right wavelength into the plantar fascia at the heel.

Not a general wellness product. Not something repurposed from a face mask or a pain pad. A doctor who understood the mechanism built it to address the mechanism.

Flexible wrap. 64 near-infrared LED chips across the heel, arch, and ball of the foot. Holds direct contact against the sole. Wavelengths third-party tested and confirmed.

The specs matched the research exactly.

I had mild plantar fasciitis myself. Had managed it with orthotics and morning stretches for over a year. Functional, but never resolved.

Week 1: Twenty minutes each morning and evening. By day five the first step out of bed no longer made me flinch.

Day 10: Walked to the kitchen in the dark without thinking about it.

Week 3: Forgot to do my morning stretches. Did not need them.

Week 7: A trail I had avoided for eighteen months. No pain during. No flare after.

Then I called Barbara.

"I need to tell you something. The treatments I gave you were not wrong exactly. But they were never going to fix this. I was treating the wrong thing. I know what is actually happening now, and I know what addresses it."

I sent her the device. Twice a day, twenty minutes, heel pressed directly against the wrap.

Barbara, week 3: "I got up at 2am last night and walked to the bathroom without turning the light on. Did not even think about my foot until I was already back in bed."

Week 5: Her husband noticed she was moving differently. She had not realized she stopped limping.

Week 8: Farmer's market. Two hours on her feet. Walked both blocks there and back.

She called me afterward.

"I thought this was just what getting older felt like," she said. "I had no idea my cells were running out of fuel."

That is what they do not want you to understand.

Your heel is not a pain problem. It is a fuel problem. The cells in your fascia cannot repair the damage because they do not have enough ATP to run the repair. Once you fix that, the repair that has been stuck in a loop for months can finally finish.

Not masking the pain. Not managing it. Fixing what is actually broken.

And here is what I need you to understand about timing.

The longer those cells go without fuel, the more the tissue breaks down, and the harder it is to reverse. Early cases respond fast. If you have been dealing with this for two, three, five years, it takes longer and success rates drop.

If your first step out of bed is something you brace for. If you have rearranged your shoes, your mornings, your whole routine. If you did the shot and watched it wear off and you are already dreading the conversation about doing it again.

It is not because you are not stretching enough.

It is not because you chose the wrong orthotics.

It is because nobody has ever put fuel into the cells that need it to heal. And nobody told you that was even possible.

FootRevive has a 90-day money-back guarantee. If your heel does not feel different, you pay nothing.

Use it every day. Twenty minutes, morning and evening. Direct contact on the sole.

89% of users reported reduced morning heel pain within the first thirty days. 73% avoided or postponed surgery.

The medical system is not coming to fix this for you. It profits more from your next appointment than from your last one.

A researcher taught me more about plantar fasciitis in one hour than I learned in twenty-two years of practice.

Time to put that to use.

Get it.

P.S. I no longer recommend insoles as a first-line treatment for chronic plantar fasciitis. I send patients home with a protocol built around getting fuel back into the cells first. Two of my colleagues have stopped speaking to me. My patients are walking without pain.

P.P.S. The cortisone shot is not treating your plantar fasciitis. It is quieting a signal in tissue that is not inflamed. You are silencing the alarm while the house falls apart. Stop silencing the alarm. Fix the house.

P.P.P.S. Barbara: "I did over twenty thousand steps at the farmer's market on Saturday. My phone flagged it as a new personal record. I have not hit that number in three years. I cried in the parking lot."
title: Podiatrist of 22 Years: "We've Been Treating Plantar Fasciitis Wrong"
linkDescription: Plantar fasciitis isn't inflammation. It's degeneration. The collagen in your fascia is breaking down faster than your body can rebuild it, because your heel has some of the worst blood supply in your body. Every night it tries to repair. Every morning you tear it open again.

bodyText:
Don't ice your heel if you have plantar fasciitis. Do this instead.

I'm going to say something that no one who's had heel pain for years wants to hear. And I don't give a sh*t if it upsets you.

The cortisone shot won't fix this. The night splint won't. The calf stretches won't. Those $180 cloud sneakers all over your feed? Those won't either. The next podiatrist appointment won't.

And that "6 to 18 months, it usually clears up on its own"? That's just going to sit there and watch your foot get worse.

Not 1 thing on that list is touching what's really causing your pain. I know. I watched my mother deal with the same thing.

10 years of Ice. Inserts. 2 rounds of shots. Then a surgery that was meant to fix it all, where they cut the band in her foot to release it. It never held right after that. A cane, then a walker. No body could ever fix it.

Then, 1 year ago, I sat on the edge of my bed at 5:40 AM and couldn't put my right foot flat on the floor.

It's happening to me. And if you sat on the edge of your bed this morning working yourself up to that first step, it's happening to you.

So read every word. It's long. But the answer is in here. And it is NOT another treatment.

I'm Denise. I'm 59, from Mansfield, Ohio. I was a nursing home aide for 26 years. On my feet all day. Lifting, turning, hauling. The lot.

For me it started small. A twinge getting up off the couch after the 10 o'clock news. A little bruised feeling under my right heel. Nothing a bag of frozen peas wouldn't sort.

2 months later it wasn't small. It was a nail through my heel every morning. Standing up made me gasp out loud.

Some days it screamed. Some days it went almost quiet. I couldn't work it out. I thought the tissue in my foot was shredding a little more every week. It wasn't. (Hold that thought. It matters later.)

I did what you're meant to do. I called the office. Waited 3 weeks. Got 10 minutes with a doctor who never looked up from the screen. "Plantar fasciitis. Common at your age. Ice it. Rest it. Lose a bit of weight." Out the door.

The pharmacy sold me gel inserts. For 2 weeks it was almost a miracle. Then it stopped. And when the pain came back, it came back meaner. Deeper. The kind no cushion could reach, because it wasn't coming from the surface.

By then I'd joined 1 of those Facebook foot pain groups. Thousands of us. All hobbling to the bathroom at dawn. All with a tip. A night splint. A frozen water bottle. A massage gun. Compression sleeves. KT tape. Turmeric. A $40 pair of heel cups off Amazon. CBD balm. 2 more pairs of drugstore orthotics. $200 max cushion sneakers that everyone swore were like walking on clouds and that had me limping by Thursday.

I spent over $400 on sh*t in 4 months. And I still couldn't pull my own socks on without holding my breath.

Then it hit me like cold water. I was doing exactly what my mother did. The same ice. The same inserts. The same "give it time." Walking her road, step by step. Towards the same chair.

They'd always told us flat feet "run in families." Nobody told me the truth. We were both treating the wrong damn thing.

By August I was a ghost. I couldn't stand long enough to make a real dinner. I couldn't walk the dog past the second mailbox before the pain had me leaning on somebody's fence like an old woman. I stopped going to my grandson's Little League. I sat down to fold laundry. And I'd be up at 5:00 AM on the edge of the bed, working up to that first step. Crying. Swearing into my sleeve so I didn't wake my husband.

The woman who used to close down every wedding reception in Richland County was googling "mobility scooter" at 2:00 in the morning. I thought I was just getting old. I wasn't. That was wrong too.

Back to the doctor. He sent me to a podiatrist. The wait was 6 weeks. And a quick mention of custom orthotics. $600, not covered.

I paid for 1 physical therapy visit I couldn't afford. $55 for a printout that said ice 20 minutes, 3 times a day, and roll a frozen water bottle under the arch. "Keep at it. Give it more time." More time. While that foot ate me alive every morning.

So I iced it. Morning, after work and before bed. And here's the thing nobody warned me about: it was making it worse. I know why now. Ice numbs it. So for an hour after every session I'd feel brave, and I'd do the dishes and carry the laundry and walk the house barefoot on a foot that couldn't tell me what was happening to it. That band under your foot isn't swollen like a twisted ankle. It's torn. Overnight your body knits those tiny tears back together. Then you get up and haul on it first thing and rip every 1 of them open again. The ice never touched any of that. It just switched the alarm off while it happened.

That's why I say don't ice your heel. Nobody ever told me the ice was only hiding the problem.

The discharge paper even admitted it: "Most cases resolve within 6 to 18 months." That's not a treatment plan. That's a shrug on letterhead.

So I stopped hunting for another treatment. And I started hunting for the cause.

Once I saw it, I couldn't un see it. Look at the road they marched me down. My mother before me.

A twinge. Ice. An insert. It fades. Better sneakers. A shot. Another shot. $600 orthotics. Surgery. A chair.

Every step just managed the pain. Not 1 step ever asked WHY it was there. We were all mopping up the puddle and wondering why the bastard kept coming back.

I'd already ruled out the easy stuff. New shoes, twice. 15 pounds gone. None of it touched the pain. Because none of it reached where the problem really lived. Not my skin. Not even really my foot. Somewhere underneath it.

I spent 2 weeks reading. Not the sponsored stuff. The real threads. Reddit at 4:00 AM. Forums full of people who'd suffered 20 years. Physical therapists on YouTube who'd gone off script from the usual advice.

Then I found 1 comment. Buried under a post. From a retired mail carrier in Oregon.

"Mine burned for 6 years. I iced it every night for 5 of them. What finally settled it wasn't a treatment. Take the insole out of the shoe you wore yesterday. Put it next to a brand new one. Look at them both from the side."

From the side. Not how it feels under your thumb. From the side. I read it 10 times.

I did it that night. Mine was flatter. Then I talked myself out of it, because it still felt soft when I pressed it.

So I ordered the first thing I could find. $17 gel insoles off Amazon. Thousands of 5 star reviews.

Week 1: nothing.

Week 2: nothing.

Week 3: still turning around at that second mailbox, I nearly wrote it all off as more snake oil.

What saved me was a chat over the back fence. My neighbor Marlene is 71. She was a certified orthotist for 35 years. Half of them in a foot and ankle clinic in Columbus. She saw me come down my porch steps sideways, 1 at a time, and came over. I showed her the insoles. She laughed, kindly.

"Oh, honey. These are worse than useless. No wonder they've done nothing. Do you want to know why?"

And standing there in her slippers, she told me the thing no 10 minute appointment ever had.

"Your arch isn't a stack of bones that holds itself up. It's a bridge, and there's a band strung underneath holding the 2 ends together. Every step, your whole weight comes down and that arch drops. It's meant to drop, that's how a foot takes a step. The only thing that has ever mattered is what's underneath it when it does.

Out on dirt, on grass, on uneven ground, the ground comes up and catches it. On a concrete floor in a flat shoe, nothing does. That band catches all of it. 10,000 times a day. And after 50 it's worse, because the fat pad under your heel has thinned and that band's gone stiff. Less padding, less give. Same concrete you stood on at 30.

That's the whole job of an insole. Be there at the bottom of the step. And almost every insole you can buy fails at it. There are only 2 ways it happens.

The soft ones pancake. They feel supportive because they push back against your thumb. Your thumb isn't 180 pounds. Under your real weight it bottoms out. Flat, at the exact instant your arch is dropping, the 1 instant it had a job to do. And it doesn't happen all at once. A new one holds a little. Every day crushes it down further and it comes back less, until it doesn't come back at all.

That's why they work for a few weeks and then quit on you. You weren't imagining that.

The other kind doesn't collapse. It just hurts. Rock hard and bulky, the sort you rip out by lunchtime and leave in a drawer. That's what your $600 is going to buy you.

So you've got one that gives out and one you won't wear. Either way, by the end of the day that arch is dropping onto nothing.

Cushion is what a thing feels like when you're not standing on it. Holding is what it does when you are. Once it's flat it isn't doing anything. It's a floor with a logo on it."

First time in 1 year, something made sense.

Then she told me why everything I'd bought had failed. And it wasn't bad luck.

"The shots? They quiet the pain for a few weeks, then fade. They never hold anything up. It's like watering the leaves of a plant when the roots are dry. The ice? Same thing, colder. It quiets the pain for an hour at night. You're not doing the damage at night. You're doing it in the 14 hours you're upright. The sleeve, the cloud sneakers? The softer the shoe, the further that arch falls before anything stops it. You went out and bought the thing that lets it drop the farthest. Not 1 of them holds an arch. You were standing on hope."

Not all insoles are the same, she said. It's what's under the arch. Whether it's still holding when your weight comes down. And whether you can stand to keep it in all day.

"This," she said, "is what I'd have sent my patients home in. If we'd ever been allowed to sell anything. It's called Xstance."

She set 1 on her step, put her foot on it, and put her whole weight down. It didn't move.

"They call it the Triple Support System, and it's the only one I know of that answers both failure modes at once.

A precision arch stabilizer, still holding at the bottom of the step, when it counts.

An impact cushioning heel pad set inside a deep, walled heel cup, right underneath the spot taking the beating. What padding you've got left under that heel bone squirts out sideways when you land. The cup keeps it under the bone instead of around it.

And a soft silicone comfort layer from heel to toe. That's the part your foot touches. Soft where it touches you, firm where your weight lands. That's why it isn't the rigid kind you rip out at lunch.

Rigid enough that it won't collapse under you. Soft enough that you'll actually leave it in. Most insoles only ever manage one of those.

The real test isn't how it feels when you put your shoes on at 6 AM. It's whether it's still holding at hour eleven."

That was the whole difference. The 1 thing I'd been missing for 1 year.

Then she told me the part I nearly got wrong.

"If you've only got 1 pair, you're only fixing it some of the time. You switch between your sneakers and your work shoes and your slippers, and your feet are shifting between something holding and nothing holding. Every day you go back to a flat shoe, you undo the ground you just made. Put a pair in every set of shoes you wear."

You put them in and you wear them every day, in every pair. That's the whole thing. Nothing to swallow. Nothing to fog your head. Nothing to clash with your other tablets. No ice tray, no timer, no frozen bottle by the bed. And they come with a 90 day money back promise. So the only thing I could lose was a few more weeks of the same.

And here's what made me cry with anger.

There's a billing code for the shot. There's a code for the imaging. There's a code for the $600 custom pair and there's a code for the surgery that put my mother in that chair. There is no code on God's earth for "your insoles went flat in March and you've been standing on nothing since." The system is built to walk you towards the codes. Not to look inside your shoe. Nobody gets paid to tell a woman in Mansfield what's under her arch.

She's nine now. Every weekend morning she comes into my room before I'm up, stands at the side of the bed, and asks the same question: "Does ya body hurt again today?"

She started asking when she was seven. She hasn't stopped, because the answer hasn't changed.

Before all this I was the mom who never sat down. Soccer practice, bike rides after school, weekend trips to the lake, Halloween on foot for three hours straight.

I coached her T-ball team the year she started. I carried her on my shoulders at the state fair when she was five and walked the whole grounds twice without thinking about it.

By 45 I couldn't walk to the end of the block without planning how long I'd need to sit in the car after. Last Halloween I took the kids trick-or-treating in flat boots and could barely walk for two weeks.

I bought the Hokas, then the Brooks, then Birkenstocks for the house, then Oofos slides for the kitchen. After the shoes came the Dr. Scholl's inserts, then Superfeet, then a night splint, then a Strassburg sock I wore to bed for months.

I paid $500 for custom orthotics that insurance wouldn't cover, because the podiatrist swore they'd fix it in a month. Within two weeks they'd given me nerve pain in both feet every time I put them on.

The cortisone shot helped for about four weeks, and I kept up with the kids at a birthday party for the first time in a year. Then it wore off, and the birthday parties went back to me sitting on the bench while the other moms ran around with their kids.

They sent me to three specialists over eight months. Podiatrist, then orthopedic surgeon, then rheumatologist. The X-rays were clean, the ultrasound showed a thickened band under my heel, and the blood work came back normal.

"It's plantar fasciitis," the surgeon said. "It's common at this age, and we've ruled out everything else."

Every single morning my feet refused to hold me up without pain, and every doctor said the same words, and the tests kept coming back clean. I'd started to wonder if I was making it up.

The alarm went off at 5:40 and I already knew what the first step would cost me. I'd swing my legs over the side, put my hand flat on the wall before my foot touched the floor. That first step felt like someone had taken a cane to the bottoms of my feet in the night.

By mid-morning I'd be at work, concrete floor, two Advil already down. No difference.

By 2pm the bottoms of my feet were the worst part of me. It felt like walking on marbles, like there was nothing between my bones and the floor.

Then I'd come home to my kids, and the math would start. If I stood long enough to cook dinner, I'd pay for it all evening. If I walked to the park and back, I was done for the night.

My sons are ten and twelve. They'd ask me to come outside and shoot hoops, and I'd say "in a little bit" and sit on the couch and never go. After a while they stopped asking, but my daughter never did.

Every time, I had to tell her no.

I went on vacation with my parents last spring, who are almost 80, and they zoomed around the whole week while I kept taking breaks for my feet. On the day everyone hiked out to the waterfall, I stayed at the hotel. My daughter came back sunburned and talking about the fish she'd seen in the pool at the bottom, and I sat there and smiled and hated that I'd missed it.

We went to the beach that summer. My family was in the water and I was in the chair, and I could see on their faces that they didn't get it.

I looked fine, and I'm 48, not 80. But my feet wouldn't let me walk across the sand without limping, and after ten minutes of standing in the surf I had to go back and sit down.

My husband and my kids have been the ones paying for this. Cranky evenings because I'd been on my feet all day at work and had nothing left for them. Weekend plans I cancelled because everything involved walking.

I backed out of the camping trip and couldn't do the corn maze. The one time I said yes to the zoo, I spent half of it on a bench while they went ahead without me.

I felt young inside. My body was in the way of every single plan my family made.

The doctor said losing a few pounds would help. I tried, and it cost me two weeks of worse pain. When my hips started aching too I got the HRT patch, and it took the hip ache and the hot flashes and left my feet exactly where they were.

After that came the walking boot, the Epsom soaks, the acupuncture. Nothing changed, and every season there was one more family outing I used to do that I didn't do anymore.

My daughter deserves her mother back. That sentence had been running through my head for two years, and I didn't know what to do with it, because I'd tried everything the doctors gave me and none of it worked.

Then my neighbor asked me a question no podiatrist ever had.

She's a nurse at a foot and ankle clinic. We were in her driveway and I was telling her I'd just backed out of the school field trip because I couldn't keep up with a group of nine-year-olds for four hours, and that I'd been dreading the Disney trip my husband had booked for winter break.

"Has anyone ever actually pressed on your heel and checked how much padding is left under it?"

I almost laughed. "I've tried insoles and I've tried orthotics, and they didn't do a thing."

She shook her head. "Press your thumb into the middle of your heel."

I did, standing right there in her driveway, and it was bone. Right under the skin.

"Ten years ago there was a thick pad of fat there," she said. "Your body's shock absorber. Every step you've ever taken landed on it."

"I'm missing fat off the bottom of my feet?"

"Plantar fasciitis was never the real problem. It's what happens when the pad goes."

"Your heel bone hits the floor about 8,000 times a day. With the pad there, that force gets spread out. With the pad gone, all of it lands on one hard point, and that hammering is what keeps the band under your heel inflamed."

"Overnight the band starts to heal. Then your first step in the morning lands bone on floor and rips it open again. That's why you hold the wall."

"What would even cause that?"

"It thins as your hormones shift. From your mid-30s on, and women's pads are thinner than men's to begin with. Your weight didn't do this, and neither did your shoes."

She looked at me. "Your life didn't get smaller because there's anything wrong with you. One part wore out, and nobody warned you."

"Once it's gone, it doesn't grow back. Researchers call it fat pad atrophy, and it keeps your heel landing on bone even on the days you rest it, even after the stretches, even when the X-ray comes back clean."

"You've spent three years treating the sore part and nothing under it."

"That first step in the morning, after a full night of sleep? That's not plantar fasciitis. That's your heel bone hitting the floor with nothing between them."

"And the marbles feeling?"

"Same thing. Pain is weight on a small spot, and comfort is the same weight spread over a big area. You can lie on a bed of nails, but you can't lie on one nail."

"But I've tried insoles," I said.

"You tried half the job," she said. "A fix has to do two jobs at once: put a real pad between the bone and the floor, and spread your weight across the whole foot so the bone doesn't carry it all. Everything you bought did one or the other."

"Drugstore inserts are the soft part, badly. A few millimetres of foam, and your bare heel squashes it flat on the first step. Your custom orthotics were the spreading part, hard plastic straight under a bare bone, which is why they hurt."

"Half the job feels like nothing."

I went home and searched "heel fat pad thinning women" and spent two hours reading after the kids were in bed. Foot and ankle journals describing the pad under the heel thinning with age and hormone changes. Everything she'd said checked out.

I texted her the next morning. "Okay, say you're right. What do I actually do?"

She called on her lunch break. "The pad doesn't grow back, so you put one under your foot from the outside. You need two parts in one insole."

"A thick pad under the heel and the front of the foot, thick enough that a bare heel can't flatten it. And a firm cradle under the arch that catches part of every step, so the heel never carries the whole load alone."

"Soft where you're bare, firm where you're not. Your heel stops hammering, and the band finally gets a rest that lasts past the first step."

"And it has to go in the slippers by your bed. The first step of the day is the one that does the damage. Your Hokas are by the front door at 5:40 in the morning."

"I keep a pair in my own slippers. We started telling patients about them last year."

This sounded too simple to me. But I'd spent three years watching my kids do everything without me. "Where do I get one?"

"You can't grab any insole off the shelf," she said. "Most of them are either thin foam or a hard shell, and the thick ones flatten out in a month."

"The one I use is Rebloom. It's a thick foam base under the heel and the front of the foot, with a firm arch cradle built into it, and you trim it to fit. It's the only one I've found that does both."

I looked it up that night after the kids were asleep. There was a 90-day money-back guarantee. After three years of shoes and shots and specialists that failed, what was one more try?

They came in four days, and I put them straight into the slippers by my bed. The first morning I still put my hand on the wall out of habit, and the step still hurt. Like ten percent less.

By day four, I got to the bathroom without touching the wall, and stood there with my hand up in the air where the wall should have been.

By the end of week one I moved them into my sneakers and got through a full day on my feet without my afternoon Advil. I'd forgotten to take it.

I'd been keeping a list on my phone all spring of how far I could walk before my feet quit. By the end of week two, it was around the block twice with no sitting in between. Triple what I'd managed all year.

Then came week three. I woke up before my alarm, lay there in the quiet, and waited for it. The marbles, the cane-strike feeling, that first-step pain that had met me every single morning for three years.

It wasn't there. I put my foot down and it held. And for the first time in three years the word for it wasn't "manageable." It was fine.

That Saturday my daughter asked if we could walk to the ice cream place, the one that's a mile each way. I said yes without doing the math first. We walked there and back and she held my hand and talked about her teacher the whole way, and I didn't think about my feet once.

The next weekend I took all three kids to the park and stayed on my feet the entire time. I shot hoops with my sons until they got bored, not until my feet quit.

Two weeks after that we did the zoo. The whole zoo, on foot, for five hours. My daughter rode on my shoulders through the bird house the way she used to, and I carried her out to the car, and she fell asleep on the drive home with her face pressed against the window.

Three years of field trips and Halloween walks and beach days and park afternoons I'd sat out, and the whole time it was never my life that had to get smaller. It was a pad.

title: Tired of Waking Up in Pain?

bodyText:
Don't stretch your calves if you have plantar fasciitis. Do this instead.

I'm going to say something that no one who's had heel pain for years wants to hear. And I don't give a sh*t if it upsets you.

The cortisone shot won't fix this. The night splint won't. The frozen water bottle won't. Those $180 cloud sneakers all over your feed? Those won't either. The next podiatrist appointment won't.

And that "6 to 18 months, it usually clears up on its own"? That's just going to sit there and watch your foot get worse.

Not 1 thing on that list is touching what's really causing your pain. I know. I watched my mother deal with the same thing.

10 years of Ice. Inserts. 2 rounds of shots. Then a surgery that was meant to fix it all, where they cut the band in her foot to release it. It never held right after that. A cane, then a walker. No body could ever fix it.

Then, 1 year ago, I sat on the edge of my bed at 5:40 AM and couldn't put my right foot flat on the floor.

It's happening to me. And if you sat on the edge of your bed this morning working yourself up to that first step, it's happening to you.

So read every word. It's long. But the answer is in here. And it is NOT another treatment.

I'm Denise. I'm 59, from Mansfield, Ohio. I was a nursing home aide for 26 years. On my feet all day. Lifting, turning, hauling. The lot.

For me it started small. A twinge getting up off the couch after the 10 o'clock news. A little bruised feeling under my right heel. Nothing a hot soak wouldn't sort.

2 months later it wasn't small. It was a nail through my heel every morning. Standing up made me gasp out loud.

Some days it screamed. Some days it went almost quiet. I couldn't work it out. I thought the tissue in my foot was shredding a little more every week. It wasn't. (Hold that thought. It matters later.)

I did what you're meant to do. I called the office. Waited 3 weeks. Got 10 minutes with a doctor who never looked up from the screen. "Plantar fasciitis. Common at your age. Ice it. Stretch it. Lose a bit of weight." Out the door.

The pharmacy sold me gel inserts. For 2 weeks it was almost a miracle. Then it stopped. And when the pain came back, it came back meaner. Deeper. The kind no cushion could reach, because it wasn't coming from the surface.

By then I'd joined 1 of those Facebook foot pain groups. Thousands of us. All hobbling to the bathroom at dawn. All with a tip. A night splint. A frozen water bottle. A massage gun. Compression sleeves. KT tape. Turmeric. A $40 pair of heel cups off Amazon. CBD balm. 2 more pairs of drugstore orthotics. $200 max-cushion sneakers that everyone swore were like walking on clouds and that had me limping by Thursday.

I spent over $400 on sh*t in 4 months. And I still couldn't pull my own socks on without holding my breath.

Then it hit me like cold water. I was doing exactly what my mother did. The same ice. The same inserts. The same "give it time." Walking her road, step by step. Towards the same chair.

They'd always told us flat feet "run in families." Nobody told me the truth. We were both treating the wrong damn thing.

By August I was a ghost. I couldn't stand long enough to make a real dinner. I couldn't walk the dog past the second mailbox before the pain had me leaning on somebody's fence like an old woman. I stopped going to my grandson's Little League. I sat down to fold laundry. And I'd be up at 5:00 AM on the edge of the bed, working up to that first step. Crying. Swearing into my sleeve so I didn't wake my husband.

The woman who used to close down every wedding reception in Richland County was googling "mobility scooter" at 2:00 in the morning. I thought I was just getting old. I wasn't. That was wrong too.

Back to the doctor. He sent me to a podiatrist. The wait was 6 weeks. And a quick mention of custom orthotics. $600, not covered.

I paid for 1 physical therapy visit I couldn't afford. $55 for 3 stretches off a printout. "Keep at them. Give it more time." More time. While that foot ate me alive every morning.

So I did the stretches. Morning and night. And here's the thing nobody warned me about: they made it worse. I know why now. That band under your foot isn't tight like a muscle. It's torn. Overnight your body knits those tiny tears back together. Then you get up and haul on it first thing and rip every 1 of them open again. Every stretch was me tearing it back open.

That's why I say don't stretch your calves. Nobody ever told me the stretching was part of the problem.

The discharge paper even admitted it: "Most cases resolve within 6 to 18 months." That's not a treatment plan. That's a shrug on letterhead.

So I stopped hunting for another treatment. And I started hunting for the cause.

Once I saw it, I couldn't un-see it. Look at the road they marched me down. My mother before me.

A twinge. Ice. An insert. It fades. Better sneakers. A shot. Another shot. $600 orthotics. Surgery. A chair.

Every step just managed the pain. Not 1 step ever asked WHY it was there. We were all mopping up the puddle and wondering why the bastard kept coming back.

I'd already ruled out the easy stuff. New shoes, twice. 15 pounds gone. None of it touched the pain. Because none of it reached where the problem really lived. Not my skin. Not even really my foot. Somewhere underneath it.

I spent 2 weeks reading. Not the sponsored stuff. The real threads. Reddit at 4:00 AM. Forums full of people who'd suffered 20 years. Physical therapists on YouTube who'd gone "off-script" from the usual advice.

Then I found 1 comment. Buried under a post. From a retired mail carrier in Oregon.

"Mine burned for 6 years. I tried it all. What finally settled it wasn't a treatment. Take the insole out of the shoe you wore yesterday. Put it next to a brand new one. Look at them both from the side."

From the side. Not how it feels under your thumb. From the side. I read it 10 times.

I did it that night. Mine was flatter. Then I talked myself out of it, because it still felt soft when I pressed it.

So I ordered the first thing I could find. $17 gel insoles off Amazon. Thousands of 5-star reviews.

Week 1: nothing.

Week 2: nothing.

Week 3: still turning around at that second mailbox, I nearly wrote it all off as more snake oil.

What saved me was a chat over the back fence. My neighbor Marlene is 71. She was a certified orthotist for 35 years. Half of them in a foot and ankle clinic in Columbus. She saw me come down my porch steps sideways, 1 at a time, and came over. I showed her the insoles. She laughed, kindly.

"Oh, honey. These are worse than useless. No wonder they've done nothing. Do you want to know why?"

And standing there in her slippers, she told me the thing no 10-minute appointment ever had.

"Your arch isn't a stack of bones that holds itself up. It's a bridge, and there's a band strung underneath holding the 2 ends together. Every step, your whole weight comes down and that arch drops. It's meant to drop, that's how a foot takes a step. The only thing that has ever mattered is what's underneath it when it does.

Out on dirt, on grass, on uneven ground, the ground comes up and catches it. On a concrete floor in a flat shoe, nothing does. That band catches all of it. 10,000 times a day. And after 50 it's worse, because the fat pad under your heel has thinned and that band's gone stiff. Less padding, less give. Same concrete you stood on at 30.

That's the whole job of an insole. Be there at the bottom of the step. And almost every insole you can buy fails at it. There are only 2 ways it happens.

The soft ones pancake. They feel supportive because they push back against your thumb. Your thumb isn't 180 pounds. Under your real weight it bottoms out — flat, at the exact instant your arch is dropping, the 1 instant it had a job to do. And it doesn't happen all at once. A new one holds a little. Every day crushes it down further and it comes back less, until it doesn't come back at all.

That's why they work for a few weeks and then quit on you. You weren't imagining that.

The other kind doesn't collapse. It just hurts. Rock-hard and bulky, the sort you rip out by lunchtime and leave in a drawer. That's what your $600 is going to buy you.

So you've got one that gives out and one you won't wear. Either way, by the end of the day that arch is dropping onto nothing.

Cushion is what a thing feels like when you're not standing on it. Holding is what it does when you are. Once it's flat it isn't doing anything. It's a floor with a logo on it."

First time in 1 year, something made sense.

Then she told me why everything I'd bought had failed. And it wasn't bad luck.

"The shots? They quiet the pain for a few weeks, then fade. They never hold anything up. It's like watering the leaves of a plant when the roots are dry. The night splint? It holds your foot while you sleep. You're not doing the damage in your sleep. You're doing it in the 14 hours you're upright. The ice, the sleeve, the cloud sneakers? The softer the shoe, the further that arch falls before anything stops it. You went out and bought the thing that lets it drop the farthest. Not 1 of them holds an arch. You were standing on hope."

Not all insoles are the same, she said. It's what's under the arch. Whether it's still holding when your weight comes down. And whether you can stand to keep it in all day.

"This," she said, "is what I'd have sent my patients home in. If we'd ever been allowed to sell anything. It's called Xstance."

She set 1 on her step, put her foot on it, and put her whole weight down. It didn't move.

"They call it the Triple Support System, and it's the only one I know of that answers both failure modes at once.

A precision arch stabilizer, still holding at the bottom of the step, when it counts.

An impact cushioning heel pad set inside a deep, walled heel cup, right underneath the spot taking the beating. What padding you've got left under that heel bone squirts out sideways when you land. The cup keeps it under the bone instead of around it.

And a soft silicone comfort layer from heel to toe. That's the part your foot touches. Soft where it touches you, firm where your weight lands. That's why it isn't the rigid kind you rip out at lunch.

Rigid enough that it won't collapse under you. Soft enough that you'll actually leave it in. Most insoles only ever manage one of those.

The real test isn't how it feels when you put your shoes on at 6 AM. It's whether it's still holding at hour eleven.”

That was the whole difference. The 1 thing I'd been missing for 1 year.

Then she told me the part I nearly got wrong.

"If you've only got 1 pair, you're only fixing it some of the time. You switch between your sneakers and your work shoes and your slippers, and your feet are shifting between something holding and nothing holding. Every day you go back to a flat shoe, you undo the ground you just made. Put a pair in every set of shoes you wear."

You put them in and you wear them every day, in every pair. That's the whole thing. Nothing to swallow. Nothing to fog your head. Nothing to clash with your other tablets. And they come with a 90-day money-back promise. So the only thing I could lose was a few more weeks of the same.

And here's what made me cry with anger.

There's a billing code for the shot. There's a code for the imaging. There's a code for the $600 custom pair and there's a code for the surgery that put my mother in that chair. There is no code on God's earth for "your insoles went flat in March and you've been standing on nothing since." The system is built to walk you towards the codes. Not to look inside your shoe. Nobody gets paid to tell a woman in Mansfield what's under her arch.

The system's hands are tied. Yours are not.

So I started. Every day. Every pair. No excuses.

Week 1: I got from the bed to the coffee pot without the counter.

Week 2: I stood a whole shift. I cried in the car afterwards. The good kind.

Week 3: I walked the dog to the second mailbox. Then past it. All the way to the reservoir and back. And I never once reached for a fence.

By week 5 I was kneeling in the garden with my hands in the soil. And when my grandson hollered "Grandma, watch this!" at his Little League game, I was at that fence, on my feet, cheering like I used to.

The first step in the morning. The socks I couldn't reach. The dancing I'd given up. 1 by 1, they came back.

Marlene checked my insoles a few months in. The way she'd checked 1,000 feet. She set them on her step and put her weight down.

"Still holding," she said. "Not a millimeter. In 35 years I hardly ever saw a foot this angry settle this well without a knife. And you did it with an insole and a bit of patience."

That was 8 months ago. Not 1 bad morning since. My feet are quiet. I gave a pair to my sister, who'd started down the same road. Hers is settling too. This isn't a good week that wears off. It held. It's still holding.

I think about my mother every single day. That chair. That window. The garden she never got back to. And the last thing she said to me.

If you're reading this on the edge of your bed working up to that first step, do not walk her road. Do not wait out 6 to 18 months while it takes your job and your walks and your Saturdays. Do not hand your good years over the way she did.
