bodyText:
I was diagnosed with plantar fasciitis at 46. I'm 51 now. Turns out that was never what was wrong with my feet.

For five years I "managed" a diagnosis that was only ever half the story.

At 46 my entire personality was black boots, and had been since I was fifteen. By 47 I was in Danskos, with a pair of giant Hokas for anything longer than an hour, and the doctors kept telling me the feet were the whole problem.

Five years of stretching my calves against the doorframe before I was allowed to take a step. Five years of rolling a frozen water bottle under my foot every night for ten minutes of relief that was gone by the time I stood up. I did everything they asked.

I bought the Hokas, then the Brooks, then Birkenstocks, then Oofos slides for the house, then a pair of Vionics. After the shoes came the Dr. Scholl's inserts, then Superfeet, then a night splint, then the Strassburg sock.

I paid $500 for custom orthotics that insurance wouldn't cover, because the podiatrist swore they'd fix it in a month. Within two weeks they'd given me nerve pain in both feet every time I put them on.

Then they sent me to a specialist. Podiatrist first, then an orthopedic surgeon, then a rheumatologist, eight months of appointments in all.

The X-rays were clean. The ultrasound showed the band under my heel was thickened, which they said just confirmed the diagnosis, and the blood work for rheumatoid arthritis and thyroid came back normal.

"Everything looks fine," the surgeon said. "It's plantar fasciitis. It's common at this age, and we've ruled out everything else."

I felt like I was making it up. The tests were clean and the doctors weren't worried, and every single morning my feet refused to hold me up without pain.

By the time my alarm went off at 5:40, I already knew what the first step was going to feel like. I'd swing my legs over the side and put my hand flat on the wall before my foot touched the floor. That first step felt like someone had caned my feet in the night.

By 10am I'd be standing at the front desk of the vet clinic where I work, concrete floor, first two Advil down. Still nothing.

By 2pm the bottoms of my feet were the worst part of me. It felt like walking on marbles, like there was nothing between my bones and the concrete.

And the math never stopped. If I walked the dog to the end of the street and back, I was done for the night. If I wore the boots to dinner, I paid for it with a week of mornings worse than usual.

I purged my closet twice. First the heels, then everything with a flat sole, and I cried in the Goodwill parking lot with the bags on the back seat. What was left was Clarks, Merrells, Vionics, and the Danskos my grandmother would have recognised.

One morning I turned the car around halfway to work and drove home, because I suddenly couldn't stand how my shoes felt on my feet and couldn't bear the idea of wearing them all day. This from a woman who used to walk all over Manhattan in plastic Payless heels.

I went to our anniversary dinner in sneakers. My husband said nothing about it, which was worse.

At the clinic I'd become the lady who shows up in cute dresses and giant Hokas.

It wasn't the pain that bothered me most, and I know how that sounds. It was standing in front of the closet every morning not knowing what to wear anymore, because nothing I loved went with the shoes I was allowed.

I looked fine on the outside. Inside, from the ankles down, I didn't know who I was anymore.

And every doctor just nodded. "That's plantar fasciitis. It's an age thing, and losing a few pounds would help."

I tried losing the pounds, and it cost me two weeks of worse pain. When my hips started aching too I got the HRT patch, and it took the hip ache and the hot flashes and left my feet exactly where they were.

After that came the walking boot, the Epsom soaks, the acupuncture. Nothing worked, and every season there was one more pair of shoes in the bag.

I started to believe this was just my life now. That I'd spend the rest of it in "supportive" shoes just so I could walk, the ones my grandmother wore in her last years, and that I was doomed to her fate. I didn't choose to need clodhoppers.

Then my neighbor asked me a question no podiatrist ever had. She's a nurse at a foot and ankle clinic. We were standing in her driveway and I was telling her I couldn't get through the grocery store anymore without sitting in the car for twenty minutes after, and that I'd just put my last pair of black boots in the donation bag.

"Has anyone ever actually pressed on your heel and checked how much padding is left under it?"

I almost laughed. "I've tried insoles and I've tried orthotics, and they didn't do anything."

She shook her head. "That's not what I asked. Press your thumb into the middle of your heel."

I did, standing there in her driveway, and it was bone, right under the skin.

"Ten years ago there was a thick pad of fat there," she said. "It's your body's shock absorber. Every step you've ever taken landed on it."

"You're telling me I'm missing fat off the bottom of my feet?"

"I'm telling you that plantar fasciitis was never the real problem. It's what happens when the pad goes."

"Your heel bone hits the floor about 8,000 times a day. With the pad there, that gets spread out. With the pad gone, all of it lands on one hard point, and that hammering is what keeps the band under your heel inflamed."

"Overnight it starts to heal. Then your first step in the morning lands bone on floor and rips it open again. That's why you hold the wall."

"What would even cause that?"

"It thins as your hormones shift. From your mid-30s on, and women's pads are thinner than men's to begin with. Your weight didn't do this, and neither did your shoes."

She looked at me. "You didn't age out of your shoes. One part wore out, and nobody warned you."

"Once it's gone, it doesn't grow back. Researchers call it fat pad atrophy, and it keeps your heel landing on bone even on the days you rest it, even after the stretches, even when the X-ray comes back clean."

"The band was sore because the bone was hammering it. You've spent five years treating the sore part and nothing under it."

"That first step in the morning, after a full night of sleep? That's not plantar fasciitis. That's your heel bone hitting the floor with nothing between them."

"And the marbles feeling?"

"Same thing. Pain is weight on a small spot, and comfort is the same weight spread over a big area. You can lie on a bed of nails, but you can't lie on one nail."

"But I've tried insoles," I said.

"You tried half the job," she said. "A fix has to do two jobs at once: put a real pad between the bone and the floor, and spread your weight across the whole foot so the bone doesn't carry it all. Everything you bought did one or the other."

"Drugstore inserts are the soft part, badly. A few millimetres of foam, and your bare heel squashes it flat on the first step. Your custom orthotics were the spreading part, hard plastic straight under a bare bone, which is why they hurt."

"Half the job feels like nothing."

I stared at her. Five years, three specialists, every test coming back clean, and nobody had ever pressed on my heel.

I went home and Googled "heel fat pad thinning women" and fell into a rabbit hole. Foot and ankle journals describing the pad under the heel thinning with age and hormone changes.

Everything she said checked out.

I texted her the next morning. "Okay, say you're right. What do I actually do?"

She called on her lunch break. "The pad doesn't grow back, so you put one under your foot from the outside. You need two parts in one insole."

"A thick pad under the heel and the front of the foot, thick enough that a bare heel can't flatten it. And a firm cradle under the arch that catches part of every step, so the heel never carries the whole load alone."

"Soft where you're bare, firm where you're not. Your heel stops hammering, and the band finally gets a rest that lasts past the first step."

"And it has to go in the slippers by your bed. The first step of the day is the one that does the damage, and your Hokas are by the front door at 5:40 in the morning."

"I keep a pair in my own slippers. We started telling patients about them last year."

This sounded too simple to me. But I'd been dragging myself through every day for five years. "Where do I get one?"

"You can't grab any insole off the shelf," she said. "Most of them are either thin foam or a hard shell, and the thick ones flatten out in a month."

"The one I use is Rebloom. It's a thick foam base under the heel and the front of the foot, with a firm arch cradle built into it, and you trim it to fit, so it goes in the boots you gave up on and not just the ugly shoes. It's the only one I've found that does both."

I looked it up that night. There was a 90-day money-back guarantee. After five years of shoes and shots and specialists that failed, what was one more try?

They came in four days, and I put them straight into the slippers by my bed. The first morning I still put my hand on the wall out of habit, and the step still hurt. Like ten percent less.

By day four, I got to the bathroom without touching the wall, and stood there with my hand up in the air where the wall should have been.

By the end of week one I moved them into my work sneakers and got through a full shift on that concrete without my afternoon Advil. I'd forgotten to take it.

Since spring I'd been keeping a list on my phone of how far I could walk before my feet quit. By the end of week two, it was around the block twice with no sitting in between. Nearly triple what I'd managed all year.

Then came week three. I woke up before my alarm, lay in the quiet, and waited for it. The caned feeling, the marbles, that first-step pain that had met me every single morning for five years.

It wasn't there. I put my foot down and it held, and for the first time in five years the word for it wasn't "manageable." It was fine.

For the first time in five years, I walked barefoot across my kitchen tile to make coffee and didn't think about my feet until the coffee was done.

That Saturday I pulled the last pair of black boots back out of the donation bag, trimmed a pad to fit, and wore them to the market for six hours. Nobody could tell.

For the first time in five years, I wore a dress to dinner with my husband with the boots instead of the giant Hokas. He looked at me across the table and said "you look like yourself again."

Six weeks in I went to my niece's wedding in ankle boots, stayed on the dance floor, and walked to the car after instead of needing a taxi. I cried in the car, and for once it wasn't from pain.

Five years of boots in a bag and dresses with the wrong shoes, and the whole time it was never my feet that had aged out of my closet. It was a pad.

I don't have a plantar fasciitis problem. I never did. And I'm not doomed to my grandmother's shoes, either.

The tall heels are still on the shelf, and that's fine, because the boots were always the point.

What I'd had was five years of a missing pad, my heel hitting the floor with nothing between them, and a sore band taking the blame.

And not one person in a white coat thought to press on my heel.

I still wear the patch, and I still do the stretches out of habit. The concrete at work hasn't changed either. But now there's a pad under my heel before my foot touches the floor.

Every morning my feet go straight into the slippers with the pad in them, and at work they go into my sneakers. There's nothing to take and nothing to do, and it takes as long as putting on shoes.

That should be the first thing anyone tells a woman whose feet started hurting in her 40s.

If you've been told you have plantar fasciitis… If you've done the stretches and the shots and the orthotics and nothing has stuck…

If your X-rays and your blood work keep coming back clean… If you wake up after eight hours of sleep and put your hand on the wall before your foot touches the floor…

If you've stopped saying yes to the walk, the market, the vacation… If you've cried over a donation bag full of shoes, and now stand in front of the closet not knowing what to wear…

I'm not saying you're definitely missing the pad under your heel. But I spent five years treating a sore band while the real problem got worse every single day, and five years dressing like somebody's grandmother over one part that had simply worn out.

Before you put another pair of shoes in the donation bag, read the heel-padding explanation I've linked below.

It's Rebloom's article. It shows the heel pad in a diagram, walks through a 30-second heel check, and explains the two jobs my neighbor was talking about: cushioning under the heel and spreading the weight across your foot.

If you've already tried insoles, there's a comparison of drugstore inserts, cushioned shoes and custom orthotics, too.

I still mourn every pair I gave away. I wish I'd understood the padding part before I started filling those bags.

Read the explanation and see the heel check here.

bodyText:
My brother died 4 months ago because his heel hurt.

I know how that sounds. I know you're reading that and thinking I've lost my mind. Nobody dies from heel pain. Nobody dies from plantar fasciitis.

But I'm going to tell you exactly how it happened. Step by step. Domino by domino. And by the end of this, you're going to understand that the thing you've been limping on for 6, 12, 18 months, the thing your doctor keeps telling you to stretch and ice and "give it time", is capable of taking a hell of a lot more from you than your morning comfort.

It took everything from my brother. And it almost took everything from me.

His name was Ray.

He was 66 years old. Retired millwright out of a paper mill in northern Wisconsin. 38 years on concrete floors in steel-toe boots, crawling under presses, standing over conveyors, walking catwalks in 12-hour rotations. He walked off the floor for the last time at 63 with a full pension, 2 bad knees, and a heel that he said felt like someone had shoved a pebble under the bone.

His GP said plantar fasciitis. Very common. Handed him a pamphlet. Told him to stretch his calves, ice the heel, buy supportive shoes.

Ray did everything they said. He bought the Hokas. $180. He rolled a frozen water bottle under his foot every night in front of the Packers game. He did the wall stretches until his calves burned. The pain dropped from a 7 to maybe a 5 for a couple weeks. Then it came back. Like it had never left. Maybe worse.

His podiatrist gave him a cortisone injection. Stuck a needle straight into the bottom of his heel, into the thickest, most sensitive tissue in his foot. Ray sat in his truck afterward and told me on the phone it felt like someone had hammered a finishing nail through his sole. But the next morning, nothing. No stab. No wince. No white-knuckle grip on the nightstand. For the 1st time in over a year, he stepped out of bed and walked to the kitchen like a normal human being.

12 days. That's how long it lasted. 12 beautiful, pain-free days where Ray was Ray again. Then the pain returned like a door slamming shut. Sharper. Deeper. Like the floor of his heel had thinned out and there was nothing between bone and ground.

He got a 2nd injection 4 months later. It lasted 8 days. The rebound was brutal. His podiatrist said the next step was extracorporeal shockwave therapy, a $4,500 package, not covered by insurance, or surgical plantar fascia release. 8 to 12 weeks non-weight-bearing.

Ray laughed when he told me. Not the good kind. The kind of laugh a man makes when he realizes the people he trusted have run out of answers.

He never did the surgery. He never did the shockwave. He just... stopped moving.

That's the part nobody warns you about. The part that doesn't show up in any podiatry brochure or orthopedic website. What happens to a man, a big, stubborn, physical man who defined himself by what he could do with his hands and his back, when his feet betray him and he decides the safest thing to do is stop using them.

Ray stopped walking the dog. He'd done it every morning for 13 years, him and Biscuit, a gray-muzzled beagle mix, 1.5 miles through the neighborhood before the sun cleared the tree line. After the 2nd cortisone shot failed, he handed the leash to his wife and said, "My heel can't do it anymore."

He stopped going to Fleet Farm on Saturday mornings. Stopped walking to the mailbox. Stopped doing the thing that had kept him sane in retirement, working in his shop, standing at his bench, building walleye lures and Adirondack chairs and wooden trucks for his grandkids.

He started sitting. All day. Recliner to kitchen table to recliner. He gained 35 pounds in 10 months. His blood pressure, which had been borderline for a decade, went through the roof. His doctor added a 2nd medication. His A1C crept from 5.7 to 6.5. Pre-diabetic. His knees started buckling from the weight. His back, which had never been great, became constant.

All of it. Every single domino. Started with a heel that nobody could fix.

I watched my brother go from a man who built Adirondack chairs and walked a beagle before sunrise to a man who couldn't get out of his own recliner without grabbing both armrests and exhaling through clenched teeth.

And the whole time, 2.5 years, his podiatrist kept saying the same thing: "Keep stretching. Keep icing. We're monitoring it."

Monitoring it. The word doctors use when they've run out of answers but can't bring themselves to say so out loud.

Last November, Ray got up in the middle of the night to use the bathroom. 2 a.m. Dark hallway. Half asleep. His heel seized the instant his foot hit the hardwood, that white-hot, 1st-step stab that plantar fasciitis people know in their bones. His foot buckled. He grabbed for the wall, missed, and went down hard on his right side. He hit the baseboard with his head and fractured his left hip on the floor.

66 years old. High blood pressure. Pre-diabetic. 35 extra pounds. A body that had been sedentary for the better part of a year.

They took him into surgery the next morning for a partial hip replacement. The procedure went fine. The surgeon said it was textbook.

On day 3 post-op, he threw a pulmonary embolism. A blood clot that formed in his leg migrated to his lungs. They coded him at 11:40 in the morning. Got him back. They coded him again at 2:15 in the afternoon.

They didn't get him back.

My brother died in a hospital bed on a Tuesday in November because his foot hurt too much to walk safely in his own hallway at night.

The death certificate says pulmonary embolism. The surgical report says hip fracture from a ground-level fall. But I know what killed Ray. 2.5 years of a medical system that handed him stretches and cortisone and night splints and monitoring while the tissue in the bottom of his foot quietly disintegrated. And when the system had nothing left to offer, it shrugged and let him sit in a recliner until his body shut down from the inside out.

Nobody killed my brother with malice. They killed him with a protocol. A protocol designed for a problem he didn't have, applied to a condition it couldn't fix, repeated month after month after month while they called it "monitoring" and billed his insurance for the privilege.

I'm telling you this because I was on the exact same path.

Same heel. Same stab. Same morning limp. I'm 63 years old. Semi-retired, I still consult on commercial HVAC projects 3 days a week, which means I'm on concrete floors in work boots more often than my knees would like. I felt the 1st stab 18 months ago, stepping out of bed on a Wednesday morning. Like someone had embedded a shard of glass in the pad of my heel overnight.

My GP said plantar fasciitis. Very common. Handed me the same pamphlet they handed Ray. Same stretches. Same advice. Same casual tone, like it was a blister.

I did the stretches. I bought the shoes. I bought the custom orthotics, $450, out of pocket. I rolled the frozen water bottle. I strapped on the night splint that kept my ankle at 90 degrees while I slept, which meant I didn't sleep, which meant I was exhausted on top of everything else.

The pain dropped from a 7 to a 5 for about 3 weeks. Then it came back. Full force.

My podiatrist gave me a cortisone injection. 11 days of relief. Then it returned worse than before. Sharper on the 1st step. Deeper through the day. And now with a new trick: every time I sat in my truck for more than 20 minutes and stepped out, the heel lit up like I was starting the whole cycle from scratch. Every rest-to-weight-bearing transition was a punishment.

My podiatrist said the next step was the shockwave therapy package or surgery. I looked at the price tag. I looked at the recovery time. I looked at my schedule. And then I looked at my brother in his recliner and I thought: that's where this road goes. I've already seen the ending.

Because here's the thing nobody talks about. The heel pain isn't the disease. The heel pain is the 1st domino. And every domino after it falls in the same order.

You stop walking. You stop moving. You sit. You gain weight. Your blood pressure goes up. Your blood sugar goes up. Your joints go bad from the load. Your balance goes because you haven't been on your feet. You fall. And then something else kills you, the clot, the fracture, the cardiac event, and nobody connects it back to the heel that started the whole cascade because plantar fasciitis isn't a "serious" condition.

It's the most serious condition nobody takes seriously. And I'm done being quiet about it.

After Ray's funeral, I stopped accepting the standard protocol. I stopped pretending that stretching and icing were going to fix something that had been getting worse for 1.5 years. I stopped treating the instructions on the pamphlet like scripture.

And I started reading.

Not blog posts. Not "Top 10 Plantar Fasciitis Remedies" listicles written by content farms who've never had a shard of glass in their heel. I read the clinical literature. Orthopedic surgery journals. Sports medicine papers. Histopathological analyses of chronic plantar fascia tissue from cadaveric studies.

And what I found made me want to drive to every doctor's office I'd ever sat in and throw their stretching pamphlet on the floor.

Here's what nobody told me. What nobody told Ray. What nobody is telling you right now.

Plantar fasciitis, the thing on your chart, the thing they diagnosed you with, the thing they're "monitoring", is the wrong word for what you have.

The suffix "-itis" means inflammation. Acute plantar fasciitis, the kind that shows up, hurts for a few weeks, and resolves with rest and ice, is inflammatory. That version responds to the pamphlet protocol. That version is what the pamphlet was written for.

But if your heel has been hurting for more than 3 or 4 months, you almost certainly don't have fasci-itis anymore. You have fasci-osis. Degeneration. Not inflammation. The tissue isn't hot and swollen and angry. It's structurally disintegrating.

The clinical literature is not ambiguous about this. Histopathological studies of chronic plantar fascia tissue, tissue taken from patients who'd had heel pain for 6 months or longer, show the same findings over and over: disorganized collagen fiber architecture. In a healthy plantar fascia, the collagen fibers run in tight, parallel, load-bearing bundles, like the cables in a suspension bridge. They absorb and distribute the force of every step across the entire span of the arch.

In chronic plantar fasciosis, those cables have come apart. The organized parallel structure has been replaced by tangled, randomly oriented scar tissue that can't handle load. The collagen architecture isn't inflamed. It's collapsed.

And it gets worse. The degenerated tissue develops neovascularization, abnormal new blood vessels growing into the damaged zone. Sounds like healing, right? It's not. In tendinopathy and fasciosis, those new vessels bring nerve fibers along with them. The tissue is literally growing its own pain wiring. That's 1 reason chronic plantar fasciitis becomes more sensitive over time, not less.

And at the enthesis, the exact point where the fascia anchors into your heel bone, the exact spot where you feel that thumbtack every single morning, the tissue undergoes myxoid degeneration. The collagen matrix breaks down into a mucoid, structurally incompetent mess. The anchor point isn't inflamed. It's dissolving.

Now here's the part that should make you furious. Because it made me furious. And if I'd known it 18 months earlier, my brother might still be alive.

Every night, when you're lying in bed, your body is trying to repair the damage. While you sleep, fibroblasts, the cells responsible for producing new collagen, are laying down fresh repair tissue across the damaged zone at the enthesis. Those new fibers are fragile, immature, and disorganized. They haven't had time to orient into load-bearing architecture. They need time and the right mechanical signals to mature into functional tissue.

The moment you swing your legs over the side of the bed and load your heel, you rip them apart.

That's not a metaphor. That's the mechanism. The 1st-step-of-the-morning pain isn't stiffness loosening up. It's the sound of your body's overnight repair attempt being torn apart at the fascial anchor point because the full force of your body weight just slammed into tissue that was trying to heal.

Then you sit at your desk. Or your truck. Or your recliner. And the fibroblasts start laying down repair tissue again. And then you stand up, and you rip it apart again. Every transition from rest to weight-bearing is a re-injury event. Every day. For months. For years. Your body builds. You tear it down. It builds again. You tear it down again. An endless demolition cycle disguised as a "chronic condition."

This is why it doesn't get better. This is why the stretches don't work long-term. This is why the cortisone shot gave you 12 days and then abandoned you.

About that cortisone. Here's the part your podiatrist probably didn't mention. Corticosteroid injections don't just suppress inflammation. They inhibit fibroblast activity and collagen synthesis. The injection that erased your pain for 12 glorious days did so by chemically shutting down the very cells that were trying to repair the fascia. The tissue was structurally weaker after the injection than before it. The rebound was worse because the drug poisoned the fire department while it turned off the alarm.

That's what happened to Ray. That's what happened to me. That's what is happening to you right now if you've had more than 1 cortisone injection and you're wondering why each one works for a shorter window and the rebound hits harder.

Your doctor is not stupid. Your podiatrist is not incompetent. They are working from a treatment protocol that was designed for acute inflammation, and it works beautifully for acute inflammation. But you don't have acute inflammation. You have chronic collagen degeneration in an avascular zone with inadequate blood supply, compounded by intrinsic foot muscle atrophy that has been silently overloading your fascia for decades. And the standard protocol doesn't address a single 1 of those 3 problems.

Not 1.

Let me break them down, because this is where everything changed for me. Understanding these 3 failures is the difference between staying on the hamster wheel for another 2 years and getting off it.

Failure 1: your intrinsic foot muscles have gone dormant.

The plantar fascia was never designed to be the primary stabilizer of your arch. That job belongs to a group of small muscles in the sole of your foot, abductor hallucis, flexor digitorum brevis, quadratus plantae. In a human walking barefoot on varied terrain, these muscles fire constantly, dynamically adjusting the medial longitudinal arch with every step.

But you don't walk barefoot on varied terrain. You wear shoes on flat surfaces. You've done it for 40, 50, 60 years. And those muscles have atrophied to the point of functional dormancy. They're still there. They still have motor units. But they've gone offline. Checked out. Silent.

When those muscles go offline, the fascia absorbs the entire arch-stabilization load. A ligament doing a muscle's job. Every step. Every stand-up. Every shift of body weight. The fascia was never built for that kind of sustained mechanical demand. So it starts failing at its weakest point, the enthesis, where it anchors into the calcaneus. Your heel bone. That's the thumbtack. That's the morning shard of glass. That's the tissue that's been degenerating for months because it's carrying a load it was never designed to carry alone.

No amount of calf stretching fixes this. No orthotic fixes this. No cortisone injection fixes this. You can stretch and ice and support and inject until the day you die. The fascia will keep failing because the muscles that are supposed to be sharing the work are asleep.

Failure 2: the repair site is starving.

The calcaneal enthesis, the exact point of maximum degeneration, the exact spot of your worst pain, sits in what the literature calls a watershed zone. Notoriously poor blood supply. Healing requires blood flow. Oxygen. Fibroblasts. Growth factors. All delivered via arterial perfusion to the damaged tissue. But this zone doesn't get adequate perfusion on its own, especially not in a foot that's been crammed into an orthotic all day and strapped into a rigid night splint all night.

Your fascia is trying to rebuild itself in a desert. The construction crew can't get to the job site because the road is closed. You can stretch and ice and rest all you want. If the blood isn't reaching the enthesis, the tissue isn't healing.

Failure 3: nobody is telling the repair cells what to build.

This one broke my brain when I read it. And it should break yours, because it's the mechanism that explains why chronic plantar fasciitis stays chronic.

Fibroblasts, the cells laying down new collagen at the repair site, are mechanosensitive. They don't blindly produce collagen in whatever shape they feel like. They respond to mechanical signals. Controlled, rhythmic, low-level mechanical loading tells fibroblasts to produce organized, parallel collagen fibers. The architecture of healthy fascia. The cable structure. The kind that can bear load.

In the absence of that mechanical signal, they produce disorganized scar tissue. Tangled. Random. Weak. The architecture of fasciosis. The kind that tears every morning.

This is the principle behind eccentric loading protocols, the gold standard in tendinopathy rehabilitation. The controlled mechanical stress isn't just "strengthening" the tissue. It's telling fibroblasts how to orient the new collagen. A cellular instruction set delivered through mechanical force.

But here's the trap. How do you deliver controlled mechanical loading to a fascial enthesis that explodes in pain every time you put weight on it? Eccentric heel drops on a stair edge, the textbook exercise, require you to load through the exact tissue that's degenerating. For most people with chronic plantar fasciosis, it's too painful to do consistently. For someone like Ray, sedentary, overweight, deconditioned, it was impossible.

The tissue needs mechanical stimulus to heal properly. But the only way to deliver that stimulus is to load the tissue, which re-tears it. The treatment and the injury are the same motion.

That's the trap. That's why people stay stuck for years. That's why the protocol fails. Not because the biology is wrong. Because there's no delivery mechanism that sends the right signal without causing the wrong damage.

My heel was a dull, grinding 4 out of 10. Not the worst it had been. But constant. That low, ugly ache that sits underneath everything you do, like a bass note you can't turn off, coloring every step, every stand-up, every moment on your feet with a hum of dread.

I was scrolling through a Facebook group for chronic plantar fasciitis. Thousands of members. Most of the posts were the same despair loop I'd been living for 1.5 years: "Has anyone found anything that actually works?" 50 comments saying "Following." 3 comments recommending the same stretches everyone already tried.

But there was 1 thread that was different. A guy in Florida, retired postal carrier, plantar fasciitis for 2 years, tried everything, had posted a 7-week update about an EMS foot mat. EMS, electrical muscle stimulation, applied to the plantar surface of the feet does 3 things that stretching, icing, orthotics, cortisone, night splints, and shockwave therapy do not do. Not 1 of those interventions addresses even 1 of these mechanisms. EMS addresses all 3 at the same time.

1st: it wakes up the dead muscles.

The intrinsic foot muscles that went dormant decades ago, the ones that should be sharing the arch-stabilization load with your fascia, are forced into involuntary contraction by the electrical pulses. Not the voluntary contraction you'd get from toe curls or marble pickups, which requires you to consciously engage muscles you can't feel and probably didn't know existed. Involuntary contraction that bypasses the brain entirely and fires the motor units directly. The muscles contract. They rebuild. They begin regaining the contractile strength they lost over 40 years of shoes on flat ground.

As those muscles come back online, they progressively take mechanical load off the fascia. Not from the outside, like a passive arch support that props up the structure. From the inside, like the muscles that were supposed to be doing the job all along finally showing up for work. The fascia gets unloaded. 2nd: it pumps blood into the desert.

The rhythmic contraction of the intrinsic foot muscles and the flexor compartment of the lower leg acts as a mechanical pump. 3rd, and this is the mechanism that changed everything for me, it sends the building instructions.

The pulsed EMS contractions transmit low-level mechanical force through the foot's musculotendinous structures to the fascial enthesis. Because his heel hurt. And nobody fixed it.

bodyText:
I was diagnosed with plantar fasciitis back in 2021. Hard to believe that was almost six years ago now.

I'm 54. I'm an elementary school administrator. I'm on my feet from the second the bell rings until the buses pull out. I'm the one who walks the building. I do laps in the cafeteria. I'm in and out of classrooms all day, and at 3pm I'm standing at the curb in whatever the weather is doing.

The first morning it happened, I thought I'd slept on it weird. I got out of bed and my left heel felt like I'd stepped on a piece of glass that wasn't there. I limped to the bathroom. By the time I'd brushed my teeth it had eased up a little. By lunch I'd forgotten about it.

It came back the next morning. And the morning after that. By the end of the second week, the first 20 steps from my bed to my coffee maker were a 7 out of 10.

I want to tell you what I've spent on this foot. Not to complain. Just so you understand who I am when I tell you what finally worked.

Two pairs of Hokas. One pair of Brooks. Three different drugstore inserts. A pair of custom orthotics from the podiatrist that cost me $387 after insurance. A night splint that I wore for six weeks and threw in the back of the closet because it kept waking my husband up. Three rounds of physical therapy. One cortisone shot that worked for about ten days. The frozen water bottle. The little blue ball. The Voltaren. The stretching app on my phone that pings me at 7am every morning to remind me I still have this thing.

Every single one of those was recommended by someone with credentials. Every single one made sense. None of them stuck.

About 14 months ago I hit a wall.

I was sitting on the edge of my bathtub at 5 in the morning, holding the orthotic I'd just pulled out of my work shoe, looking at the dent my heel had worn into it, and I thought: I cannot keep doing this for the rest of my life.

That's the thing nobody warns you about with chronic foot pain. Chronic foot pain makes you a mathematician. You start running a step budget. You know every step costs something, so you make less of them, and it gets into your head. You count the steps from your bed to the bathroom. You park closer to the door. You stop volunteering for the field trip. You decline the wedding two states away because you can't imagine being on your feet that long in dress shoes. Your life gets smaller in a hundred ways nobody else notices because they happen one decision at a time.

My husband said something to me that week that stuck. He said, “You used to walk Sasha around the lake. When was the last time you did that?”

I couldn't remember. That's what got me. I literally couldn't remember the last time I'd walked the lake.

A friend of mine, she's a teacher at the same school, she'd had her own bad year with a knee, told me she'd been seeing a PT who'd helped her. Not a podiatrist. Not an orthopedist. A physical therapist who specialized in gait and foot biomechanics. She said he'd told her something about feet that nobody else had told her in five years of treatment, and within two months she was hiking again. She gave me his number.

I went to see him in March of last year.

His office is in a strip mall next to a smoothie place. He's maybe 40. He sat me on a table and watched me walk barefoot across the room twice. Then he asked me to take off my sock and hand it to him. I thought that was strange but I did it. He turned the sock inside out, stretched the toe end open with both hands, and let it go. The whole front snapped back into a tight tube.

He said, “This is the shape your foot has been held in for fifteen hours a day. On top of everything else”.

He explained it like this, and I'm going to say it the way he said it, because the way he said it is what I needed to hear.

Your arch isn't held up by your shoe. It's held up by the small muscles inside your foot. The ones that run from your heel to your toes. Those muscles only fire when your toes can spread and grip the ground. When your toes are jammed into a single chamber for fifteen hours a day, those muscles stop firing. The arch loses its active support. The fascia, which is the ligament that runs along the bottom of your foot, ends up carrying load it was never designed to carry alone. That's when it gets inflamed. That's the pain.

He said: your orthotic is holding your arch up from below while your sock is preventing the muscles that should be holding it up from doing their job. Every sock you've ever owned has been quietly sabotaging every shoe you've ever bought.

I sat there with my sock in my hand.

It wasn't that I'd failed at treating my foot. I'd been treating it out of sequence. Every input I'd added was being undone by an input I didn't know was working against me. And once he said it, it was obvious. A compression shirt still feels tight under a bulky jacket. That's what was happening to my foot every day. The orthotic was lifting the arch and the sock was squeezing the forefoot back into a tube right on top of it.

Then he handed me a pair of socks. Slots for each toe, like gloves for your feet. He told me to wear them every day for six weeks and call him if nothing was different. He said the brand was MARO. They were merino wool, and the only ones he'd found that didn't have nylon or polyester running through the toe pockets.

I'm going to tell you what happened, and I'm going to be honest, because I've been on the receiving end of too many ads from women who claim they were cured in three days.

Week one, nothing. If anything it felt weirder. My toes weren't used to being separated.

Week two, I noticed that the first 20 steps in the morning were a 5 out of 10 instead of a 7. That was the first time anything had moved the needle on the morning pain in a year and a half.

By week four I'd stopped flinching when I got out of bed.

By week six I walked Sasha around the lake. It took us 38 minutes. I cried a little in the car after. Not because my foot hurt. Because it didn't.

I'm not telling you the fasciitis is gone. There are still mornings, usually after a long day on hard floors, where the first few steps remind me what it used to be. But the flares don't stack on top of each other the way they did. The math has changed. I'm not counting steps to the bathroom anymore.

My husband noticed before I did. He said, "You're walking different. You're not limping out to the car." I hadn't realized I was limping to the car. I thought I'd been hiding it.

Here is what I want you to take from this if you're still reading.

You haven't failed at treating your foot. You've been doing real work, the shoes, the inserts, the stretches, the shots, and you've been doing it on top of an input you didn't know was there. The closest layer to your foot, the one you put on without thinking every morning, has been quietly pulling your forefoot back into a tube for as long as you've been doing the rest of the work.

A note on what I learned about these socks.

After a few months of using the pair the PT handed me, I thought the magic was just the toe-pocket design. So I went on Amazon and bought two cheap pairs of toe socks to fill out my drawer. Both were synthetic, made from nylon and polyester, which is what most toe socks are made of. They worked mechanically, the slots were there, but my feet sweated in a way they hadn't in months, and one pair wore through at the big toe in about six weeks. That was when I understood it wasn't only the toe pockets. It was also what sat against my skin all day.

MARO, the brand that the PT actually recommended, uses Australian merino wool, organic cotton, and a tiny amount of spandex that's fully encased in cotton so it never touches your skin. The merino is what holds up under boots and work shoes for a 10-hour day. They also make an organic cotton version for warmer weather and indoor work. I keep both. The merino is what I wear to school. The cotton is what I wear around the house.

I've now bought MARO for my mother, who has had Morton's neuroma in her right foot for nine years and had given up on finding anything that helped. I bought a pair for my sister, who teaches third grade. I bought a pair for my friend from work, the one who sent me to Bob in the first place. I bought four pairs for myself and I rotate through them every week.

If you've spent the last few years upgrading your shoes and your inserts and your stretches and you've quietly stopped expecting anything to actually change, this is the one thing I'd ask you to try before you give up.

The toe socks are here: https://wearmaro.com/collections/socks
— Helen

bodyText:
Turns out I don't have plantar fasciitis and you might not either.

I'm 52. I've had this in my right foot for two years and four months.

You know the mornings. That first step out of bed is the one that tells you what kind of day you're going to have. I used to sit on the edge of the mattress and just look at the floor. Actually look at it. Like it was a thing I had to negotiate with.

Then it stopped being just mornings.

It became the whole house.

I have not been barefoot in my own home in two years.

Not once. crocs on before my feet touch the carpet. crocs on to make coffee. crocs on to walk down my own hallway at eleven at night to check the back door. I keep a pair by the bed. I keep another pair by the couch so I don't have to cross the living room in socks. My husband walks around barefoot like it's nothing and I watch him do it the way you'd watch someone do a card trick.

And at night, the splint. That plastic boot strapped to my leg in my own bed.

That's the part nobody talks about. It's not that your foot hurts. It's that you are wearing footwear inside your own house at all hours except for when I'm sitting down. Always relying on something to soften the step even at the grocery store, I'm leaning on the cart. Not pushing it. Leaning.

I want to say what it takes from you and I don't know how to say it without sounding dramatic. So here's the plainest version.

I stopped planning things.

Not big things. I stopped planning the farmers market. I stopped saying yes to a hike because I didn't know what my foot would be in three weeks. My daughter asked me to come out for a long weekend and I said maybe. I said maybe to my own daughter because of my foot.

I did everything they told me.

Three podiatrists. Custom orthotics, the expensive ones. The cheap ones before that. Stretches every morning. The frozen water bottle. The spiky ball. Calf raises. Going up a shoe size. The night splint. A cortisone shot I was so scared of I nearly walked out of the office.

The shot worked. For about five weeks. Then it came back and it came back worse.

Two years of doing everything right and nothing moving.

The breaking point was a Tuesday in March. I was standing in my kitchen and I couldn't get to the sink. That's the whole story. It was nine feet away and I stood there and did the math on whether it was worth it. And I thought: this is my life now. This is just what it is.

My podiatrist had started using the word surgery. Not pushing it. Just letting it sit on the table between us.

I went home and I sat in the car in my own driveway for twenty minutes.

I got a second opinion. Not because I'm brave. Because I was out of moves.

The man I ended up in front of has been doing feet for twenty years. Older. Not slick. The kind who doesn't fill the silence while he's thinking.

He watched me walk. He asked me how long. I said two years and four months.

And he put his pen down and said, "Then you're being treated for the wrong thing."

I laughed at him.

The kind where I knew I was right, I'd had three podiatrists. I'd had an MRI. I had a diagnosis written on paper. I said, I have plantar fasciitis. Everyone agrees I have plantar fasciitis.

He said, "You did. Two years ago."

And I sat there in that chair and I could feel my ears getting hot. Because if that was true, then two years of my life were a mistake. And I would rather have been sick than have been wasting my time.

I looked at him with a confused but angry look, like I wasn’t sure if he was telling the truth or not

He saw the look on my face and explained it to me.

The word ends in "itis." Itis means inflammation. And when this starts, that's a fair description. You overload the fascia. You get tiny tears in it. Your body sends inflammation, because that's what a body does when something tears. That's not the disease. That's the repair crew showing up.

The trouble starts when the repair crew never gets to finish the job.

Because you cannot stop using your foot. You have to walk to the bathroom. You have to stand at the sink. So the tissue gets torn again before it's finished healing from the last time, and again before it finishes healing from that, and it never once completes a repair. 

And a tissue that never completes a repair does not stay the same. It changes.

He told me the fibers in there are supposed to lie down straight and tight, like the strands of a rope. When the healing keeps getting interrupted, they come back disorganized. Weak. The rope stops being a rope and starts being frayed cord.

That has a name. It's not fasciitis anymore. It's fasciosis.

Osis, not itis. Not inflammation. A degeneration.

I made him say it twice.

Degeneration. My foot wasn't sitting there inflamed and waiting for the swelling to go down. It was breaking down. The tissue itself was falling apart, getting structurally worse, month over month, for two years, while I iced it and stretched it and strapped it into a plastic boot at night.

He drew it on the back of a chart.

Overload. Tear. Start to heal. Overload again before it heals. Tear it worse. Start to heal. Overload again.

Every step you take rips open the thing that's trying to fix itself.

That's the whole disease. Not "my foot is inflamed." My foot was a rope that never got a single day to knit back together, and it was coming apart one strand at a time.

And once he said it, two years of failure rearranged themselves in front of me.

The mornings. I always thought the morning was bad because the foot got stiff overnight. It's worse than that. At night, off your feet, the fascia finally goes slack, and your body starts trying to patch it. That's the only window it gets all day.

But it's a bad window. That tissue sits at the end of the line, furthest from your heart, and lying still in bed you're barely moving any blood down there at all. So your body does the repair with almost nothing to build with. What it lays down overnight is thin. Weak. Half a patch.

Then you stand up. And your whole body weight goes down through that patch before it ever had a chance to harden.

That's what the first step is. That's the pain. It isn't stiffness. It's you tearing open the only repair your body managed all night, and it tears easy, because there was never enough blood down there to make it strong.

Every morning of my life. Ripping open the one thing my body tried to build while I slept.

Then the splint. Two years I slept in that thing. It holds your foot at a right angle so the fascia stays under a gentle stretch all night. And that does work, in a way. If the tissue is held taut, it can't go slack, and relax, so there's nothing there to tear in the morning and the first step doesn't hurt as much.

It buys you a quieter morning by taking away the one window your foot had. It parks that tissue in limbo all night, every night. Not stretched enough to tear. Not slack enough to heal.

All that splint ever bought me was a quieter first step. But as soon as it came off the rope kept fraying.

The stretches. I was pulling on a cord that was already coming apart and calling it treatment.

The orthotics. They cushioned the landing. They propped the arch from underneath. They did nothing about the tearing and nothing about the healing. A pillow under a wound.

The cortisone. That one hurts to say out loud. Cortisone is an anti-inflammatory. It goes after inflammation. It does not reorganize one collagen fiber and it does not stop one tear. It quieted the alarm for five weeks while the rope frayed on. And when it wore off I got the same foot back, five weeks worse, and I blamed my body.

Nothing I did failed because I did it wrong. Or it was a scam 

All of it failed because every last one of those things was aimed at the alarm and not at the fraying rope.

I asked him why nobody had told me this in two years.

He was honest with me. He said the first-line treatments are the first-line treatments. They get written down, they get handed out, and for most people they work. Most people get better and everybody feels good. The ones who don't get better keep coming back, and they get the next thing on the list, and then the shot, and then the conversation about surgery.

Then he said the quiet part. There's no money in telling you the tissue needs a chance to heal. There's money in the injection. There's money in the operation.

So I asked him what actually stops it.

He didn't hesitate. He said you have to break the cycle in two places at once. You have to take the load off it while you're on your feet, because you can't stop being on your feet. And you have to get blood down into it, because the fascia is at the very end of the line, furthest from your heart, and blood is what rebuilds a tissue.

Then he opened a drawer.

He took out a sleeve and put it in my hand.

It's like a compression sock with the toes open, and there are straps that wrap over the top and lock down underneath the arch. Thin. It disappears inside a shoe.

He told me he's been doing this twenty years and he didn't learn this in a classroom, he learned it watching people like me come back for a fourth and fifth visit. And that once he understood what was actually happening in there, he started sending patients to this instead of to the next injection.

He said the straps hold the arch so the tissue stops getting torn open with every step you take. And the compression drives blood down into a fascia that has been starved for months and can finally rebuild.

He said this is the only thing he's found that goes after both halves of that cycle at once.

I'll be honest, I still didn't believe it. I have a drawer at home full of things that didn't work.

I put it on that night the way you eat a salad you don't want.

It goes on like a sock. You pull the straps snug across the arch and you feel them take hold, like a hand cupping the bottom of your foot from underneath.

And I stood up. And I put my weight down wrong, the way you do when you're not thinking, and I braced for the thing that always happens.

It didn't happen. The pain wasn’t gone but it wasn’t unbearable, interrupting or the kind that has you reaching for a railing. 

That was the whole event. Nothing shot up through my heel. I stood in my kitchen at ten at night and put my weight on that foot again on purpose, just to check.

Two days later I walked to the bathroom in the morning without doing the thing I do, where I hold the doorframe and lower my heel down in stages.

I just walked.

I said "huh" out loud, to nobody.

Three weeks in, I made dinner and stood the entire time.

And then came the day I found out it was real.

My sleeve was in the wash. I had the whole day at home ahead of me and nothing to put on, and I remember thinking, fine. It's one day. I'm not going anywhere.

By the afternoon I felt it. Not the old thing. Nothing close to the old thing. A dull ache coming up through the arch, low and steady, the way a bruise reminds you where it is.

I sat down at my own kitchen table and I understood two things at once.

This dull ache used to be my good day. That was the best my foot ever felt for two years, and I used to be grateful for it.

And I hadn't thought about my feet in three weeks.

Not once. Not standing at the sink, not on the stairs, not getting out of bed. Three weeks of my life where my feet were just my feet. Until the one day my sleeve was in the wash

I sat there with my hand over my mouth.

That's when I believed him.

I've been wearing them since April.

I went to the farmers market on a Saturday and I never once limped, I went to every stand I wanted to and not just the ones close to the parking lot. 

I did the whole grocery store, both sides, and I was pushing the cart. Pushing it. I got to the car and realized I hadn't leaned on a single thing, and I sat in the driver's seat and cried, which I'm not going to apologize for.

And a month ago I got up in the night for a glass of water, and I was halfway down the hall before I understood what I was doing.

I was barefoot.

Standing in my own hallway in the dark on my own two bare feet.

Two years. And I didn't even notice I was doing it.

That's the thing I would have paid anything for. Not "less pain." I wanted to stop thinking about my feet. I wanted my house back.

They're called Koprez Foot Sleeves.

If you've had this longer than a few months, hear the one part that matters. What's wrong with your foot now is that it’s never getting the chance to heal. The stretching and the icing and the inserts and the splint are not failing because you're doing them wrong. They're failing because they're aimed at the alarm bell. And that fascia is tearing open every morning before you've had your coffee and it is not being allowed to finish a single repair.

Every month you stay on the list, that rope frays a little further.

There's a 30-day guarantee, so if you wear them and nothing changes, you say so and they make it right. No trial that quietly turns into a subscription. Nothing to mail overseas.

You wear them for a month and you find out.

Put them on and go stand in your kitchen.

That's all I'd ask you to do.

I won't call it a miracle. I'll say I wore shoes in my own living room for two years, and I don't anymore.

bodyText:
My mom is the kind of woman who doesnt just "do" things, she masters them. She has the best garden in the neighborhood and her sourdough is legendary. But over the last couple of years, I noticed she was starting to shrink.

It wasnt just age. It was a quiet, steady retreat from the things she loves. First, she stopped taking the dog for those long morning walks. Then, she stopped cooking the big Sunday dinners, and suddenly our kitchen was full of takeout containers. I think I just assumed she was getting tired, or maybe just slowing down. I felt this weird guilt, like I should have noticed sooner that she was struggling.

The breaking point happened last month. My parents have been planning a trip back to Italy to visit the spot where they honeymooned forty years ago. It was supposed to be the trip of a lifetime. Then, my dad told me they were cancelling it.

When I asked her why, she finally broke down. She told me she has been dealing with this stabbing, ice pick feeling in her heels for two years. She called it plantar fasciitis, but she had been hiding how bad it really was because she didnt want to be a burden.

She had tried everything. I saw the drawer full of drugstore insoles and those rubbery heel cups that never stayed in place. She spent 400 dollars on custom orthotics from a podiatrist that insurance wouldnt cover, and she had two cortisone shots that did nothing but leave her sore. She even tried one of those rigid night splints, but she told me she actually threw it across the room at 2 AM because it was so uncomfortable.

It was heartbreaking. She felt like the floor was moving under her and she just couldnt trust her own feet anymore.

I started researching, because I couldnt stand the thought of her giving up on Italy. I found a study that reframed the entire problem. It suggested that focusing only on the heel is like putting a bandage on a leak without fixing the pipe. It pointed toward the ankle as the real source of the instability.

The research explained the gap she was stuck in. The rigid braces she tried locked the joint but made the muscles stop working. The compression socks just squeezed her leg but didnt actually stabilize the ankle. She was stuck between a "cage" and a "sock" and neither one stopped her gait from overloading her heel.

The breakthrough in the study was a specific kind of flexible stabilization. Instead of a rigid wall, it used adjustable straps that could actually be tuned to the ankle. It provided the alignment of a brace but the flexibility of a sleeve, so the muscles could still fire. It was the first time I saw a solution that didnt force her to choose between stability and mobility.

I found a solution based on those adjustable straps and sent it to her. I didnt even tell her what it was, I just told her to try it for a month.

Three weeks later, I got a text. It was a photo of her and the dog, halfway through their old morning route. She told me "the floor isnt moving under me anymore."

She still has bad days, and I wouldnt say shes suddenly a marathon runner, but the light is back in her eyes. We are actually looking at flights to Rome again.

I want to show you the study I found first, because it explains why the usual stuff doesnt work.

bodyText:
🦶 WHEN SHOULD YOU STOP TRYING TO TREAT PLANTAR FASCIITIS YOURSELF?

Heel starts hurting.

So you Google it.

Then comes the stretching…

The frozen water bottle…

New shoes…

Inserts…

Rest…

Maybe a massage gun…

And three months later you're still taking those painful first few steps every morning.

So when is it time to stop experimenting on your own and get it evaluated?

Here are a few signs.

1️⃣ IT'S NOT GETTING BETTER

There's nothing wrong with trying simple conservative options first.

But if you've consistently been working on the problem and you're seeing little or no improvement, that's information.

Instead of endlessly adding another stretch, shoe or gadget, it may be time to have someone evaluate what's actually happening.

2️⃣ IT KEEPS COMING BACK

Maybe you rest for a few days and feel better.

Then you go for a run…

Play pickleball…

Work a long shift…

Or simply start walking more…

…and the pain returns.

If you're stuck in a cycle of pain → rest → feel better → activity → pain again, I'd want to know why.

3️⃣ YOU'RE CHANGING HOW YOU WALK

This is a big one.

If you're limping, walking on the outside of your foot or avoiding putting weight through the heel because it hurts, don't just ignore it.

Now you're changing the way the rest of your body moves to compensate for the pain.

4️⃣ YOU'VE BEEN BUYING SOLUTIONS INSTEAD OF GETTING ANSWERS

$150 shoes.

$300 orthotics.

Massage tools.

Braces.

Compression socks.

Another pair of inserts.

None of those things are automatically bad.

But eventually you have to ask:

“Am I actually improving—or am I just getting better at managing the symptoms?”

5️⃣ YOU'RE NOT EVEN SURE IT'S PLANTAR FASCIITIS

Not every case of heel pain is plantar fasciitis.

Other problems can cause pain around the heel and foot, which is one reason persistent or unusual symptoms deserve a proper evaluation.

And if you have significant swelling, redness, numbness, weakness, an injury, inability to bear weight, fever, or rapidly worsening pain, seek appropriate medical care rather than assuming it's routine plantar fasciitis.

⚡ THIS IS WHY I CREATED THE FIRST STEP METHOD™

My approach isn't:

“You have heel pain, so let's just rub your heel.”

I want to look at the bigger picture.

How are you moving?

Where are you restricted?

What movements reproduce the pain?

What happens when we address those areas?

I use Rapid NeuroFascial Reset® (RAPID NFR) as part of this process.

RAPID is a hands-on technique that works with the nervous system and painful or restricted tissues. Depending on what I find, treatment may involve the foot, ankle, calf and other related areas rather than only the painful spot.

Then we reassess.

Walk again.

Move again.

Do the thing that hurt before.

Did something change?

That's the question I'm interested in.

You don't necessarily need another gadget.

Sometimes you need someone to take a fresh look at the problem.

👇 How long did YOU try treating your heel pain yourself before finally asking for help?

And if you know someone who has a closet full of shoes, inserts, braces and massage tools because of their heel pain…

send them this post. 😂

— Derrick

bodyText:
I took a full week off walking and my heel felt the same within three days of coming back. That's when I knew rest wasn't actually fixing anything.
I'm 46. I've been dealing with plantar fasciitis for about two years. Morning stiffness. 

Afternoon burning. That deep heel rigidity where you press your foot to the floor before standing just to check what kind of day it's going to be. 

The steps that used to be automatic became calculated, then painful. 

Gripping walls on the way to the bathroom is like some kind of pre-morning ritual you never signed up for.

I did what made sense. I took more rest days. Stopped walking for exercise. Cancelled weekend hikes. When that didn't change anything, I took an entire week off my feet. 

No standing at work, no errands, nothing.

My heel felt great by day five. I was convinced rest was the answer and I just hadn't been taking enough of it.

First day back felt amazing. Second day was solid. By day three—just three days after coming back—I was right back where I started. Same stiffness. Same morning calculation. Same floor press test.

I spent $400 on podiatrist visits over the next few months. 

The advice was always some version of "reduce activity" and "listen to your body." I was already doing both. I dropped another $150 on treatments—custom orthotics, night splints, compression socks. None did anything. Not subtle improvement, not slow progress.

Nothing. The orthotics were $520 for what turned out to be expensive plastic inserts.

I was stuck. Not getting worse. Not getting better. Just permanently stuck in this cycle where my heel never fully reset and I couldn't figure out why rest, the thing that's supposed to fix everything wasn't working.
The conversation that changed it happened on a Thursday.

There's a woman I work with. Early fifties, dealt with plantar fasciitis longer than me, same activity level. I'd noticed she never seemed to deal with the same heel issues anymore. No morning limp. No calculation before standing. Just stood up and walked.

I asked her about it while we were having coffee. I was flexing my foot under the table, which I didn't even realize I was doing until she pointed it out.

"That used to be me," she said. "Constant heel management. I thought it was just chronic plantar fasciitis."
"What changed?"

"I stopped thinking about it as a rest problem. It's not a rest problem."
I didn't get what she meant.

"Your muscles recover between rest days because they have massive blood flow," she said. "Blood delivers nutrients, clears waste, repairs tissue. That's why your calves feel ready after two days. 

Your fascia doesn't have that. It's poorly vascularized tissue dependent on circulation for everything—nutrients, waste removal, tissue repair. That circulation moves slowly. Way slower than blood to muscles."
"So the rest days aren't long enough?"

"It's not about length. When you rest, you stop adding load. That's real. But rest doesn't improve the circulation to the tissue. It doesn't speed up the clearing of inflammation. It doesn't upgrade the recovery environment. It just pauses the input. 

So if your fascia environment is already compromised from months of accumulated inflammation and at your activity level, it almost certainly is taking a week off doesn't fix that. 

It just gives you a short window where the load drops below the threshold. Then you come back and you're right back to the same compromised baseline within a few days."

That hit me like a wall. Because that's exactly what happened.
"So rest removes load but doesn't rebuild the environment," I said.
"Exactly. You've been thinking about it like you just need to stop damaging it. But the tissue environment is broken. 

The circulation is shut down. Doing nothing doesn't fix the underlying problem."
"So what does?"

She told me about something she'd been using daily for the last six months. A topical treatment and before I could say anything, she held up her hand.

"I know. I was the same. Creams are pointless. I tried lidocaine patches and arnica gel and neither did anything. 

But here's what I didn't understand until someone explained it to me: those products aren't built for this. Lidocaine numbs surface skin. 

The penetration is terrible, maybe 1mm deep, and the formulation has nothing to help reach fascia tissue. Arnica is surface anti-inflammatory. Neither one was ever designed for poorly vascularized tissue under chronic inflammation. 

Testing them and concluding topicals don't work is like testing hand lotion on broken bone and concluding creams don't work."

She told me about Senzio. Said it was penetration-optimized, formulated with botanicals that actually restored circulation, and built specifically for the kind of deep tissue damage that most cream companies don't even address. 

She said the people who designed it understood that fascia needs circulation restoration, not surface numbing.
"What did it feel like?" I asked.

"First few days, nothing. I almost stopped. Around day five, my mornings started changing. Not my walking, my mornings. The heel stiffness got quieter. Not gone. Just quieter. Like the volume turned down. 

By week two, I stopped doing the foot thing." She mimicked pressing her heel to the floor. "You know, the morning check. I just stopped because there was nothing to check. My heel wasn't a thing I was managing anymore."

I ordered it that night. Not because I believed her. Because the specificity of what she said—mornings, not walking; quieter, not fixed; weeks, not days—sounded like someone describing something real, not someone selling something.

First three days: nothing.

I mean genuinely nothing. I checked the jar to make sure it wasn't empty because I was convinced I'd been sent plain lotion.

Day five: something shifted.

I can't tell you the exact morning. But somewhere around day five, my pre-standing ritual got shorter. I was still checking my heel in bed. But the stiffness wasn't as deep. 

The tissue cooperated faster. The morning went from its usual ten-minute negotiation to maybe three minutes of just... standing up. It was subtle enough that I almost dismissed it.

Week two: I stopped checking.

Not a conscious decision. I just noticed one morning that I'd gotten out of bed and walked to the kitchen without doing the floor press test first. My heel wasn't perfect—it was just fine. Not a thing I needed to assess before starting my day.

I'm three months in now. Same activity level. Same work schedule. I didn't add rest days, didn't change my routine, didn't start new stretching. I added daily application and gave it time.

The honest truth is that I spent more on rest days, podiatrist visits, orthotics that did nothing, and splints I never wore in the last two years than a full year of Senzio would cost. 

All of it managed around the tissue. None of it supported what was happening inside it.

Here’s why Senzio works when rest doesn't
Beeswax Carrier Technology

Standard creams sit on surface. Molecules too big to penetrate. Senzio uses beeswax carrier. Pushes through skin layers. Forces compounds into fascia tissue where circulation has failed.

Circulation-Restoring Botanicals
Angelica Sinensis opens blood vessels. 
Comfrey triggers tissue repair. Frankincense calms chronic inflammation. Myrrh activates circulation in poorly vascularized tissue.

Not surface numbing. Not pain blocking. Circulation restoration.
Senzio offers a 60-day money-back guarantee. If your mornings don't start feeling different, send it back. Full refund. That's what got me to try it. The risk was basically zero.

Here's what I wish someone had told me two years ago:
Rest removes the load. But if the circulation inside the tissue is already shut down, more rest doesn't fix that. 

It just delays the next time you feel it. You need something that actually restores the circulation environment—not just something that pauses the damage.

You've got two options.

Keep resting more. Keep hoping the week off will finally be the one that fixes it. Keep doing the morning floor press test and managing the stiffness.

Or try the one thing that actually addresses what rest can't: daily circulation restoration built for tissue that can't heal on its own.
60 days. Twice application daily. See what changes.

Your fascia doesn't need more rest. It needs circulation it can't get on its own.

P.S. - I'm not going to tell you it's a miracle. My heel isn't invincible. I still feel soreness after long days. But the baseline is different. Mornings feel like mornings. And I stopped accepting that permanent low-grade stiffness was just the price of living with plantar fasciitis.

bodyText:
I had a stroke at 62. My left ankle never came back.

One morning I was fine. Teaching my water aerobics class, planning a trip to see my grandkids in Colorado, living my life.

The next morning, I woke up and the left side of my body wasn't mine anymore.

They call what happened to my ankle "foot drop." The nerve signals from my brain don't reach my foot properly. So my ankle just... hangs. I can't lift it. I can't control it. I drag it everywhere I go.

That was 7 years ago. I'm 69 now.

The doctors were honest with me. They said the brain can sometimes rewire itself, but there are no guarantees. Physical therapy might help. Might not.

So I did the therapy. Three times a week for two years. I did the exercises at home. I wore the big plastic brace they gave me—the one that went up to my knee and made me look like a robot.

My ankle got a little better. Maybe 20%. Enough to walk with a cane instead of a walker. But the foot drop never went away.

And then something else started happening.

Because I was walking differently—dragging my left foot, putting all my weight on my right—my right foot started to break down.

First it was just soreness in the morning. Then it became stabbing pain in my heel the moment I stood up. Then it spread to my arch.

Plantar fasciitis. That's what the podiatrist called it.

"It's because you're compensating," she said. "Your right foot is doing the work of two feet. It's not designed for that."

So now I had a left ankle that didn't work, and a right foot that was screaming at me every morning.

One foot I couldn't control. The other I couldn't stand on.

I'm not going to lie to you. There were days I didn't want to get out of bed.

Not because I was depressed—I've always been a fighter. But because I knew what was waiting for me when my feet hit the floor.

Pain. Instability. The shuffle to the bathroom, gripping the wall. The fear that today might be the day I fall and can't get back up.

That was my life for almost 5 years.

Then about 8 months ago, my daughter sent me a package.

No note. Just a pair of what looked like socks.

I called her. "What are these?"

"Bamboo ankle sleeves. Just try them, Mom. Please."

My daughter is the researcher in our family. She's always sending me articles, supplements, things she's found online. Half of it I ignore. But she's also the one who found my neurologist after the stroke—the one who actually helped me. So I listen to her.

"How is a sock going to help a stroke?" I asked.

"It's not a sock. It's compression. But it's made of bamboo so it won't irritate your skin or make you hot. Just try them for a week. If they don't help, I'll shut up forever."

She wasn't going to shut up forever. We both knew that. But I put them on anyway.

The first thing I noticed: they were comfortable.

That sounds stupid. But you have to understand—I've worn every brace, wrap, sleeve, and compression sock known to medicine. They all squeeze too tight, or slip down, or make my feet sweat, or dig into my skin.

These didn't do any of that. They were snug—I could feel the compression—but they didn't feel like a medical device. They felt like... I don't know. A hug for my ankle.

I wore them around the house that first day. Didn't notice much.

I wore them to bed that night because I forgot to take them off.

When I woke up the next morning, I stood up out of bed—and the heel pain wasn't there.

I stood there for a second, waiting for it. That ice-pick feeling I get every morning when the plantar fasciitis wakes up.

Nothing.

I took a step. Then another. Then I walked to the bathroom without gripping the wall.

My left ankle still had the foot drop—that's nerve damage, that's not going away. But it felt more... stable. Like something was holding it in place. Keeping it from rolling.

And my right foot? The one that's been punishing me for 5 years of compensating?

Silent. For the first time in years.

I called my daughter that afternoon.

"Okay. What are these things?"

"They're bamboo ankle sleeves. The bamboo keeps your feet warm without overheating, which helps with circulation and stiffness. The compression supports the joint and reduces swelling. And they're gentle enough to sleep in, so you get 8 hours of therapy while you're not even trying."

"Why didn't anyone tell me about these 5 years ago?"

"I don't know, Mom. But they're working, right?"

They were. They are.
