title: Step into Comfort👟

bodyText:
I ordered the Footstr InsoleX to fix my kid’s flat feet...

And then I panicked.

Was my kid going to even like these?

What if he wore them once and pulled them straight back out of his cleats?

What if this was just another pair of insoles that ended up sitting in the bottom of his soccer bag?

I'd been through that before.

Custom orthotics were the worst.

And not because they didn't work.

They actually did.

When my son wore them, I could see that his feet weren't rolling inward nearly as much.

The problem was everything it took just to get there.

First we had to see a specialist.

Then the assessment.

Measurements.

The fitting.

Then we waited for them to be made.

Then went back again to make sure everything fit properly.

Hundreds of dollars later...

we finally had these custom orthotics that were supposed to solve the problem.

And my son hated wearing them.

They were hard.

Bulky inside his soccer cleats.

He complained that they hurt his feet.

At first I kept trying to convince him to give them another chance.

“Just wear them for practice.”

“Give them a few days.”

“You'll get used to them.”

Eventually I gave up.

I started finding the $400 orthotics sitting in the bottom of his soccer bag instead of inside his shoes.

All that money.

All those appointments.

All that waiting.

And they weren't helping anyone sitting underneath a dirty jersey.

Then a few months later, I finally convinced him to try them again.

He pushed his foot into his shoe...

stopped...

and looked at me.

“Mom, these don't fit anymore.”

His feet had grown.

Of course they had.

He's a kid.

I hadn't even really thought about that when we bought them.

Then I learned that growing kids may need their orthotics replaced around every six months.

So I did the math.

$400 twice a year.

$800 a year.

And he still had years of growing left.

By the time my son stopped growing, I could've spent thousands of dollars on custom orthotics.

Thousands...

on something I still had to argue with him to wear.

And customs weren't the only thing we'd tried.

Pharmacy insoles.

Too flat. Barely any structure.

Gel heel inserts.

Soft, sure. But they didn't do much for the way his feet rolled inward when he ran.

Heel cups.

Different shoes.

Stretching.

Rest.

We kept trying things.

Some helped a little.

Some did basically nothing.

But eventually we always seemed to end up in the same place.

His feet were still rolling inward when he played.

His knees were still bothering him after harder practices.

And I was still searching for another answer.

So when I saw Footstr...

I was interested.

But I definitely wasn't convinced.

The one thing that made ordering easier was the price.

Compared with going through the custom-orthotic nightmare again...

Specialist.

Fitting.

Waiting.

Hundreds of dollars.

Footstr felt like a pretty small gamble.

Still...

cheap doesn't matter if your kid won't wear them.

So if you just ordered Footstr...

Or you're about to order...

Let me tell you exactly what happened.

Day by day.

So you know what to expect.

THEY ARRIVED FRIDAY AFTERNOON

The first thing I did was take them out of the package and bend them in my hands.

They weren't what I expected.

The top felt soft.

The whole insole had some flex to it.

But underneath the arch...

there was actual structure.

Not that flat piece of foam I'd gotten from pharmacy insoles.

And not the rock-hard feeling of my son's custom orthotics either.

I bent one again.

Flexible.

But not floppy.

That immediately got my attention.

Because that had basically been the problem with everything we'd tried.

The comfortable stuff didn't give him enough support.

The supportive stuff was so rigid he wouldn't wear it.

Footstr looked like it might actually sit somewhere in the middle.

But I'd spent enough money getting excited about things in my hands.

The real test was getting them onto his feet.

FRIDAY EVENING

My son was sitting at the kitchen table when I brought over one of his cleats.

I'd already taken his old insert out and slipped the Footstr inside.

He looked at the shoe.

Then at me.

“What is it?”

“Another insole.”

He gave me the look.

You know the one.

So I told him:

“Just try it. If you hate it, take it out.”

He pushed his foot inside.

Stood up.

Walked across the kitchen.

Stopped.

Walked back.

I was waiting for:

“No.”

Instead he looked down at his feet.

Took another few steps.

Then shrugged.

“These are way softer.”

Okay.

Good start.

But I wasn't celebrating.

Walking around our kitchen for thirty seconds is very different from sprinting, cutting and stopping for an entire soccer practice.

I'd been fooled by first impressions before.

So I went to bed thinking:

We'll see tomorrow.

SATURDAY — DAY 1

Soccer practice.

This was the first real test.

Before he ran onto the field I told him:

“If they bother you, take them out.”

I didn't want him suffering through them because he knew I'd spent money.

He nodded.

Practice started.

Twenty minutes.

Still playing.

Forty minutes.

Still playing.

Then the entire session.

And I swear I spent half of practice watching his feet.

Waiting for him to jog toward the sideline.

Waiting for the cleat to come off.

Waiting for him to pull the Footstr out and hand it to me.

It never happened.

He finished practice with them still inside his cleats.

When he walked over, I immediately asked:

“How were the insoles?”

He shrugged.

“Fine.”

That was it.

And weirdly...

that was exactly the answer I wanted.

I didn't want him obsessing over his insoles.

I wanted him thinking about soccer.

Still...

one practice is one practice.

SUNDAY — DAY 2

I put them into his regular sneakers.

And then I waited.

Normally my son notices everything I put inside his shoes.

Too high.

Too stiff.

Feels weird.

Shoe feels tight.

This time?

Nothing.

We went through almost the entire day before I finally asked:

“You still have those insoles in?”

He looked confused for a second.

Then remembered.

“Oh. Yeah.”

That got my attention.

He had basically forgotten about them.

TUESDAY — SECOND SOCCER PRACTICE

This was the day I was really waiting for.

Because almost anything new can survive one wear.

The real question is:

Will a kid keep wearing it after the novelty disappears?

That's where we'd lost the custom orthotics.

Again...

they worked.

When he wore them, his inward rolling looked better.

But eventually he started pulling them out before practice.

I'd argue.

Then bargain.

“Just wear them for half the session.”

Then I'd find them in the bag anyway.

So this time I said nothing.

I didn't remind him about Footstr.

I didn't ask whether he had put them in.

I just watched.

Full practice.

Still inside his cleats.

He came off the field sweaty.

Hungry.

Exhausted.

But he hadn't removed his shoes halfway through practice.

He hadn't complained about something hard digging into his foot.

He hadn't handed me an insole.

They just...

stayed in.

That sounds small.

After everything we'd been through?

It wasn't.

WEEK 1 — THE FULL PICTURE

Before Footstr:

$400 custom orthotics.

Specialist appointment.

Assessment.

Measurements.

Fitting.

Waiting for them to be made.

Trying to convince my kid to actually wear them.

Eventually finding them sitting in his soccer bag instead of underneath his feet.

Then the cheap pharmacy inserts.

Easy to wear.

But almost completely flat.

Gel heel pads.

Comfortable...

but not the structured support I was looking for.

So it felt like there were two choices:

Comfortable enough for my kid to wear... but barely any structure.

Or:

Enough structure... but so rigid he refused to keep them in.

After one week with Footstr:

He was wearing them.

That was the first big difference.

Sneakers.

School shoes.

Soccer cleats.

I wasn't arguing with him before practice.

I wasn't digging through the bottom of his bag afterward.

And for the first time I felt like we'd found the middle ground we'd been missing.

Soft enough that my kid would actually wear them.

Structured enough to support his arch when his foot started rolling inward.

And with cushioning underneath his heel for all the running, jumping and pounding his feet take during sports.

WEEK 2

This was when I stopped thinking quite so much about the insoles...

and started noticing everything around them.

Normally after soccer I could tell how practice had gone before my son even said anything.

The way he walked toward the car.

How quickly he kicked his shoes off.

Whether he started rubbing his knees.

Nothing was suddenly perfect.

He's still a nine-year-old playing soccer hard.

He still gets tired.

He still gets sore.

But I wasn't seeing the same ritual after every single practice.

And most importantly...

the Footstrs were still in his shoes.

Every day.

That mattered.

Because even the best support in the world can't help much when it's sitting at the bottom of a sports bag.

WEEK 3

One night I noticed something strange.

The ice pack was still in the freezer.

Normally after a hard week of soccer, getting it out had almost become automatic.

That week...

I hadn't.

Not because I'd made some decision to stop using it.

I simply hadn't thought about it.

Neither had my son.

Again...

nothing dramatic.

No miracle.

Just one little thing that used to be part of our routine...

that suddenly wasn't happening as often.

WEEK 4 — THEN I PULLED THE CUSTOM ORTHOTICS BACK OUT

I got curious.

Part of me still wondered whether we'd been stupid to abandon something we'd spent so much money on.

So I asked my son:

“Try your customs again.”

He rolled his eyes.

Eventually agreed.

I put them into his shoes.

He pushed his foot down...

stopped...

and immediately said:

“Mom, these don't fit anymore.”

At first I thought he just didn't want to wear them.

Then I looked.

His feet had grown.

And that was the moment the economics of this whole thing really hit me.

I'd spent around $400 on those orthotics.

Specialist.

Fitting.

Waiting.

Getting them adjusted.

Convincing him to wear them.

Eventually giving up.

Then finally getting him to try them again...

only to realize he'd already outgrown them.

So again I did the math.

$400.

Twice a year.

$800 every year.

My son is nine.

He has a lot of growing left.

By the time his feet stop changing, I could have spent thousands.

And I want to say this again because it's important:

The custom orthotics did work when he wore them.

That's not why I stopped using them.

I stopped because the whole process was a nightmare.

Appointments.

Fittings.

Waiting.

Hundreds of dollars.

A rigid device my kid hated.

And then...

just when I finally convinced him to give them another chance...

his feet were already too big.

I did not want to start all over again.

That's when Footstr's price stopped looking merely “cheap”...

and started looking practical.

Four pairs for $30.

Instead of hundreds of dollars for one custom device.

And four pairs meant I didn't have to move one insole around every day.

One pair in his school shoes.

One in his sneakers.

One in his soccer cleats.

One for another pair he wears regularly.

That is a completely different decision from:

“Do I want to spend another $400 and hope my kid actually wears them this time?”

THEN I STARTED LOOKING AT WHY THEY FELT SO DIFFERENT

I wanted to understand why he was keeping Footstr inside his shoes when he had fought the customs so hard.

There were three things that made sense.

1 - FLEXIBLE ARCH SUPPORT

Footstr isn't a completely flat foam pad.

There is structure underneath the arch.

When the foot starts rolling excessively inward, that support gives the arch something underneath it instead of simply following the collapse.

But it still flexes with the foot.

Walking.

Running.

Cutting.

Playing.

The goal isn't to lock his foot into one rigid shape.

It's to give it a steadier base while he's moving.

2 - HEEL CUSHIONING

Kids playing sports take an insane amount of repeated impact.

Sprint.

Stop.

Jump.

Land.

Sprint again.

Footstr combines the arch support with cushioning underneath the heel.

So there's comfort where the foot lands...

and structure where it needs support.

3 - THE STRENGTHENING EXERCISES

This was the other big reason I liked them.

I didn't want our long-term plan to be:

“Put something in his shoe forever and hope.”

The insole and the strengthening work have different jobs.

The insole supports the arch and heel during the activities that put the most demand on his feet.

The exercises give the muscles around his feet something to actually work on outside the shoe.

Support during activity.

Strengthening work over time.

That made much more sense to me.

WHY I DON'T WANT TO GO BACK

The pharmacy inserts?

Easy to wear.

Not enough structure for what I wanted.

The custom orthotics?

Plenty of structure.

Expensive.

Rigid.

A whole specialist process.

Quickly outgrown.

And most importantly...

my kid wouldn't consistently wear them.

Footstr landed in the middle.

More structure than the flat inserts we'd tried.

More flexible than the customs he'd rejected.

Cushioning under the heel.

Support under the arch.

Something he could actually keep inside his cleats while playing soccer.

And inexpensive enough that keeping up with a growing kid didn't feel ridiculous.

WHAT I WOULD EXPECT IF YOU JUST ORDERED

First time they put them on:

Don't expect fireworks.

Honestly, the best answer might be:

“They're comfortable.”

Or:

“They're fine.”

That's a win.

You don't want your kid thinking about the thing inside their shoe.

First practice:

This is the first real test.

Cleats tightened.

Feet getting hot.

Running.

Jumping.

Cutting.

See whether your kid actually keeps them in.

That's what mattered most to me.

First week:

Watch the ordinary things.

Are they still wearing them?

Are you fighting about them before practice?

Are they pulling them out halfway through?

What do they say after the activities that normally bring on complaints?

Over the next few weeks:

Keep your expectations realistic.

Footstr isn't going to magically rebuild a growing foot overnight.

It's giving the arch and heel support during the activities that demand the most from them...

while the strengthening exercises give you something proactive to work on as they grow.

IF YOU JUST ORDERED...

Don't panic like I did.

When I clicked order that Tuesday night, I genuinely wondered whether I'd just bought another pair of insoles my kid would refuse to wear.

A few weeks later...

I was holding his $400 custom orthotics that he'd already outgrown...

while Footstr was still sitting inside his soccer cleats.

That comparison pretty much answered the question for me.

IF YOU HAVEN'T ORDERED YET...

If your kid's feet roll inward...

Their feet, heels or knees complain after sports...

Or you've already been through the nightmare of expensive custom orthotics they won't consistently wear...

Footstr gives you a much simpler place to start.

Flexible arch support.

Heel cushioning.

A strengthening program.

And support designed around active, growing feet without locking them against something hard and rigid.

Right now, you can get four pairs for $30.

So instead of constantly moving one pair between shoes, you can keep them where your kid actually needs them.

School shoes.

Sneakers.

Cleats.

Sports shoes.

For me?

That was a much easier decision than:

Another specialist appointment.

Another fitting.

Another wait.

Another $400 custom orthotic.

And another argument with my kid about whether he'd actually wear it.

bodyText:
No matter which brand makes them, running shoes have all been offered with ever-increasing amounts of padding, cushioning, and support in recent years.

Think about it.

Every year, the soles get thicker. The arch supports get taller. The foam gets softer. The marketing gets louder.

More cushioning. More structure. More technology between you and the ground.

And I used to believe every word of it. I used to think more padding meant more protection. More support meant stronger feet. A thicker sole meant a safer step.

I was wrong.

I believe running shoes can be the most destructive force to ever hit the human foot.

Not just running shoes, either. Walking shoes. Hiking boots. The everyday sneakers most of us wear from morning to night.

They're dangerous.

And my belief, after years of dealing with the consequences, is that they cause the very injuries they're supposed to reduce. That by encouraging you to move in a way which is unnatural to the human leg, they actually cause the damage.

Here is what nobody tells you when you lace up that next pair of cushioned shoes.

Most shoes today are squishing your toes together. Locking your feet in like casts. And blocking the muscles from doing any real work.

Your foot has over a hundred muscles, tendons, and ligaments. It was designed to flex. Spread. Grip. Stabilize. Sense every surface beneath it and respond in real time.

But when you encase it in a stiff, elevated, foam-padded shoe, you take away every job it was built to do.

The toes can't spread. The arch can't load naturally. The small stabilizing muscles that are supposed to fire with every single step just... stop. They have nothing to do. The shoe is doing it for them.

And this does not happen overnight.

It happens slowly. Over years. Over decades.

You don't notice until one day you're standing on a curb and your ankle wobbles. Or you step off a trail onto loose gravel and your balance feels off. Or you realize you haven't walked barefoot on grass in so long that it actually feels uncomfortable.

That's not aging.

That's years of damage building up without you even realizing.

Flat feet. Collapsed arches. Pain up the entire chain. Sore knees. Tight hips. A lower back that aches after a walk around the block.

And what do most people do when the discomfort starts?

They go buy more cushioning.

They buy the shoe with the thicker sole. The insert with the higher arch. The orthotic that promises to correct everything.

And for a while, maybe it feels a little better. Because padding feels nice. Support feels safe.

But underneath all that foam, the feet are getting weaker. The muscles are shutting down further. The toes are being squeezed tighter. And the cycle continues.

More support. Less capability.

More cushioning. Less feedback.

More dependency. Less trust in your own body.

I tried the cushioned shoes. I tried the arch-support insoles. I tried the gel inserts. I tried the $200 walking shoes that were supposed to be engineered for comfort.

None of them addressed what was actually happening.

Because none of them gave my feet permission to work again.

Here's the crazy part.

Once you free your feet, everything else starts improving.

Posture. Balance. Strength. Even joint discomfort.

When the feet can finally spread and grip and sense the ground the way they were designed to, the rest of the body stops compensating. The ankles stop wobbling. The knees stop absorbing force they were never meant to handle. The hips settle. The back releases.

It is not magic.

It is what happens when you stop treating your feet like they need to be carried and start letting them do the job they were built for.

But here is the problem.

You can't just walk barefoot everywhere.

Glass. Sharp rocks. Hot pavement. Wet tile. Debris you can't see. The world is not set up for bare skin on the ground, no matter how good it might feel.

And that is exactly why I started wearing SuperSocks.

Not ordinary socks. Not padded slippers. Not another pair of minimalist shoes that still feel like shoes.

SuperSocks are the world's first sock that gives you true barefoot freedom without any of the risks.

I wear them for walking. For hiking. Even for running.

They're made from Dyneema, a material 15 times stronger than steel. That gives them serious cut resistance. I've walked over glass and sharp rocks. Zero damage. They handle pebbles, all rocks, all the pokey, sharp kind of things. They may not go through the material and actually cut you.

They're slip resistant, too. I never worry about slipping, even on tile or wet surfaces. That alone changed how I move indoors.

But what I love most is how my toes finally move freely.

Five individual toe compartments. Not crammed together. Not squeezed into a narrow toe box. Each toe has space to spread, flex, and grip the ground the way it's supposed to.

That is what makes your feet come alive again.

When your toes can finally splay and your foot can actually feel the surface underneath, you start noticing things.

You feel the cool tile in the kitchen. The texture of a wooden deck. The firmness of packed earth on a trail. The subtle slope of a sidewalk you've walked a thousand times without ever really sensing.

All of that feedback is information your feet were designed to receive. Information that helps your body balance, stabilize, and move more naturally.

And shoes have been blocking it for years.

These are also true grounding socks. You're actually connected to the earth. That's helped lower my stress and improve my sleep. It's not placebo. It's real.

They're ultra light. Dry fast. Pack small. I bring them on every trip. No more bulky sandals or hot shoes. Just one pair of SuperSocks, and I'm set.

If you're looking to go raw, nature barefoot, this is the next step away from skin to ground.

Here is what the first few weeks looked like for me.

The first time I put them on, I noticed how thin they were. Not flimsy. Thin in the way that lets you actually feel what's underneath. I walked across my kitchen floor and could sense every tile edge. That was new.

By the end of the first week, I was wearing them around the yard. On the driveway. Down the sidewalk. The Dyneema held up to everything. The grip kept me steady on every surface. I stopped thinking about where I was stepping and started just walking.

By week two, I noticed my toes spreading more on their own. Not because I was stretching them. Because they finally had room to do it naturally, while I moved.

By week four, my balance felt different. Steadier. Not dramatic. Just quieter. I stopped reaching for the railing on the porch steps. I stopped second-guessing my footing on the uneven path behind my house.

By week eight, I was hiking in them.

Real trails. Loose rock. Roots. Creek crossings.

No sore feet. No worries about where I step. And I feel more energized after a walk than I have in years.

My posture's better. The low back tightness that used to settle in by afternoon started fading. My knees stopped aching after walks.

It's amazing what a difference the right footwear can make.

Or, more accurately, what a difference it makes when your feet are finally allowed to participate in your own movement again.

These are better than any $200 barefoot shoes I've tried. And I have tried them. The rigid soles. The enclosed toe boxes that claim to be wide but still press the toes together. The bulky designs that defeat the entire point of going minimal.

SuperSocks are none of that.

They're a sock. With serious protection. With grip. With the durability to handle outdoor terrain. And with the freedom to let every part of your foot do what it was designed to do.

Machine washable. Quick drying. Light enough to fold into a pocket.

One pair replaces the sandals, the house shoes, the gym shoes, and the backup hiking footwear.

I believe running shoes can be the most destructive force to ever hit the human foot.

The toes can't spread. The arch can't load naturally. The small stabilizing muscles that are supposed to fire with every single step just... stop. They have nothing to do. The shoe is doing it for them.

WARNING: I made a huge mistake after buying Footstr insoles for my son. Don't do what I did.

I almost threw them away.

Three weeks after they arrived, I nearly pulled them out of his cleats and tossed them in the trash.

Not because they weren't working.

Because of what happened after he started wearing them.

Let me explain.

My son is 9, he plays soccer, and somewhere over the past year I had quietly accepted that sore feet were just part of who he was.

The slow limp to the car after practice.
The ankles rolling inward every time he stood barefoot.
Me planning our weekends around how much his feet could handle.

Our doctor looked at his flat feet, shrugged, and said he'd probably grow out of it.

So I went down the internet rabbit hole.

That's when I found Footstr. Insoles made for kids who overpronate, with flexible arch support, heel cushioning, and a foot strengthening program.

Honestly, it seemed too simple. We had already spent $450 on custom orthotics. What was a kids' insole going to do that those couldn't?

But the reviews from other soccer parents sounded exactly like my house.

So I ordered.

=====

MY FIRST MISTAKE

I didn't tell my husband.

Not because he wouldn't be supportive.

I just didn't want to get his hopes up. Or mine.

I pulled the old orthotic out of my son's cleat, slid the Footstr in, and handed him the shoe like it was nothing.

By week two, something strange happened.

He was still wearing them.

That might sound small, but the $450 custom orthotics lasted about two weeks before I started finding them at the bottom of his soccer bag. He hated how hard they felt under his feet.

The Footstrs just stayed in his shoes. School, practice, the park. I never had to argue once.

And I noticed something else. He stopped kicking his shoes off the second he got in the car.

=====

THE REAL PROBLEM STARTED IN WEEK THREE

Saturday game.

Normally I watch the second half differently than the other parents. I'm not watching the ball. I'm watching my son's run, waiting for it to turn into that heavy, flat-footed jog that means his feet are done.

But this time?

Nothing happened.

He just... played.

The whole game.

Afterward he walked to the car talking about a goal he almost scored, and climbed in like a kid whose feet had never once been a topic in our family.

That night after dinner, he asked my husband to go kick the ball around in the yard.

I tensed up. Evenings were usually when his feet and legs were finished for the day.

But before I could say "maybe tomorrow," he was already outside.

=====

HERE'S WHERE I ALMOST MADE MY BIGGEST MISTAKE

That next week, I caught myself watching him constantly.

Waiting for the limp to come back. Waiting for him to wake up with sore legs again. Waiting for the other shoe to drop.

And when it didn't, I did something ridiculous.

I decided it couldn't be the insoles.

I nearly took them out and put the custom orthotics back in. The expensive ones. The prescribed ones. The "real" ones.

Because somewhere along the way, I'd been trained to believe that if a solution isn't expensive and complicated, it can't actually be doing anything.

$450 and a specialist appointment felt serious.

A comfortable insole my kid actually liked wearing felt too easy.

I'm so glad I stopped myself.

Because the customs never really had a chance to help him. They were so stiff and bulky inside his cleats that he wouldn't keep them on his feet.

And support sitting at the bottom of a soccer bag isn't supporting anything.

=====

WHAT I FINALLY LEARNED

That was the week I sat down and actually researched what was going on with his feet.

I found a study of 92,000 adolescents. The ones with moderate to severe flat feet had nearly double the rate of knee pain and low back pain compared to kids with normal arches.

Another study from 2025 looked at school aged kids specifically. Children with flat feet scored 42 percent higher on a clinical pain scale than their classmates, and they were measurably less active because of it.

Neither study proved that my son's feet were behind every complaint he ever had.

But they explained something I'd been watching for a year without understanding it.

When his arch rolled inward under his weight, his whole leg was working from a wobbly base. Every sprint, every cut, every landing started from a foot that collapsed a little with each step.

Then I finally read what was actually behind the Footstr design.

Structured arch support that flexes as he runs instead of locking his foot in place the way the customs did. It helps reduce that excessive inward rolling while he's wearing them.

Heel cushioning, so all the pounding from running and jumping has a softer place to land.

And the part I didn't appreciate when I ordered: the strengthening program.

The insole and the exercises have two different jobs.

The insole supports his arch and heel during the activities that put the most demand on his feet. The exercises give the muscles around his feet and arches something to work on outside the shoe as he grows.

Support during activity. Strengthening work over time.

This wasn't just a softer version of the orthotics.

It was the first thing that felt like a plan instead of another thing we bought after he was already hurting.

=====

THE SIDE EFFECT NOBODY WARNS YOU ABOUT

About two months in, my husband said something on the drive home from a game that stuck with me.

"He hasn't stopped talking since he got in the car."

He was right.

I hadn't realized how quiet those drives had gotten over the past year. How much of our family's energy went into managing his feet. The ice, the rest days, the bargaining over whether he could handle practice.

I'm not going to tell you his feet became indestructible. He still gets tired. He still has sore days after a big tournament.

But the sore days stopped running our week.

=====

WHY MOST "SOLUTIONS" NEVER WORKED FOR US

Before Footstr, we tried the whole list.

Custom orthotics. To be fair, when he actually wore them, his ankles didn't roll inward as badly. But they were rigid, bulky inside his cleats, $450, and he'd outgrow them within the year. Support your kid refuses to wear isn't support.

Pharmacy inserts. Soft, cheap, and completely flat. They just followed his foot down as the arch collapsed.

Rest. His feet always felt better after a week off. And the complaints always came back once he was playing again.

Better shoes. They helped a little. But the support stayed home every time he switched into his cleats.

None of it dealt with what was happening underneath him. A foot rolling inward under his weight, step after step, all day long.

=====

WHAT I WISH SOMEONE HAD TOLD ME SOONER

If your kid's ankles roll inward when they stand.
If their shoes wear down faster along the inside edge.
If they limp after practice, ask to sit out, or say their feet are tired before they are.

Please don't spend a year like I did, telling yourself it's just growing pains.

And if you do try something and things start getting better, don't make my mistake.

Don't talk yourself out of it just because it was simple.

I spent three weeks waiting for the bad news to come back before I let myself believe the good news.

Watching your kid walk to the car talking about the game instead of his feet... you're allowed to believe that.

bodyText:
I ordered the Footstr InsoleX to fix my kid’s flat feet...

And then I panicked.

Was my kid going to even like these?

What if he wore them once and pulled them straight back out of his cleats?

What if this was just another pair of insoles that ended up sitting in the bottom of his soccer bag?

I'd been through that before.

Custom orthotics were the worst.

And not because they didn't work.

They actually did.

When my son wore them, I could see that his feet weren't rolling inward nearly as much.

The problem was everything it took just to get there.

First we had to see a specialist.

Then the assessment.

Measurements.

The fitting.

Then we waited for them to be made.

Then went back again to make sure everything fit properly.

Hundreds of dollars later...

we finally had these custom orthotics that were supposed to solve the problem.

And my son hated wearing them.

They were hard.

Bulky inside his soccer cleats.

He complained that they hurt his feet.

At first I kept trying to convince him to give them another chance.

“Just wear them for practice.”

“Give them a few days.”

“You'll get used to them.”

Eventually I gave up.

I started finding the $400 orthotics sitting in the bottom of his soccer bag instead of inside his shoes.

All that money.

All those appointments.

All that waiting.

And they weren't helping anyone sitting underneath a dirty jersey.

Then a few months later, I finally convinced him to try them again.

He pushed his foot into his shoe...

stopped...

and looked at me.

“Mom, these don't fit anymore.”

His feet had grown.

Of course they had.

He's a kid.

I hadn't even really thought about that when we bought them.

Then I learned that growing kids may need their orthotics replaced around every six months.

So I did the math.

$400 twice a year.

$800 a year.

And he still had years of growing left.

By the time my son stopped growing, I could've spent thousands of dollars on custom orthotics.

Thousands...

on something I still had to argue with him to wear.

And customs weren't the only thing we'd tried.

Pharmacy insoles.

Too flat. Barely any structure.

Gel heel inserts.

Soft, sure. But they didn't do much for the way his feet rolled inward when he ran.

Heel cups.

Different shoes.

Stretching.

Rest.

We kept trying things.

Some helped a little.

Some did basically nothing.

But eventually we always seemed to end up in the same place.

His feet were still rolling inward when he played.

His knees were still bothering him after harder practices.

And I was still searching for another answer.

So when I saw Footstr...

I was interested.

But I definitely wasn't convinced.

The one thing that made ordering easier was the price.

Compared with going through the custom-orthotic nightmare again...

Specialist.

Fitting.

Waiting.

Hundreds of dollars.

Footstr felt like a pretty small gamble.

Still...

cheap doesn't matter if your kid won't wear them.

So if you just ordered Footstr...

Or you're about to order...

Let me tell you exactly what happened.

Day by day.

So you know what to expect.

THEY ARRIVED FRIDAY AFTERNOON

The first thing I did was take them out of the package and bend them in my hands.

They weren't what I expected.

The top felt soft.

The whole insole had some flex to it.

But underneath the arch...

there was actual structure.

Not that flat piece of foam I'd gotten from pharmacy insoles.

And not the rock-hard feeling of my son's custom orthotics either.

I bent one again.

Flexible.

But not floppy.

That immediately got my attention.

Because that had basically been the problem with everything we'd tried.

The comfortable stuff didn't give him enough support.

The supportive stuff was so rigid he wouldn't wear it.

Footstr looked like it might actually sit somewhere in the middle.

But I'd spent enough money getting excited about things in my hands.

The real test was getting them onto his feet.

FRIDAY EVENING

My son was sitting at the kitchen table when I brought over one of his cleats.

I'd already taken his old insert out and slipped the Footstr inside.

He looked at the shoe.

Then at me.

“What is it?”

“Another insole.”

He gave me the look.

You know the one.

So I told him:

“Just try it. If you hate it, take it out.”

He pushed his foot inside.

Stood up.

Walked across the kitchen.

Stopped.

Walked back.

I was waiting for:

“No.”

Instead he looked down at his feet.

Took another few steps.

Then shrugged.

“These are way softer.”

Okay.

Good start.

But I wasn't celebrating.

Walking around our kitchen for thirty seconds is very different from sprinting, cutting and stopping for an entire soccer practice.

I'd been fooled by first impressions before.

So I went to bed thinking:

We'll see tomorrow.

SATURDAY — DAY 1

Soccer practice.

This was the first real test.

Before he ran onto the field I told him:

“If they bother you, take them out.”

I didn't want him suffering through them because he knew I'd spent money.

He nodded.

Practice started.

Twenty minutes.

Still playing.

Forty minutes.

Still playing.

Then the entire session.

And I swear I spent half of practice watching his feet.

Waiting for him to jog toward the sideline.

Waiting for the cleat to come off.

Waiting for him to pull the Footstr out and hand it to me.

It never happened.

He finished practice with them still inside his cleats.

When he walked over, I immediately asked:

“How were the insoles?”

He shrugged.

“Fine.”

That was it.

And weirdly...

that was exactly the answer I wanted.

I didn't want him obsessing over his insoles.

I wanted him thinking about soccer.

Still...

one practice is one practice.

SUNDAY — DAY 2

I put them into his regular sneakers.

And then I waited.

Normally my son notices everything I put inside his shoes.

Too high.

Too stiff.

Feels weird.

Shoe feels tight.

This time?

Nothing.

We went through almost the entire day before I finally asked:

“You still have those insoles in?”

He looked confused for a second.

Then remembered.

“Oh. Yeah.”

That got my attention.

He had basically forgotten about them.

TUESDAY — SECOND SOCCER PRACTICE

This was the day I was really waiting for.

Because almost anything new can survive one wear.

The real question is:

Will a kid keep wearing it after the novelty disappears?

That's where we'd lost the custom orthotics.

Again...

they worked.

When he wore them, his inward rolling looked better.

But eventually he started pulling them out before practice.

I'd argue.

Then bargain.

“Just wear them for half the session.”

Then I'd find them in the bag anyway.

So this time I said nothing.

I didn't remind him about Footstr.

I didn't ask whether he had put them in.

I just watched.

Full practice.

Still inside his cleats.

He came off the field sweaty.

Hungry.

Exhausted.

But he hadn't removed his shoes halfway through practice.

He hadn't complained about something hard digging into his foot.

He hadn't handed me an insole.

They just...

stayed in.

That sounds small.

After everything we'd been through?

It wasn't.

WEEK 1 — THE FULL PICTURE

Before Footstr:

$400 custom orthotics.

Specialist appointment.

Assessment.

Measurements.

Fitting.

Waiting for them to be made.

Trying to convince my kid to actually wear them.

Eventually finding them sitting in his soccer bag instead of underneath his feet.

Then the cheap pharmacy inserts.

Easy to wear.

But almost completely flat.

Gel heel pads.

Comfortable...

but not the structured support I was looking for.

So it felt like there were two choices:

Comfortable enough for my kid to wear... but barely any structure.

Or:

Enough structure... but so rigid he refused to keep them in.

After one week with Footstr:

He was wearing them.

That was the first big difference.

Sneakers.

School shoes.

Soccer cleats.

I wasn't arguing with him before practice.

I wasn't digging through the bottom of his bag afterward.

And for the first time I felt like we'd found the middle ground we'd been missing.

Soft enough that my kid would actually wear them.

Structured enough to support his arch when his foot started rolling inward.

And with cushioning underneath his heel for all the running, jumping and pounding his feet take during sports.

WEEK 2

This was when I stopped thinking quite so much about the insoles...

and started noticing everything around them.

Normally after soccer I could tell how practice had gone before my son even said anything.

The way he walked toward the car.

How quickly he kicked his shoes off.

Whether he started rubbing his knees.

Nothing was suddenly perfect.

He's still a nine-year-old playing soccer hard.

He still gets tired.

He still gets sore.

But I wasn't seeing the same ritual after every single practice.

And most importantly...

the Footstrs were still in his shoes.

Every day.

That mattered.

Because even the best support in the world can't help much when it's sitting at the bottom of a sports bag.

WEEK 3

One night I noticed something strange.

The ice pack was still in the freezer.

Normally after a hard week of soccer, getting it out had almost become automatic.

That week...

I hadn't.

Not because I'd made some decision to stop using it.

I simply hadn't thought about it.

Neither had my son.

Again...

nothing dramatic.

No miracle.

Just one little thing that used to be part of our routine...

that suddenly wasn't happening as often.

WEEK 4 — THEN I PULLED THE CUSTOM ORTHOTICS BACK OUT

I got curious.

Part of me still wondered whether we'd been stupid to abandon something we'd spent so much money on.

So I asked my son:

“Try your customs again.”

He rolled his eyes.

Eventually agreed.

I put them into his shoes.

He pushed his foot down...

stopped...

and immediately said:

“Mom, these don't fit anymore.”

At first I thought he just didn't want to wear them.

Then I looked.

His feet had grown.

And that was the moment the economics of this whole thing really hit me.

I'd spent around $400 on those orthotics.

Specialist.

Fitting.

Waiting.

Getting them adjusted.

Convincing him to wear them.

Eventually giving up.

Then finally getting him to try them again...

only to realize he'd already outgrown them.

So again I did the math.

$400.

Twice a year.

$800 every year.

My son is nine.

He has a lot of growing left.

By the time his feet stop changing, I could have spent thousands.

And I want to say this again because it's important:

The custom orthotics did work when he wore them.

That's not why I stopped using them.

I stopped because the whole process was a nightmare.

Appointments.

Fittings.

Waiting.

Hundreds of dollars.

A rigid device my kid hated.

And then...

just when I finally convinced him to give them another chance...

his feet were already too big.

I did not want to start all over again.

That's when Footstr's price stopped looking merely “cheap”...

and started looking practical.

Four pairs for $30.

Instead of hundreds of dollars for one custom device.

And four pairs meant I didn't have to move one insole around every day.

One pair in his school shoes.

One in his sneakers.

One in his soccer cleats.

One for another pair he wears regularly.

That is a completely different decision from:

“Do I want to spend another $400 and hope my kid actually wears them this time?”

THEN I STARTED LOOKING AT WHY THEY FELT SO DIFFERENT

I wanted to understand why he was keeping Footstr inside his shoes when he had fought the customs so hard.

There were three things that made sense.

1 - FLEXIBLE ARCH SUPPORT

Footstr isn't a completely flat foam pad.

There is structure underneath the arch.

When the foot starts rolling excessively inward, that support gives the arch something underneath it instead of simply following the collapse.

But it still flexes with the foot.

Walking.

Running.

Cutting.

Playing.

The goal isn't to lock his foot into one rigid shape.

It's to give it a steadier base while he's moving.

2 - HEEL CUSHIONING

Kids playing sports take an insane amount of repeated impact.

Sprint.

Stop.

Jump.

Land.

Sprint again.

Footstr combines the arch support with cushioning underneath the heel.

So there's comfort where the foot lands...

and structure where it needs support.

3 - THE STRENGTHENING EXERCISES

This was the other big reason I liked them.

I didn't want our long-term plan to be:

“Put something in his shoe forever and hope.”

The insole and the strengthening work have different jobs.

The insole supports the arch and heel during the activities that put the most demand on his feet.

The exercises give the muscles around his feet something to actually work on outside the shoe.

Support during activity.

Strengthening work over time.

That made much more sense to me.

WHY I DON'T WANT TO GO BACK

The pharmacy inserts?

Easy to wear.

Not enough structure for what I wanted.

The custom orthotics?

Plenty of structure.

Expensive.

Rigid.

A whole specialist process.

Quickly outgrown.

And most importantly...

my kid wouldn't consistently wear them.

Footstr landed in the middle.

More structure than the flat inserts we'd tried.

More flexible than the customs he'd rejected.

Cushioning under the heel.

Support under the arch.

Something he could actually keep inside his cleats while playing soccer.

And inexpensive enough that keeping up with a growing kid didn't feel ridiculous.

WHAT I WOULD EXPECT IF YOU JUST ORDERED

First time they put them on:

Don't expect fireworks.

Honestly, the best answer might be:

“They're comfortable.”

Or:

“They're fine.”

That's a win.

You don't want your kid thinking about the thing inside their shoe.

First practice:

This is the first real test.

Cleats tightened.

Feet getting hot.

Running.

Jumping.

Cutting.

See whether your kid actually keeps them in.

That's what mattered most to me.

First week:

Watch the ordinary things.

Are they still wearing them?

Are you fighting about them before practice?

Are they pulling them out halfway through?

What do they say after the activities that normally bring on complaints?

Over the next few weeks:

Keep your expectations realistic.

Footstr isn't going to magically rebuild a growing foot overnight.

It's giving the arch and heel support during the activities that demand the most from them...

while the strengthening exercises give you something proactive to work on as they grow.

IF YOU JUST ORDERED...

Don't panic like I did.

When I clicked order that Tuesday night, I genuinely wondered whether I'd just bought another pair of insoles my kid would refuse to wear.

A few weeks later...

I was holding his $400 custom orthotics that he'd already outgrown...

while Footstr was still sitting inside his soccer cleats.

That comparison pretty much answered the question for me.

IF YOU HAVEN'T ORDERED YET...

If your kid's feet roll inward...

Their feet, heels or knees complain after sports...

Or you've already been through the nightmare of expensive custom orthotics they won't consistently wear...

Footstr gives you a much simpler place to start.

Flexible arch support.

Heel cushioning.

A strengthening program.

And support designed around active, growing feet without locking them against something hard and rigid.

Right now, you can get four pairs for $30.

So instead of constantly moving one pair between shoes, you can keep them where your kid actually needs them.

School shoes.

Sneakers.

Cleats.

Sports shoes.

For me?

That was a much easier decision than:

Another specialist appointment.

Another fitting.

Another wait.

Another $400 custom orthotic.

And another argument with my kid about whether he'd actually wear it.

bodyText:
I'm a podiatrist. I've made custom orthotics for thousands of kids over 35 years. Last month I refused to make a pair for my own son.

I want to explain why. Because there is a sentence I have never once said out loud in an exam room in 35 years.

Nobody told me I couldn't say it. There's no rule. I just never said it, because I'm the one who makes the orthotics.

I'm not staying quiet about it anymore.

My name is Dr. Blane. I've run a small podiatry practice for most of my adult life. A big part of what walks through my door is a mom and a kid somewhere between seven and thirteen, and the kid is limping.

Usually it's a soccer kid. Sometimes basketball, sometimes dance. The mom says he's complaining after practice, or he's asking to sit out, or she's noticed his ankles roll inward when he runs. Almost always she's been told it's growing pains by somebody before me.

Here's what happens next, and I've done it thousands of times.

I have him stand on the plate. The scan comes up on the screen and I turn it toward his mom. She sees the arch flattened out and the pressure sitting on the inside of the foot, and her face changes, because now it's real.

I take a mold of his feet. Three weeks later the customs come in. I slide one into his sneaker, he stands up, and the foot sits perfectly. Held right where it should be. Mom sees it. She pays somewhere around $450, because insurance almost never covers it.

And I say the thing I've said thousands of times.

"He'll grow. Let's see you back in six months."

Six months later they're back. His foot grew. The customs don't fit anymore. And the limp is the same limp.

That's when Mom says it, a little embarrassed, looking at the floor instead of me.

"Honestly, he hasn't really been wearing them."

And I nod. And I measure him for the next pair.

I've heard every version of it. He pulls them out at halftime because they dig in. They're in last year's sneakers, not the cleats he actually plays in. They're at the bottom of the soccer bag under wet socks. One dad brought a pair back still in the box.

Every scan on my screen looked perfect. Every foot in my office sat exactly where I put it.

And the kid was still limping to the car.

The first few years you tell yourself it's the parents not enforcing it. Or the kid being difficult. By year ten you stop telling yourself stories. By year fifteen you start keeping a drawer.

I started that drawer in 2009. It's the bottom drawer in my exam room, and it's full of outgrown custom orthotics that parents brought back hoping I could resize them. I can't. A custom is molded to one foot at one moment, and a nine-year-old's foot is a different foot by spring.

I'm not going to tell you how many pairs are in there. It would sound like I'm making it up.

I want to be honest about something before I go further, because you might be reading this thinking I'm some kind of hero for saying it.

I'm not. I've made a lot of money making custom orthotics. Millions of dollars over 35 years, if I'm being honest with you. It paid for my practice, my staff, and my house.

I'm not going to call custom orthotics a scam, because they're not. When one is in the shoe, it does exactly what it's built to do.

But nobody in that exam room measures the wearing. Not me, not the mom, not anyone. I get paid the day the orthotic is made. I get paid again six months later when it's outgrown. Whether it spent those six months inside a cleat or inside a bag has never once shown up on an invoice.

That's not corruption. It's just a business that gets paid on the fitting, not on the wearing. And I was very good at fitting.

That was the deal I made for 35 years.

Last month the deal blew up.

My son is nine. He plays soccer three days a week and he'd play seven if we let him. He came off the field on a Thursday and sat down on the curb with his cleats still on, and he didn't get up when the other kids ran to the parking lot.

I asked him what was going on.

"Dad, my feet hurt after every practice now."

Not once. Every practice. And I'm a podiatrist, and I hadn't noticed.

That night I had him walk across the kitchen floor in his socks while I sat on the tile and watched. Both ankles rolling inward with every step. The inside of his heel taking the landing. I have seen it thousands of times on other people's kids, and I'd never sat on my own floor and looked.

Saturday I brought him to the office and stood him on the plate. The scan came up. The same flattened arch. The same pressure on the inside edge. I've seen that exact picture more times than I can count.

The next step is the easiest thing in the world for me. I have the mold kit in the next room. I have the order form in the drawer above the one full of outgrown orthotics.

I sat at my desk with that form and I did not fill it in.

Because I knew exactly what was coming. I'd watched it thousands of times. The customs would come in. They'd sit perfectly on the plate. And by October I'd be finding them at the bottom of his soccer bag, and he'd be sitting on that curb again, and I'd be looking at the same scan of a foot that had grown out of a $450 prop it never wore.

I drove home and my wife asked what was wrong. I told her I couldn't do it. She's been married to a podiatrist for a long time. She didn't argue.

That week is when everything changed for me.

I did what I hadn't done since residency. I sat down and actually read. Not the catalogs from the orthotic labs. Not the sales reps. The studies on kids' feet, the ones I'd stopped keeping up with somewhere around year ten because I thought I already knew the answer.

And I understood something I now can't believe I didn't understand.

What the foot looks like in my office was never the thing that mattered.

I want to say that again, because it took me most of that week to accept it. What the foot looks like in my office was never the thing that mattered. What the foot is doing on a field at 4:30 on a Tuesday is the thing that mattered.

I'd been treating the scan. I'd never treated the Tuesday.

Here's what's actually going on inside a kid like mine, in plain English.

The arch is supposed to work like a spring. It flexes when the foot lands and pushes back when the foot pushes off. That's how a kid runs for two hours and comes home tired but fine.

When the arch rolls inward, that spring gives out under load. The foot lands and just keeps collapsing. The heel takes the hit from a bad angle. The muscles and tissue along the inside of the foot get pulled with every single step, and a nine-year-old at soccer practice takes thousands of steps.

That pull, over and over, is the ache my son was feeling on the curb.

And it doesn't stay in the foot. The ankle has to follow the foot. The knee has to follow the ankle. A study of 92,000 adolescents found that kids with moderate to severe flat feet had nearly double the rate of knee pain and low back pain compared to kids with normal arches. That's association, not proof of cause, and I'll be careful to say so. But it's not nothing.

The one that stopped me cold was a 2025 study on school-aged kids specifically. Kids with flat feet scored about 42 percent higher on a standard pain scale than their classmates. And they were measurably less physically active.

Read that second part again. They hurt more, so they move less.

That's the curb. That's "can I sit out today." That's every mom in my office who said her son used to love practice.

I had those numbers on my wall for years. I'd never once thought about what they meant on a Tuesday.

Now I'm going to tell you what a custom orthotic actually does, because I had to sit with this myself before I could admit it.

A custom orthotic is a brace. It holds the foot in a position. When it's in the shoe, the arch is held up and the roll is reduced. That's real, and I've watched it help kids who wore them.

But it's a hard shell, and the reason it holds so well is the same reason a nine-year-old pulls it out. It doesn't flex when the foot flexes. Inside a tight cleat it presses and digs. Kids tell their moms it hurts more with it in, and I've heard that sentence in my exam room more times than I want to count.

So the kid stops wearing it. And when it's out of the shoe, nothing about that foot is any different than it was before I molded it. The brace did its job for exactly the hours it was in.

And even when it is in, holding a foot in place doesn't ask the muscles around the foot to do anything. It does the job for them.

Then the foot grows, and the $450 brace expires.

That's the machine I'd been running for 35 years. A prop that works when worn, that most kids won't wear, with a six-month shelf life. And a scan that looked perfect every single time.

I went through the rest of the menu that week too, the same way I'd heard parents go through it for decades.

Rest. Rest is free and every doctor says it first. It works, in the sense that the foot stops hurting because the foot stops running. Then he goes back to practice and the roll is exactly where it was, and the ache comes back with it. Rest, play, hurt, rest. Kids hate it and moms hate watching it.

Drugstore gel inserts. Soft, cheap, and my son would wear them. But there's no structure under the arch. A flat insert just follows the foot down as it collapses.

Supportive sneakers. Genuinely helpful for school. Useless the moment he laces up cleats, which is the exact moment his feet hurt.

Exercises on their own. This is the one that embarrassed me. Strengthening work is real and I know it's real. But it takes months to show up, and in the meantime the kid is on the curb tonight. And here's the part I have to own: in 35 years I had never once handed a family the exercises. I handed them the mold kit.

Every one of those options does one job. None of them do both.

That's the thing I finally saw sitting at my kitchen table with my son's scan on my laptop.

There are two different jobs here, and I'd been selling one of them as if it were the whole answer.

The first job is support during the hours that put the most load on the foot. Practice. Games. Recess. School hallways. And it only counts if it's in something a nine-year-old will actually keep in his cleat, because support sitting in a bag isn't supporting anything.

The second job is strengthening work outside the shoe. Simple, short, a few minutes a day, so the muscles around his feet and arches get asked to do something instead of being held the whole time. That's the part that makes it a plan for a growing kid instead of a prop with a shelf life.

Support while he plays. Work while he doesn't. And enough consistency that both actually happen.

I sat there thinking about that bottom drawer. Every pair in it was job one, done in a way the kid wouldn't tolerate, with job two never mentioned. Thousands of families paid me for half an answer, and I said "see you in six months" to every one of them.

That was the moment I stopped being a quiet podiatrist.

I wrote down what I'd actually want under my own son's foot, which I had never done in 35 years for anybody.

More structure under the arch than drugstore foam. Flexible enough to bend when his foot bends instead of fighting it. Soft enough on top that a nine-year-old forgets it's there. Cushioning under the heel, because that's where every landing starts. Thin enough to fit in a cleat. Cheap enough that when his foot grows in six months, replacing it isn't a decision. And something to go with it that actually gives him the exercises.

Then I did what a podiatrist does before trusting anything. I went and looked.

I found Footstr on a thread of soccer parents I'd never have read before that week. Moms comparing what their kids would and wouldn't keep in their shoes. Somebody had posted it with a sentence I'll never forget: "first pair he doesn't hate."

I read everything on the site the way I'd read a lab spec. It's soft on top with a structured, flexible support underneath the arch. It cushions the heel. It's built to help reduce the inward roll at the arch and ankle while the foot is in the shoe, without locking the foot in place like a hard shell. It's sized for kids and it fits in cleats. And it comes with a strengthening program, the exercises I'd never once handed anyone.

It comes as a four-pack. I understood why immediately. My son has cleats, school sneakers, indoor shoes, and the beat-up pair he wears everywhere else. One insole in one shoe would be support for a third of his day. Four pairs means it's just in his shoes, all of them, and nobody has to remember to move anything.

Four pairs cost less than the sales tax on one custom. I'll get to that.

I ordered them Saturday night. I did not fill in the order form.

I want to be honest about the first few days, because I know what parents want to hear and I'm not going to say it.

It wasn't anything.

He put them in his cleats before Tuesday practice and said "these are squishy" and ran off. That was the whole review. No miracle, no announcement.

Then the small things started.

WEEK 1: He finished Thursday practice without sitting down on the curb. He still said his feet were tired. But tired isn't hurt, and I've spent 35 years learning the difference.

WEEK 2: My wife pulled his cleats out of the bag to bang the mud off, and the insoles were still in them. Both of them. I've found thousands of customs in bags. I had never once found a support still in the shoe.

WEEK 3: We started the exercises. Five minutes on the living room rug after dinner, and I turned it into a contest so he'd do it. He beat me at the single-leg one and would not let it go. That was the first time in my career the strengthening part actually happened in a house.

WEEK 4: Tournament weekend. Two games Saturday, one Sunday. He played every minute of all three. On the drive home he asked if we could stop at the park. I said his feet must be exhausted. He said, "They're fine, why?"

WEEK 6: I brought him back to the office on a Saturday and stood him on the plate.

I'm not going to tell you the scan showed a brand new arch. It didn't. Six weeks doesn't rebuild a foot and I'd be lying to you if I said an insole does that. The roll was still there under load.

What was different is everything the scan can't see. He'd worn support every hour that mattered, without one argument. He'd done the work outside the shoe. And the limp I'd watched on my kitchen floor was gone.

I stood there looking at the screen, at the same picture I'd turned toward thousands of moms, and I did not reach for the order form.

And for the first time in 35 years, I didn't say "see you in six months."

There's no six-month appointment. When his foot grows, we open the next pair.

Monday morning a mom came in with her ten-year-old. Soccer. Limping after practice. Ankles rolling in when he walked down my hall. I stood him on the plate, turned the screen toward her, and she asked me the question I've been asked thousands of times.

"So which orthotic do you recommend?"

And I finally said the sentence.

"The orthotic I make is only as good as the hours your kid actually wears it. And most of them don't."

She just looked at me. Then she said, "Nobody's ever told me that."

I know. That's why I'm writing this.

I'm writing this because I can't keep doing it.

I can't keep turning a screen toward a mom, taking her $450, and saying "see you in six months" when I know where that orthotic is going to end up.

If your kid is coming off the field limping, or asking to sit out, or telling you his feet hurt after every practice now, and somebody has told you it's growing pains, I want you to read this twice. The pain isn't coming from nowhere. Kids with flat feet hurt more and move less, and it's measured. Your eyes aren't lying to you.

If you already paid for customs and you're finding them in the bag, you didn't fail. Your kid didn't fail. You were handed a brace built for a scan, not for a Tuesday. Support at the bottom of a soccer bag is supporting nothing.

If you've tried rest and gel inserts and better sneakers and your kid is still limping to the car, it's because each of those does one job. None of them does both.

Footstr. Four pairs, so it's in every shoe he actually plays in. Flexible support under the arch, cushioning under the heel, and the strengthening program to go with it. The thing I put under my own son's feet instead of the mold kit in the next room.

Right now the four-pack is $30.

I want to sit on that number for a second, because I've spent 35 years on the other side of it. A custom is $450. It expires every six months. That's $900 a year for a prop most kids pull out by halftime. Thirty dollars gets support into all four pairs of shoes at once, and when his foot grows, you open the next pack instead of scheduling the next appointment.

If your kid has practice this week, get it in his cleats before then. Every practice on a collapsed arch is another practice on the curb.

You don't have to be the mom in my exam room looking at the floor.

Dr. Blane, DPM, 35 years

P.S. I want to be clear about something. If your child has custom orthotics and actually wears them, and they're helping, keep them in his shoes. That's between you and your podiatrist and I'm not arguing with it. This letter is for the kid whose customs are in the bag. That's most of them. Nobody measured it, so nobody told you.

P.P.S. The exercises are the part I keep coming back to. Thirty-five years and I never handed a single family the strengthening work. Whatever you decide about the insoles, do the five minutes on the rug. Make it a contest. You'll lose the single-leg one.

No matter which brand makes them, running shoes have all been offered with ever-increasing amounts of padding, cushioning, and support in recent years.

Think about it.

Every year, the soles get thicker. The arch supports get taller. The foam gets softer. The marketing gets louder.

More cushioning. More structure. More technology between you and the ground.

And I used to believe every word of it. I used to think more padding meant more protection. More support meant stronger feet. A thicker sole meant a safer step.

I was wrong.

I believe running shoes can be the most destructive force to ever hit the human foot.

Not just running shoes, either. Walking shoes. Hiking boots. The everyday sneakers most of us wear from morning to night.

They're dangerous.

And my belief, after years of dealing with the consequences, is that they cause the very injuries they're supposed to reduce. That by encouraging you to move in a way which is unnatural to the human leg, they actually cause the damage.

Here is what nobody tells you when you lace up that next pair of cushioned shoes.

Most shoes today are squishing your toes together. Locking your feet in like casts. And blocking the muscles from doing any real work.

Your foot has over a hundred muscles, tendons, and ligaments. It was designed to flex. Spread. Grip. Stabilize. Sense every surface beneath it and respond in real time.

But when you encase it in a stiff, elevated, foam-padded shoe, you take away every job it was built to do.

The toes can't spread. The arch can't load naturally. The small stabilizing muscles that are supposed to fire with every single step just... stop. They have nothing to do. The shoe is doing it for them.

And this does not happen overnight.

It happens slowly. Over years. Over decades.

You don't notice until one day you're standing on a curb and your ankle wobbles. Or you step off a trail onto loose gravel and your balance feels off. Or you realize you haven't walked barefoot on grass in so long that it actually feels uncomfortable.

That's not aging.

That's years of damage building up without you even realizing.

Flat feet. Collapsed arches. Pain up the entire chain. Sore knees. Tight hips. A lower back that aches after a walk around the block.

And what do most people do when the discomfort starts?

They go buy more cushioning.

They buy the shoe with the thicker sole. The insert with the higher arch. The orthotic that promises to correct everything.

And for a while, maybe it feels a little better. Because padding feels nice. Support feels safe.

More support. Less capability.

bodyText:
I am going to say something that every parent who's watched their kid limp off a soccer field needs to hear.

It might not be growing pains.

It might be his feet.

I'm not a doctor. I'm a mom who spent almost a year telling my nine-year-old the same four words everyone kept telling me.

"You'll grow out of it."

What I finally noticed at a Tuesday practice is something I still can't stop thinking about.

Read every word of this before you let him quit.

My son is nine. He's played soccer since he was four. Last fall, a couple of months into the season, he started coming off the field holding his knee.

Just under the kneecap. Always the same spot.

At first it was only after games. Then it was after practice. Then it was on the walk from the field to the car.

I remember the exact night I stopped calling it a phase.

He came off the field slower than everyone else, one hand on his knee, cleats still tied when he sat down on the curb by the parking lot.

He didn't want help getting to the car. He just wanted to get there.

Normally the ride home is nonstop. Who scored. Who got yelled at. What he wants for dinner.

That night he was quiet until we hit our street.

Then he said, "Can you just tell coach I'm sick tomorrow?"

He wasn't sick.

He just didn't want to hurt again.

We'd already been to Dr. Reeves. He's been our family doctor since my son was three, and he was careful and kind and completely right.

"It's Osgood-Schlatter. Very common in active kids his age. His body's growing. Rest it, ice it, and he'll grow out of it."

So we did exactly that.

Ice after practice.
Stretching before bed.
Ibuprofen when it got bad.
A week off when it got really bad.

And to be fair...

rest worked.

That was the confusing part.

We'd pull him for a week and he'd stop limping. He'd tell me it felt fine. He'd be begging to go back by Thursday.

Then he'd go back, and within two or three practices we were right back on the curb by the parking lot.

Rest.
Better.
Return.
Pain.

Over and over.

I asked other parents. I asked his coach. I read every Reddit thread I could find at eleven at night.

Every single one said some version of what Dr. Reeves said.

He'll grow out of it.

And I wanted that to be enough. Honestly, I needed it to be enough, because it meant nothing was actually wrong and we just had to be patient.

But if rest was the whole answer, why did the pain come back every time he played?

One night after he'd gone inside I sat in the driveway with the engine off and typed an email to his coach.

"Hi, I think we're going to sit out the rest of the season."

I didn't send it. But I wrote it.

He was nine, and I was one click away from ending the thing he loved most because I didn't know what else to do.

The next practice, I did something I'd never once done in five years of soccer.

I stopped watching his knee.

I watched his feet.

And I saw it.

Every time he planted to change direction, his ankle rolled in underneath him. His arch flattened out against the inside of his cleat. Then he'd push off, and the whole leg would twist a little to catch up.

Not once. Every single stride.

I went home and pulled out his cleats. The inside edge of each one was worn down like someone had been sanding it.

His school shoes were the same. So were his sneakers.

I'd been looking at those shoes every day for months.

A few nights later I found a study that made it worse.

Researchers looked at more than 92,000 adolescents and found that kids with moderate to severe flat feet had nearly double the rate of anterior knee pain and intermittent low back pain compared to kids with normal arches.

Anterior knee pain. The front of the knee.

The exact spot my son grabs when he sits down on the curb.

Now, that study didn't say flat feet caused his Osgood-Schlatter. I'm not going to tell you it did.

But it wrecked one comforting assumption I'd been leaning on for a year.

That because he was nine, the way his feet moved couldn't really matter yet.

So I went back to Dr. Reeves. Not to argue. Just to ask.

"Could his feet have anything to do with this?"

And I'll never forget how honest he was about it.

"They could. When a kid comes in with knee pain, we look at the knee. That's where it hurts, so that's where we check. I don't usually have them take their shoes off."

Nobody was hiding anything from me.

The knee got all the attention because the knee was where it hurt.

Then he explained it in a way that finally made sense.

Every sprint, every cut, every landing starts at the ground. If the foot rolls in too far on every step, the ankle follows it, and the knee ends up working above that movement thousands of times every practice.

Osgood-Schlatter is already an irritation right where the tendon pulls on the growing bone below the kneecap. Extra strain from below doesn't help.

So we'd been resting the knee, and the knee would calm down.

Then he'd go back out on the same feet, doing the same thing, and the strain would start piling up again.

Rest treated where it hurt.

It didn't change what was happening underneath him.

That was the part I hadn't understood.

And look, some kids really do just grow out of it. I believe that.

But mine was limping every single week, and in a full year nobody, including me, had looked at his feet.

Dr. Reeves suggested support. Something under the arch to keep the foot from collapsing so far inward, especially during sports.

So we tried the thing everyone tries first.

Pharmacy inserts.

Soft, flat, twelve dollars. He said they felt "squishy." I watched him at the next practice and his foot rolled in exactly the same way. The foam just followed the collapse. It didn't give the arch anything to work against.

So we went the other direction.

Custom orthotics.

Appointment. Assessment. Casting. A three-week wait. About $400 by the time we walked out.

And to be completely fair...

they worked.

When he wore them, I could see the difference. His ankle stayed steadier when he planted.

For about a week I thought we were done.

Then I started finding them in the bottom of his soccer bag.

Under the shin guards. Under the dirty socks. One time, under half a sandwich.

They were hard. They were thick. They made his cleats feel a size too small. And he was nine, so "wear them anyway" lasted about as long as you'd expect.

$400 of support sitting in a bag, supporting nothing.

Four months later I got him to try them again and he pulled his foot right back out.

"They don't fit."

His feet had grown. Of course they had.

That's when I did the math on $400 twice a year for however many years it took.

And that's also when a different worry crept in. Even if I found something he'd actually wear, wasn't I just putting a cushion under the problem? What happens when he takes it out?

So I knew what I was looking for now.

Structured enough to keep his foot from collapsing.
Flexible enough that he'd forget it was there.
Cheap enough to replace when he outgrew it.
Something for school shoes, sneakers and cleats, so the support didn't stop when the shoes changed.

And some way for his feet to actually get stronger, not just get propped up.

I found Footstr in a parent thread. Another mom, another kid with knee pain, another soccer bag full of orthotics.

What made me actually order was that it had both halves.

The insole has a structured arch that flexes with the foot instead of locking it in a hard block. That was the exact middle ground between the foam that did nothing and the customs he refused to wear. It supports the inside of the arch, which is where his foot kept caving in, and helps reduce that excessive inward roll while he's moving.

There's cushioning under the heel, so every landing has a softer spot to start from instead of jarring straight up the leg.

It fits in regular shoes, sneakers and cleats. And it comes as a four pack for $30, which meant one pair in his school shoes, one in his sneakers, one in his cleats, and a spare for when he outgrew them.

Four pairs for less than a tenth of one custom orthotic.

And then the part I hadn't seen anywhere else.

It comes with a strengthening program. Short exercises he does at home, outside the shoe, for the muscles around his feet and arches.

The insole doesn't strengthen anything. It supports his foot during the hours that put the most demand on it. The exercises are the part that's meant to help his feet get stronger over time.

Support during activity. Strengthening work outside the shoe. Both, consistently.

For the first time, it felt like a plan instead of one more thing to do after he was already hurting.

Here's how it actually went.

WEEK 1:

I didn't watch his knee. I watched his bag. Every day I checked whether the insoles were still in his cleats.

They were. He never mentioned them once. That was the first sign, before anything else.

WEEK 2:

He finished a full practice. He still rubbed his knee a bit in the car, but he walked to the car instead of limping to it.

WEEK 4:

Saturday game, two halves, no curb. He jogged off the field with the rest of the team and asked if we could get food on the way home.

He'd stopped asking me to tell coach he was sick.

WEEK 6:

The ride home was nonstop again. Who scored, who got yelled at, what he wanted for dinner.

I couldn't get a word in.

I'm not going to tell you it cured his Osgood-Schlatter. It didn't. He still gets sore after a hard week. He still needs rest days.

But the loop broke. He's not going back onto the same collapsing feet every time the knee calms down.

And he's still playing.

I see the posts every week now.

"He limps after every practice but the doctor says it's just growing pains."

"Rest helps but it comes right back the second he plays again."

"She's nine and she asked to quit gymnastics. I don't know what to do."

"We spent $400 on orthotics and I found them in her backpack."

You didn't miss it.

Rest worked. The diagnosis was right. Everyone who told you he'd grow out of it was being honest with you.

That's exactly what made it so hard to see. When the answer works for a week, nobody keeps looking.

So here's the one thing I'd ask you to do.

Watch his feet at the next practice. Not the knee. The feet. Then look at the inside edge of his shoes.

If you see what I saw, put support under his arch and let him keep playing.

Slide the insoles into the shoes he already wears. Do the exercises with him at home. Then, before you watch his knee, watch his bag. If they're still in his cleats after a week, you're most of the way there.

I'm not promising you it fixes everything. I'm promising it's worth trying before you send the email I almost sent.

Four pairs for $30, here: https://getfootstr.com/products/footstr-insolex

That's less than one copay. It's a fraction of one custom orthotic he might not wear.

He's nine. He shouldn't have to decide whether soccer is worth the pain.

Neither should yours.

EDIT: A few parents have messaged asking if this is okay to use alongside what their doctor already told them to do.

Yes. It's not a replacement for rest, ice, or your doctor's plan. Nothing here asks you to skip that.

It's support during the hours he's actually loading his knee, which is the part rest never covers.

If you want to ask your doctor first, ask. Mine had no problem with it. He was the one who suggested support in the first place.

Same link: https://getfootstr.com/products/footstr-insolex

P.S. I keep coming back to that soccer bag.

$400 of custom support. Made for his feet. Sitting under a sandwich.

Not because they didn't work. They did.

Because he was nine and they hurt and I couldn't win that fight every single morning.

Support only counts when it's under the foot. That's the whole thing I got wrong for a year.

Four pairs. His cleats, his sneakers, his school shoes, and a spare: https://getfootstr.com/products/footstr-insolex

P.P.S. He limped for almost a full year.

I sat in the car after every practice and told myself the same thing I'd been told.

He'll grow out of it.

I wrote the email. I had my finger on the button.

And the whole time, the answer was in the shoes I picked up off the floor every night.

I got there late. But he's still playing.

Your kid is still lacing up.

Still throwing the bag in the back seat.

Still asking what's for dinner.

You have not run out of time.

Watch his feet before you let him quit: https://getfootstr.com/products/footstr-insolex
